en: The Tattvaṭīkā: A Commentary on the Śrībhāṣya composed by the venerable Nigamānta Mahādeśika. Homage to the illustrious Rāmānuja! The Tattvaṭīkā, a commentary on the Śrībhāṣya, authored by the venerable Nigamānta Mahādeśika.
May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians,
the preeminent Vedāntācārya, dwell forever within my heart.
Victorious is that sage Tīrthaṃkara, an ocean of compassion, whose ornament is forbearance;
he is like a dark cloud over the mountain of Kailāsa, for the thirsty seekers are satisfied by the waters of his speech. || 1 ||
Self-established, rivaling a mountain of pure crystal, whitening the three worlds with splendors akin to nectar,
and accompanied by the tumultuous neighing of infinite horses according to the three Vedas—
We praise the Great One, whose horse-like face has destroyed every blemish. || 2 ||
Having bowed down to the preceptor Varada and also to Vādihaṃsāmbuda,
this *Tattvaṭīkā*, which explains the true meaning of the commentaries on the Sūtras at the conclusion of the three Vedas, is now composed.
Let this work, which is neither too concise nor overly prolix, and which conforms to all principles of logic, be accepted by those who know the essence. (4)
The futile adherence of Śaṅkara and others has been cut down in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*;
however, the body of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] is clearly demonstrated here. (5)
By the teacher and sage Śrī Vedāntācārya, born of the lineage of Viśvāmitra,
the perpetual dispelling of all vain disputants is here performed.

Adorned as the crest-ornament of the entire series of the Vedas, this banner-cloth of victory is now fastened upon the palace-roofs of the minds of the skillful— the commentary on the words of the Lord of Ascetics (Śaṅkara), during the twenty-eighth exposition consisting of both what was heard and what was reflected upon.
In this regard, we shall set forth ten meanings for the commentary beginning with the word "akhila.
First, the statement concerning the triad beginning with the subject matter (viṣaya) is established. (8)
Since that meaning is based on the Sūtra, this verse—which consists of its detailed exposition and is characterized by the definition of a Bhāṣya—is indeed faultless. (9)

Although the aphorism *athāto brahmajijñāsā* is directed toward the necessity of the inquiry into Brahman for one who desires to know Brahman, it nevertheless applies by implication to the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and other preliminary requirements of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], just as the aphorism on the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). And thus it has been said:
"This first aphorism, *athāto dharmajijñāsā*, was composed..."
"The purpose of the inquiry is to declare the object known as Dharma.
Likewise, here too— Brahman is the object, and [liberation] is the purpose by virtue of being that which is to be attained.
And he also declared the relationship [between Brahman and the inquiry] by way of [Brahman] being the object of the desire to know. || 10 ||

For the meaning of the word *brahman* is unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśayabṛhattva*). This is because the word is derived from the verbal root *bṛh* with the suffix *manin* and the augment *am*, according to the rule *bṛheram ca*; and as Yāska has stated: "Brahman is that which is pre-eminent (*paribṛḍha*) in every respect. As for the etymological explanation found in the *Ātharvaṇa* which also mentions the quality of expansion—stating, "It is called the Supreme Brahman because it expands (*bṛhati*) and causes expansion (*bṛṃhayati*)"—and the well-known Puranic tradition which says, "Because of its expanding and causing expansion, it is designated as Brahman"; [these refer to the same].

Therefore, there is no contradiction, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*); for the quality of nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇatva*) is itself a specific form of greatness (*bṛhattva*). This is the meaning: that which is great by its own nature is also great by virtue of being nourishing. To avoid the redundancy of using another word for what is already expressed, the contraction of a general term follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull. Thus, in accordance with this principle, the word *bṛhat* refers to something other than the greatness consisting of the quality of nourishing; as it is said: "He whose name is Viṣṇu is celebrated in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas. Consequently, some maintain that the meaning of the word *brahman* is simply greatness characterized by the absence of any limit or superior degree.

Others, however, maintain that like "vastness" (*bṛhattva*), "expansiveness" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*)—as being without limit or superior degree—is also the meaning of the word *brahman*; for they argue that this is supported by the natural force of the separate mention [in the etymology], "it grows large (*bṛhati*) and it causes to grow (*bṛṃhayati*)," as well as by the natural force of the inclusion of both [qualities] together. We, however, say: since there is no contradiction in either case, we explain it in both ways. Here is the summary of this point: "Vastness is the meaning of the word *brahman*, while expansiveness is its differentiation; or else, expansiveness is the meaning of the word *brahman*, just like vastness. (Verse 11)

Alternatively, it may be understood as a conjunction of "vastness" (*bṛhattva*) and "nourishing" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*). Having all this in mind, it was stated in the commentary on the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa*: "For that which is to be characterized is [Brahman], which is infinitely unsurpassed vastness and nourishing, because the root *bṛh* has that as its meaning. And the fact that these two qualities surpass all others is established by their being unlimited and by the authority of Yāska’s *Nirukta*. For when a term is used without limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), no restriction is intended by the wise;
this is stated according to the maxim: "The relationship between word and meaning is established [by usage]. (12)

Such Brahman is the primary subject matter of this scripture, and it is the supreme goal to be attained; for the meaning of the two etymologies has been explained by two [verses]. The fact that Brahman is the object of attainment is established by the mention of its "expansiveness" (bṛṃhaṇatva); for here, expansiveness is said to be the means for attaining oneself. (13)

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction in the etymological derivation (abhidhāna) "it causes to grow" (*bṛṃhayati*) with respect to the root *bṛhati*; for there are two distinct etymological statements based on two roots established as *bṛha* and *bṛhi*, both meaning "to grow. Since the intention concerns the general sense [of growth], the inclusion of another root is permissible. Furthermore, because that root is marked with the *it*-augment, the addition of the *num* augment is correctly applied. (14)

And the purpose (prayojana) in this case must necessarily be stated. Regarding this, they also say: "For of any scripture whatsoever, or even of any action, as long as the purpose has not been stated, by whom would it be grasped?"

"Furthermore, this science called Mīmāṃsā, which rests upon many other branches of knowledge, cannot be properly studied if its purpose has not been stated beforehand. And: "The relationship [of the treatise] consists in its being a means of determining Brahman, which is the subject matter; or in its being a means of attaining it, which is the purpose. As for the purposes consisting of liberation—which is accomplished by the inquiry intended by the word *jijñāsā*—and the protection thereof, which is rooted in that [liberation], they signify its status as a cause, either directly or indirectly, according to their respective roles."
In all undertakings of treatises, the wise state the connection;
for if it were mere incoherent chatter, an intelligent person would not engage with it. (15)

Thus, the venerable author of the commentary (Bhāṣyakāra), specifically proclaiming the triad of subject matter and so forth—which belongs to the Sūtra itself—for the sake of focusing the listeners' intellects and for the sake of their desire to undertake [the study], first composes at the outset a benediction (*maṅgala*) in the form of a prayer of devotion to his chosen deity. This benediction, established by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), is intended to ensure the completion of the work he intends to begin without obstacles and to promote its increase; it serves to pacify any suspected impediments. Although he has already performed this benediction himself, he records it here by recounting his own deed for the purpose of instructing his disciples and for the sake of their greatest auspiciousness. He begins with the words: "akhila... (all...).
Those who desire auspiciousness conduct themselves by following the conduct of their teacher; this very point is stated here based on the Vedic revelation that "these [teachings] belong to us. (16)

The description of the objects of salutation is also established by implication, since it speaks of that reality which is the most auspicious and supreme of all. And it has been said: "This nature of being the saluter and the object of salutation consists of the low and the high. Here, the statement of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) is expressed through words ending in the locative case. The phrase "in the crest of the Vedas" (*śrutiśirasi*) summarizes the intermediate subject matter;
for just as the subject matter of a Vedic sentence is stated to be Brahman.
In the very same way, the culmination of the three Vedas (the Upanishads) is proclaimed as the final word of the Sūtra. || 17 ||

The threefold purpose of the treatise (*sādhya-prayojana*) is proclaimed by the words "illumination" (*vidīpti*), "refutation" (*vinata*), and "protection" (*rakṣā*). Here, "illumination" (*dīpti*) means excellence (*viśiṣṭa*); it is "illumination" because of its distinction. That [distinction], however, arises from critical inquiry (*vicāra*). As they have said: "When Dharma is being cognized through the Veda as the instrument (*karaṇa*), Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill the requirement of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)."
And it is said in the *Nyāyasudarśana*:
"When the Supreme Self is being known by means of the Vedāntas as instruments,
they know this Uttaramīmāṃsā to be the *itikartavyatā* (the procedural method)."

And it is said: "Even though the Veda possesses authority characterized by independence, this [work] serves to remove doubt, error, and delusion caused by the dullness and faults of the learner's intellect.
The statement of the purpose (prayojana) provides certainty regarding the ascertainment of the author's reliability;
even when that is doubted, it kindles the desire to acquire the work as something established. (18)

In that regard, even though the general possession of a purpose has been ascertained, it is nonetheless necessary to state the specific purpose required by oneself. Herein, the relationship (*saṃbandha*) is also indeed indicated, because the comprehension of the relationship is inseparable from the mention of the scripture (*śāstra*), its purpose, and so forth, which serve as the substrata of that relationship.

The nature of being an inquiry (*vicāratva*), the nature of being an object of inquiry (*vicāryatva*), the nature of being determined (*nirdhāryatva*), as well as the other [corresponding qualities], and the nature of being attained (*prāpyatva*) and the nature of being the means of attainment (*prāpakatva*)—this is what is called "relationship. (Verse 19)

In this regard, the collection of topics—beginning with the "three realities" and the "five objects"—which has been embraced with great reverence by those who know the inner science (adhyātmavid), is not written out in detail here, as it is to be understood by the wise themselves.
In the first verse, the primacy of the subject matter and so forth was proclaimed;
now, the primacy of the practice of auspiciousness (maṅgalācāra) is described. (20)
And although that practice of auspiciousness (maṅgalācāra) is not seen in some texts, it is to be inferred from its cause and its result. For they say:
"The cause is the commencement of what is intended, and the result is its completion without obstacle and its further increase; therefore, the practice of auspiciousness is desired."

The meaning is that the commencement of the treatise, conjoined with [factors such as] completion without obstacles, serves as a qualification for the specific qualified person (adhikārin) therein. And it has been stated by the authors of the *Vivaraṇa*: "In this case, the qualification is conjoined [with other factors], like the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice; just as in the *jāteṣṭi*, the birth of a son is the occasion (*nimitta*)."

Even in your view, there must be the assumption of results such as purity residing in the son, which are mentioned in the *arthavāda* passages. Nor is there any complexity [in our position], because when the result serves as a qualifier, it facilitates engagement [with the rite]. For if there were only the result [without the qualification], the censure would be inexplicable; for censure does not apply to the non-performance of what is merely desired (*kāmya*). Alternatively, some explain that the salutation to the Lord and other auspicious rites were not performed in the works of Śabara and Śaṅkara because those texts do not propound a Supreme Lord (*īśvara*).

Nor do the most orthodox thinkers, such as Pakṣila and others, explain that they fail to perform auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) even when the [auspicious] occasion is present. Some, however, have explained that because the word *pramāṇa*—which denotes the Lord (*Īśvara*)—is employed at the outset, the sage Pakṣila has indeed performed the auspicious rite. Alternatively, if it were the case that he did not perform the auspicious rite, how could the fruit be accomplished? As for those who have performed the auspicious rite, any deviation from the result depends upon defects in the action, the agent, or the means.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācāra*) is unnecessary because there is no injunction stating, "One who desires the completion of what has been begun should perform an auspicious rite"? [Reply: This is indeed the talk of those who have not mastered the Vedas and have not studied Mīmāṃsā; for it is precisely the unopposed practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) that serves as the basis for inferring a foundational authority (*mūla-pramāṇa*). From that very source, its status as being defined by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*) is established. Nor should it be argued that the fruit [of the rite] is observed even in the absence of the performance of auspicious rites; for since this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, such an observation must also be dependent upon specific merits (*sukṛta*) acquired in other lives.

Nor should it be asked: "What is the use of this practice of auspicious rites? That [primary cause] alone bestows the fruit. For there is no certainty regarding the existence of that [cause], and because the occasional rite (naimittika) which follows upon its occasion is necessary, being established by the traditional conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

"For one who is about to begin something, having abandoned the fulfillment [of the rite] already present in his mind, the postulation of some other result does not please those who are wise in policy. (21)

Even when devotion is being invoked, it should proceed without obstructing the fulfillment and accumulation [of merit], and both she (Devotion) and those two (the parents) should do so through that blessing.
For devotion is the most auspicious thing and the cause of true awakening and other virtues;
therefore, because it is the foremost of all, the aspiration for devotion is the best.

Alternatively, because of the different types of devotion, we consider here that everything— such as prostration, worship, and so forth— is indeed auspicious and worthy of being invoked as a blessing.

It might be argued: "Let the practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācāra*) be granted for now; however, the composition of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalanibandha*) is improper because it is not seen in those respective commentaries. This is not so, because of its utility and because it is not prohibited.
First, there is the instruction of the students through the mention of his own work;
furthermore, the attainment of the greatest auspiciousness is its fruit, as previously stated. (15)

In the Dramiḍabhāṣya and other works, [it is said]: "Homage to Brahmā, the sole abode of preeminent qualities, the seed-vessel for the multitude of moving and stationary beings, the protector of the cosmic egg; homage to Jaimini, who causes to burst open the secrets of the Vedas hidden within their caskets, his mind kindled by logic."

This practice must indeed be observed because it is seen in such [scriptural passages] as "Salutation to the Teachers" (*namo'stvācāryebhyaḥ*). It has already been stated that the conduct of those who deny the existence of God is not to be followed. Furthermore, this is established by the legal principle that when there is a conflict between Smṛti (tradition) and Ācāra (custom), Smṛti alone is more authoritative. Moreover, the practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācāra*) is recorded therein: "For those who are endowed with the practice of auspiciousness, who are ever self-restrained, and who perform recitation (*japa*) and oblations (*homa*), no misfortune occurs," and so forth.
The act of auspiciousness (maṅgalakriyā) is described as being identical in form to the three instruments [of action];
therefore, the inclusion of an auspicious opening at the beginning of a work is also supported by valid authority.
In former times, the foremost among the Pulastya lineage, through the practice of constant repetition,
have declared that at the commencement of all undertakings, one should perform an invocation for auspiciousness.

The practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācāra*) is seen in the *Purāṇas* as "having prostrated and saluted," which consists of bowing down to the guru and so forth. For this very reason, commentators—suspecting that [the opening of] the *Yuṣmadasmad* [section] might be a flawed composition—declared it to be auspicious by virtue of its contemplation of the reality of the inner self (*pratyaktattva*). That, however, is weak, because even there the contemplation of the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad*) comes first, and because the *ragaṇa* (the syllable-group 'ra'), which has fire as its deity, is placed in the middle due to its lightness. The hymns beginning with "May Mitra be propitious to us" (*śanno mitraḥ*) are remembered by the wise as numbering one hundred.
These should be recited by the wise at the times of performing ritual actions. || 28 ||
Thus, the objection regarding the composition of this verse is unfounded. Furthermore, we observe in some works such expressions as "having bowed to the Lord, the Cause" and so forth.
Moreover, the fact that this [work] begins with the letter 'A' is due to the intention of performing an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).
As for its completeness, it is easily understood even if the word "entirely" (*nikhila*) were not stated. (29)
Even if this syllable here has another meaning, it becomes auspicious by the very nature of being the name of Viṣṇu, according to the logic of spontaneous sounds such as those of a conch shell. (30)
And at the outset, [the meaning] was described by Pāṇini and others as well;
furthermore, they accepted that words such as "atha" (now/then) in a sūtra have a different primary sense, yet their specific purpose is also understood.
In this context, even a negative particle may signify auspiciousness by way of negating deficiency;
for the conceptualization of this [negation] as either auspicious or inauspicious depends upon the specific object being negated. (32)
They know that even the mention of the suffering to be destroyed at the outset is auspicious;
therefore, in this negation of imperfection, the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori) remains unimpaired. 33.
In this entire work, the inclusion of the word "agaṇa" at the very beginning serves solely for the removal of obstacles, as it is the cause for the completion of one’s lifespan. (34)
In this *gama*, the *nagaṇa* is indeed distinguished for all [verses].
Regarding that, they know there are eight other meanings in the first four-line stanza. (35)
The summary of the definition of Brahman is an exposition of the first aphorism, which is inseparable from the procedure for distinguished auspicious rites. (36)

The summary of the four chapters consists of two types of purification of the object of meditation, the refutation of opposing views, and the prevention of the commencement of [further] objections. (37)

Furthermore, the complete removal of all factors that are contrary to one's desired undertaking is indeed the method relied upon by the wise, for they intend to express many points that are consistent with the subject at hand. (38)

Indeed, the authors of the Vārttika, in their explanation of the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "In the world" (*loke*), state: "They declare six meanings for the Bhāṣya passage beginning with 'In the world':
[the first is] a general exposition (*sarvavyākhyā*), [the second] a censure (*upālambha*), and others likewise [the third] a rejection (*pratyākhyāna*)."

"Some [hold that] the word *atha* [serves the purposes of] exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) and praise (*stuti*); this is the refutation [of those views]. The *Bhāṣya* states: "Those words which are well-known in common usage in their respective meanings should, whenever possible, be understood in those very same meanings within the Sūtras; their meaning should not be imagined through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, nor should it be artificially defined (*paribhāṣitavya*). It is called a "complete commentary" (*sarvavyākhyā*) because it describes the entire system of meditative practice (*samādhi-prakriyā*) correctly from beginning to end; it is called a "reproach" (*upālambha*) because it demonstrates the opposite of the methods found in the commentaries of Bhavadāsa and others.

Because it is stated that the Sūtra does not require an explanation due to its inherent nature of conveying its own literal meaning, the Sūtra is not explained; this constitutes a "rejection" (*pratyākhyāna*) because it rejects the explanation of the Sūtra by asserting that the Śruti itself is explained by the Sūtras. When there is a conflict between the Śruti and the Sūtra, since the Sūtra must somehow be interpreted through methods such as *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) by abandoning its natural meaning, the acceptance of the text exactly as it stands is discarded; this constitutes a "limitation" (*parisaṃkhyā*).

The praise of the author of the Sūtras is due to the description [of the Jaimini-sūtras] as having the inherent nature of conveying their own literal meaning. Although the word *atha* necessarily conveys its well-known meaning [of "then" or "thereafter"], the opponent objects that its meaning of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is not established because no such usage is seen in other texts; thus, this is the refutation of the word *atha*. Such is the division of the meaning of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). "Just as six meanings were stated by them within a single Commentary, in the very same way, we shall explain ten meanings here as well. (Verse 39)
First, the sixfold meaning, beginning with "explanation" (vyākhyā) and so forth, serves as an illustration;
likewise, those respective meanings have been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya of Pakṣila and other works. (40)

Just as the authors of the Sūtras and others, desiring to encompass various meanings, have formulated [doctrines] to be accomplished through the repetition and application of the Tantras, so too have they been conceived by us in that very same way. (41)

For indeed, within a single sūtra—namely, "because an object is apprehended through both seeing and touching"—there is established a multitude of points such as the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the permanence of the self (*ātman*), the plurality of the sense organs, the stability of objects, and the distinction between qualities and the possessor of qualities.

Thus, here in the statement of the meaning of the Sūtra, the summary of the subject matter to be explained is [contained] in the word *brahma*; its etymological derivation is shown by the two feet [of the first Sūtra]; and its auspicious nature (*śrīnisatva*), which is the supporting mark (*liṅga*), is [shown by the second foot]. The word *atha*, which expresses immediate succession, is established according to the order of the subject matter and the order of the principal elements within the "Crown of Revelation" (*śrutiśiras*). The specific cause for the commencement [of the inquiry], expressed by the word *ataḥ*, is grasped by the word *vidīpta*. The word *mama* serves as an illustration of the qualified person (*adhikārī*) who possesses the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), which is established by implication.

Because the remaining portion has as its object the most excellent reality and is itself sweet, it expresses a specific means for the goal of the benediction; by thus intensifying the passion indicated by the suffix *san* regarding the inquiry into Brahman as its object, it dispels the delusion that the inquiry need not be commenced from the very beginning. Of the two meanings of the Sūtra, the first has been established by implication through its result.
Here, however, the meaning of the Sūtra is expressed directly; therefore, there is no tautology. (42)

In the summary of the complete characteristics established in the second Sūtra, "Brahman" is the object to be defined (lakṣya), while the remaining [characteristics] constitute the collection of its definitions (lakṣaṇasamāhṛti). || 43 ||
Valid cognition does not arise from a mere enumeration; rather, critical examination is based upon definitions.
Since the definition is primary here, its presentation is indeed appropriate.

For here, the attributes such as being the creator of all effects and so forth, as well as being the object of worship for those seeking liberation, the bestower of liberation, the primary object of knowledge according to the Upaniṣads (trayyanta), the abode of Śrī, the essence of existence, and the supreme goal to be attained, are all taken into account; through their presence or absence, there arises a discernment of the superiority or inferiority of devotion, which either obstructs or facilitates final emancipation.
Indeed, a unique attribute is defined as a *lakṣaṇa* (defining characteristic).
The multiplicity of such attributes serves as the cause for the awakening of the intellect. (45)
The difference between the defined does not follow from the plurality of definitions;
for the wise know that it is contradictory definitions that constitute differentiation. (46)

The summary of the meaning of the four chapters (*caturadhyāyī*) is as follows: the phrase "in the supreme Brahman" states the primary subject matter, which distinguishes it from what is to be known through other sections of the Veda. Through the two quarters [of the first verse], the dual meaning of each pair of chapters is summarized—namely, that which consists of the established subject matter and that which consists of the subject matter to be accomplished. By the phrase "shining at the crest of the Śruti," there is an extraction of the meaning of the four aphorisms (*catuḥsūtrī*) which serve as the introduction; this is because the intended sense of the restrictive designation "shining *only* at the crest of the Śruti" is to exclude both non-connection with this specific means of knowledge and connection with anything else. Non-connection with the Śrutis, as well as connection with other means of knowledge, is thereby precluded.
What need is there for us here to state a restrictive determination by means of these four sūtras? || 47 ||
However, the proponents of the *ekadeśin* (partial) view have explained this as a statement of the meaning of the first sūtra. [Objection:

But how can there be an exclusion of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that it is established by memory (*smṛti*) and so forth as well? [Reply: Not so; for it is established by logic (*nyāya*) that their validity is derived solely from being rooted in that [direct perception]. By this, the suspicion of the sublation of Śruti due to conflict with Smṛti is dispelled. Furthermore, the fact that Śruti acts through the medium of Smṛti is the same even when there is a sublation of the means of proof. In that case, if it is rooted in Śruti, Smṛti itself is the refuge. As it has been said: "But in case of conflict, it should be disregarded; for when there is no [conflict], there is inference [of its basis]."

And he will say: "If it is argued that this would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other [Vedic] Smṛtis. Through the two terms *śrīnivāsa* (the Abode of Śrī) and *bhakti-rūpa* (whose form is devotion), the true nature of the goal to be attained and the means to attain it is established. Furthermore, His supremacy—as understood through the fourfold definition (*catur-lakṣaṇī*) in the manner previously described—is fourfold. The word *mama* (of mine) serves as an illustration of the means and the qualified aspirant (*adhikārī*). Here, if only the word *bhuvana* (world/universe) were used, or even if the qualification *sakala* (all) were added, one might suspect it refers only to the majority of worlds; therefore, by using the term *akhila* (entire/without exception), its absolute completeness is expressed, thereby distinguishing Him from Brahmā and others.
When [the matter] is stated by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), the firmness of the meaning is perceived;
therefore, there shall be the accomplishment of the desired object and the warding off of the undesired. 48.

For Caturmukha (Brahmā) and others do not possess the status of being the cause of all things. Indeed, they are not the causes of their own [creation], nor of those [creations] preceding or following them, nor of the pure creation (*śuddhasṛṣṭi*) and so forth residing within other cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*); rather, in the individual creation (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*) and so on, they have restricted offices and are directed by another. Furthermore, although the word *bhuvana* here is conventionally established as referring to a specific collection of effects, it may also refer to effects in general by way of implication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because in this context conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*). The compound *janmādi* is a *bahuvrīhi* that includes the qualities of its members (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), just as in the case of the rule "all pronouns [beginning with *sarva*]" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*).
When a substance that is eternally established is determined according to its observed state, its various conditions—
such as birth, persistence, and so forth— arise through the power of the diversity of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

With the intention of expressing that properties such as "space-ness" (ākāśatva) and so forth are adventitious, even though their respective substances are eternal, [qualities] such as origination are also taught in scripture. (50)

Just as for others, color and other qualities appear in eternal substances through the process of transformation, so too do the various states appear to us within the substance of the three guṇas through the conceptualization of others.

The states beginning with birth (*janman*) are said to be manifold, distinguished as *nitya*, *naimittika*, and so forth. Birth (*janman*) is the acquisition of self-existence by that which was previously non-existent. Stability (*sthiti*) or steadfastness (*sthemā*) is the non-destruction of an object whose form has been acquired through birth, provided the causal conditions for its destruction are absent. Now, one might ask: how is the word *sthemā* formed, and how does it have the meaning of "stability"? For it is not derived from the root *sthā* (to stand) like [words ending in] *-ana* or the like; nor is it within the scope of the rule *pṛthv-ādibhya imanij vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.122).

Although by the rule *priyasthira-* etc., the word *sthira* undergoes the substitution of *stha*, and in that context the three suffixes beginning with *tu* (i.e., *tara*, *iṣṭha*, and *imanic*) are prescribed; nevertheless, in this case, the suffix *imanij* occurs only after the substitutes for *priya*, *uru*, *guru*, *bahula*, and *dīrgha*, and not after others, because [the group] is not recited among the *pṛthvādi* group. Nor is that group an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Therefore, how is this usage justified? To this we reply: "The established usage [is derived] from actual practice (*prayoga*), while the formation of *sthemā* results from the application of the rules for suffixes and so forth."
Or rather, this word is unbroken [as a single term] from the perspective of its not being derived from a verbal root (adhātu). || 52 ||
For indeed, there is an application of that [term] in the *Nyāyatātparyaṭīkā*:

"The stability (*sthemā*) of entities will be established," and so forth. And in the *Tātparyapariśuddhi*, during the examination of doubt (*saṃśayaparīkṣā*), it is stated that even for a Buddhist or others who maintain [theories] such as momentariness, since their proof has been instantly shattered by the opponent's proof, a definitive ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) of stability and so on arises without any doubt, because all suspicion of error has been completely eliminated. Furthermore, there are usages by great poets such as: "The glories of the ten-faced one (*daśānana*) were devoid of stability."
Thus, its correctness is established here by the abundance of well-known usage by many scholars. Furthermore, its etymological derivation is possible, as it has been said:

"In the Nirukta and in Grammar, it is stated that names are born from verbal roots (dhātu); and [the name] Śakaṭāyana says they are derived from 'the son of a cart' (śakaṭasya ca tokam). That which does not arise from a specific meaning of the word-base must be inferred from the suffix and the root."

Or, let there be no division into *prakṛti* (base) and so forth, since according to different schools of thought, the indeclinable (*prātipadika*) is spoken of as being indivisible; this is indicated by the words "and a noun" (*nāma ca*) and so on. For the purpose of establishing that such usages are not to be excluded, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* introduces the various types of rules, such as those beginning with *bahula*, in many ways. (53)
We do not regard as true grammarians those who, while surrounded by many scholars proficient in various systems of grammar, declare that certain words are ungrammatical. 54.
The learned remember that etymological derivation follows the usage of distinguished authorities; therefore, it is altogether improper to find fault with usages that are not contested. (55)

The word *bhaṅga* does not denote absolute destruction, because that is expressed by the word *rakṣā*, and because the purpose (*prayojana*) must also be stated separately, just like the subject matter (*viṣaya*). Therefore:

Just as in passages such as "to Him who is the sole cause of the birth, sustenance, and destruction of the world," there is a separate mention here according to the logic of the Brāhmaṇas and Parivrājakas; however, even for those who claim that in [passages] such as "to Vinatā" and so on, He merely bestows desired fruits like bondage by virtue of possessing the bodies of Indra and others, there would necessarily be a contraction of meaning regarding the word *sthiti* (sustenance). For this very reason, the Teachers have stated that it is not appropriate to include liberation (*mokṣa*) even as a specific object denoted by the compound "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*), which stands in apposition with the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here, because the specific distinction [of liberation from the others] is not clearly manifest.

In this very context, when the meaning of the Purāṇa is stated as "the sport consisting of the creation, maintenance, destruction, entry, and control of the world," since it is impossible for this [definition] to conform to what has been stated by others—whether that be distant from one's own statement or stated in another of one's own works—it is appropriate that those factors most essential to the triad of birth and so forth, such as the entry into those [beings], are also included therein. This is because they are implied by the sense (ārthatva), whereas the literal expression (śābdatva) of the former [creation, etc. is secondary. Furthermore, by this, the Lord's independence from auxiliary causes is established, because of the logical consistency in describing the birth and so forth—which reside within His own effects—as His sport (līlā).
And by the very manner stated in "May I be," etc., its status as the material cause (upādānatva) is also indicated. || 56 ||
For those who watch a dancing person, the dance is not a pastime (līlā), but rather a mere perception;
however, when that [dance] is centered upon the body, birth and so forth become a pastime. (57)
They have declared that being the substrate (upādānatva) consists in the connection with different states;
a state is defined as an adventitious property that is not established separately [from its substratum]. (58)
O All-pervading One, through the medium of the individual soul (jīva) and by Your own essential nature, these states exist;
they are faultless, while the description of You as "changeless" refers to something other [than these states]. (59)

And for this very purpose, the reasoning regarding "entering within" and so forth is employed here. Consequently, by demonstrating that everything else has its body in Him, it is stated that He alone—having the Pradhāna and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) as His body—performs the divine play of birth and so on.
Those who have reached the further shore of the Upaniṣads have declared this intention: "Therefore, creation and the rest belong to Him alone; residing in all beings, He is the benefactor. (60)

Nor is there any contradiction here regarding the application of the word *bhuvana* (world) in its intended specific sense, for this is justifiable in the same way as [the expressions] "one whose play consists of independent worldly activities" (*svatantrabhūtaceṣṭālīla*) and so forth. Furthermore, there is no contradiction even if the term extends to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) without being extracted [as a separate referent], as in the expression "Viṣṇu is the worlds" (*bhuvanāni viṣṇuḥ*). Thus, the *Vivaraṇa* states: "The word *bhuvana* intends the non-sentient [matter] together with the sentient self (*sajīvātmaka*), because causality is perceived in that very manner in the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*); Brahman, however, is mentioned separately."

Alternatively, the meaning of the word *brahman* is that which is distinguished [from all else], and for that very reason [it is so called]. Furthermore, there are other meanings stated in the *Tātparya-ṭīkā*: because it is an effect (*kāryatva*), the term "play" (*līlā*) is used figuratively in relation to birth and the rest; or, because birth and the rest are its effects, it is that whose play consists of birth and the rest; or, it is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose play [is manifested] in the creation of the worlds and so forth"; or, it is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *tatpuruṣa*, meaning "that whose play is the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution [of things]. These [meanings] are stated by way of its majesty (*vaibhava*), as they are not contradictory even when the primary meaning has been explained.
In this way, by the word "birth and the rest" (*janmādi*), its cause is indicated through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Alternatively, the two meanings are considered to be: "He whose divine play consists of birth and so forth," or "He for whom birth and so forth are the play. (31)
A conscious being would not engage in action without aiming at some desired object;
however, the claim that this is not the case for one who has already attained their goal is here refuted by common worldly usage.
Whatever is desired by Him, that is accomplished; thus He possesses the fulfillment of all desires.
Therefore, He who is heard of as being endowed with the play of the objects to be attained should not be dismissed as being like an ordinary worldly being.
Even that which begins with "Fullness is Brahman" (pūrṇam adaḥ) does not contradict what has been said;
on the contrary, it is consistent with it, because [Brahman] is filled both by itself and by another. (34)

To demonstrate that even this [Brahman] acts according to its own will, independent of any other purpose, there is the illustration: "as a child with toys. The aphorism intended to convey this is: "But like the world, it is for sport," and so forth. Even by stating the reason [for creation], the meaning of the section on "Concordance" (Samanvaya) is established. Furthermore, the word "sport" (līlā), following the maxim of the "sample from a cooking pot" (sthālīpulāka-nyāya), serves as an indicator for the meaning of the section on "Non-contradiction" (Avirodha). By this term, which denotes an activity performed for one's own pleasure based on one's own intelligence, agency is shown to be non-contradictory to being the material cause.

By virtue of being distinguished by its subtle primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it may be the material cause (*upādāna*) and, through volition (*saṃkalpa*), the agent (*kartṛ*). In this way, its status as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is also to be maintained through its role as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the collection of auxiliary factors. For an instrumental cause (*nimitta*) is that which is employed for the production of the effect in a form distinct from being the locus of transformation; it is not something entirely other than the material cause. Indeed, the terms "one" (*eka*) and "without a second" (*advitīya*) in the causal statements are intended to convey both [meanings]. This is further corroborated by passages such as "He, having meditated" (*so 'bhidhyāya*). The section beginning with "the egg" (*aṇḍa*) and ending with "the host" (*vrāta*) is devoted to defining the means (*sādhana*).

Therefore, "bowing" (*nati*) here refers to mental prostration according to the prescribed rule, consisting of the various forms of knowledge mentioned in the section on the "Accumulation of Qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhārapāda*). The prefix *vi-* has various meanings; thus, those possessing it are "the bowed ones" (*vinatāḥ*). Alternatively, the prefix *vi-* may refer to the distinction of detachment (*vairāgya*) and other qualities established in the first two chapters (*pādas*). The diversity among these bowed ones arises from the differences in stages of life (*āśrama*) and so forth, as described in the section on the "Limbs of Knowledge" (*vidyāṅgapāda*). This applies even beyond that.

The distinctions among gods and others mentioned previously should also be understood here. The word *bhūta* (being), by virtue of its etymological derivation from the cessation of suffering (*tāpa*) and the presence of proficiency in the means for its removal through a particular body, expresses the state of being a seeker (*arthitva*) and so forth. Furthermore, the verbal root portion (*dhātu*) denotes "existence" (*sattā*)—either in the form of being endowed with pure intellect as stated in "they know him as existing," or as the "absorption into Brahman" (*brahmanirveśa*) taught in "here he attains Brahman."

In this context, the term *vrāta* (multitude) refers to those who are connected to the *bhūtas*, as indicated by the genitive case expressing a general relationship; otherwise, there would be no dependence on the word *vrāta*. For here, there is neither a collective undertaking nor the attainment of results through association alone, as is the case with *satra* sacrifices. Furthermore, the acquisition of results is not universal, unlike the case of residents of Sāketa. Thus, the scriptural declarations such as "in his lineage no inferior persons perish" and "no animal, human, or bird among his kin remains ignorant of Brahman" are widely applicable.

For in expressions such as "the assembly of kings" (*rājapariṣad*), both the king and others are intended to be expressed. Some maintain that by the word "various" (*vividha*) is intended the diversity of agents desiring various fruits—such as cattle, sons, food, heaven, or self-sovereignty—and by the mention of a "multitude" (*vrāta*), the great number of individuals devoted to those respective means is intended. We accept this as a statement of the [text's] grandeur (*vaibhavavāda*). And they say: "Of all the alternative explanations, two purposes are desired:
either dissatisfaction with the previous [explanation], or the complete pervasion of the subject matter."

In this context, according to the sequence of the chapter on the fruits [of action], the term "protection" (rakṣā) includes the pacification of obstacles to the attainment of the supreme state, such as suppression and so forth. || 65 ||
But when obstacles are completely destroyed, the happiness and so forth that are attained by their very nature are attained in their entirety;
thus, in this context, the perfection of that [state] is achieved as a matter of fact.
Alternatively, "protection" (rakṣā) is understood as the granting of desired objects;
for it protects one from the despondency caused by the failure to obtain them. (67)
According to the principle that greater effort entails a greater entitlement to the fruit, there is no fault in the statement regarding the protection of the four types of devotees. (68)

This is also to be understood from the *Śrutisūtra* on the quality of being the giver of bliss (*ānandayitṛtva*). Here, the word "one" (*eka*) has the sense of "principal"; for in passages such as "even I would give up my life," when there is a conflict with that [principle], there is mentioned the renunciation of everything else that is most desired but contrary to it. Alternatively, it is for the sake of preventing punishment that leads to hell and other lower realms even if others are negligent; for their going to the domain of Yama is prohibited, as it is observed: "Indeed, the devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavatas*) do not go to the domain of Yama."

Furthermore, because it is taught as a mere instruction that "some calamities may even occur right here for them," and because of such statements as, "Dīkṣā is a firm resolve; one should not abandon this vow of mine. By the mention of *dīkṣā*, self-interest is indicated; for indeed, the protection of chariots, horses, elephants, and so forth is for the sake of the king. [The compound] is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose single *dīkṣā* is in protection"; or, since *dīkṣā* has the nature of an action (*kārya*) regarding protection, there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term to that protection; or it should be construed as "one who has a single *dīkṣā* toward protection. For punishment, mutilation, and the like are seen [to be applied] when another commits an offense.
For indeed, when a prince commits an offense, a light punishment is observed. || 69 ||
Even for one enjoined to perform a task as a means to a result, those who prioritize the bestower of the result are the ones who grant the fruit;
kings grant the fruit to those who perform service for the king.
The preeminence of the bestower of the fruit is understood from that very fruit. (70)

By the statement of Vinatā’s son (Garuḍa), the cause of bondage—namely karma and so forth—is shown to be removed through the subduing of evil deeds accompanied by that song; for this very reason, the objections regarding partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) are also avoided. The word *śruti* is conventionally established as referring to the eternally heard Veda, based on the principle of immediate consensus; this is likewise stated in such passages as "when the relationship between word and meaning is established. By this, the absence of defects in the speaker is proven.

And the authority of the Vedas was established in the very first pāda by the absence of defects in their cause and the absence of any subverting cognition, because it is impossible to infer an author for them, since they were manifested exactly as before at the beginning of each Kalpa, and because designations such as "Kāṭhaka" do not establish a specific author. "Head" refers to the supreme portion, being preeminent due to its primary focus on Brahman. "Radiance" means manifestation; that, moreover, arises from the understanding of established facts (siddhārtha) as stated in the first adhikaraṇa.

The term *viśabda* (the prefix *vi-*) denotes *vaiśiṣṭya* (distinction), which here consists in the absence of any mention of other deities. By the passage beginning with "That indeed is Agni," it is intended that words such as "Agni" and so forth ultimately refer to the Embodied One (the Supreme Self), and that there is an exclusion [of the individual soul] by virtue of the two qualities mentioned in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 1.1.2): being the cause of the world and having self-sufficient human purpose (*svataḥ-puruṣārthatva*). Through the mention of this specific characteristic, the meaning of the third Sūtra is established by the principle of the negation of the remainder (*śeṣa-niṣedha-nyāya*).
Thus, the summary of the *Nyāyasudarśana* regarding this point is as follows:
"Lack of etymological derivation, difficulty of comprehension, establishment through another [means], and lack of fruitfulness."
"These very [objections] have indeed been refuted by the four aphorisms as having their root in the lack of an undertaking.
And likewise, the teachers Senaśvara and others state in the *Nyāyasaṃgraha*:
"Because of the absence of proficiency, because of the difficulty of comprehension, because of being established by another [means], and because of fruitlessness..."
Having raised the doubt that [the Self] might be non-existent, he refuted it by establishing each respective point through four logical arguments (*nyāya*).
By this, the excellence of the resulting valid cognition (*pramiti*)—which culminates in the inquiry "What is Brahman? and so forth, similar to the inquiry "What is Dharma? and so forth—is stated.

Now, if the word "Brahman" were used here in a general sense, it would then be qualified by the word "Śrīnivāsa. But this is not the case, because it has been established elsewhere that [the term] is used figuratively in other contexts; because in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 1.1.2), the etymological definition is stated as "Brahman is that which is unsurpassably great and which causes growth"; and because in the *Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 1.4.23), it is stated: "Even though the word 'Brahman' is unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), its usage is sometimes seen applied figuratively to the individual self (*pratyagātman*)," and so forth.

And in the section concerning the ether (*viyadadhikaraṇa*), there is a Sūtra: "And [the word may apply] to one [thing], as in the case of the word 'Brahman'"; and regarding that, the Bhāṣya says: "Just as the word 'Brahman' is used in a secondary sense for the Pradhāna in the passage, 'From that this Brahman is born—name, form, and food'—and yet in that same context, in the passage, 'By austerity Brahman is built up; from that food is produced,' the Bhāṣya states: 'Because the word Brahman has its primary meaning only in the Supreme Brahman.'"

Furthermore, the term *śrīnivāsa* is not a qualifier here intended to exclude a metaphorical usage—as in the case of the word "other" (*para*)—since the purpose is already fulfilled by the word *parasmin* alone. Nor does it serve to convey the meaning through a synonym because of its lack of common renown despite being established in one sense, for such a connection is impossible; indeed, there is no syntactic connection here like that in the expression "the cuckoo is *pika*," due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) and because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). And this is not tenable, according to the maxim: "When a single unified sentence is possible, a split in the sentence is not desired."

It is incorrect to claim that the name "Śrīnivāsa" is one where the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) has been abandoned in favor of a specific meaning derived from etymology (*yoga*), because this point has already been covered by the passage beginning with "ale. Furthermore, the word *brahman*, which denotes the universal, appears in certain places: first, in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, there is a juxtaposition of terms such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Brahman" with the intention that each subsequent term serves as a qualifier for the preceding one. Also, in the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa*, it is stated that words such as "Being" possess a common form.

In the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* as well, it is stated that words such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Brahman," occurring in the same context, when qualified by the word "Nārāyaṇa" within that same context, lead to the understanding of Him alone. In the *Pāśupatādhikaraṇa* also, it is stated that words such as "Being," "Brahman," and so forth—occurring in the same context as the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīt*)—establish Nārāyaṇa Himself as the Creator mentioned in the creation-texts.

Therefore, how is this so? It is thus: when there is a mutual contradiction within a text accepted as authoritative, the contradiction must first be resolved on the basis of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). That very conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *brahman* which was established from the outset as referring exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is what is accepted everywhere. [This applies even where] it is common...

The statement regarding [the word] *anya* (other) may be intended to dispel the suspicion that it has a meaning other than what is accepted by those who—based on the observation of its usage in various scriptures and so forth, as well as the contradictions of proponents of false views—regard it as a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) like the word *ātman*, or as having both an etymological (*yoga*) and a conventional (*rūḍhi*) sense, or as possessing a mere conventional sense. Thus, even in such commentaries as "‘Brahmaṇi’ is a general term, while ‘Śrīnivāse’ is a specific term," the same principle applies.

Likewise, here, through the inclusion of the common [meaning], there would be the specific determination "Śrīnivāsa. Alternatively, following the singular conventional meaning of the word *brahman* itself, that very [reality] is qualified by the term *śrīnivāsa*; for she (Śrī) is resorted to by all, and she is the one who takes refuge in Him. For this very reason, the maxim of the "goat and the animal" (*chāgapaśu-nyāya*) is intended here; otherwise, even the status of being the "four-faced one" (Brahmā) and so forth might be suspected.

For this very reason, even the meaning of the term *puruṣa*, which is unique to the Supreme Reality—as expressed in the mantra, "Hnīḥ and Lakṣmī are Your two wives"—is further qualified by Śrī’s status as His consort. By this, the conventional usage of the word *brahman* for the Supreme is established, just as it is through [attributes] such as causality. Furthermore, the connection with the most well-known alternative name (*śrīnivāsa*) is applied to Brahman, who is the referent of the term *śrīnivāsa*. Alternatively, in order to establish the supremacy of *śrīnivāsa*, He must be qualified as being denotable by the word *brahman*, based on the cause of His vastness in His manifested form (*prakṛtākāra*).

It is stated that the Supreme Brahman, though defined by the pentad of attributes such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) which characterize its essential nature, is specifically qualified as the Abode of Śrī (*śrīnivāsa*), and is thus the object to be known through the *Brahmavidyā*. This is because it is declared that "His taking refuge in Śrī is eternal, both in His essential nature and in His form; He has the Śrīvatsa on His chest and possesses eternal Śrī. In this context, passages such as "the peaceful and infinite" (*śāntānanta*) should also be kept in mind. By this, it is suggested—through the prayer that "may there also be other well-known manifestations such as those in the Paryaṅka-vidyā"—that this means of attainment is the most delicious (*svādutama*) among all others to be reached. Thus it has been said:
Where is the ascent to the summit of heaven, characterized by rebirth?
And where is the recitation of "Vāsudeva," the unsurpassed seed of liberation? Thus it is said.

The sense is that [the Lord is the object of devotion] for one who is in the state described by the words, "O Blessed One, I am grieving," and so forth. "In the Supreme" (parasmin) means in Him who is the ultimate limit and the supreme goal, as declared in the scripture: "That is the limit, that is the supreme goal," because He is the ruler of all and the giver of unconditioned bliss, and because He constitutes the pinnacle of what is to be accomplished and attained. By mentioning His being the "attainable" (prāpyatva), the purification of the state of liberation—established by such passages as "He is indeed this Bliss"—is also accomplished. Alternatively, "supremacy" (paratva) refers to His being the absolute limit of all excellence, such as omniscience and other qualities, which are necessary for creation and other cosmic functions. Thus, the object of worship—the perfected, attainable form of the Lord who is approachable through both His supremacy and His accessibility—has been purified.
Excellence devoid of accessibility does not provide benefit;
likewise, accessibility devoid of excellence does not provide benefit. (71)
However, regarding the purification of the means for the goal to be accomplished,

the two terms "intellect" (*śemuṣī*) and so forth are employed here to exclude the notion that devotion consists merely of worship and the like, and that wisdom takes the form of mere reflection and so on. (72)

This is a summary of the terms *vedanā* and so forth, according to the principle of cattle and other animals which will be explained later—their specific resting points: *śama* (tranquility) is peace; it shows that wisdom (*buddhi*) has tranquility as its constituent part. *Bhakti* (devotion) is love for a venerable object. And love is a particular state of the intellect (*dhī-viśeṣa*), such that by means of which intellect it is to be accomplished, as desired by others.

It is logical that the true nature [of devotion] is precisely such [as described]; this has been stated in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* with reference specifically to *bhakti*: "That particular object by which knowledge is qualified and intended to be the generator of happiness—that very knowledge of that object is itself happiness; no other distinct category of entity is perceived apart from it, and because the conventional usage of 'being happy' is established by that alone. And it is said: "Devotion (*bhakti*) is defined as contemplation preceded by affection.
Thus, the meaning of the entire scripture, from head to foot, has been described here in this manner.
The established usage [of these terms] will occur according to their respective places, depending on the intention to denote them. || 73 ||

Thus the meaning of the treatise has been set forth in sequence. Specifically, by following the progression of the "Chapter on the Two Liṅgas" (Ubhayaliṅga-pāda), the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is refined—because, even though the reality of Brahman was established in the preceding two chapters, this chapter establishes its particular excellence of power (*prabhāva-viśeṣa*), and because it declares the multiplicity of the Vidyās.

Here, through the passage beginning with "akhila" and so forth, by describing the Supreme as the cause of the birth and so forth of even the dream-phenomenon and the like, and by stating its excellence of supremacy, the intention of the four sections beginning with "Sandhyā" is revealed: namely, that the Supreme possesses unimpeded and manifold powers (*akuṇṭhita-vicitra-śaktitva*), which is the cause of the dream, deep sleep, and other states for those who possess a field (*kṣetrin*).

By the two words "vidīpte" (blazing) and "śrīnivāse" (abode of Śrī), there is an indication of a group of qualifiers consisting of positive injunctions and mutual non-sublation; furthermore, by the employment of the word "para" (the Supreme) as used in the aphorism "na sthānato 'pi parasya," this [verse] is cited for the purpose of establishing the dual-natured character [of Brahman]. Through the inclusion of the entry into the sentient and insentient and so forth, and by the force of the word "līlā" (sport), the doubt that the Self might, even in part, incur ignorance is rejected, thereby calling to mind what was stated in the *Ahi-kuṇḍala* section.

By stating "in the highest" (*parasmim*), the meaning of the section "from that, the Supreme" (*paramataḥ*)—which refers to the cause—is also fully explained. By the words "to Vinata" and so forth, the teaching of the section "from that, the fruit" (*phalamataḥ*) is demonstrated. Regarding the remaining [sections], there is an indication of the desire to meditate upon the goal already established by the sense.
Furthermore, the object of meditation is refined here by another method:
previously, the procedure for the chapter on the two genders (*dviliṅga-pāda*) was thoroughly purified.
The meaning determined by the Nārāyaṇānuvāka and other such passages is stated here.

For here, by the words "entirely" (*akhila*) and so forth, the status of being the cause of all is stated; by "Vinata" and so forth, the state of being known through all sciences for the sake of liberation is stated; and by the phrase "blazing at the summit of the Vedas" (*śrutiśirasi vidīpta*), the fact that the Supreme Brahman is the sole object propounded by all the Upaniṣads is stated. Then, regarding the statement that He is the abode of Śrī, the intended meaning is as follows: in passages such as "But the Cause alone is to be meditated upon," scripture declares that the Cause of all is precisely what must be meditated upon by one seeking liberation. That very [Cause] is expressed by terms such as "Being" (*sat*), "Goodness" (*cit*), and "Brahman."

Furthermore, these [scriptures] do not have different subjects, because it is stated that the cause of the world is one everywhere, making alternatives or combinations impossible; and because once the authority of the entire Veda is ascertained, it is improper to abandon any part of it; otherwise, according to the maxim of the broken jar, there would be no way to avoid discarding the rest. Thus, their having a single subject being established, [the conclusion is reached that the cause is] Nārāyaṇa, who is the locus of the conventional usage found exclusively in the Mahopaniṣad, which is consistent with numerous uncontradicted purāṇic expositions (upabṛṃhaṇa) that are predominantly composed of truths concerning the negation of Brahmā, Īśāna, and others.

The Lord of Śrī alone, as denoted by the word "Being" (Sat) and other such terms, is the meaning of the word [in question]. Furthermore, the determination that the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) concerning the Cause is Nārāyaṇa is established in the *Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa*. It is logical that all statements regarding the Cause have a single referent with the *Puruṣasūkta* recited in all the Vedas; and it is established in the subsequent section (*uttarānuvāka*) that the one propounded therein is the Lord of Śrī. As for the term "Hiraṇyagarbha" when referring to the Cause—

By the very Vedic text, "Born from the waters, Hiraṇyagarbha... and so forth, the fact that [the Puruṣasūkta] has Śrīpati as its subject is demonstrated. In this way, by the recognition of the meaning of the words in the Puruṣasūkta, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and others are also explained. Therefore, what is established here is confirmed by such statements as, "That wherein all the Vedas become one," and "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known.

For this very reason, through the unanimity of the Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, and Uttara-Nārāyaṇa Anuvākas, [it is shown that] the word *brahman* refers to Śrīnivāsa; thus, Śrīnivāsa alone is the meaning of the word *brahman*.

And the refutation of opposing views has been performed from one part of the treatise; it is now manifested here in this verse-summary of the treatise’s meaning by means of various specific terms. (75)
In this context, every word manifests the reality of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious;
even in a single entity, that manifestation occurs with reference to the differentiation of its parts. (76)

In the same way, one who is devoid of wisdom and desires to invalidate perception here by means of [cognitions] based on objects, sense-faculties, both, or neither, while being free from defects, is merely deluding himself. (77)
If the distinction between the position that difference is real and the position that difference is false were itself false, there would be a contradiction on all sides. (78)

Without contradicting the manifestations, qualities, and form described in statements that have no other purpose, passages such as "not this, not this" and so forth must be interpreted as referring to the Lord.
But the Śruti is eternally faultless and possesses intrinsic validity;
regarding matters beyond the reach of ordinary experience, it should not be cast aside as mere extraordinary speech intended for one's own desires. (80)
Subsuming the parts together with their remainders and the remainder itself into a single unity, the statement that "all is one" even eclipses the doctrine of manifoldness (anekāntavāda). (81)

For one who declares this entire universe to be non-absolutist (anekānta), there can be no occurrence of attachment or aversion toward a thesis to be proven or a position to be refuted, nor any other such biases. || 82 ||

And this employment of the negative particle (nañ) is meaningful, conveying understanding according to its conventional derivation; it refutes the "indefinability" of non-existence by means of uncontradicted cognition. (83)
This non-existence is either a different state of being or a distinct category of entity;
in either case, how could it possess a nature if that [nature] were devoid of intrinsic being? (84)
By stating that all things arise, he rejects the eternality of the four types of atoms, the mind, and space; however, the eternality of the other [entities] is established through scripture. (85)

Those who deny the existence of the action explicitly stated by the verbal root *sajjāyate* are refuted by the mention of the world (*bhuvana*) as produced from a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose meaning is existence (*sattā*). (86)

Indeed, conceptualization that is free from both existence and non-existence is purposeless, because there is no distinction between it and the contradiction stated regarding the positions of being and non-being. (87)

But in the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, no other alternative is possible for those who intend to speak of modifications such as the manifestation, superimposition, or emission [of the universe]. (88)
Obstruction [of the self] is established by the birth [of the body], as shown by the Śruti and other authorities;
if manifestation were beginningless, there would be no purpose for causal agents. (89)
If one desires that [change] to be adventitious, why not desire it to be so in other cases as well?
For emission (*visṛṣṭi*) is indeed accepted in some instances, and even expansion (*vikāsa*) is merely another state.
If there were identity between the manifestation and that which possesses it, there would be a contradiction, as in the Sāṃkhya position;
for this implies that a single entity is both the efficient cause and the material cause. (91)
He spoke fallacious arguments as set forth by the Yogas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others, such as:
"The Creator is the inherent cause (samavāyin) in the union of self and other, and is the maker of the universe. (92)
One should not conceive of a permanent conjunction in the case of the fluctuating elements;
for even the individual soul (jīva) is observed there, producing its own pleasure and other experiences.
Since the status of being the inherent locus of agency cannot be abandoned even by the followers of Kaṇāda,
and since the thought "May I become many" implies a modification,
[the objection] was countered by pointing out that creation occurs through the medium of the body.
Because birth and all other states occur for everyone in a sequence, and because they are designated as "one," the position that [the self] is a stream of momentary destruction is here refuted. (95)
For inference, which depends on stability, cannot establish the non-existence of that which is stable; nor can perception [establish it], because it is sublated by another unshakable perception. (96)
The doctrines concerning creation and dissolution,
though declared by those who have ascended to the level of the "Half-Lokāyata" to be false in their ultimate meaning, are here set aside as such.

By speaking of "entry" (anupraveśa) and so forth, he refuted—according to scripture—the notion that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is caused by sublation (bādha), identity (aikya), and the like. || 98 ||
Those who claim here that [the word] possesses a single referent consisting of multiple distinct objects due to its co-referentiality with various qualified objects are refuted. (99)

In this context, the doctrine of the Cārvākas and others has been refuted through reasoning based on logical reasons (*hetu*) and so forth; furthermore, the position that asserts the absence of bliss (*nirānanda*) has been dismantled with ease. (100)

Because [the status of being the creator] is established through extensive learning and the like, and because it is free from even a trace of contradiction, the impossibility of [the individual soul] being the creator is stated in the view of identity by means of the very expression "līlā" (sport). || 101 ||

In this context, [the Self] cannot tolerate the superimposition, burning, or conceptualization of the two [intellect and mind], which are merely modifications of ignorance and are eternally insentient by nature. (102)

In this context, the superimposition consisting of volition cannot tolerate conceptual construction, because both [the object and the subject] are insentient and are merely modifications of ignorance. (103)

Furthermore, according to the doctrine that Brahman consists of three parts, when the Lord is in deep sleep and is equalized with the insentient and the individual soul, there can be no possibility of his engaging in divine play or exertion. (104)

His state of deep sleep is contradicted by the scriptural testimony of his eternal omniscience; furthermore, it is difficult to avoid the lack of sovereignty resulting from the fact that his awakening and so forth are dependent upon time. (105)
The claim that deep sleep and waking occur prior to volitional resolve is incorrect,
because it would entail the abandonment of infinite experience and bliss, which is logically untenable.

Neither the insentient [matter] can will, nor can the individual soul (jīva), whose senses and so forth are unestablished; nor can the Lord, who is peaceful and faultless, bring about what is not beneficial for Himself.
Therefore, even though he is a portion of the Lord and eternally awakened, he does not possess such a mode of conduct;
for he who is not omniscient does not know the identity of his own self with that of all enjoyers.

In this context, the identity of nature between the individual souls—such as Vinatā and others—and their mutual relationship, as well as their identity with the Lord, is refuted by their respective authoritative means of knowledge. (109)

If one perceives the self through direct perception as "I am not omniscient," then even by the power of that perception, the notion of identity with an omniscient being could not possibly arise for him. (110)
Others have also formulated this in a sutra: "Because of the established distinction of diverse selves.
[This verse] elucidates the association with contradictory attributes through various modes of expression. (111)
The doctrine of non-attachment is refuted by the diversity of castes and other such factors;
furthermore, for one desiring liberation, that dharma has been rendered steadfast throughout the duration of life.
The term "those beyond the stages of life" (atyāśramin) refers to those who have attained excellence through their connection with the stages of life;
and it is established that they are heard to be unstained by sins even through negligence on their part. (113)

Beyond that, the fact that [the Lord] is the sole object of worship for all the gods, as stated in the opening sūtra, is manifested through various expressions for the sake of attaining the supreme state of each respective deity. (114)
By using the word *vrāta* (multitude), which indicates the infinity of living beings, [the author] has warded off the objection that universal liberation might occur prior to this point. || 115 ||
Due to the infinity of the self, there is infinity for both the unliberated and the liberated;
this occurs through gradations of infinity according to the principles of existent substance and so forth. (116)
"If one soul was previously unliberated from here due to the non-arrival of the cause, why does one not see that same state [of being unliberated] among many? (117)
By stating that there is no further becoming after liberation, eternal liberation is refuted;
nor can one's own essential nature (svarūpa) be liberation, because that would involve the contradiction of the already established being something yet to be accomplished.
The claim made by others— that heaven and so forth result from ritual action, its power, the *apūrva*, and the like—
has been refuted by the authoritative Veda through its teaching on the *dīkṣā* that protects the one who performs it.

But when the requirement for an injunction is met by the Vedic purpose itself being shown through direct scriptural statement (śruti), it is improper to abandon what is heard [in the text] and so forth, according to the principle of the Rātrisatra and other such cases. (120)
Because the activities of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), such as protection from danger and so forth, are demonstrated,
the status of these two as mere witnesses (*sākṣin-mātratva*), which was stated in various places, is set aside.

The doctrine of the non-eternality of the Vedas, the path abandoned by the Vedas, and [the view] that the subject of inference possesses a similar class (sapakṣa)—all these have been refuted through reasoning based on scripture and other authorities. || 122 ||

Establishing that the Lord possesses qualities and is therefore subject to transience and other such defects, [the opponent] has his hair of arguments singed away by the radiance of the Vedānta texts which apprehend the very nature of the subject. || 123 ||
The claim of unknowability and even ineffability put forward by those of false views has been refuted by the teaching that [Brahman] is radiant as the culmination of the Vedas (nigamānta).
The claim that Brahman is "heard" [in scripture] as something unfit for worship and so forth is refuted by the statement that the Supreme is the object of knowledge, worship, and the like. (125)
For those who claim that there is no all-pervasive entity, the term "Brahman" demonstrates an immeasurable vastness in order to refute their respective means of knowledge. (126)

If the all-pervasive reality is denied on the grounds that it is incompatible with the division of parts and so forth, then that same objection is unavoidable regarding atoms as well; moreover, if it were non-existent everywhere, there would be a contradiction with one's own words.

For one who abandons an all-pervading cause because it is impossible to perceive its negative concomitance (vyatireka), he demonstrated that its establishment occurs precisely through the fact that the uncontradicted scripture is established. (128)
He declares that properties such as causality, even though they possess counter-correlates, are not merely conceptual, because they are cognized by means of valid cognition in that manner. (129)
The relationship is accepted on the principle that it establishes itself as well as others;
let it be understood that this is neither for the sake of infinite regress nor for the sake of over-extension. (130)

By the term *śrīnivāsa*, which here expresses the meaning without doubt, those [objections] regarding identity with or equality to the Trinity, or the possession of another manifestation, are refuted. (132)

In the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), an indirect statement (*anyokti*) based on etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) and the like has a supreme referent; it rests upon that which is qualified by those [attributes], provided that the indicative marks (*liṅga*) thereof are not established otherwise. (132)
The theories propounded by outsiders with false views—which postulate a Supreme Being transcending the three forms—are refuted by the declaration of the supremacy of Śrīnivāsa, who is Brahman. (133)
By using the word "supreme" (*para*) to indicate that one "attains the supreme," [the author] has refuted the notion that the attainment of one's own self and so forth constitutes only a lower state.
There is neither non-existence nor diminution of the experience of others for one who is free from sin;
however, let it be figuratively said that "one is liberated" when karma has been exhausted without remainder. (135)
For it is heard in scripture that His otherness is unrestricted even from those who are liberated and so forth;
therefore, the doctrine of absolute equality in all attributes is also refuted. (136)
In this context, the scriptural mention of "becoming one" (ekībhāva) is intended to signify the unity of their mode;
for when pure and impure water are mixed, scripture demonstrates that they become identical.
Having described the brilliance of the three Vedas, it was further stated that, due to the injunction regarding devotion,
verbal knowledge cannot possibly result in direct perception.
In order to dispel the claim of those who assert that the self is not the referent of "I," the term "mine" (mama) was employed to demonstrate that the self is indeed the referent of "I. (139)

By the two words "intellect" (śemuṣī) and so forth, it is demonstrated here that the cognition of the object, its conceptualization, and the view that the meaning of the sentence is a single unity are not the means [to liberation]. || 140 ||
