By demonstrating here that there is a distinction between the knower and the cognition through the use of the possessive pronoun "mine," he refuted the view that the cognition which grasps objects is the self.

"The statement of difference, such as 'this is my own nature,' is merely figurative; otherwise, it would be incorrect due to the absence of [actual] existence and because of the consequence of over-extension. (142)
There is no natural sublation of cognitions regarding the knower and the known; unless, through fallacious reasoning, one points out a counter-example to the intellect. (143)
We consider that he, by distinguishing his own intellect through its object, its locus, and its inherent nature, has refuted those who would seek to refute it. (144)

But for those who thus maintain the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul and the Supreme, the commencement of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā] here would be contradicted by three [authoritative works]. (145)
Since bondage, being illusory, is sublated by the very cognition of reality, it is difficult to maintain that this treatise must be commenced with that [bondage] as its primary subject. (146)
By demonstrating that this established truth is destroyed without supreme devotion, he has refuted the undertaking of the opponent. 147.
O wise one, one should not desire to know [the Self] through the abandonment of knowerhood and so forth;
for if the "I" (ahamartha) were already established as a knower, it would not undertake its own destruction. (148)
A certain fool desires his own destruction for the sake of pacifying his own suffering;
it is not so here, because of the establishment of the abiding state of one's own self in which afflictions have been eliminated. (149)
Thus, this refutation applies even to the position that the individual soul is a reflection of Brahman;
for even the Lord is not an object of inquiry, since His omniscience is universally accepted as being superimposed.

In this case, even the status of being an object of inquiry is sublated by the very specific description of one whose form is devoid of all particularities consisting of existence and non-existence. (151)
And because its status as an object has been abandoned, its being an object of inquiry is destroyed;
for here there is no reflection upon the conditioned, nor does that [reflection] bring about the cessation of delusion. (152)
For there can be no desire to know that which is unknowable; if it were such, how could it be unknowable?
Furthermore, nothing can exist that is free from these two alternatives, because that would involve a contradiction. (153)
As for the claim that "if it were an object of knowledge, it would lack selfhood like a jar or similar things," that is incorrect;
for the two [selfhood and being an object of knowledge] are observed together, just as in the case of fire and its heat, both of which are real entities.
Furthermore, the contradiction between the object and the agent [of cognition] is woven into the very fabric of one's own perception;
for there is no contradiction in what is perceived, nor can perception itself be denied. (155)
If it is "unknowable" (avedya), then in that state of being unknowable, knowability would have been accepted;
if it is "unknowable" in the sense of being truly unknowable, then knowability remains unrefuted. (156)

Whether the thing is considered "unknowable" and thus "inexpressible," or even if it is expressible, it would nonetheless be expressible, because the word "inexpressible" itself is connected to that which is expressed. (157)

Statements such as "He spoke without words" and so forth, which express the ineffability of the Supreme Self, would be meaningless if there were no contradiction with His own words and other such [evidences]. (158)
Because it is consciousness (*jñāna*), the Self has neither the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatā*) nor the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtā*);
its nature as consciousness, however, is established by its own self-luminosity, which is free from what is seen or heard. 159.

Moreover, by asserting that the Lord's splendor resides in the very crest of the Vedas, [the author] reveals the opponents' disregard for the conclusions of the three Vedas regarding those matters. (160)

"Since the self-luminosity of cognition is established by such [arguments] as 'cognition is self-luminous because it is an act of intelligence' and 'the object of dispute is false because it is perceptible,' what is the use of reflecting upon the conclusions of the Upanishads? (161)

If that contemplation is for the sake of accomplishing the meditation on [Brahman] with attributes and so forth, it may be so; but if it is for the sake of establishing non-dual knowledge, then it is useless, because it is in contradiction with that [non-duality].

If you maintain that such reflection is for the sake of some other result, then, in that case, the status of the *Śārīraka* as a treatise primarily concerned with liberation would be lost for you. (163)

It is not possible for you to claim that "the cognition produced by the Vedic statement sublates that which is inferential," because [in your view] the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is independent [of such sublation]. 164

For in cases of delusion, such as [the perception of] a snake in a rope, sublation is observed to occur without distinction between inference and verbal testimony; let it be so in this case as well for you. (165)
For you, perception produced by words is difficult to establish and fruitless, since even from a word-referent that is beyond the senses, sublation is admitted in some cases. (166)

Nor is it logical to claim that a statement is [authoritative] for one who lacks the capacity for inference, because the scripture is established as a means of valid cognition regarding that which is not accessible through any other means of knowledge. (167)

The method of investigating statements endowed with numerous restrictive rules is superior; it is based on worldly perception and capable of inferring [the truth] from scripture and other sources. (168)
If it is argued that for those who know such inferences, error does not occur, [we reply] that for those who know such statements, the same holds true, except in cases of delusion. (169)
In the doctrine of duality-nonduality (dvaitādvaita) as well, such an undertaking is untenable;
for nothing is inconceivable to the Omniscient One, nor is it [inconceivable] due to his identity with the individual soul.
Even if there were a difference here, whether due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or by its own nature, what would it matter?
For there is no inequality resulting from differences such as Rāma and others, because of the equality of their oneness in omniscience. || 171 ||
And in all incarnations, those who eternally know all things declare that [the Lord] experiences deep sleep, delusion, suffering, and so forth, according to the manner of an actor. (172)
Furthermore, it cannot be said that cyclic existence occurs by one's own will, because the desire of another is your life-force, and from that root arises existence. (173)
If one who has realized the identity with his own living self is capable, he may overcome worldly existence;
if he is incapable, how could he seek the Supreme for the sake of liberation? (174)

Therefore, [the Lord] declared the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) to be devoid of any touch of non-difference, [distinguishing them] by such categories as the protector and the protected, and the guardian and the guarded. (175)
Thus, the commencement of the treatise is rendered unfavorable by both proponents of difference and non-difference, as they have been refuted. (176)

In our own system, however, because [the treatise] arises from a subject distinguished by the purpose of self-protection, all causes for not undertaking the scripture have been completely shaken off here. (177)

The claim that "whether known or unknown, it is not an object of inquiry" is incorrect, because [the nature of the object] is described precisely through the distinction between its known and unknown aspects. (178)
"By enjoining the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) with reference to the established subject (dharmin);
in this very manner, the proponents [of logic] have also accepted inference. (179)
Even though the general capacity for understanding is established through the treatises regarding specific details,
it is held that with respect to supramundane objects, [that understanding] arises from co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra).

This scripture is not without an object, because its object is stated in the Vedic revelation: "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon. Nor is that [Self] established through error or by another means of knowledge, because it shines forth clearly within the very crest of the Vedas (the Upanishads) without contradiction. Nor has it been determined [by other means], because the two preceding sections [of the Veda] have a different purport; and because there is no occasion for it in other scriptures, and because those scriptures contain contradictory statements.

Nor is it indefinable, like the number of crows or teeth, because it is described as being protected by its own nature of expansion dependent upon itself, similar to a vast treasure deposited in one's own house. Furthermore, liberation is not already established, as that would contradict perception and other means of valid knowledge. Nor can it be accomplished by another, because the very person who is bound through the creation of the body and so forth is the cause of his own liberation. Nor can it be obstructed by another, because this [Self] possesses an absolute sovereignty over all existence, being without equal or superior.

Nor is that [attainment] difficult to reach, because he is solely dedicated to that one goal. It is not endless through such things as returning again, like heaven and so forth, because punishment and the like have ceased without remainder. Nor does it have a result that is merely equal [to its cause], because infinite happiness is obtained by means of an easy path. Furthermore, there is no lack of qualified aspirants here, because it is indicated both generally by the phrase "one who has bowed down to various beings" (*vinatavividhabhūta*) according to the scripture, and specifically by the word "mine" (*mama*).

The objection that this system should not be commenced because it lacks the characteristics of a specific school (*pratitantra*) is also refuted by the fact that it is spoken in its unique, uncommon form. (181)

For it is heard that the state of being the body of all, the state of being the limit of all, and other such matters are established in this very [text]. Alternatively, even if every undesirable point has not been stated here, what follows from that?
Therefore, one should consider what is authoritative, whether it be the position of others or otherwise. (182)
And since tenets have been established by others through conceited measures, how could there not be a commonality [of views] due to the vastness of space and time? (183)
Who here is capable of either explaining or even comprehending that abundant reasoning which resides within the intention of the Commentator?
Nevertheless, virtuous people, perceiving even this small portion shown by us as having a hundredfold fruit, will savor it. 184.

In this very context, by means of the reasoning concerning the supreme subject matter and so forth—which is implicitly contained within the auspicious invocation consisting of the praise of the Supreme Guru and others—the unbeginnability (*anārabhyatva*) of this treatise is also refuted.

[The work is] the nectar of the words of Pārāśarya (Vyāsa), extracted from the midst of the milk-ocean of the Upaniṣads; it is the reviver of the life-force of the self when its vital breath has departed due to the blazing fire of saṃsāra.
May the wise ones of this earth daily drink from that [work] which was well-guarded by the ancient masters, situated far beyond the reach of many opposing views, and honored by its own words.

Then, having paid homage to Hṛṣīkeśa with the words "Salutation to that Blessed One, Vyāsa," and so forth, he dispels any suspicion of illegitimacy regarding his intended treatise by means of an intermediate subject-matter and reasoning that contains auspiciousness in the form of the invocation of his lineage-guru according to traditional practice—beginning with "The son of Parāśara" and ending with "will be explained.
[For] that which is spoken with deceit or spoken through delusion is fruitless, lacks support, is obscure, difficult to maintain, devoid of understanding, and not radiant in the eyes of others. (185)

An objection is raised here: "If this treatise were like the Lokāyata and other such systems—spoken by deceivers, rooted in error, purposeless, unaccepted, clear in meaning yet impossible to lead toward the intended goal, lacking qualified students, or redundant because its purpose is already fulfilled elsewhere—then it should not be explained. The term *Parāśara* refers to one who pierces (*āśṛṇāti*) others—namely, those of external and false views—with the arrows of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). His offspring is *Pārāśarya*. The specific mention of *Pārāśarya* is for the sake of clarity, to show that the son of such a person could not be otherwise than his father.

And the Śruti says: "He, Vyāsa Pārāśarya, said... Here, his own quality is pervaded by the quality of his father. One should not think that the name Bādarāyaṇa belongs to someone other than the author of the Sūtras; for [the Śruti states]: "Satyavatī obtained from Parāśara, on the island of Badarikāmiśra, the son Bādarāyaṇa, the infallible subduer of enemies."

This is because of such well-known traditions. Furthermore, his authorship of the *Brahma-sūtras* is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The Great Yogin, Lord Hari himself, having descended through Parāśara upon Satyavatī, raised up the Vedas that had been lost."
He divided them into four parts, and again into twenty-four;
likewise into a hundred, into one, and also into a thousand.
"Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of understanding its meaning, further composed the Brahma-sūtras in twelve ways, by which their status as 'sūtras' [aphorisms] is clearly established.

Thus, the statement of the Lord, who perceives the future—"and by the words of the Brahma-sūtras"—was either composed later than the sūtras themselves within the Mahābhārata, or He Himself bound it there. Furthermore, since that work, whether existing previously or to be realized in the future, is cited as having the sūtras as its subject matter in the form of those very words, there is no contradiction regarding the sequence of priority and posteriority.
Alternatively, because the traditions of the Smṛtis and the Sūtras have been established from time immemorial, their mutual acceptance does not lead to contradiction. (186)

And the commentator on the works of others has said: "Salutation to Vedavyāsa, the author of the Brahma-sūtras, the second creator, the incarnation of the power of knowledge of the Blessed Lord Hari."

The commentary explains that by the word *sudhā* (nectar), the author demonstrates the enjoyability (*bhogyatva*) of this meaning. Furthermore, in the analysis of the compound *vacasaḥ sudhā* ("the nectar of speech"), the word *sudhā* functions figuratively (*gauṇī vṛtti*). Alternatively, in accordance with the context of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), the meaning indicated by the word "speech" is itself represented as being nectar. Or else, the aphorism (*sūtra*) itself is represented as nectar; the expression "extracted" (*uddhṛta*) is used because it has been drawn out by way of the meaning consisting of the logic arising from the investigation of the Upaniṣads.

Now, one might ask: since [the nectar] is brought forth by the syllables of its own words (*nijākṣara*) which are embellished by *śleṣa* (punning), how can there be a compound here using the term "upamita" (that which is compared) and so forth? It is thus: the commonality of sweetness (*svādutvasāmānya*), which is indicated by the compound, is not explicitly stated here; yet there is no fault even when something other than that is employed, as in the example, "Where is the ocean of the Bhāṣya so exceedingly deep? Alternatively, the nature of contrast (*vaidharmyarūpatva*) may be applied to all the qualifiers here: for nectar is brought forth by the syllables of another Vedic hymn (*chandas*) which are metaphorically treated as "immortal syllables" (*amṛtākṣara*), whereas this [nectar] is brought forth by its own syllables alone.

Nectar, it is said, was extracted from the midst of the ocean of pure milk; this Upaniṣad, however, was extracted from the midst of the ocean of milk [of all scriptures]. In this manner, the rest should also be applied accordingly.
Through similarity (*sādharmya*), the establishment of sweetness is achieved, as well as the cognition of its being the sweetest;
through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the difference should be contemplated here by the wise. (187)
The application of that specific universal which one intends to express is what is prohibited;
however, a statement whose object is a different universal is not contradictory. (188)
However, the intended universal (sāmānya), such as sweetness and so forth, is what is meant;
that [universal] is not expressed directly, and by that means the compound is established. (189)

In poetry and scientific treatises, the use of a compound whose general sense is not intended to be expressed is frequently observed; therefore, a compound in this instance does not constitute a fault. (190)

The word *upaniṣad* is used for the purpose of clarifying the intended meaning of the word "head," just as [the term] *amṛta* is used for the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhībhyaḥ*). It is said that it "sits near" (*upa niṣīdati*) because it is eternally and immediately connected [to its object]; thus, it expresses that which has no other purpose. Accordingly, there is this statement: "Or, it is called *upaniṣad* because it sits near (*upaniṣaṇṇatvāt*). Regarding this, the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya* states: "For this knowledge is established in the deep. And regarding that, the *Vāmana-ṭīkā* says: "It sits near (*upaniṣaṇṇā*) in the profound Brahman."

The aphorisms are the subject matter of the commentaries; the Upaniṣads are the subject matter of those aphorisms; and Brahman is the subject matter of those Upaniṣads—such is the sequence of subjects. Their respective purposes are also as appropriate. And the Āraṇyaka is [the essence] from the Vedas, according to the Śruti.

The description of [the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā] as a "milk-ocean" is due to its being the most delicious essence of the "cow" (the Upanishads) and because of its infinity, profundity, and so forth. By describing it as such, its conformity with all the Vedas is manifested through its similarity to the milk that exists from the center to the very limits [of the ocean]. By the mention of its being "extracted," it is shown that the subject matter is not artificial and has been grasped from its very root. The phrase beginning with "saṃsāra... states the intermediate purpose most urgently required, in accordance with such Vedic texts as "If one knows that Brahman exists" (*asti brahmety evaṃ vedet*); furthermore, it is because the Sūtras find their final rest in the determination of the meaning of the [Vedic] sentences.

Having unified [the elements] with the acids, there arises *saṃsāra* for one who has entered the stream of births and so forth. Alternatively, *saṃsāra* is *karman*, that by which one wanders; it is described as "fire" because even heaven and the like consist of the threefold suffering (*tāpatraya*). "Kindling" (*dīpana*) is the rising of the flames of afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth; and this is the state of destruction for that which is conjoined with it, due to its being contrary to liberation (*apavarga*). Its manifoldness—fivefold, threefold, twofold, and so on—is explained in various places according to the distinctions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest.

In this context, the meaning of the prefix *vi-* is "distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭya*), due to its bringing about various sufferings such as those pertaining to the body. Here, "Prāṇa" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the cause of the vitalizing breath (*prāṇana*) for living beings; for it is said:
"No mortal lives by the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or the in-breath (*apāna*);
rather, they live by something else, upon which these two depend."

This is based on such scriptural passages as, "The life-breath of the life-breath," and "They enter into the very life-breath. Furthermore, *prāṇa* is recorded in lexicons as meaning "the sacred syllable *praṇava*," "the individual soul (*jīva*"), "life-force," and "the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It has become something "gone away"—that is, situated far distant—even though the scriptures reveal it through hidden methods and other means; from ancient times until today, it has attained the status of being known as "non-existent Brahman" (*asadbrahma*). The prefix *vi-* signifies that it has not been even slightly smelled [perceived] by any one of the means of knowledge, such as hearing and so forth.

Or rather, having departed specifically, even though He manifests Himself by descending of His own accord, He is difficult to perceive because of His state of withdrawal. Herein, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is knowledge. Because the individual selves have that [knowledge] as the essence of their quality, they are spoken of as being "parts" of Him. In this context, "departure" refers to extreme contraction. It is the restoration to life of those whose vital breaths have departed.

The term "establishment" (*sthāpanam*) refers to the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) such that it cannot be led astray by external false views (*bāhyakudṛṣṭi*); through this, it is a concise exposition of the supreme purpose as declared in the *Rakṣā*. In that context, however, the prefix [in *sthāpana*] serves merely to exclude the notion of [merely] attaining one's own self [through meditation]. The "former teachers" (*pūrvācāryāḥ*) are those other than the Buddhists and Jains. Protection (*rakṣā*) is "instructional" (*aupadeśikī*) only at that time and in that place; but it is called "well-protected" (*surakṣā*) in its "textual" (*grānthikī*) form because of its non-interruption over time and so forth. Indeed, the state of being protected was indicated by the venerable Rāmānuja regarding the meaning of the Upanishads (*trayyantārtha*), as proclaimed in the works of the venerable Yāmunācārya, such as the *Ātmasiddhi*. (Verse 191)

Through the two words *sudhā* (nectar) and *surakṣita* (well-guarded), there is an implied praise of the speaker: nectar is indeed firmly protected by the preceptor of the gods, the discus, the machine, and so forth. Even though it is well-guarded, he states that it has been disturbed by those of false vision who have abandoned the traditional lineage—this is expressed by the word *bahu*. "Many" refers to mutually contradictory opinions, or the opinions of many; the "conflict" (*vyāghāta*) caused by them is a manifold pervasion of affliction; the meaning is a contradiction with one's own natural intellect.

By this, she is situated far away from the understanders, being fit for non-understanding, incomplete understanding, or distorted understanding due to the varying degrees of *rajas* and *tamas* in their minds.
Lack of awakening and false awakening are both opposed to the awakening to reality;
even when there is no certain awakening, they remain as states that produce such [false] cognitions. (192)
If it were censured by the virtuous, it would not be accepted by later generations;
nor would the pursuit of that [censured] view be true for one who desires to conceal the truth. (193)
If it were accepted by those with false views or by outsiders, which would be one's own position to be protected, and which would be the position of another? (194)

Therefore, in this [treatise] consisting of four chapters, having intended the underlying cause regarding both the section on the means (sādhana) and the section on the refutation (ākṣepa), the two have been presented according to their distinction. (195)

But the nectar (*sudhā*), due to the fear of being struck down by Daityas and others who hold contrary views, remained at a distance. Alternatively, because it was to be brought forth for the purpose of ransoming herself when Suparṇī had been defeated by Kadrū and was in a state of great mental conflict, it remained far away in the third heaven. To show how even his own explanation avoids incapacity through the refutation of others' contradictions, he says: "brought near" (*ānītām*)—that is, established in its own meaning close to the intellect. By this, the relationship between the explanation and that which is explained has been purified.

He clarifies this in order to exclude other types of interpreters, such as those who seek only worldly success or those who act merely as formal practitioners, by stating: "by its own syllables" (*nijākṣaraiḥ*). Because the context concerns speech, "its own syllables" refers to the syllables of the *sūtra*, as will be stated later. As explained in the *Vivaraṇa*: "That meaning alone which the syllables of the *sūtra* convey by their own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*) is the traditional one; for it is the natural disposition of a speaker to employ words that express his intended meaning, and the purpose of employing words is to communicate to others."

The sense is that when there is mutual contradiction among many commentaries, the intrinsic consistency of the subject matter (*vyākhyeya-svārasya*) is what establishes the correct tradition. "Sudhā" (the nectar) refers to [the commentary] which brings along the immortal syllables (*amṛtākṣara*) that are the limbs of the *Gāyatrī*, as they are well-known from the *Saura* and *Sauparṇa* narratives; or alternatively, it means "by my own words. It was not mentioned in that way [in the previous verse] for the sake of establishing the *Sudhā* through the *Tantra* (systematic method). The gods, who are "well-minded" (*sumanasaḥ*), are the enjoyers of this *Sudhā*.

Alternatively, those who partake at every occasion of the terrestrial *sumanas* flowers—which have been brought by the *suparṇa* birds presiding over the *gāyatrī*, transformed into the form of the *soma* creeper, and consumed during the *ekāha* and other sacrifices—are the Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the [flowers] in the form of speech, they are described by the author himself elsewhere as "those who are excluded from [the sphere of] injunctions," such as in the passage "they desire to know," and as "those who possess the knowledge that discriminates between the essential and the non-essential. By this, the transmission of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is also taught.

For this is indeed heard in the *Chāndogya*: "A father should impart this Brahman-knowledge to his eldest son, or to a worthy disciple (*praṇāyya*), but to no one else whatsoever; even if one were to give him this entire earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, this [knowledge] is far more than that. A "worthy disciple" (*praṇāyya*) is one who is fit due to being humble, free from malice, upright, and so forth. Indeed, it is not appropriate to use the term "earthly flowers" as a mere designation for "brāhmaṇas," because the *Mīmāṃsā* is intended only for those of the three twice-born castes who have studied the Veda.

For those who are wise by their own nature and have attained the heavenly realms and so forth, there is generally no need for a commentary on the Sūtras; even if such a need exists, they have already achieved their purpose through works such as the Vṛtti, which are suited to those of vast intellect. Therefore, the mention here of [this work] being "earthly" is not in vain. Let them drink; let them experience bliss without effort. For effort consists in the churning and the bringing forth of the nectar (sudhā). It is "daily" because of its extreme profundity and its supreme charm. The intention is that this nectar was churned up by the author of the Sūtras like Hari, and brought down by the author of the Bhāṣya, that lord among the twice-born. 196.
The ancient teachers have condensed the extensive commentary on the Brahmasūtras composed by Bhavad-Bodhāyana; following their view, the words of the Sūtras will now be explained.

Nevertheless, why [compose this work] out of respect for the creation of instruments that provide no assistance, like a lamp in the daytime? Let the pure and ancient explanations, which have not been interrupted, be set in motion. To this he replies: "By the Blessed One" (*bhagavat*). Here, the word *bhāva* refers to the excellence of spiritual awakening as described in such passages as "the origin and the dissolution," and so forth; by this, there is an exclusion of Śabara, Śaṅkara, and others. The mention of its "extensiveness" implies that it is difficult to master for those of the present day. In this context, the "former teachers" (*pūrvācāryāḥ*) are Brahmanandin and others.

He indicates the obscurity resulting from the extreme brevity of those [works] by the phrase "they condensed. The intention is that [he refers to] treatises whose purpose is to establish the meaning set forth in the sūtras. He says "in accordance with their doctrine" in order to suggest that the statements of others do not derive from an authentic tradition.

[The author] says "the syllables of the sūtras" (*sūtrākṣarāṇi*) because the sūtras—being concise in syllables yet rich in meaning, light, indicative of their own sense, and composed of very few syllables and words—require an exposition. The word *akṣara* is used here with the intention that there be no difficulty regarding the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the objection of others—that the sūtras should be understood according to their literal possibility—is not to be accepted. And it has been said by Bhāskara: "Because [the commentator] introduces his own intention by means of the concealment of the intended meaning of the sūtras..."

"This [work] has been explained by others; in order to prevent that [misinterpretation], we shall explain it. We shall state merely the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*), for the implied meaning (*sūcya*) is difficult to express in detail. Furthermore, the fact that a *sphoṭa* distinct from the power of the syllables (*akṣara-śakti*) is not to be postulated is also what is implied. In the phrase "they will explain" (*vyākhyāsyanti*), the prefix (*upa-sarga*) and the verbal root (*dhātu*) together suggest—conforming to the understanding of contemporary people—a style that is neither too concise nor too diffuse, as well as clarity of expression. Alternatively, the two particles (*nipāta*) signify excellence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) and preeminence (*prābalya*).

The word-split (*padaccheda*), the statement of the meaning of the words (*padārthokti*), and so forth should be understood. The meaning of the Sūtra, beginning with "akhila" and ending with "etadanta," is being described; thus, the definition of a commentary (*bhāṣya*) previously stated—namely, that it consists of the summary of the meaning and serves that purpose—is established here.
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).
Here, this word "atha" (now/then) signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*). The word "ataḥ" (therefore/from this) indicates the state of being a cause for what has preceded.

In order to demonstrate the dependence upon an explanatory commentary (*vyākhyā*), he takes up the aphorism with the word "Now" (*atha*). An objection is raised: Here, the combined form "atha-ataḥ" is not appropriate because it is impossible for them to have separate meanings prior to their emergence [as a compound], and because one part would be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, a strained interpretation is not permissible when a natural one exists. Although the word *atha* is well-known in the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), even that established meaning is set aside by observing its specific, useful, and unique function [in this context]. For this very reason, it does not refer to a subject matter other than the one under discussion, as neither of the two possible alternatives is observed. Moreover, an inquiry [into the meaning of *atha*] would be pointless and unanswered [if it were merely "immediacy"].

The word *kārtsnya* (entirety) means a statement that does not require further expectation; for a reflection on only a single part does not constitute a complete doubt. Therefore, it must have the sense of "commencement. Indeed, the author of the Sūtras commences [the work] here. Or, it has the sense of "auspiciousness," as it is recorded in tradition: "The syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, they are both considered auspicious at the beginning."

To this he replies: "Here" (*atra*). By the verb *bhavati*, there is a restatement of the natural sense of the word *atha*. By the two words *atra* and *ayam*, there is the exclusion of exceptions. Here, in this Sūtra, which has the purpose of making the latter portion of the Veda the object of inquiry, [the author] distinguishes the completed subject matter—which consists of the inquiry into ritual action—from any other preceding event, whether from something arbitrary or from something common to other parts [of the text], because the mention of mere immediate succession would be purposeless. This [Sūtra] is endowed with the word *atha*, as in "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and "Now, therefore, the desire to know that which pertains to the sacrifice and that which pertains to the person" (*athātaḥ kratvarthapuruṣārthajijñāsā*), and so forth.

For this word *etad* (this) has its natural sense (*svarasa*) toward that which is under discussion, and this case-ending [the ablative] signifies causality. Thus, when "therefore" (*ataḥ*) has been stated in a general sense, and the specific [cause] has been implied by the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), once that [desire] has occurred, the natural sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not set aside. Some say that the word *atra* (here) is intended to manifest the capacity of the combined usage of *atha ataḥ* independently [of each other]. By the word *atra* and so forth, the non-relevance of other meanings here is indicated. To explain: first, we shall reject its meaning as an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*).

Is this [auspiciousness] due to its mere proximity to that which has an unintended meaning, or because it expresses that meaning? It cannot be the first, because it is improper to include in a sentence something that does not convey a meaning, because auspiciousness—which serves merely as the purpose of the scripture—cannot be syntactically connected with the meaning of other words, and because even an intended different meaning can be justified by depending on mere proximity. Nor can it be the second, because [the word "atha"] functions merely as an indicator (*dyotaka*); for instance, in the phrase "Now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), even though they express a meaning, words such as "is commenced" (*adhikṛtam*) are stated through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

However, this is not with the intention of asserting that [the word *atha*] is the denotative expression of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). Even if it were denotative here, the connection of auspiciousness would still have to be explained. For even if the utterance of an auspicious word serves the purpose of the subject at hand, its establishment as auspiciousness is properly understood as a secondary result (*anuniṣpatti*).
Indeed, the traditional teaching on auspiciousness states the analogy of the sound of a drum:
"Both the speaker and the listener obtain auspiciousness through these two. (197)

Otherwise, there would be the necessity of [interpreting] the word *brahman* as referring to something else, or [accepting] a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) of the sentence, or [the need for] the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "let it be" (*bhavatu*). This is because the word *brahman* denotes the most auspicious reality (*tattva*), which is uncreated and supreme among all things. Furthermore, neither the auspiciousness of the reason nor that of the probandum is restated (*anūdyate*) or enjoined (*vidhīyate*) here, as that would be purposeless; for there is no suspicion of their being contrary [to the conclusion] in this context, since there is no negation. The Nyāya-sūtras are intended for the removal of doubt.

Now, it might be argued that the auspiciousness of the inquiry should be made known, and therefore there is an injunction for it, which serves that purpose. Even this is weak, because there is no further expectancy once the reason "therefore" (*ataḥ*) has been stated, and because stating an additional qualification would be useless. Furthermore, its being for the purpose of "commencement" is also incorrect, since no doubt arises as to whether it has begun or not, and because it would be pointless to state the commencement of something already understood as an object to be accomplished.

Furthermore, the word *atha* does not express or indicate that the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is fit to be commenced, because there is no conventional usage (*avyutpatti*) for it to imply the action "to commence," as no other action is present in its meaning. Otherwise, even in the case of words indicating conjunction and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of connecting them with a word meaning "fit" by intending [the sense] "to conjoin" and so on. Moreover, the very word *ārabdhavyā* ("should be commenced") must be supplied as an ellipsis.

In that case, what is the purpose of the word *atha*? Nor is it intended here to indicate an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), since that is already established by the inherent expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*) [of the sentence], and because it is improper to abandon a well-known meaning in favor of a strained interpretation. The immediate succession between the word "yoga" and the "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) was set aside only out of necessity; but here, there is not even the sense of commencing a treatise. For [the word *atha*] has another [meaning].

*Vicāra* (investigation) is something other than *anuśāsana* (instruction), and it is not that which is being introduced here. Now, one might argue: "Let Brahman be the subject under discussion by virtue of its being that which is to be made known (*jñāpyatā*). This is not so—because of the delay caused by hearing [the word] as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), because of the absence of the words "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) or "instruction" (*anuśāsana*), and because the word *jijñāsā* lacks synonymy with *mīmāṃsā*, it does not present [Brahman] as that which is to be made known. For this very reason, it should not be said that "investigation is the subject under discussion by virtue of being understood as something to be performed," since the point would already be established by proving that the investigation must be commenced, making any other word redundant when what is required [is already met].

Because it is illogical for there to be no dependence on what precedes, and because stating both [the preceding and the following] would result in prolixity, therefore, the natural and uncontradicted immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) alone is established here. Consequently, the base of the word *ataḥ* could refer to something present in the mind even if it is yet to be mentioned, and the suffix is one that functions in all cases. Thus, in expressions such as "therefore silence" (*atha maunam*), it has a different meaning. Furthermore, the meaning of the ablative case is manifold. Therefore, he says "the word *ataḥ*" to show that no specific meaning is established [from the word alone].

In this case as well, there is this same implication for you ladies, due to the inherent force of the context (*svārasyāt*), and because of the co-occurrence with the subsequent term, just as before. The reason that was to be stated—namely, that the inquiry into ritual action serves as a cause for the inquiry into Brahman—is refuted by the fact that such a cause is not perceived. Furthermore, that which is yet to occur in relation to the inquiry into Brahman cannot be its cause. Nor can the purpose (*prayojana*) itself be a cause in its own right, because that would lead to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, the desire for that [inquiry] has already occurred.

Furthermore, for the suffix of the word *pratyaya*, its meaning as another case-ending (*vibhaktyantara*) or its status as an ablative (*apādānatva*) and so forth is irrelevant to the present context. Only the mere form (*svarūpa*) of the word *ayam* is appended [to the word *atha*]. Therefore, what is intended here is the state of being joined with the word *atha*. Nor does this involve a circular dependency (*mithassaṃśraya*), because the natural fitness of the words and their inherent meanings are established by themselves and do not depend on one another for their own existence; they depend on each other only insofar as they act as mutual auxiliaries. Alternatively, the word *ayam* need not be appended at all.

[Objection: Is it not the case that one of the two words, *atha* or *ataḥ*, is sufficient? For this is a sūtra. [Reply: Not so; because there is an abundance of purpose. The word *atha* is intended to indicate independence from other treatises that might intervene in the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*). The word *ataḥ* is intended to eliminate the failure to establish the qualifying and qualified portions of the reason for the inquiry into Brahman—which resides in the initial cognition as having a purpose not obtainable elsewhere. [The word *ataḥ* is intended to eliminate the failure to establish the qualifying and qualified portions of the reason for the inquiry into Brahman—which resides in the initial cognition as having a purpose not obtainable elsewhere.]
Even in the case of an immediate [cause], there is no causal efficacy; even when there is causal efficacy, there is delay.
This pair, along with its meaning, is observed to be like two sections of an arrow-shaft. (198)
For one who desires to abandon one thing here, a second thing to be abandoned will follow;
for inquiry itself will imply its own authority and its own cause. (199)
Therefore, in this Ārambha-sūtra, as in the Dharmacintā and other sūtras, he set forth the triad beginning with the proposition (pratijñā) separately by way of reversal. 200.

For one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga) and the Upaniṣads (saśiraska), and who—having understood that the fruits of mere ritual action (karma) consist of little more than a few bones and wood—has conceived a desire for liberation, there indeed follows immediately thereafter the inquiry into Brahman, which possesses infinite and eternal fruit.

In this context, what kind of conduct (*vṛtta*) is that which must necessarily be relied upon? And what kind of conduct is yet to be practiced, by which there is an implication of a specific mode of conduct? Furthermore, even if these two occur in a temporal sequence, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect between them? Once that is established, the logic of the grass, the flint, and the gem (*tṛṇāraṇimaṇinyāya*) would apply. The causal relationship between those two is indicated by the words "born from" (*saṃjāta*) and so forth, in contrast to the "small and unstable fruit" and the "infinite and stable fruit. Here, the words "established" (*sthita*) and "unstable" (*asthira*) refer respectively to being devoid of destruction and being characterized by persistence. In this [work], action and knowledge consist of the nature of definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).

Its "attainment" (*adhigati*) is its acquisition; or it is the understanding [of karma] as having small and unstable fruits through such passages as "having examined the worlds" (*parīkṣya lokān*). The connection of the fruit with the knowledge of action occurs by way of its performance. Alternatively, "having small and unstable fruits" is an adjective qualifying the action itself. The word "mere" (*kevala*) serves to exclude those actions that are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge which culminates in liberation. The compound "infinite and stable fruit" (*ananta-sthira-phala*) qualifies Brahman by way of a *karmadhāraya* construction; or, by way of a *bahuvrīhi*, it qualifies the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) as being the indirect cause of liberation.

By the prefix *sam-* (in *samyag*), independence from external causes and immediate succession (*ānantarya*) are indicated. For the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) arising from the practice of Sāṃkhya and other systems, or produced merely by the perception of suffering, does not generate the thorough contemplation of Brahman. The intention is that once the vain hope for endless fruits in mere ritual action has been discarded, and because the obstacles thereto have ceased, the intellect increases through the abundance of proficiency; thus, when the most intense longing for liberation has reached the state of a complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there would be no delay in the inquiry into Brahman.
However, in the absence of other obstacles, there is indeed immediate succession (*ānantarya*) here for us.
Therefore, there would be no over-extension [of the definition], as this is likewise accepted by others.

By the words "having studied" (*adhītya*) and so forth, [the author] makes known that there is no occasion for practicing other systems of thought which might strengthen the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*). The statement regarding the study of the Veda with its six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)—to the effect that "the Veda should be studied without ulterior motive"—is made either to increase the preliminary understanding of the fruit that generates the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), or to establish a specific proficiency restricted solely to the Veda. Regarding this, the *Tūlikā* states: "The mention of the 'limbs' (*aṅga*) is for the purpose of establishing the investigation of the purpose (*prayojana*), which is the motivator for inquiry."

By employing the term *saśiraska* (with its head) to indicate a distinction based on the excellence of the fruit, the author points out that in the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), the word *svādhyāya* refers to the two parts [of the Veda] in their fixed order; that the three sections (*trikāṇḍī*) intended for the investigation of that [Veda] constitute a single treatise (*ekaśāstrya*); and that the sequence [of the sections] is indicated. The sense is that there is no "head" not embraced by the injunction for study, such that it would not be subject to investigation. Here, the word *veda* expresses the fitness to convey human goals and their means; from this alone, the initial cognition (*āpātadhī*) that generates the desire for investigation is established.
By means of the two words ending in the genitive case, the subject matter (*adhikārin*) is extracted.

Regarding what was stated by some at the beginning of their commentary on the *Karmasūtra*: "Even though the meaning of the word 'atha' (*athaśabda*) and so forth is well-known, why is it described here? Some say it is for the sake of illustration; others, who maintain that words have multiple meanings, explain that Bhavadāsa, having extracted [the meaning] from the whole, describes the power of the individual part alone, as in the case of the eighth [note] and so forth. This is not very elegant here, because the explanation of the two words was introduced precisely to address the doubt concerning an exception to their well-known meanings.

The desire to know Brahman is *brahmajijñāsā*. In the term *brahmaṇaḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), because of the specific rule: "The sixth case is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows. Although the status of the object is established even if the genitive is taken in its general sense of relation—since the desire to know necessarily requires an object—nevertheless, since the explicitly stated meaning should be preferred over what is merely implied by necessity, the genitive is understood here as denoting the object.

Even regarding the third case, since the application of the suffix could occur in various ways, he analyzes the compound to specify its particular meaning: *brahmaṇo jijñāsā* (the desire to know Brahman). For here, first of all, the genitive (*vyāsa*) is not possible, because it would lack connection with the act of desiring (*jijñāsā*). For this very reason, it cannot be a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), even though it might be capable of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), due to the reversal of the qualifier and the qualified and because it would be useless for the intended meaning. Furthermore, the accusative case is precluded by its connection with a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*).

Although a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) would be possible because Brahman is the cause of all things, there would be no justification for the mention of "objects" (*viṣaya*) and so forth, nor could there be an implied qualification of the *vṛtti* (the commentary). Furthermore, a compound with a fourth-case ending in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is prohibited here; for Kātyāyana has stated: "In a compound denoting 'being for the sake of that,' one must specify the relationship between material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-grahaṇa*). And they say: "Since a word ending in the fourth case is compounded with its material cause (*prakṛti*)—as in the case of 'sacrificial post-wood' (*yūpa-dāru*) and the like—to express the sense of being for its sake, therefore there is no compounding here [in the case of Brahman]."

Likewise, it cannot be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), because Brahman lacks the status of being a recipient. Even in the case of a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), the sense would only establish that [Brahman] is the object (*viṣaya*). This is the intended meaning. Therefore, since the meaning is already grasped by the compound here, it is appropriate to explain it by bringing the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) into proximity. Thus it is said: "Thus, because the meaning is contained within the compound, it is fitting to explain it here by means of the proximity of the meaning of the case-ending."

The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) as "starting point" (*apādāna*) and so forth is disconnected from the sentence and requires the insertion of missing words (*adhyāhāra*). The impossibility of [Brahman] being the primary agent (*kartṛ*) is indicated by the very expression "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*), following such passages as "seek to know that" (*tadvijijñāsasva*). For the primary Brahman would not itself desire to be known, since it is by its own nature all-seeing. And it is said in the *Nyāyatattva*: "He who always knows everything simultaneously through direct perception by his own nature."

However, one who possesses only limited knowledge (*kiṃcijjña*) should not be called the "agent" (*kartṛ*), because [the status of agent] follows from the very beginning for one who has studied the Veda and desires to determine its meaning. By stating that [the object] is the "object" (*karman*), its status as the primary focus (*viṣayatva*) and its being the purpose (*prayojanatva*)—by virtue of being that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*)—are established. Therefore, the sense is that even though the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) and so forth exists, it need not be mentioned here. Nevertheless, let the genitive of possession (*śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī*) apply in a general sense; however, the specific [relationship] is not to be stated because it is obtained through propriety (*aucitya*). To this, he says: "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*).

Since the application of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is already established by the rule for specific relations, that which is stated in the rule concerning "lack of expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣa*) is more appropriate than that stated in the rule concerning "expectancy" (*sākāṅkṣa*). In that case, although the injunction is similar for both [types of] qualifiers, because the agent is common to both transitive and intransitive verbs, whereas here it is not possible for it to be the meaning of the agent, the intention is that it is proper to present the object (*karman*) which is most specifically required.

Now, one might ask: what is the use of a verbal operation (*śabdavyāpāra*) when the meaning is already obtained? Nor does this render the specific grammatical instruction (*pratipadānuśāsana*) useless; for its purpose lies in ensuring the correctness of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by prohibiting the accusative (*dvitīyā*) even when there is an intention to express the object (*karman*) and so forth.

Therefore, a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) does not set aside the possessive genitive (*śaiṣika-ṣaṣṭhī*). And when that [genitive] is accepted, since even those things connected by a mediated relation are included within it, the means (*upāya*) and so forth—which are related to Brahman—are also connected to the desire to know (*jijñāsā*); thus, the fact that they constitute its object is established by implication. Consequently, the further purpose is to indicate that the entire subject matter of the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras) is to be investigated. To this he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi*). "Inclusion" (*parigrahaḥ*) means grasping on all sides; that is, the inclusion of [Brahman] along with its adjuncts (*sānubandha*). However, in the subsequent text...

By the statement "it is grasped" (*gṛhyate*), the intention is merely that the connection with the attendant factor (*anubandhin*) is not directly expressed by the word (*aśābdatva*). This is because, due to its transitivity—its inherent nature of first generating an expectancy for an object (*karman*)—the establishment of its being for the sake of the object means that, by excluding the status of agent (*kartṛtva*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) effectively culminates in the specific sense of the object. With the intention that in usage intended for communicating to others, a cause for delayed cognition should not be accepted, he says: "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

For in this case, there is no postulation of a capacity for what is already obtained through implication; rather, it is said that what is expressed by a word whose capacity is already established is better than what is merely implied. But is it not improper to say "from implication," since—according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*—it will be stated later that the general capacity [of a word] extends as far as the particular? Do not say so; for that [general capacity] grasps only the particular [as such], not properties such as being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth; indeed, the capacity of the word "cow" does not grasp specific qualities such as being a spotted cow (*khaṇḍatva*).

Nor should it be mistakenly thought that there is a relinquishing of the *anubandhi* (the subordinate element) even when the denotative [meaning] is grasped here; for in all cases, inquiry has as its object that which resides in the intellect as a subordinate element (*anubandhin*). If it is argued that even so, an implication (*ākṣepa*) is admitted, this is true—yet it is better that the status of being the object of one [of two actions] be considered verbal (*śābda*) due to the implication of the status of being the object of both, let alone the implication of the status of being the object of the primary part. The particle *eva* (only/just) expresses the greater strength of that which is the cause of immediate cognition.

How can *brahman* be the object (*karman*) [of the verb] according to grammar? [One might argue: "The suffix *san* is applied when there is a desire for an action that has the same agent as the root's action" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkādicchāyām vā*), and thus only knowledge (*jñāna*) would be the object. This is not so; even when the suffix *san* is present, the distinction between transitive and intransitive status follows the base verb (*prakṛti*). For this very reason, the grammatical rule "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*) is taught with reference to the object of the base meaning. Furthermore, in expressions such as "Dharma is to be desired to be known" (*dharmaḥ jijñāsitavyaḥ*), Dharma and the like possess the status of an expressed object (*abhihitakarman*).

But even so, it is not denotative, because there is no meaning for the case-ending of the *upapada*; for if that [case-ending] were meaningful merely by virtue of its usage, it would follow that it is so in cases such as *gāvī* and the like. Nor is there any expressive power (*śakti*) in those cases. The expressive power of the word does not reside in *gāvī* and the like; rather, the word *go* is remembered from it. Then, by means of that [word *go*] present in the mind, the genus "cow" (*go-jāti*) is cognized. (202)

The usage of authoritative persons (*āpta-prayoga*), however, may occur even when there is no referent, because it is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*); for such usage is observed elsewhere as well, and it is so accepted. Furthermore, the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) is intended merely for the specific manifestation [of forms]. Since the cognitions of those respective meanings are established otherwise, and since a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) is not to be postulated for what can be obtained from another source, and because it is improper to postulate multiple capacities when other means exist, linguistic capacity is not the operative factor here.

That is not so—just as the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is meaningful and possesses multiple meanings by virtue of rules such as "kartṛkaraṇayoḥ... and so forth, likewise [it is so] by virtue of rules such as "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti... and so forth. Nevertheless, there is no impairment of its inherent power (*śakti*). Here, the proximity of another word merely manifests the power, but does not instill it; just as in the case of words like "go" which have multiple meanings. Or else:

In this context, although [the status of] being denotative (*ābhidhānikatva*) does not apply, the term "denotative" is used to indicate that [the objecthood] is equal to what is expressed by words (*śābda*), as it is established by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) whose specific function (*vṛtti*) is sanctioned by a particular grammatical rule (*viśeṣānuśāsana*). By the word "denotative," the fact that objecthood (*karmatva*) is established by the denotation of the sūtra is understood; furthermore, this is because the examination of the nature of the *upapada* is not delayed, since it consists of an examination of what is conveyed by the word itself.

One might object: "In this case, since there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the compound, how could it denote or indicate [the object]? Nor can it be said that even an unexpressed ending might denote it through recollection, for even the use of an ending is merely for the sake of bringing about the cognition of that meaning. This objection should not be raised. For there is no evidence for a rule that one must necessarily recall a case-ending when the meaning is understood from a compound; moreover, such a rule would result in the total abolition of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and other such functions everywhere. Furthermore, the distinction between the two [types of objects] lies in the fact that the genitive case denotes [one type]. Thus, in the absence of a denoting element, how could the status of being an object (*karmatva*) be either denotative or coextensive with that [denotation]?
Do not say so, provided that what is intended is either a general relation or the specific state of being an object.
Indeed, because of the elision of the case-ending, the indication must be accepted as being inherent in the base itself.

Now, if it is held that [the word] is denotative (*śābda*) because the characteristic [of denotation] is established through the identity of the expression (*abhidhāna-samatva*) with respect to the meaning of the injunction (*asuśāsana*), then this is equally true even when [the word] has the action as its meaning. However, some maintain this: whether in a compound (*samāsa*) or in an analytical form (*vyāsa*), the same expressive power (*śakti*) resides in words with and without case-endings, according to the maxim of the words *dadhi* and *dadhy*. Therefore, even by a base-form (*prakṛti*) whose case-ending is elided, the connection is not to be understood through indication (*lakṣya*); for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed a function directed toward another entity related to the expressed meaning, and a relation itself is not a related entity.

And [the meanings of] *karmatva* (objectness) and so forth are of the nature of a relation. Thus, although the result of the relation is established through this self-explanatory (*svaparanirvāhaka*) mechanism, it is observed that even for those lacking such discrimination, there arises an understanding of the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) based on the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, even if a relation exists, it does not serve as the cause for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for one who does not know it, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, since the usage cannot be explained otherwise and because any suspicion of such an alternative explanation is barred by the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), the meaning of the case-ending must be denoted (*abhidheya*) even in a compound (*samāsa*).

The same principle applies even to cases where there is an elision of case-endings. Now, it might be argued that in the word *niṣādasthapati*, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is rejected in order to avoid the fault of implying a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the meaning of the case-ending; how then can there be primary denotation (*ābhidhānikatva*)? If that were the primary sense, then in a conflict between what is already established and what must be inferred, only the established should be accepted, and thus no further assumption of entitlement (*adhikāra*) could apply elsewhere. This is not so. For it has been demonstrated that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) possesses greater strength than prior syntactical dissociation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because it results in a cognition that is free from delay.

According to this principle, verbal usage proceeds with rapidity. Now, if it is argued that the meaning [of the compound] follows the natural tendency (*svārasya*) of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), then there is no regard for the specific determination [of the case-ending], because it does not contradict the meaning. What was stated regarding the case-endings of subordinate words (*upapada-vibhakti*) should also be understood to apply to compounds (*samāsa*).
This [explanation] may be either a statement of rhetorical flourish (*vaibhavavāda*) or a declaration of ultimate truth (*paramārthokti*).
However, the claim that it is based on denotation (*ābhidhānika*) is more appropriate, as it serves to demonstrate the swiftness of the intellect. (204)

Nor should one suspect a prohibition of the compound with a genitive case ending in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) on the grounds that "a genitive used in the sense of the [specific] rule of application (*pratipadavidhāna*) is not compounded"; for there exists a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) stating that "a genitive connected with a *kṛt* suffix is indeed compounded."

Thus, the impropriety of using the genitive case in the sense of the object has been refuted. In that regard, he also dispels the suspicion regarding the prohibition of compounding—by the words "na ca" (and not). By the phrase "of the genitive in the sense of the object," it is indicated that the general rule for the *pratipadavidhāna* (specifically prescribed) genitive is subject to restriction. The exception to compounding applies only to that [genitive] which is taught by the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* ("the genitive of the root *jñā* when it does not mean 'to know,' provided it is used with the instrument"); however, even if the genitive of the instrument occurs in some instances with the root *jñā* (or *jānāti*) when it means "to perceive" (*avedanārtha*) and is joined with a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *ya*, it is not to be considered there, as seen in the example *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he perceives the ghee"). He states the restriction on the prohibition: "due to connection with a *kṛt*[-suffix]."

Thus, this counter-objection is a refutation of the exception, because that [exception] exists. The sense is that it is not merely by observation in usage. In this way, compound (samāsa), which is the cause for forming a single word, has first been explained.

And by the word *brahman*, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) is denoted, who by His very nature has all defects removed and possesses an infinite multitude of excellent, auspicious qualities beyond measure.

In this regard, because it is heard that the first constituent part (*prakṛtyaṃśa*) of the word [Brahman] has its basis in its etymological meaning, there may arise elsewhere a suspicion that its primary sense is determined by observed usage. Dispelling the claim that [the term] refers to such intended objects as the partless pure consciousness, the enjoyer, the enjoyed, the controller, the aggregate, the Lord who possesses those parts, or pure Being (*sanmātra*), and rejecting the figurative application (*upacāravṛtti*) in his own preferred sense, he explains the two qualities of being "vast" (*bṛhat*) and "expansive" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) as being unlimited in order to establish its absolute supremacy, stating: "And by the word *brahman*. The particle *ca* (and) serves to dispel the aforementioned doubt.

By the words "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) and so forth, the undesirable consequence that [Brahman] would be unfit for inquiry—due to being imagined by others as having defects, being devoid of qualities, being inexpressible, or being unknowable—is refuted. Furthermore, the state of being free from all defects is a specific form of greatness (*bṛhattva*) conducive to its nature as the "Expansive" (*Bṛṃhaṇa*). The fact that the injunctions and prohibitions regarding qualities and so forth fall within the scope of the principles of general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*) is indicated by the two qualifiers. For those learned in the science of logic know it to be better to restrict the application of a general rule than to assume that it has a different purpose by setting aside a specific injunction. (Verse 205)

The point is this: even if there is a dispute regarding the falsity or truth of the opponent's position, since the defects intended for refutation—whether by way of superimposition, limitation by adjuncts (*upādhi*), or as an inherent portion—would reside in the Supreme Brahman, it would follow that omniscience and other attributes would be destroyed precisely because of that [residence], and thus the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) would be untenable, resulting in contradiction with the Śruti and other authorities. In its own nature, the category of non-sentient objects (*acit-padārtha*) possesses states worthy of receiving different names: those possessing afflictions and so forth are "bound" (*baddha*); those lacking some afflictions and so forth are "seekers of liberation" (*mumukṣu*); and those in whom even that is absent are [liberated].

Those who possess the absolute cessation of that [suffering] are the liberated ones (*muktas*); even though they possess the absolute absence of that [suffering], because their state is dependent on another, they are the eternal ones (*nityas*). By means of such approaches as "having all defects eliminated through the gradual entry of the intellect," these are the things to be excluded (*vyavacchedyas*) regarding the first qualification. In that context, by the word "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*), if the intention is to express beginninglessness, the liberated ones are excluded; if the intention is to express non-dependence on another, [the eternal ones are excluded].

And the eternal [entities] are excluded. In the second case as well, all of them [are excluded], because of the injunction of qualities impossible in others; or rather, they are indeed eternal. For even though their knowledge and other attributes are equal to those of Brahman, their dependence on another is established, and their power is inferior to His. And the author will state this in the explanation of the word "infinite" (*ananta*) in the passage concerning Truth (*satya*) and so forth: "The eternal [entities] are excluded, having forms and qualities that are surpassed. Indeed, they do not pervade the universe, nor are they the embodied selves of all.

By the word *atiśaya* (excellence), it is indicated that the "increase" (*vṛddhi*) mentioned in the grammatical roots is "surpassing" (*atiśāyana*). By the qualification "without limit," there is a statement that this culminates in a state of absolute non-surpassability, as demonstrated by the sequence of multiplication increasing tenfold. The position that the Lord’s possession of qualities such as knowledge and bliss is occasional, whereas His power (*śakti*) is eternal, is refuted by the connection with the word "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). The word *gaṇa* (group) is used to indicate the various subordinate groups of qualities, which consist of the expansion of each individual quality such as knowledge.

And it is said in the *Ṣāḍguṇyaviveka*: "Though You possess infinite qualities, only six are primary; for by these alone, even all others have been placed within the womb of the universe, just as by You."
Thus [it is said].

Here, the compound *anavadhikātiśaya* (limitless excellence), while qualifying the "group" (*gaṇa*), effectively qualifies the "qualities" (*guṇa*) by virtue of the principle that "when each member of a group is understood through a word denoting excellence, the assembly of the wise is implied. Otherwise, the meaning of the whole compound would not be established. Furthermore, when a simpler solution is available, the use of a non-appositional *bahuvrīhi* is improper. In cases such as *śailajanmā* ("born from a mountain"), this [non-appositional usage] is accepted due to the force of traditional usage (*āgati*).

Having examined this in accordance with the agreement of the Sūtra and such scriptural passages as "He who is to be known," [the author] states "Puruṣottama" (the Supreme Person), intending to express: the extraction of the object of inquiry denoted by the term *brahmapuruṣa*; the fact that all Upaniṣads have the same purport as the *Puruṣasūkta*; the impossibility of the Lord being a superimposed part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman; and the specific distinction of such a one from other deities such as Prakṛti, as explained in the *Gītā*. Here, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood.

Although in this case there is a reversal of the sequence [of words] in a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is no compounding with the genitive in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Nevertheless, starting from "These two persons... up to "...but the Supreme Person is another," because the inferior is mentioned as its counter-correlative, the compounding occurs by virtue of being relative terms. Alternatively, by the phrase "higher even than the Imperishable," a compound with the ablative (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is indicated. The division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), however, is intended according to usage. For this very reason, the locative is also compounded even in the sense of selection.

And words such as "supreme" (*uttama*) and so forth have been thus established by those versed in grammar. However, one who says, "Let Puruṣottama be [the name] by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)," is contradicted by scripture (*śruti*) and other authorities; for it is stated by the Omniscient One: "Therefore, in this world and in the Veda, I am celebrated as Puruṣottama. It is now explained: [He] is made the primary object of reference through the primary mode of signification (*mukhyavṛtti*). By this, those who maintain that the word *brahman*—which has that [Puruṣottama] as its sole name—is used there only in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) are refuted, as are those who claim that figurative usage occurs even within the scope of conventional meaning.

The word *brahman* is applied everywhere by virtue of its connection with the quality of greatness (*bṛhattva*). And that which possesses greatness—both in its essential nature and in its qualities—to an unlimited and unsurpassed degree is its primary meaning; and that is the Lord of All alone. Therefore, the word *brahman* functions in its primary sense only there. Consequently, when it is applied elsewhere, it is figurative due to a connection with a mere fraction of those qualities, because it is illogical to assume multiple meanings, as is the case with words such as *bhāva*.

One might object: "Could there not be a primary application [of the term 'Brahman'] elsewhere as well—either by way of a genus (*jāti*), like the word 'cow' and others; or by way of an action (*kriyā*), like the word 'cook' and others; or through arbitrary convention (*yadṛcchā*), like the name 'Dittha'? To this he replies: "In all cases. This means: in instances where the word "Brahman" is applied, such as to the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) and so forth. Among those disparate objects, neither a genus nor an action that excludes everything else is observed. Furthermore, the quality of being "expansive" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*) is dependent upon "greatness" (*bṛhattva*); therefore, if that were the basis [for the application of the word], it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, "greatness" (*bṛhattva*) is in each instance both the contextually relevant and the intended meaning. Nor should we overlook the well-known etymological sense of the verbal root *vṛdh*—as "unconditioned growth"—which serves as the basis for the application of the word *brahman*. Therefore, the point is that when other possible derivations exist, the term is not used merely by chance. The particle *hi* indicates either well-known usage or a reason. If it were argued that this [word *brahman*], like the word *bṛhat*, would be based solely on the quality of greatness, he says "no": "greatness" (*bṛhattvam*). This greatness is said to be "on all sides" (*sarvataḥ*) because it is unrestricted, pertaining both to its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and to its qualities (*guṇataḥ*).

By that [term *bṛhat*], there is the exclusion of those things whose nature is delimited and which lack the greatness of attributes, as well as the exclusion of attributes themselves. By the word "of this" (*asya*), the distinction from the word *bṛhat* is shown; for that [word] does not tolerate a specification of a limit such as "this is Brahman from here," nor the use of comparative suffixes like *-tara* or *-tama*. In passages such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," "All that has been declared is this threefold Brahman," and "When one finds this triad, that is Brahman," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other things because they constitute its body—just as in the expression "I am a god"—but it is not a case of applying the word "Brahman" to those various individual objects.

The statement regarding the threefold nature is made with reference to the distinction of being the impeller (*preritṛ*) and the distinction between the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*). In the passage "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," the qualification "Supreme" (*param*) is intended to exclude a figurative sense; therefore, the intention is that His greatness (*bṛhattva*) alone is not the [etymological] cause [of the name]. To the objection that, due to the rule of usage, there might be a greatness reaching its ultimate limit in various instances, he says: "And He..."—meaning, He is the substratum of unlimited greatness.

"Sarveśvara" (the Lord of All) is a designation indicating the state of being free from all limitations such as superiority or poverty, because His name is recited as "Ajassarveśvara" (the Unborn Lord of All). The scriptures declare that unsurpassed greatness—consisting of the governance of all and so forth—belongs to Him alone. The intention of the restrictive particle (*eva*) is to establish that others possess this nature only through dependence on Him, and even that [dependence] does not exist for them. He states the consequence—that in the absence of a cause, the effect cannot exist—because no other cause is possible elsewhere: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).

Therefore, since the absence of denotative power [in the primary sense] exists in each case, and since both the connection (*sambandha*) and the possession of qualities (*guṇayoga*) are possible everywhere, he states that there is a restricted usage in certain instances such as the *prakṛti* (the source), etc., with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the intended meaning: here, the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) does not arise from mere connection, nor is there a metaphorical function (*gauṇī vṛttiḥ*) based on some similarity; rather, it is the quality of that [source], namely unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśayabṛhattva*), or even a trace of it, which constitutes a transcendent greatness. Because the restriction of figurative application is based on that, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And they employ the word *brahman* as a name (*nāmatayā*) according to their wish, with the intention of praise or blame, toward that which is proximate to the primary referent and toward that which possesses an excellence of its qualities. Now, it might be argued: "When the primary meaning is available, there can be no figurative usage (*upacāra*); and since the word *brahman* does not have multiple powers (*śakti*), one should not postulate another power even for a single instance, much less for many. To this we reply: even for such a word, a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) must be postulated to account for the restriction of its employment. Just as in the case of words like *paṅkaja* (mud-born), there is a single restrictive factor—namely, the quality of being a lotus—and so on.

It has not been seen. Therefore, to the objection that "the capacity [of a word] must be differentiated according to its usage," he replies with the words "aneka" (multiple). For when examining the usage of a word whose capacity is already established, one first follows the primary sense.
