However, in the investigation of capacity, if a subsequent usage is otherwise accounted for by a single capacity, no further capacity should be postulated due to the fault of complexity (*gaurava*). Otherwise, even metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) would be lost; yet such usage does exist, as established in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa*. The intention is that in some cases, however, the postulation of multiple capacities occurs out of necessity. But the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭukas*), disregarding the extraction of meanings from words, [proceed as they do].
The state of having multiple names is studied for the purpose of training in the proficiency of application.

The intention here is that the answer has already been given to the objection: "Since this 'transcendent greatness' (*lokottara-bṛhattva*) is stated to be the defining factor (*niyāmaka*) in this case, by that very same reason other [entities] should also possess primacy; otherwise, why would the reverse not occur? In accordance with the maxim: "Knowing that one should give an answer to those who are in disagreement even regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he spoke the opinion of the elders," he cites the statements of the *Purāṇas*—beginning with "In that pure [state] called Great Sovereignty" (*śuddhe mahāvibhūtyākhye*)—and so forth, as opposed to other [texts].

By the passage ending with "only by way of metaphor," it is stated that the primary application of the word *bhagavat* belongs only to that which possesses the fullness of its etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*). Furthermore, in another Purāṇa it is said: "This word *bhagavat*, as well as the word *puruṣa*, apply without qualification (*nirupādhī*) to the eternal Vāsudeva."

The position of the Dārṣṭāntikas is also established in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "O great sage, the word *brahman* is used in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtta*) for that alone [the sun], because of its frequent application in the Veda and because of its connection with [auspicious] qualities," beginning thus, and concluding: "In that [sun] alone, when it is employed, the connection of qualities is most abundant; therefore, this [term] is used in its primary sense there, whereas elsewhere it is used figuratively (*upacārataḥ*)."

That very [Brahman] is to be inquired into for the sake of immortality by those afflicted by the threefold suffering; therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is Brahman, the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). *Jijñāsā* is the desire to know (*jñātum icchā*). Since desire has that which is desired as its primary element, it is knowledge (*jñāna*)—the object of desire—that is enjoined here.

"Let it be that His power resides in one [deity] alone; yet, since there is no differentiator in this Sūtra, why should it not be secondary? To this, he replies with the word "tāpa" (suffering), following the logic of such authoritative texts as: "There is no remedy other than the elixir of Nārāyaṇa; he who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worships another deity is a fool who, while thirsty on the banks of the Gaṅgā, digs a well. For here there is no sublation of the primary sense, because the Blessed Lord is the independent Master.

This meaning is established for another [subject] who is not independent, because through these supporting passages such as "When he sees the other, the Lord, as the beloved," it is stated that the worship of the Supreme alone is what removes the threefold suffering. The sense is that He alone is what "should be reflected upon" and "should be sought"—that is, He is what is heard in scripture as the object of inquiry. Although the word *brahman* has multiple meanings, he states that in this particular usage, this is the only intended meaning; thus, the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) is intended to provide specific reinforcement even regarding the subsequent ascent (*anvāroha*).

For even in the views that [the word "immortal"] has multiple conventional meanings based on causes such as genus (*jāti*) or quality (*guṇa*), a specific meaning would be established by the other words uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Alternatively, there is a restatement of multiple meanings through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) regarding both the primary and secondary senses. Since the two statements—"knowing him thus, one becomes immortal" (*amṛta*) and "having known him thus"—are indicated respectively by the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) and the particle "only" (*eva*), the non-contradiction of the two is pervasively established.

[Objection: Is it not impossible to determine that "He alone" [is the object] here, since we see that He is to be sought even in the inner self (pratyagātman) in such passages as "That [Self] is to be sought," and because He too will be defined in such passages as "The Self, on account of Scripture"? [Reply: This [objection] he refutes by way of a conclusion with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is: "by the power of the words and by the inherent nature of the subject matter at hand. Both of these are intended by the two terms beginning with "the Lord of all" (sarveśvara). The meaning is: that which is the object of the desire to know (jijñāsā), and which is most desired to be attained through that desire to know.

For here, the Supreme is primarily the object of inquiry; however, for the sake of ascending to devotion toward Him, one's own self must also be contemplated as a qualifying attribute within the practice of *ahaṃgraha* (identifying with the Self). Furthermore, it will be stated later that in passages such as those concerning Prajāpati, the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is taught solely for the purpose of the primary higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) under discussion.

In this context, does the suffix *san* have the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) or not? It cannot be the first [alternative], because the root is not listed in rules such as *gup-ti-j-kid-bhyaḥ san*. Nor can it be the second, because if investigation (*vicāra*) is intended, there would be a contradiction in denoting a desire for that [investigation], and it would contradict the definition of a *sūtra*.

And because [the term *jijñāsā*] cannot be used in a figurative sense (*upacāra*), he analyzes the word "to know" (*jñātuṃ*) in order to support the latter [interpretation] while not accepting the former. Now, one might object: since the word *jijñāsā* has the meaning of the suffix as its primary sense, knowledge (*jñāna*) is submerged within it and thus cannot be the object of injunction; furthermore, desire (*icchā*) is not dependent on the person [as it would be for an action], nor is it produced by its own cognition, because it depends upon the suitability of the object—such that it would be impossible in the absence of that [suitability]—and because it is not perceived [as such]. To this, he replies: "Of desire... (*icchāyāḥ*).

Since it serves the purpose of accomplishing its own object, the action in the form of desire possesses primacy with respect to its own object, just as the acts of sprinkling and so forth do; this is established by the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.7]. Furthermore, in that rule, the primacy of the verbal root's meaning must be understood in a functional sense (*ārtha*). That which is not already established is what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Therefore, the intention here is that it is not appropriate to intend a relationship with the desire by means of a word expressing that desire.

In that case, one might ask: "Should not mere knowledge (*jñāna*) alone be stated? What is the use of the term 'realization' (*pratyaya*), which is like the teat on the neck of a goat? To this, the reply is given according to the maxim that each subsequent term indicates an increasingly superior meaning: "that which is desired" (*iṣyamāṇam*). The intention is that the term "being" (*san*) is purposeful, because it indicates that the knowledge in the form of inquiry—which is prompted by natural inclination due to its being a subject matter that is both doubtful and purposeful—is not scripturally enjoined (*vaidha*) like meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like. Furthermore, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) here, by virtue of propriety, refers to the specific type of knowledge already described.

However, it is not reasonable to assume that [the author] intended to imply the investigation by way of knowledge regarding the nature of passion, its objects, and their results; for that would cause a delay in understanding, and what is intended can be stated directly.

This is at the commencement of the latter portion of the treatise known as Mīmāṃsā. The sense is that this is exactly the same in cases such as "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (athāto dharmajijñāsā) and so forth. Objection: But how can there be a statement of an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding an inquiry that is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), nor can there be a statement of an injunction here with reference to restrictive rules (*niyama*) such as approaching a teacher and the like; for [such rules] are already implied by logic (*nyāya*), and because no prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) could arise if such restrictive rules were prohibited. Reply: Not so. For the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) here is intended to negate the misconception that even what is prompted by natural inclination need not be commenced.
Indeed, even if a desire for inquiry has arisen, it may be set aside by the arguments presented in the prima facie position.
Those who are sinking are supported by means of reasoning, preceded by proficiency in the established [truth]. || 207 ||

Because the ritual action known from the first part of the Mīmāṃsā yields fruit that is meager and unstable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman—which is to be understood from the subsequent part—yields infinite and inexhaustible fruit, it is stated that after the knowledge of ritual action which has preceded it, for that very reason, Brahman must be known. Thus says the author of the Vṛtti: "After the mastery of ritual action as it has been practiced, there arises the desire to know Brahman."

And he will state the unity of the two systems of inquiry—into ritual action and into Brahman—in the passage: "This Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā] is joined with the Jaiminīya consisting of sixteen chapters; thus is the establishment of the unity of the scripture."

In this work, *Tātparyadīpikā*, it appears as if the author intends to set forth the historical account mentioned by Yādavaprakāśa and the establishment of the non-commencement of the inquiry into Sāṅkhya and other systems; setting that aside, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Mīmāṃsā. In the root *māṅ* (to measure), either the form *mān* is derived through a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), or, from the root *māna* (in the sense of honoring), this word is formed with the suffix *san* (denoting desire) following the rule *mānbadha*, etc., without the addition of the desiderative marker *i*. As for the statement of the grammarians that *māniḥ* is used in the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*), it is because the meanings are not far removed from one another.

For the extraction of the primary denotation (*śakti*) of this term [mīmāṃsā] is established through the usage of the elders in reference to a venerable inquiry (*vicāra*)—arising from a specific desire to know (*jijñāsā*)—or to the excellent method (*nyāya*) associated with it. And they have said: "All reasoning designated as *mīmāṃsā* originates from the Veda," and so forth. However, when applied to the treatise (*śāstra*) which consists of a compendium of such methods, the word *mīmāṃsā* is used in a secondary or metaphorical sense (*bhākta*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction in describing it as "known" and "to be understood" by means of its division into prior and subsequent parts. Here, the construction of the sentence begins with "pūrvavṛttāt" (from what has preceded), while the remainder serves to support the logical reasons (*hetu*) found therein.

The instruction on the sequence of investigation is based on the Sūtra; however, in this [treatise], the unity of the Śāstra and its sequence are stated here as intended by the author of the Sūtras. (208)

By the two terms "prior portion" (*pūrvabhāga*) and "subsequent portion" (*uparitanabhāga*), the unity of the treatise—which consists of explanations arranged in a fixed sequence—is indicated. The cause for this is the sequential nature of the Veda, which is to be explained; this is shown in the word-connection (*padayojanā*) by the term "together with the introduction" (*saśiraska*). There is no tautology, because there is a difference in purport between the presentation of words and sentences. "Of that which is known" means of that which has been ascertained. "Of that which is to be understood" means of that which is to be determined as being present in an uncontradicted initial cognition. "Of the knowledge of Brahman" means of the meditation upon Brahman.

Because here, when there is the intention to express the nature of Brahman alone, the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is redundant; because it is more appropriate to grasp a specific result by placing it on the same level as "the action that has been known"; because it is improper to speak of knowledge—whether in the form of inquiry or in the form of ascertainment—as something to be attained; and because [such knowledge] is not enjoined with respect to the stated fruit.

Thus, here, according to the principle of coordination (*samanvaya*), although Brahman is to be known primarily as the infinite and imperishable fruit itself, it is also to be known as the object of its own worship because that worship is the means to attain that infinite and imperishable fruit; therefore, its mention as a subordinate element is also entirely appropriate. However, by the statement "Brahman is to be known," its primary status is revealed. In this context, the reason for its being a subject of inquiry is its presence in the mind through an initial cognition characterized by purposefulness.

However, for that [inquiry] which occurs after the inquiry into karma, there is dependence on it once obstacles have been stilled; and as for "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), it is the absence of any other such requirement. Therefore, with reference specifically to the particular inquiry that extends until the fulfillment of the dispassion (*nirveda*) mentioned in the scripture, [the sūtra says] "from that very [karma]."

Thus it has been said. Here, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended to exclude the possibility of a deficiency in the cause (*hetu*), for it is improper to negate a cause that is already established as restrictive. Some, however, say: "Since the investigation into Brahman might otherwise follow from other causes—leading to the undesirable consequences of its being non-essential or of Śūdras being entitled to it—this teaching is intended to show disregard for any cause other than the knowledge of ritual action (*karmadhī*). In this regard, there would be much impropriety, as neither the primary thesis nor its reason, nor the reason for a further thesis, would have been stated.

By the very exclusion of the impossibility of the specific probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) being preceded by the intended cause, the rejection of other causes and so forth follows as a matter of course; this is indeed logical. "To be known" (*jñātavya*) means "to be investigated" (*vicārya*). It will be stated that "investigation must be performed. Here, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of fitness (*arha*). In the phrase "from the knowledge of action" (*karmajñānāt*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*) likewise refers to investigation (*vicāra*).

By stating "it is said that Brahman is to be known," those who claim the meaning of the sentence is "Brahman alone is to be known"—thereby suggesting its inherent propriety and providing a logical justification—are refuted. For this Sūtra is intended to remove the objection regarding the lack of necessity for inquiry. Since the fact that Brahman is to be known has not been established prior to this point, the restriction that "that [alone] is to be known" does not arise. Furthermore, how can one speak of the necessity of inquiring into a specific established entity without first proving the possibility of words having established entities as their referents?

The proof for that [non-difference] follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*; moreover, a construction involving mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa-yojanā*) is not tenable. Here, it is also incorrect to claim—as one might in the case of the *Codanā-sūtra*—that there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and an exclusion of connection with something else (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*) both in terms of word and meaning, and that there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because a mere thesis (*pratijñā-mātra*) that is not supported by reasoning is untenable. Furthermore, the claim that "increasing faith in Brahman" and "the negation of others" are useful for the subject at hand is weak; even if those were accepted as theses, a reason (*hetu*) must still be inferred here.

However, if one were to attempt its refutation, it would be redundant, as its establishment has already been achieved by the section beginning with *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* up to the end of the *Tarka-pāda*. Furthermore, how can a denial of it be asserted here by those who state that the portions not mentioned in the *Śārīraka* are to be understood through Sāṅkhya and Yoga? As for the point that portions contrary to the Veda are not to be respected, this was already established prior to the *Virodha-adhikaraṇa*; yet, while strengthening his own stated positions regarding word-meanings and sentence-meanings even through the commentary (*vṛtti*), he demonstrates here the agreement between his work and their own composition by following their system, saying: "Thus he says."

The author’s intention is also that the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) serves as a cause [for the inquiry into Brahman], by virtue of its being established as preceding [the inquiry into Brahman] in an invariable manner (*ananyathāsiddha*). Here, "attainment" (*adhigama*)—defined as that by which something is attained—is synonymous with "inquiry" (*vicāra*). The mention of "desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) is to be understood in the same way as the mention of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*).

To establish the meaning of the Sūtra he himself has stated, he also corroborates the unity of the scripture (*śāstra-ekya*) which was indicated [earlier], saying: "he will state. This is a future reference (*bhaviṣyan-nirdeśa*) regarding another section of the work that is yet to be explained. The expression "being joined together" (*saṃhitatva*) is used with the intention that the unity of the scripture here does not merely consist in belonging to a single branch of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*), but rather in forming a single continuous composition (*eka-prabandhya*).

The meaning is that once the unity of the investigation into the nature of the entire Veda’s meaning has been established, the two sections—the *Karma-kāṇḍa* and the *Brahma-kāṇḍa*—are joined together according to the maxim of "the lost horse and the burnt chariot," because each is incomplete in itself and thus possesses a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Furthermore, this commentary indicates the causes for the delusion regarding the division of the scripture and the means to dispel them: by using the term *Śārīraka*, which shows that the subject matter concerns all embodied beings (*sarva-śarīrin*), it makes known the difference in scope; and by the very pointing out, with the finger as it were, of the difference between the purpose and the qualified person (*adhikārin*) through the word "this" (*etat*), as well as the manifestation of the non-contradiction of their meanings. [This is indicated] by the phrase "by the follower of Jaimini."

This indicates the apprehension of a division [of the work]. The resolution, however, is given by the phrase "by that which has sixteen characteristics," meaning by the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) consisting of twelve chapters (*adhyāya*). Here, that [work] emerged in three ways from the author of the Sūtras, according to the sequence: from the sage Jaimini, from Kāśakṛtsna, and from Bādarāyaṇa—concerning the spheres of ritual action (*karman*), the deities (*devatā*), and Brahman (*brahman*), respectively. Thus [ends] the *Tattvaratnākara*.

Furthermore, because of the statement [of Jaimini] and because of his conduct, any apparent contradiction should be understood as being resolved through figurative usage (*upacāra*). By employing a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) with the phrase "by means of the sixteen characteristics," it is shown that differences in intermediate subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth do not contradict the unity of the treatise. By the very expression "by Jaimini," it is indicated that the suspicion of a contradiction in meaning arises from a lack of understanding regarding the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the Sūtras; for Jaimini will indeed show agreement (*saṃvāda*) with the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras) on many points concerning its subject matter.

In passages such as "Jaimini [holds this] for the sake of pacifying delusion" (*vyāmohaśāntyai*), there is the mention of a disagreement in certain places and its subsequent refutation. In cases such as "Jaimini [regards] the highest stage" (*parāśaṃ jaiminiḥ*), the absence of lifelong stages of life (*naiṣṭhika-āśrama*)—though not explicitly sūtrized by Jaimini—was certainly mentioned at some point and then rejected as a restatement, for the purpose of preventing those with desires from turning away from the duties of the householder. Otherwise, it would be inconsistent to speak of agreement with Jaimini regarding the prohibition of falling from the lifelong stage and so forth, as in the passage: "But for one who has become that [ascetic], there is no returning to the other state, even according to Jaimini. (*tadbhūtasya tu nātadbhāvo jaiminer api*).

Jaimini [asserts] a lack of qualification [for certain rites] due to the impossibility [of their performance] in the Madhu-vidyā and others; Jaimini [also asserts] the existence [of a single authorship] because there is no statement contradicting the unity of the scripture even in cases such as the *vikalpa* (optionality), since a slight difference in expression does not contradict that [unity], just as there is a difference in the explanations given by the same author himself. By the mention of "being composed as a whole" (*saṃhitatva*), it is established that differences or non-differences in the authors do not necessarily entail differences or non-differences in the treatise, according to what is observed. For when there is a connection of meaning, it is logical for a joining to occur through the intention of either one [author] or the intention of both.
This is because there is no contradiction with the primary subject matter due to the firmness of the dialogue with Brahmā.
However, a contradiction with what is non-primary is set aside by virtue of the intended meaning (tātparya). || 209 ||

Or rather, just as in the case of filling a remainder after removing the obstructed parts of a palace imagined by another, here too the possibility of speaking of "junction" (saṃhitatva) arises. || 210 ||

Therefore, the distinction between the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* and the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā* is established by the difference in the objects they seek to expound, just as there is a distinction between the six sections (*ṣaṭka*) and the distinction between the chapters (*adhyāya*). The Mīmāṃsā-śāstra begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and concludes with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), following a specific sequence determined by particular logical connections.

To the unreflective inquiry, "Whence then is the manifestation of that difference, and even if there were such a difference, how could there be unity in the continuum? [the author] clarifies what is intended by the second section with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). This means: "from the authoritative tradition supported by reasoning. By the statement that [this] is what he intends to establish, it is indicated that the sections concerning the ritual portion (*karmakāṇḍa*) and the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) lack any intent toward refuting the corporeal form (*vigraha*) and so forth; for they are devoted solely to establishing the excellence of ritual action and the like, even for those who lack a definitive ascertainment of the true nature of the deity.

For it has been stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "Just as for the venerable Jaimini, the presentation of the fruit of ritual action was intended to increase one's faith in that action. And this has been explained in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "In the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, hyperbolic statements (*ativādāḥ*) were made so that those who have not heard the Vedānta might not lose faith in ritual action. Here, "hyperbolic statements" refers to declarations made with another purpose in mind. The intention is that even by that much, the suspicion regarding the lack of authority of the Śruti—based on reasons such as its connection with impermanent things as asserted by outsiders—is dispelled; and from that very fact, one's own desired goal is established.

Moreover, in this same manner, within the first pāda of the ninth [chapter], regarding the two topics under discussion—namely, the fruit (*phala*) and the deity (*devatā*)—under the heading "Nor [is there a distinction] because of the injunction, for their qualities [are derived from that]" (*na codanāto hi tādguṇyam*), we shall explain those sūtras concerning the deity which begin with "Or the deity would be the motivator" (*devatā vā prayojayet*). [The view is: the substance to be given with reference to a deity would not be motivated by the deity. Why? Because it is logical that the action itself, which serves as the means to the fruit, is the motivator, just as in the case of agriculture and similar activities.

To this, he says: "Or rather, the deity should impel [the sacrificer], because the eating is for its sake," as in the case of a guest. The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the doubt. The deity, who is the intended recipient of the oblation (*havis*), should impel the seeker of fruit toward the propitiation of itself. Why? Because the eating is for its sake; that is, because the eating of the oblation and the offering of it are for its sake, being subordinate to it. For the deity, being the recipient (*sampradāna*), acts as the primary factor and impels the substance and its offering toward its own purpose.
Even though the deity is subordinated in sentences where the action is the primary focus, [it remains the principal].
By the power of their respective mantras and so forth, they possess a predominance of meaning. || 211 ||

Nor should it be argued that the deity is not an agent because of the absence of the fivefold attributes such as a physical body (*vigraha*); for its existence [as such] is established by uncontradicted evidence consisting of traditional texts (*smṛti*), figurative usage (*upacāra*), and the observation of other scriptural passages (*anyārthadarśana*). Therefore, just as a guest possessing a body and other attributes is to be worshipped and employs the service rendered toward his own purpose according to his desire, so too does the deity. Furthermore, regarding the term *ārthapatya*: "artha" means prosperity (*vibhūti*) which is attained (*aryate*) or sought after (*arthyate*). Consequently, one should not suspect that [the deity] is unworthy of worship due to the absence of such [prosperity], or that it is ineffective because it does not bestow what is desired.

Indeed, the Supreme Deity rules over everything, while another [deity] appointed by Her exercises various powers according to their respective jurisdictions. Nevertheless, that independent Deity would not be pleased by anything, nor does She please anyone; therefore, how can She be the motivator? To this he says: "And therefore, there is a connection with That."

Therefore, even though [the deity] is indifferent, the connection between the one performing the service and the attainment of their desired fruit is established through the metaphorical application of memory (*smṛti*) and so forth—on the grounds that the deity, who is endowed with compassion and generosity according to the policy of a king of men, becomes pleased while being served; such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word 'śarad', the sacrificial act (*yajña-karma*) should be the primary element. Here, the phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates a partial acceptance while setting aside the previous position.

Although the fivefold attributes of a deity, such as its physical form and so forth, are difficult to deny; although the recipient (saṃpradāna) is primary in relation to the substance and other factors; and although sacrifice (yajña), being synonymous with the propitiation of a deity, has that deity as its purpose; and although in established scriptural statements we learn the nature and other details of both the higher and lower deities for their own sake—even so, in the injunctions regarding what is to be done, ritual action in the form of sacrifice and the like is primary because it is enjoined as the means to achieve results such as heaven. Thus, by appearing as something to be accomplished, it motivates the person toward activity; and the deity and all else are entirely subordinate to the action.

Now, is it not the case that we hear from scripture that the deity who bestows the fruit is primary by virtue of being the object of worship? To this, he replies: "The scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate. For we hear of the deity as having become subordinate with respect to the offering of the oblation (*havis*); the deity-pleasure, which is presented through mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and which constitutes the *apūrva*, is adopted as the medium for the fruit arising at a later time for the enjoined action, which is itself momentary. Therefore, although the deity possesses actual primacy, it is subordinate to the action—just like the verbal primacy that motivates one desiring the fruit.

"It is not the primary motivator. If that is so, how then does the guest function as the motivator? He explains it thus: "In the case of a guest, there would be a predominance of him [and] an absence of [independent] action. For it follows that the guest is the predominant factor with respect to hospitality; otherwise, since there would be no motivator for the action intended for his sake, that [hospitality] would be absent. If it is argued that the injunction for the ritual service of him is itself the motivator, he replies to that: 'Because it is a counter-measure.
For the injunction for the rite of hospitality is indeed given solely as a counter-measure to the arrival of the guest."

But when a deity is summoned by a person engaged in ritual action, the deity remains present for the sake of that person's desired object; it does not follow from this that [the deity] is itself employed [as an instrument] by that person.
But when a guest arrives of his own accord, one should carry out his desired purpose; by complying with what he desires, one is prompted to perform that service for him. (213)

Therefore, the statement regarding the preeminence of the guest (*atithi*) is based on a distinction between what has been attained and what has not yet been attained. Just as there is never any harm in performing the ritual service for a guest even if that guest possesses a physical body and so forth—in fact, it rather results in the attainment of the guest's true nature—likewise, we see no success in refuting the deity’s possession of such attributes either. If it is asked, "What is the fruit even in establishing [the deity] as secondary (*guṇībhāva*)?", it is the increase of faith in ritual action even among those who have not yet determined the actual preeminence [of the deity].
Thus, in these Sūtras, regarding the prior and subsequent positions:
This indicates that [the teachings] concerning possession by deities and so forth are not to be rejected. || 214 ||

Regarding the unity of the body and other such points asserted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, their refutation does not appeal to those who recognize the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognition. (215)

Through the application of memory, through observations of other meanings, and because it was spoken by himself, that which he uttered cannot be denied by those other than nihilists merely on the basis of words alone. (216)

If one denies the meanings of what has been heard through non-perception and fallacious reasoning, then by falling into the views of the Cārvākas and others, the possibility of denying everything arises. (217)
The claim that the grammatical compounds and so forth heard [in scripture] are merely figurative is born of delusion;
for you, however, there is the burden of postulating the non-existence of the powers of what has been heard and so forth. (218)
When considering what could serve as the gateway for the fruit of that which is momentary, it is better here to accept the scriptural formulation of the gateway rather than a fabricated one. (219)

The fact that the deities have action as their purpose and that ritual acts have them as their purpose is established through different aspects; therefore, they do not deserve to contradict one another. (220)
By establishing the meditations on the sun and other objects upon the sacrificial fire, Bādarāyaṇa indicated that the preeminence of the deities is established by the very nature of the matter.
Furthermore, the perception of the form of a deity that has not been accomplished is not appropriate elsewhere;
nor should a procedure based on such perception be postulated for every case where there is no contradiction. (222)

Furthermore, the practice of austerity by the deities is not contradictory, because it is logically consistent with their engagement in such acts for the purpose of pleasing their own superior Lord. (223)
And for the Ruler, who desires to establish dharma by means of the *ghuṇī* [wheel] and follows the dictates of his own karma, there shall be the engagement in various specific dharmas. (224)

The qualities and activities of those [beings] who are animals, immobile, or lifeless, as well as their remedies, are considered by the deities through continuous mental application; this too has been heard in the scriptures.
According to the specific type of oblation offered, there is the bestowal of various fruits; likewise, by the principle of the king and others, there occurs provocation through prohibited acts. (226)

If the nature [of the deity] in relation to the oblation and so forth is according to scripture, then it is appropriate that the respective nature of the one to be propitiated be accepted as such. (227)
Even though the meaning of a mantra is established through explanatory passages (arthavāda), where no contradiction is observed,
the Smṛti rooted therein is also not subject to sublation, just like its own source.

And in various modes and in its specific distinctions, there is the conceptualization of different deities through the application of their respective names, for the purpose of establishing that they are the objects of those [offerings]. (229)
Those nihilists who, failing to recognize their own dullness, have spoken of dullness among the believers here, are to be pitied by those of subtle vision. (230)
Even when the substance and the deity are common [to two mantras], the substance is more powerful;
this is because, whether [the object] is perceptible or imperceptible, it follows the authority of the established means of knowledge.
The sacrificial nature of a substance established through perception is the domain of scripture;
likewise, the distinction lies in the essential form of the deity and its status as a religious duty (dharma). || 232 ||
Because it depends upon perception and other means of knowledge, cognition derived from scripture is delayed;
for that reason, there is a relative weakness even among the indicators such as direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The disparity between the material object and the deity does not arise from their being real or unreal;
for if the deity were false, how could it possess attributes such as differentiation? (234)
Whether its nature consists of words connected with meaning, or whether it consists of mere sound, or even as it is grasped exactly as heard—verily, the deity is truly real. (235)
Success through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth is accepted as being taught;
why then is that which is innate at birth not also accepted among the gods? (236)

It is not appropriate to assume [the existence of a substance] here, as in the case of the injunction for Devadatta to see another place, because the injunction regarding the nature of the word is more consistent. (237)

And according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* and other such [Vedic] injunctions, by following the requirements of the ritual rules, the deities are established as bestowers of fruits because they themselves constitute the fruit. (238)
Thus, by this ancient method, the view that there is no divine being has been refuted;
the remainder will be addressed in the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "tadupari" (above that). || 239 ||

The author of the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya* has also stated: "Starting from the words 'the form of the Creator of the universe is indeed manifest,' [he says] 'for the form of a formless deity is not taught, since the scripture speaks of things as they truly are. Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not previously stated that explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi*), whereas in the *Samanvaya* section it was stated otherwise? How, then, is there no contradiction? It is thus: because the two proceed by way of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda*). And this is observed in other scriptures and in other sections of the work.

In this manner, contradictions imagined through false views (*kudṛṣṭi*) elsewhere must also be pacified. The phrase "like the division of the *ṣaṭka*" serves as a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) regarding the *Karmakāṇḍa*, while "like the division of the chapters" applies to all three *kāṇḍas*. The word "and" (*ca*) here is intended to include other unstated divisions, such as those between the *pādas*. Furthermore, the separate treatment of the *Śārīraka* from the *Devatākāṇḍa* is established by way of a counter-argument based on that same principle of separation. Now, he clarifies—on the basis of what is already established in the commentary—the removal of the notions that [the *Brahmasūtra*] lacks a sequential order of topics (*vinnakrama*) or that it constitutes a distinct work (*bhinnaprabandha*), by stating: "The treatise of Mīmāṃsā."

The meaning is: "by a specific connection," that is, by a relationship such as that of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). And this [connection] is explained in the *Viṃśatilakṣaṇī* as the state of being accomplished by a single effort because of having a single purpose. This is for the sake of manifesting the unity of the work (*ekaprabandhya*). "With a specific order" means with a fixed sequence; the intention is that there is no sequence here based merely on the occasion (*avasara*) as in other treatises. In this regard, the distinction is as follows: "In this system, study is already established prior to inquiry (*vicāra*) by virtue of the injunction.
Therefore, inquiry by one who has not studied the Veda is forbidden by the Śruti. (240)
The sequence of the twenty characteristics is not based on scriptural injunction (vaidha), but rather is logical (yauktika);
therefore, any consideration of a reversal of that order is revealed as improper.

By the word "beginning with" (*ārabhya*) in the *Dharmajijñāsā* Sūtra, the promise to investigate the entire meaning of the Veda is indicated, since the term "dharma" (*dharma*) encompasses all established entities (*siddha*), things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the higher and the lower, and the cause of the support of the universe. A promise to investigate only the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) may also be established therein either by way of a governing principle (*tantra*) or through repetition (*āvṛtti*). On that basis alone, the statement in the *Sāra* that the purpose is the investigation of ritual action is justified. From the two specific promises regarding the two portions, the general promise is understood, just as in the *Nyāyasūtra*, where the mention of the "balancing of similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) and "balancing of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*) implies the "balancing of the counter-attribute" (*pratidharmasama*). All of this has been stated in the *Saṅgatimālā*.

Nor should it be said: "Since the entire subject is established by the initial proposition alone, what is the purpose of the subsequent specific propositions? For this is appropriate here as well, just as in the preceding chapters, because they serve purposes such as removing specific doubts. Furthermore, this opening—"Then, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*)—and so forth, is not an irrelevant matter; for the intended meaning is that just as elsewhere there is a fixed sequence due to logical connection (*saṅgati*), so it is here. For in this context, since that which lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be defined, the first chapter was devoted to the definition of the means of valid cognition.

Once the authority of the Veda as a whole was established, and since distinctions among its contents would be impossible if there were no difference in their meanings—rendering all [notions] such as being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) untenable—an inquiry into the differences in the meaning of the scriptures proceeded immediately after the inquiry into the means of knowledge (*māna*). Some say this is the "inquiry into the difference of the scriptures" (*śāstrabheda-cintā*). In that regard, once the difference [between rituals] is established through distinct words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*), the definition of the subsidiaries (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) proceeds by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and title (*samākhyā*).

In the fourth [book], there is an inquiry into what serves the ritual (*kratvartha*) and what serves the person (*puruṣārtha*), for the sake of establishing that only the subsidiaries (*śeṣa*) are to be employed by their principals (*śeṣin*); some say this is an investigation into "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which consists in the requirement of an injunction (*vidhyapekṣā*). Once the items have been enjoined, the order (*krama*) is set forth in the fifth [book] through direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual sequence (*pāṭha*), procedure (*pravṛtti*), and the primary [element] (*mukhya*). When the meaning of the scripture has been established as possessing a specific order, the performer (*prayoktṛ*) of that [ritual] is declared in the sixth. Thus, once the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been taught, the general principle of extension (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) is established in the seventh; and in the eighth, its specific applications (*anubandhiviśeṣa*) are treated.

In the ninth [book], there is a manifold modification (*ūha*) of mantras and other elements that have been extended by analogy (*atideśa*). In the tenth [book], there is sublation (*bādha*) of those things obtained through extension, occurring either because they serve no purpose in a particular case, because they are already obtained from another source, or because of an explicit prohibition. In the eleventh [book], there is the principle of ritual economy (*tantra*), which applies when both [the primary and secondary acts] possess the capacity for separate performance and share identity in place, time, and so forth. In the twelfth [book], there is the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), which occurs when one act falls within the middle of another performance and depends upon that performance for its execution.

They summarized this as follows: "By means of [the topics of] dharma, intellect, non-difference, auxiliaries, application, sequence, agents, beginning, specific place, particularity, doubt, refutation, and the connection with the tantra. Thus, once the ritual action had been deliberated upon in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa* (the section on deities) through its four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*), the very deity to be worshipped by each respective rite was extracted (*nirakṛṣyata*) by means of distinctions in essential nature, attributes, and excellence.

And at its conclusion, because of his vision of Hari, the elders who know the truth state that he offered this introductory remark regarding what was to be investigated: "They call him Brahman; they call him Brahman. Thereafter, in the final section (the *anta-kāṇḍa*), the Supreme Deity—who is to be worshipped through all the duties taught in the twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*) either directly or through an intermediary, and whose body comprises all deities as determined by the subsequent four chapters—is intended to be examined.

In that regard, the first chapter establishes the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all causal statements with Brahman by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "The concordance of sentences with Brahman—having excluded [the possibility of] being without an object and having an object other [than Brahman]—is demonstrated here by means of the first chapter. In the second chapter, the removal of any suspected contradictions therein is treated.

By those two [chapters], the establishment of Brahman is shown; by the third and fourth, the excellence of the means and the fruit [is shown] according to the order of origination (*utpatti-krama*). Thus, the specific sequence of the twenty chapters has been indicated merely by way of direction. Well then, in this case, how is the priority of the group of four [chapters on] the sixteen-fold [breath-control] established? For even in the case of a reversed order, it is not [contradictory].

There is no contradiction; for the authority of the Vedas and so forth, though being a prerequisite (*upajīvya*), can be established in their proper place within the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras), or one might engage in reflection on Brahman after having heard only that much. This is not so, because regarding the three aims of life (*trivarga*) practiced since time immemorial, the agent first becomes attached [to them] until he perceives their defects; such is the sequence of meaning.

Although there is no difference between the two cases regarding the immediate perception of limited or unlimited fruits, according to the maxim, "If one can find honey in the mud itself," it is better to first undertake the contemplation of karma—which is free from the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) shaken off by the exertion of knowledge independent of ritual action—rather than the exertion of knowledge that is dependent on such action. Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, which constitutes a constituent part of that [knowledge], depends upon the understanding of the meanings of its constituent elements, such as sacrifice (*yajña*). Likewise, in the various types of knowledge (*vidyā*), the investigation into injunctions for viewing sacrifices and their parts as deities depends upon the determination of the specific attributes of those visualizations (*dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the cognitions regarding the examples such as the piling of bricks (*iṣṭakacita*) are dependent upon the subject matter to which they are applied (*dārṣṭāntika*). Since the portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) abounds in both ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman, the sequence of inquiry into them is also logical according to the order of study established by the beginningless tradition (*sampradāya*). Moreover, this is the primary sequence here, due to the order of the arising of the subordinate and principal elements consisting of ritual action and meditation (*upāsanā*). Thus it has been stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "Because the relationship of cause and effect between the knowledge of ritual action and [the knowledge of] Brahman is accepted, the priority of ritual action is established, and the posteriority of the other."

And because those two [the primary rites] occur in a sequence, their investigations likewise follow that same order; this occurs precisely by the principle of "primary sequence" (*mukhyakrama*), as in the case of the subsidiaries of the Sārasvata sacrifice. Just as in the passage, "There are two Sārasvatas; this indeed is the divine couple," when there is no determination regarding which of the two sacrifices produced from the pair should have its subsidiaries performed first, the priority of the Sarasvatī sacrifice is established by its *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; and by that sequence, it is stated that its subsidiaries alone take precedence—according to the rule: "Or rather, by the sequence of the primary, because the subsidiaries exist for its sake. This is because the principles well-known in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) are summarized here.
Remember also that the section on Brahman would be in vain, as it was in the preceding chapters. (242)

The explanation of things not previously understood, as well as their establishment by means of refutation, and in some cases an exception—thus the meaningfulness of this [treatise] is established here. (243)

Now, if the Mīmāṃsā concludes with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement," then—since it is accepted that the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras] have as their qualified seeker one who is dispassionate, and since there is the certainty of a faultless and infinite fruit therein—no one would succeed in performing the means for results such as heaven. Consequently, the injunctions regarding optional rites (kāmya-vidhis) would suffer invalidity characterized by non-performance.

Not so—those who, out of delusion or due to obstacles, rest content after investigating merely ritual action; those who, desiring only fame, gain, honor, and the propagation of their teachings, might contemplate the meaning of the Upanishads; or those whose dispassion has later subsided through the force of destiny—even if they have heard the *Śārīraka*, such persons would abandon the dharma of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*).
Even a wise man, when afflicted by illness, may engage in unwholesome things;
why then should that which is desired not likewise occur even in a person of intelligence regarding forbidden matters? (244)
Even great beings are said to possess a dual cultivation due to desire;
for some, gradual liberation is likewise declared. (245)

For instance: first of all, by the injunction "one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," the grasping of the collection of syllables called the Veda—which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*—is prescribed by the act of study itself. The phrase beginning with "for instance" (*tathā hi*) is stated for the sake of establishing the sequence and the logical consistency of the present subject matter: the inquiry into Brahman as a single unified science and the effort toward that inquiry. (Verse 146)

Regarding this, keeping in mind the following dilemma—namely, whether one views that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) might occur even before the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), and thus desires it to precede even the study [of the Veda], or whether it simply precedes the determination of ritual action for one who has already studied the Veda—the author negates the first alternative with the word "first" (*prathamam*). The *Vivaraṇa* explains that the word "for now" (*tāvat*) demonstrates the universal consensus regarding the immediate succession to the study [of the Veda].

By this, it is suggested that—just as inquiry (*vicāra*) occurs immediately after study (*adhyayana*)—it is impossible for anyone who properly reflects on both karma and Brahman to abandon the following points: (1) that the subject matter to be explained possesses the nature of a single continuous composition with a fixed sequence, established by a single injunction regarding the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of study; (2) that study, by the force of its injunction, has the entirety of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) as its object; and (3) that for that very reason, inquiry likewise has the entirety of one's own Veda as its object. Alternatively, the word *tāvat* may be used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

And by that [injunction], because there is no opportunity for other treatises due to the mandatory study preceded by the instruction in purificatory conduct (*śaucācāra*) immediately following the initiation (*upanayana*) at eight years of age and so forth, any prior state such as the "fourfold means" (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*)—which might otherwise be presumed to be its root—is excluded. By accepting the self-injunction (*svavidhi*) "one's own Veda is to be studied," its application is intended. By the statement "the acquisition of a mass of syllables through study," the attainment of refinement (*saṃskāra*) is indicated. Here, the particle *eva* (only) illuminates the fact that this is the result of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

Although this injunction for study is obligatory (*nitya*) because of the sin incurred by non-performance and the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from its performance as a specific occasion (*nimitta*), nevertheless, since the visible fruit (*dṛṣṭa-phala*) cannot be abandoned, once the mass of syllables has been grasped through study undertaken for the sake of accepting that fruit, there is no room here for any other cause of grasping [the meaning]. For even one who asserts that study is for the sake of the Vedic injunction (*niyoga*) must, by implication, prohibit reading from books and the like; it is for this very reason that there is also censure of those who read from written texts.

By the three [verses] beginning with "That which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*," it is indicated that neither merely a portion of one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*) nor the meaning of the Veda is what is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*; rather, the sense is that study according to the traditional sequence is sanctioned by injunction. "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is enjoined and understood as the fruit; the meaning is that while other means might be possible for this fruit, it is restricted to this specific means. For restriction (*niyama*) applies to something other than that which is already established by the particle *eva*.

Although there is no restriction regarding the essential nature of grasping the syllables, since that can be accomplished through other means as well, nevertheless, the restriction is justified on the grounds that the utility for recitation (*jāpa*) and so forth applies only to what has been acquired through formal study (*adhyayana*). Those who assert a restriction regarding the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) are likewise saved by this same reasoning.

In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of that study is and how it is to be performed, the following are prescribed through such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age and teach him," and through specific instructions regarding vows and observances such as: "Having performed the *upākarma* ceremony on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada according to rule, a Brāhmaṇa, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months."

Surely, by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), one understands merely that one's own Vedic text (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied. By that much alone, there is no obstruction to the opportunity for other scriptures which serve as causes for the attainment of the fourfold qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth; for it is possible to study [those others] even after that. Whether one studies them without the preliminary rites or having studied [the Veda] once, let one practice other scriptures—regarding this, [the author] clarifies the nature, time, and eligibility of the study itself with the word "that" (*tat*); the meaning is that the initial study is established by the universally accepted obligatory injunction (*nitya-vidhi*).

What is its form? Does it consist of independent utterance like *japa* and so forth, or is it non-utterance; or is it based on a different principle like the study of the Gaudas, or is it non-repetitive like a *pārāyaṇa*, or is it repetitive like the threshing of grain? By the word "form" (*rūpa*), the inclusion of the fruit is intended; thus, even for the *Tūlikā*, the point is that it takes the form of repetition as long as the [text] is being grasped. "How? refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

With the intention of showing that there must necessarily be a distinction and a state of uniformity (*aikarasya*) between those supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) which are accepted as being for the purpose of study—despite being subject to doubt regarding their purpose of teaching—and those [texts] which are to be supplemented, he makes this specific mention by dividing them with the words "and by these instructions. The statement "having performed the *upākarma*, one should study" establishes the intent of the Śruti, namely that "one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) should study"; for it is precisely for the sake of the study of one who has been initiated that the *upākarma* and other rites are prescribed. "Yuktaḥ" means attentive, or else, engaged in the observances (*vrata*) and so forth.

Those for whom the fifth [month] is half are called "half-fifth" (*ardhapañcama*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), those statements previously mentioned that are consistent with the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) are included, such as: "But from this point forward, one should regularly recite the *Chandas* during the bright fortnights; and one should thoroughly recite all the *Vedāṅgas* during the dark fortnights. The specific vows (*vrata-viśeṣa*) include the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, and others, together with their introductory rites (*sopākṛti*).

The specific rules (*niyama-viśeṣa*) concern the distinctions in time for the study of the limbs and the main body of the Veda, divided according to the bright and dark fortnights, the half-month, the fifth month, and so forth; they also concern matters of place and so on, such as the rule: "One must not study in the presence of a *Śūdra*."

Thus, it is understood that study (*adhyayana*) is the acquisition of the mass of syllables (*akṣararāśi*), consisting of the repetition of what is uttered by a teacher who is learned in the Vedas and endowed with self-qualities such as steadfastness in good conduct produced by the lineage of virtuous ancestors; and this [acquisition] is characterized by the observance of specific vows and restraints.

One might object: "Since the Vedic injunction *upanayīta tam adhyāpayet* (he should initiate him and teach him) prescribes the duty of the teacher, how can it be a rule requiring study? And how, by means of this implied scriptural authority (*upātta-śruti*), is the prevention of the opportunity for other scriptures established? To this he says: "In this manner. This means: by the method of enjoining the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), which is established by one's own injunction supported by the previously shown Vedic and Smṛti texts; [and] by [the qualities of the teacher] such as "one who is well-born and endowed with knowledge" (*abhijana-vidyā-samudeta*). By these, the teacher—

One should not suspect that the passage is primarily intended as an injunction for teaching, because of the principle regarding the description of the qualities of a priest (*ṛtvij*); it is with this intention that the statement beginning with "in a lineage of the virtuous" (*satsantāne*) is made. Here, the words "composed" (*samāhita*) imply both proper conduct and personal qualities. The term "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) serves to clarify the state of being fully endowed with knowledge. Furthermore, teaching by one who is unfit is prohibited; however, if such qualities are lacking, the matter is remedied. Likewise, the loss incurred by the student is stated in passages such as, "He indeed enters from darkness into darkness."

The fact that these qualities belong to the student is made explicit by such statements as "he should seek out a preparer" and "in him alone [resides] the culmination of knowledge and action. Just as for those who maintain that the injunction to teach is the primary rule, the qualifications of the student—such as being eight years old—are for the sake of the teacher, so too the qualifications of the teacher are for the sake of the student. To indicate this parallelism (*pratibandī*), the phrase "endowed with specific vows and observances" and so forth has been cited; for the two words ending in the genitive case also qualify the eligible person (*adhikārin*) through their specific observances, and because one who is initiated at eight years of age is already governed by the injunction to study.

By the phrase "the teacher's utterance followed by the student's non-independent (anūñcāraṇa) utterance," independent utterance as well as the suspicion that reflection might fall outside the scope of the treatise on study are excluded. Just as, according to another view, the proximity of a pupil suitable for teaching is considered a beneficial factor because it has a visible result for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), so too, in this view, the proximity suitable for the non-independent utterance [is the beneficial factor]. And such is the intended meaning.

In this first chapter, disregarding specific details such as "once," "not once," "twice," or "thrice" according to the logic of threshing (*avaghātanyāya*), he says—"the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables"—with the intention that the purpose of repetition is established by the attainment of its result. By this, it is also implied that the desire to grasp the syllables is a qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) of the seeker. Even though it is adopted as a fruit, its status as such is like being husked [of grain];
and its utility in rituals such as sacrifice is likewise difficult to deny, even for the act of grasping itself. (247)

If one desires the knowledge of the meaning as the fruit here, whether through injunction (*vidhi*) or permission (*anujñā*), it is difficult to maintain that its status as a compulsory duty (*nityatva*) would be lost due to its connection with a fruit. (248)

However, those who, regarding the injunction for compulsory study (*nityādhyayana-vidhi*) as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), postulate heaven as the fruit—unspecified by any particular qualification—on the basis of the *Viśvajit* principle, and who [hold] the knowledge of meaning as the fruit in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), are also refuted by this [argument]. For it is logical that the apprehension of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), being a perceptible result, possesses the status of a fruit because it culminates in happiness, just like the knowledge of meaning and so forth, even though it is distinct from happiness itself.

Thus, by both [the preceding statements], the nature of the meaning of the first study—namely, what form it takes—is demonstrated as being the non-omission [of the text] and the result of grasping the mass of syllables. And so the commentary explains: "For the function of a verbal root (*dhātu*) consists in a collection of momentary actions delimited by a single result, as in 'he cooks rice'; otherwise, there would be the consequence of violating the designation of the present tense. For the meaning of the word 'present' is that which has begun but is not yet completed."

However, if action—which is momentary—were the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then because the moment of action known prior to the utterance of the word has already perished, and because the subsequent moment is yet to come, and because a simultaneous moment cannot be known and thus is not an object of the word, [action] would not be established as having a beginning or an end; for even if it were perceptible by the eye, its beginning and completion could not be proven due to its destruction in each moment and the impossibility of defining a beginning, middle, or end. Therefore, he states that the term "studying" (*adhyayana*) applies to a collection of momentary actions delimited by the result of apprehension.

The statement that study consists of the non-simultaneous recitation performed by one who has been initiated by a teacher clarifies that both injunctions—“one should initiate” and “one should teach him”—prescribe that [the study] must be preceded by the initiation and other rites performed by the teacher.

[Objection: But surely, the statement "one should teach" must be intended as a restrictive rule regarding the means of livelihood (vṛtti). [Reply: Not so; for even one who has not been initiated is seen to teach for that purpose, which would render the injunction for initiation useless. Nor is there a restriction regarding sequence, such as "one should teach only one who has been initiated," because that would result in the statements such as "a Brāhmaṇa of eight years" becoming irrelevant. Furthermore, it is entirely inconsistent to claim that the instruction here is for some other purpose. Nor can a restriction regarding initiation be suspected here, since no other source is observed that establishes it. If it is argued that a Smṛti is observed, we say no, because the mention of "eight years" and so forth would be useless [if initiation were already established].

O King, there is no statement here regarding two means of livelihood (*vṛtti*), because initiation (*upanayana*) is not enumerated as one such means. Even if that were the case, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be untenable due to the absence of a motivator (*prāpaka*), as has already been stated; furthermore, this has already been answered. Therefore, this is simply an injunction required by the act of study (*adhyayana*). And in this context, the injunction is a motivator (*prayojaka*), like the injunction "one should cause [another] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*); for teaching (*adhyāpana*) itself, like officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*), is already established as being for the purpose of livelihood and thus is not something to be enjoined.

Therefore, in this context, an eight-year-old Brahmin, desiring to acquire the Veda, having been initiated by a teacher in the manner described, should approach him and study while observing the vows and rules as prescribed. This establishes the meaning of the scriptural injunction for study, including its supplementary elements. For this very reason, it is incorrect to assume that the performance [of study] is prompted by something else simply because no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is heard of in the injunction for study; for the same applies to the injunction for teaching, as nothing is heard there either, and the assumption [of another prompter] would be equally applicable to both. Furthermore, such an assumption is not made here.

The establishment of this [obligation] follows from the mere modification of the case endings in passages such as "A Brāhmaṇa... for those desiring offspring and so forth, and because it is supported by the Smṛti rule, "A Brāhmaṇa should study. If it is argued that a child cannot be prompted by its own injunction because it lacks knowledge of its own entitlement (*adhikāra*), we say no; for, according to the logic of the *niṣādasthapati* (the chief of the Niṣādas), the performance is possible through others who are cognizant of that entitlement. Indeed, well-wishers themselves perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) for children and others who do not know their own entitlement, since they themselves understand their utility.
As for Vedic study, however, it is reasonable for even a child to engage in it through the instigation of authoritative persons and the like, based on the inference of its fruitfulness.
For those who maintain that constant study is prompted by desire, how can there be in that case the characteristic of a mandate (niyoga) having the performance of the action as its objective? [249]
If it is claimed that [the means of knowledge] function according to their own rule for the awakened, but otherwise for the unawakened,
then in the fabrication of such a distinction in application, there would be the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya).

And as for the claim that, in the case of a student who has completed the hardship of study, the knowledge of meaning—which is perceived prior to reflection—is accepted as the purpose because it is the object to be accomplished by the injunction of study; that too is weak, because once study is established through another means, it is improper to postulate a further purpose for it based on an effect that is already established without being its motivator; for, like other obligatory rites (*nitya*), this too can be shown to have the mere performance of the injunction (*niyoga*) as its sole purpose.

If it is argued that something other than the seen [result] is also permitted, we say no; for there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting even incidental gains such as profit and honor, since they too would be permitted by the injunction here. Nor can it be said that the injunction permits only the knowledge of meaning because it is useful for the performance of dharma, and nothing else; for wealth and so forth are also useful for that purpose, and thus they too would be granted permission. While it may be possible for the knowledge of meaning to assist all injunctions, one does not disregard other seen results on the basis of this much distinction alone. (251)

If you argue that wealth and the like provide assistance through their own inherent power, then knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda] should likewise arise from its own power; it would not be subject to the brow of an injunction. (152)
In its actual meaning, that [injunction] is authorized and brought forth by the very power of the word;
let it be relied upon by the injunctions for sacrifice, giving, and so forth, which are themselves dependent [on it]. (253)

Moreover, for a single [action], a dual nature consisting of both injunction and permission would follow, as would the status of being both a primary and a subordinate action, with respect to its object. (254)

Therefore, it is a matter of common experience even in your own villages that at the very time of beginning the study, teachers and others, intending the welfare of the boy—either by their own intelligence or through the instruction of others—act as the motivators for him. No one, however, is seen engaging in such activity with the thought, "I must assume the role of a teacher for another. Furthermore, those who wish him well, while instructing him, point out to the child the future results [of his actions].

And in the *Chāndogya*: "I shall dwell as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under the Blessed One; I shall approach the Blessed One," thus Jābāla said to Gautama; and he replied, "Bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the teacher acts solely for the sake of the disciple, and that the student must obtain the sacrificial fee (*vara*) and other such requirements from him. For this very reason, the claim made by some—that study is motivated by the teacher's attachment arising from greed for the acquisition of wealth and the like—is refuted.

In order to establish that even if its own injunction (*svavidhi*) cannot be the motivator, the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*) is nonetheless untenable as a motivator: for it is not possible to induce a boy to act without first making him understand his own purpose, since otherwise the acquisition of wealth and the like would be impossible; otherwise, the teacher’s engagement would have to be by force. Therefore, in the injunction for the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary sciences, the Brahmin and others explicitly mentioned [in the text] are the qualified agents who intend their own welfare; thus, there is no motivation from another source.

By this, the argument raised by some—that if one does not accept the impulsion (*prayukti*) of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), then since the impulsion of the ritual injunctions (*kratuvidhi*) must necessarily be resorted to, even Śūdras and others desiring those respective fruits would have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for study—is refuted; for study is impelled by its own injunction, which has a fixed agent (*niyata-kartṛka*), just like the rite of consecrating the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Furthermore, the objection regarding the lack of a stated qualification (*adhikāra*) in the injunction for study is also refuted by stating that the result is the apprehension of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), which is a visible effect (*dṛṣṭa*) similar to threshing (*vaituṣya*).

The Smṛti passage beginning with "upanīya" (having initiated) also does not enjoin teaching, nor does it take the status of being an *ācārya* as its fruit; for it is intent solely upon deriving the word *ācārya* by way of restating a specific form of teaching already established elsewhere—just like the derivation of words such as *upādhyāya*—and there is no reason here to assume an intention beyond that. Nor is there a single, distinct kind of *ācārya*-ship [separate from teaching], as there is no evidence for it. If it is argued that this [distinct status] is assumed because no other basis is observed, we say no.

This is because we observe that the cause for the application of the term [‘Ācārya’] is the exclusion of absolute non-connection with the acts of initiation (*upanayana*), instruction (*adhyāpana*), and the imposition of restrictive rules (*saniyama*). For this very reason, the application of the word ‘Ācārya’ is justified even after the time of initiation and so forth, following the logic applied to the term ‘Upādhyāya’. However, previously [before initiation], due to the difficulty of anticipating the future, there is no usage [of the term], owing to both doubt and the absence of knowledge regarding the perception of the cause. Furthermore, if the Smṛti text here were intended merely to etymologically derive the word, its source is clearly seen to be simply the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

If, however, it were intended for the purpose of the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), one would have to postulate that it is rooted in a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) of a non-worldly meaning; and when there is a conflict between what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what is to be postulated (*kalpya*), the established alone should be accepted. Furthermore, the Vedic hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* and so forth is compatible here—even if there is no status as a subordinate member (*anaṅgatva*)—merely by virtue of the similarity mentioned in the Sūtra, such as having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), as in the case of "having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām iṣṭvā*). Now, an objection might be raised: "On account of the natural force of having a common agent and because there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgitva*) would be established through a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*). This is not so; for the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* resides in Smṛti, and it may even be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
In this case, the indicative mark (liṅga) residing in the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is indeed stronger, because it is immediate.

The *upanayana*—heard in the scripture as "the Brahmin [initiation]" (*brāhmaṇam*) by virtue of being a singular refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the student (*māṇavaka*)—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) specifically to the student's study (*adhyayana*), due to the internal indicative mark (*antaraṅga-liṅga*) of its residing in the ritual action (*karmasthatā*). This is so even though it stands in proximity to both the fruit-bearing activities of studying and teaching, which consist of the operations of the one to be prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*). If it were for the sake of another purpose, there would be a mediated connection (*praṇāḍyā*). Thus, since it is enjoined to study by the scriptural indicative mark (*śrauta-liṅga*), any assumption that it is an auxiliary to teaching would involve the contradiction of enjoining what has already been enjoined (*viniyukta-viniyoga-virodha*).

For a non-vedic statement (*aśruti*) based on Smṛti is not capable of subverting a vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*); this is because it is obstructed by a double delay: Smṛti depends upon its own source (the Veda), and a subsequent restatement (*anūkti*) depends upon a prior statement. [Objection:

But surely, from the ātmanepada ending prescribed by the rule *svarita-jitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*, initiation (*upanayana*) should be an auxiliary to the teaching (*adhyāpana*) residing in the initiator. [Reply: It would not be so, because it is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *sammānana*.

The Grammarians (Śābdikas) maintain that this undertaking [of the sūtra] has the sense of "not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāya*). They argue that "intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*) means the connection of the fruit with the agent alone, whereas "not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāyatva*) is simply the absence of such a restriction. If this is argued, it is not so; for even in the case of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by rules such as *svarita-jitaḥ* in the example *ādadhīta*, the fruit is connected to both [the agent and another]. Nor is it the case that the fruit of the action cannot be connected to two conscious beings; for that is observed even in the passage, *jāyāpatī agnimādadhīyātām* ("the husband and wife should establish the sacred fire"). Furthermore, the claim that "connection with a conscious being other than the agent" is what is meant is also refuted.
