From the perspective of authoritative sources (*prāmāṇika*), in all scriptural matters, since there are scriptural declarations of fruits in the form of pleasure directed toward one who is not the agent but the object of worship (*ārādhya*), there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the loss of the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) endings in rules concerning the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Furthermore, in passages such as "one should sacrifice while practicing sorcery" (*abhicaran yajeta*), a fruit appropriate to that [act] is accepted even for the enemy (*bhrātṛvya*). And in the case of "he chooses the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*), the fruit is established for those being chosen as well. Since the term "fruit of the action" (*kriyāphala*) is intended to refer to the immediately subsequent fruit, its connection with the agent constitutes the state of being "intended by the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*).

As for the argument that the *Sammānanādi-sūtra* must serve to establish the connection of the agent with a remote result, this too has already been answered; for there is a deviation [in the rule] even in cases such as "one should establish" (*ādadhīta*). Indeed, in this case, the result—namely, the status of being one who has established the fires (*āhitāgnitva*)—belongs to the establisher, though it is mediated by the consecration of the fire. Now, one might object: "The result for the establisher is simply the accomplishment of the consecrated fire, which serves as the basis for future obligatory and optional sacrifices; thus, there is no connection with a remote result. Do not say so.

In this case as well, the result for the initiator (*upanetṛ*) is simply the accomplishment of the student who has been consecrated by the initiation rite (*upanayana-saṃskṛta*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering the sūtra concerning "honoring" (*sammānana*) and so forth superfluous. If it is argued that the two sūtras are purposeful because the immediate result is either desired or undesired by the agent, we say no; for even an initiator who desires the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) cannot logically be one who does not desire the consecration of the person being initiated. Therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here is used solely to establish the connection of the result with the agent. Likewise, by the expression "he should teach," the result does not accrue to the agent. Thus, in this manner, study is not prompted by another injunction.

And as for reflection (*vicāra*), is it enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*)? Not the first, because the [objection regarding] the lack of a subject matter and a fruit has already been refuted. Not the second, because it would not exceed what is prescribed.

For even the teacher, having caused [the student] to grasp the *svādhyāya*, may then desist. But if [reflection] were prompted by compassion and the like, then it was already established that this would be the case even previously. (256)
Therefore, thinking that the entire system of Mīmāṃsā would fail under the Guru’s doctrine, those who sought to establish the original position refuted it. (257)

And study (*adhyayana*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedic text (*svādhyāya*), because from the injunction "the Vedic text is to be studied," it is understood that the Vedic text is the object (*karman*).

Although the opportunity for other treatises is thus blocked by the limit of grasping the syllables (*akṣara*), there might still be the doubt that this [opportunity] could arise once the syllables have been grasped. To prevent that even thereafter, he clarifies—by rejecting the position that study is the object of an injunction—that it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya*, as previously indicated, stating: "study" (*adhyayanam*). The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of removing that doubt; or rather, its order is displaced, serving to conjoin its nature as a refinement with [the fact of] its being repeated many times and so forth.

By those who assert that "consecration (*saṃskāra*) is intended for the person alone through [rites such as] recitation and sprinkling," it is accepted that even the consecration of study belongs to the agent alone. Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt that the intended meaning is not established, he says: "The Veda (*svādhyāya*). And it has been stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "In the enumeration of consecrations, the consecration of the syllables is indeed appropriate; for the Veda is clearly the ritual act, and it is that which is directly consecrated.
Those who understand the conferring of excellence upon the person to be achieved by means of sprinkling and so forth—[this is what is meant].
They too did not abandon their status as conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and karma in various instances. || 258 ||
The impression (saṃskāra) produced by various specific actions resides in the person;
this is because it is determined that, when conjoined with those [actions], it brings about the respective effects. (259)

In this context, since the study [of the Veda] is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*), its status as an object (*karmatva*) serves as the reason; thus, there is no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This is the intended meaning: for here, no other meaning for the suffix *tavya* is possible. Consequently, whether the accusative case-ending or the suffix *tavya* etc. signifies the object, there is no distinction; and although grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) exist for the sake of the action, because the verbal sense (*bhāvārtha*) residing in the substance is for the sake of the substance, the principle of "threshing" (*avahanti-nyāya*) is appropriate here.

Furthermore, it is established that the acts of threshing and so forth constitute the *saṃskāra* (preparatory refinement) of their respective substances, as stated in the section on "Difference" (*Bhedalakṣaṇa*): "These [actions] are twofold, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*). By the phrase "of one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyasya*), the impossibility of [the Veda] being something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth is indicated; for it is certainly not something to be produced, since its sequence is established from time immemorial, and because there is no conventional usage of constructing sentences [anew] in the manner of previous utterances. Nor is it something to be modified (*vikārya*), since no change of state is observed, as in the case of milk turning into curd.

Nor does it consist merely in being something to be attained, for that would be incompatible with its having other functions [such as recitation]. Therefore, the understanding of its status as an object (*karman*), supported by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), is the reason for its being something to be refined (*saṃskārya*).

For "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) indeed means the production of fitness for another purpose. And it is appropriate for the Veda (*svādhyāya*) to be something to be refined, because it brings about the knowledge of the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as well as their means; and because, through recitation (*japa*) and so forth, it serves as a means even in its own form.

Now, one might ask: even if it is understood to be an object (*karman*), how can the Veda (*svādhyāya*)—which is not enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) and the like for any specific purpose and is not itself a material substance (*adravya*)—be that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*)? To this he says: "For [the word] *saṃskāra* [is used] in the sense of a well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). The particle *hi* indicates a well-known fact; the word *nāma* signifies excellence, reaching as far as the consensus of others. Here, the expression "making it fit for another function" is stated with the intention of referring to a refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by the study of the Veda, which is to be realized and is useful for future purposes. Alternatively, the definition of refinement (*saṃskāra*) here is "the conferring of an excellence upon something already existing."

[This has been] explained. Consequently, even though [the *paridhi* sticks] are already employed [elsewhere], the term "fitness for another effect" (*kāryāntara-yogyatā*) must somehow be applied here with the intention of expressing a fitness that is conducive to that [other effect]. For it is heard in scripture that even when they have been used as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), they remain fit for another effect in that very same form, namely, the benefit of the sacrificial fire (*bhūta-upakāra*). The underlying point is this: it is not the case that they cannot be consecrated simply because they have not been [previously] assigned [to a specific role]; for even in the absence of a formal assignment, their status as objects of consecration is possible by virtue of their utility [for the sacrifice].

Furthermore, there is an application (viniyoga) both general and specific, such as "the Hotṛ priest acts with the Ṛgveda" and so forth. Nor is it the case that [the Veda] cannot be an object of refinement (saṃskāra) because it is not a substance; for there is no contradiction provided it has been acquired through study as previously described. Moreover, the fact that [the Veda] is an object of apprehension is universally accepted even in the case of qualities and other categories.

Even though the excellence (*atiśaya*)—consisting of the Lord’s grace—which is to be accomplished by the action enjoined, does not reside in the Veda itself, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because that very excellence, being attained through study and apprehended by the cognition of the object of worship, is restricted by the scripture to the subsequent action appropriate to it. Whether or not an imperceptible excellence arises in rice and other materials through acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the aforementioned principle applies universally.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in such instances as "one offers the flour-grains" (*saktūñ juhoti*) and "gold is to be worn" (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*), even though there is an understanding of an object (*karman*) devoid of being something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) does not have the substance as its purpose? Similarly, in injunctions for muttering (*japa*), such as "the Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) and "one should study the Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhīyīta*), the understanding of [the Veda] as an object (*karmatva*) is no different. Therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that regard; or else, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even there [the Veda] is something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) all at once. To this, he says: "Being something to be refined... (*saṃskāryatvam*).

The point is this: because it is impossible for flour and the like to have utility either in the past or the future, and because recitation (japa) and the like necessarily have as their object the syllables already grasped, and because it would be cumbersome to postulate multiple latent impressions (saṃskāra), and because no other utility accomplished by the impressions of recitation and so forth is observed, and because a fruit is heard [in scripture], one abandons the notion of a latent impression in those cases; however, it would not be so here, since the status of these as ritual actions (karma), once understood, remains uncontradicted.

On this very point, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states: "We maintain that the first study [of the Veda] is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*), because it is measured by its status as an action and because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) serves a further purpose, even though no specific fruit is heard [in the injunction]. If one were to claim that even recitation (*japa*) and the like are purificatory acts, then the first study would not be a purification, since it does not serve all [subsequent uses] of the Veda. Consequently, the status of the Veda as an object of action (*karmatā*) would be contradicted everywhere; therefore, the first study is a purification, while the others are actions for the sake of the meaning (*arthakarman*)."

In this case, the fruit must be that which is mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice. Here, the wise maintain that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is an unintentional object (*anīpsita-karma*), whereas in the first [type of action], it is considered an intentional object (*īpsita-karma*), and the ritual act is regarded as being for its sake. If even recitation (*japa*) and the like were merely purificatory acts (*saṃskāra-karma*), then since the Veda—which is the object to be purified by all such purifications—would have its utility solely in the comprehension of meaning (*arthāvabodha*), all studies would become acts aimed at that meaning. This is because such comprehension would be useless regarding those portions of the ritual not authorized for performance (such as the *hum* and other interjections). Therefore, all studies of the Veda are indeed acts whose purpose is the comprehension of meaning.

In that case, there would be a destruction of the status of *svādhyāya* as an action (*karman*). Therefore, the first study alone is the sanctification (*saṃskāra*). [Objection: Even here, the argument is established as illogical because no utility is observed; for if utility were postulated solely on the basis of its being something to be sanctified, it would result in circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). And they say: "A rule of sanctification (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) does not enjoin the object to be sanctified; rather, a rule of sanctification—which culminates in sanctification—applies to that whose utility is already determined by another means of knowledge, and it does not postulate a purpose for the object to be sanctified. To this, he says: "For the sake of dharma" (*dharmārtha*). For it is because no utility is observed that the scriptural injunction regarding the action is sublated in the case of *saktu* (barley flour) and similar instances.

The sense is that, because various purposes—both seen and unseen—are observed for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), it is not logical to regard it as something not to be refined (i.e., not a *saṃskāra*), just as in the case of *saktu* (groats) and other such items. Here, the statement that the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are to be known through the Veda is intended to demonstrate that the entire [Veda] is to be investigated (*mīmāṃsitavya*), by showing a commonality of purpose that persists throughout all its parts; and it is also intended to show that those [aims] taught in non-Vedic scriptures are not to be trusted. Even though some objects of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) and their means are established in the world, it is appropriate that wealth and pleasure in the form of the sovereignty over the three worlds, as well as their means, are to be known through the Veda.

The operation of the scripture is established even regarding worldly objects and desires (*artha* and *kāma*) in relation to means such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice. However, although *dharma* is perceptible in its nature as a substance and so forth, it is grasped by the scripture specifically as a means to stability (*dhṛti*). As they say: "For their status as means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is always understood from the Veda; and since their nature as *dharma* consists in that very [status], it is therefore not within the range of the senses."

Furthermore, liberation (*mokṣa*) is not perceptible to people such as ourselves. As for [arguments] such as "the self is at some time devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because it possesses non-eternal specific qualities, like a jar," these do not constitute valid inference because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). If one were to state a subverting argument against the counter-example by relying on the scriptures that teach liberation, then the inference would be rendered futile. However, since liberation consists in the experience of Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss, there is no possibility of the application of a logical reason [to prove its absence]; if, instead, one were to attempt to prove the opposite of that, it would contradict scripture (*āgamabādha*).

Moreover, it can also be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is never devoid of all its specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), because it possesses the nature of self (ātmatva), just like the Lord (Īśvara). In this context, just as the object [of desire] is the means for accomplishing the human goal, dharma—which is itself a specific quality—is also a means for accomplishing that same human goal; therefore, it too is designated by the term "means" (sādhana). Furthermore, it should be understood that both the Mantras and the Arthavādas appropriately convey the fourfold aims of human life (caturvarga) or assist in conveying them.

Even in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others such as the Vajra, there is no injunction toward what is harmful (anartha), because they merely provide instruction on the instrumental part (upāyāṃśa) for achieving desired ends, such as the destruction of enemies.
And from other terrible means, a remedy may be obtained here;
for they declare that malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) can be overcome by a light expiation.
Furthermore, it is taught that "one who does not practice sorcery shall fall into the six [hells]";
by this, they understand that killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) is consistent with dharma.

But surely, the capacity to convey extraordinary human goals and so forth exists even in the Smṛtis and other texts; therefore, if the purpose is to be accomplished by something else, what is the use of the Veda’s refinement? Furthermore, there is no comprehension of meaning in cases such as the *hum* and other ritual interjections. Moreover, in the case of portions that have not been previously understood or intended for performance by a particular person, even if such comprehension were present, it would be of no use because it would lack the quality of leading to actual performance. Thus, in this context:

Because the utility of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is obtainable through other means, because it is impossible for the act of recitation (*adhyayana*) to be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the entire Veda, and because a refinement of only a single portion is not supported by the words [of the injunction],—and since, in the absence of its being an injunction of refinement, the alternative that it serves as a mandatory purpose (*niyoga*) would necessarily follow—it says: "by means of *japa* (muttering), etc. By the word "etc.," "retention" (*dhāraṇa*) is included. "Even in its own form"—the meaning is: not only by way of the knowledge of the meaning. Alternatively, "teaching" (*adhyāpana*) may be understood by the word "etc."

Then, by its own nature—that is, by the mere nature of that which has been shaken off—according to such Smṛti texts as, "The wise man, upholding the Ṛgveda... The intended meaning is this: knowledge is indeed accomplished solely through the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) as acquired through formal study.

The [Vedas] are to be lived by according to the prescribed rules; however, the supplements (upabṛṃhaṇas) do not possess the capacity to be means for achieving dharma and so forth independently. Moreover, there is a scriptural text: "By constant study of the Vedas, by truth, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. Such well-known purposes as the recitation of mantras (japa), which cannot be accomplished by any other means, justify the fact that even those portions intended for those who are ineligible or purposeless are fit to be objects of refinement (saṃskārya).

Furthermore, the rule regarding recitation (*japa*), even when its subject matter is mere vocalization, does not contradict the fact that Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) has meaning as its primary purpose; for if it were to contradict all rules, it would result in self-contradiction. Nor is there a conflict with the distinct application (*viniyoga*) [of the same text] to two purposes, because there is no multiplicity of purposes through a single form. Thus states the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "By its own nature it serves the purpose of recitation and so forth, and by its own power it conveys the meaning; there is no contradiction due to the difference in forms, just as in the case of fire's burning and illuminating."

The intended meaning is this: since an infinite variety of purposes arises from the Veda once it has been refined by study, who would strive elsewhere for such goals without the inquiry [into its meaning], given that they are found within the study of the scriptures?
Thus, the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables, just like the recitation of mantras accompanied by restrictive rules.

One might object: "Surely, by one who has understood the utility [of study], the knowledge of the meaning must also be accepted as the fruit of the injunction; however, by one who has not understood the utility, even the grasping of the syllables cannot be recognized as a fruit. Therefore, since it is directly useful for performance, let the knowledge of the meaning—just like the grasping of the syllables—be the perceptible fruit of the injunction to study. He refutes this objection under the guise of a summary of the present topic with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning is: "in the manner of determining the nature of the enjoined act, its fruit, and so forth."

The state of being "possessed of mantra" (*mantravattva*) and the state of being "possessed of observance" (*niyamavattva*), which reside in the non-deficient pronunciation [of the Veda], are figuratively attributed to their fruit when that fruit is grasped. "Mantras" refers to those that are constituent parts of the *kāṇḍavrata* and other such rites, as well as those to be recited during the period of study, such as "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*). "Observances" refers to those previously mentioned. Some maintain that the expression "possessed of mantra" is stated by way of illustration: just as the study enjoined regarding a mantra is accepted as culminating merely in the apprehension of the syllables, so it is here as well.

Others, however, maintain that it should be understood as follows: just as in the case of the rites to be performed at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), such as for one who has just been initiated regarding the mantras for placing fuel on the fire (*samid-ādhāna*) and so forth, so it is here as well. Others say it is "like *hum* and so forth," meaning like specific mantras used for neutralizing poison and the like. By the words "only" (*mātra*) and "conclusion" (*paryavasāna*), the cessation of the injunction before or after the grasping of the syllables is negated.

The point is this: the word "study" (*adhyayana*) does not denote the knowledge of meaning, because such a relationship has not been established [by usage], and because in expressions such as "one becomes a Brāhmaṇa after having studied something," it is impossible for it to have meaning as its primary referent. Rather, with respect to the study that is the object of the injunction, there is observed a result that is an immediate goal, all-pervasive, and unavoidable.

If one were to postulate that something other than that [knowledge] is its fruit, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate that even a remote goal is the fruit, it would follow that the performance of the ritual—which is itself to be accomplished by that knowledge—would also have to be considered its fruit, just like the knowledge itself. Moreover, the state of being required immediately after the subsequent injunction is equal for both the grasping of the text and the knowledge of its meaning. If the knowledge of the meaning were indeed taught as having the ritual action as its object, then one might accept it even when it is non-pervasive or remote; however, this is not the case. Therefore, the knowledge of the meaning must be accepted solely on account of its utility.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, according to the logic of the *Samanvaya* section, it is proper to establish that the knowledge of meaning alone is the result by virtue of being an end in itself? [Reply: It is not so; for that [logic] was stated only with respect to those portions teaching Brahman as unsurpassed bliss, whereas here, because we are considering the fruit of the study of the entire [Veda], it is improper to posit such a heterogeneous result. [Objection: But in cases such as "Listen to the words of the elders," it is observed in common experience that the injunction to hear the sentence culminates in the knowledge of its meaning. [Reply: No, because the intent in such cases is merely the instruction to listen to some particular sentence serving as a landmark on the path—like a tree—and we observe that this is not always the case.

Furthermore, in some cases, the purposefulness of an instruction consisting of hearing a statement is accepted as being directed toward the meaning only out of necessity; however, this is not the case here, as it is observed in common worldly experience. [Objection: But surely, through scriptural passages such as "He who, indeed, [uses] a mantra whose seer, meter, and deity are unknown," and through Smṛti texts such as "That which is recited without knowing the seer and the meter, being uncomprehended," the knowledge of the meaning is established as something that must necessarily be accomplished by stating the defects in the opposite case.

It is stated that in the absence of that [knowledge], study is fruitless, whereas in its presence, the attainment of all human goals occurs: "This man is a mere pillar, a bearer of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning; he who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness and, with his sins shaken off by knowledge, goes to the world of Brahman. Therefore, the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas is mandatory (*vaidha*). This is not so.

Just as for one who has reached the age of passion (*rāga*), a fault is incurred by failing to engage in sexual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and so forth, while the attainment of progeny (*santati*) and other benefits is recorded in the Smṛtis as the fruit resulting from performing it according to the rule—so too would it be here. Therefore, the statement "one should know these [details] in each mantra" is intended to mean that at the time of performance, one must recollect the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes for each individual mantra. For this very reason, the prohibition against using a mantra whose seer and other details are unknown (*avidita-ārṣeya*) refers only to that much.

Therefore, since the praise of the knowledge of meaning through such passages as "He who has studied [the Veda] is a mere post, and he who deliberates on the sacrifice [without understanding it] is likewise" encourages spontaneous engagement, and since this knowledge of meaning is necessarily required, one should not assume that the injunction for study extends so far as to include that knowledge—even within the context of a ritual injunction. This is because [the injunction] is independent [of such knowledge], because an injunction remains indifferent toward what is already established by other means, and because even if it were to extend that far, it would not terminate in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by itself.

As for the objection raised by some: since the injunction to study extends as far as the knowledge of the meaning—on account of such scriptural passages as, "Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher, according to the rules, and having returned at the conclusion of the duties to the teacher, performing righteous acts in his household while reciting his own portion of the Veda in a pure place," and so forth; and on account of Smṛti texts such as, "Having studied, one should bathe"—the knowledge of the meaning, which consists of the Self, is also employed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent of ritual action, being for the sake of that action; therefore, [the Self] is to be seen and heard.

Since the Self—declared as the object of inquiry in such passages as "It should be reflected upon, It should be meditated upon; It is to be sought, It is to be desired to be known"—is established as a subordinate element of ritual action (karmaśeṣatva) by not contradicting its inherent fitness for refinement (*saṃskāryatva*), just like rice that is to be pounded; and since statements such as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman" declare that even one subject to karma is indeed Brahman; and since universal authorship (*viśvakartṛtva*) is possible through the medium of karma; and since, when there is a conflict between what is already established and what must be postulated, it is logical to adopt the established; and since the individual soul (*jīva*), having attained the status of agent in rituals, is fit for refinement for the sake of those very rituals—this being the case while the Vedānta texts have the individual soul as their primary referent—[the Upanishads do not teach a separate, disembodied Self].

Since there is no possibility of a scripture whose subject matter is an Īśvara distinct from that [Veda], for what could this single scripture and its sequential order be postulated? That argument, too, is refuted by the fact that [the texts] conclude merely with the acquisition of the syllables. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras, by using such expressions as "having studied" (*adhītya*) and "having returned home" (*abhisamāvṛtya*), does not assign the knowledge of meaning to the status of being a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣatva*); for the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* rests merely upon the identity of the agent and so forth. Even if such an assignment were made, meditation (*upāsanā*) is indeed something other than the knowledge of meaning required for the performance of rituals.

The knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts consists of this very nature [of Brahman]. Furthermore, the Self to be meditated upon is established by Scripture itself as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), and is not merely a conceptual construction. Moreover, the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the individual soul and Brahman—just like the coordination between non-sentient matter and Brahman—is for another purpose, as it would otherwise contradict their identity. And let the injunction of such knowledge stand as it is; even so, there is no contradiction.

Since the one to be propitiated, like the agent, must be investigated as being for the sake of the ritual action (*karman*), and since it is established by scripture that he is distinct from that which is subject to *karman*, the existence of a separate section (*kāṇḍa*) for the investigation of that [divinity] is established. Even though, in this context, the knowledge of the meaning remains subordinate to the performance of the rite, the subsequent conclusion reached is that it may also, according to its respective portion, be subordinate to the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the Supreme Brahman.

Nevertheless, since it is improper to overlook the grave offense found in the first section when the objection is rooted in the very basis of the effort toward knowing the meaning, the word "mātra" (only) is used in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya with the intention that, rather than adopting a concessive argument (*anvāruhyavāda*), one must here effect a total severance of the root.

Since it is observed that the Vedic study acquired through formal recitation inherently possesses the capacity to bring about the understanding of a purposeful meaning, a person who has completed his studies, upon seeing at first glance the purposeful meanings understood from the studied Veda, spontaneously engages himself in listening to Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the inquiry into Vedic sentences aimed at determining the specific nature and details of those meanings.

In that regard, once the nature of ritual action has been ascertained, one observes that the fruits of such actions are limited and impermanent; yet, upon hearing certain Upaniṣadic passages within the portion of the Veda acquired through study, there arises an initial intuition that immortality constitutes an infinite and stable fruit. Consequently, one becomes qualified for the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, which consists of an inquiry into the Vedānta passages aimed at reaching a definitive conclusion regarding that [immortality].

Now, an objection: since the injunction to study culminates merely in the acquisition of syllables, the meaning of the Veda—even if it is perceived—cannot be the intended object of that injunction because it serves another purpose; therefore, the Veda would be meaningless. Furthermore, the injunction to study would not culminate in human welfare, and Mīmāṃsā itself could not be commenced, as its scope would be nullified by the Smṛti rule, "Having studied, one should bathe," which precludes the opportunity for such inquiry.

Dispelling the doubt as to how there could be identity [between them] and demonstrating the unity of the scripture—which consists of the Veda as the subject matter and its commentary as the exposition—by way of their having a single object, [the author] also indicates the meaning of the opening sūtra of Mīmāṃsā: "In the study... Here, by the words *adhyayana* (study), *svādhyāya-nirṇaya-vicāra* (determination and inquiry into one's own recitation), and *adhīta-veda* (one who has studied the Veda), the unity of the subject matter, the fruit, the nature, and the qualified person (*adhikārī*) of Mīmāṃsā is manifested. By the word *gṛhītasya* (of that which has been grasped), the cessation of the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*) is expressed.

The statement that [the Veda] shows a purposeful meaning is intended to make known that it culminates in the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "By its very nature" means without depending on the operation of an injunction; the phrase "by one who has mastered the meanings of words and sentences" is to be supplied. This is the underlying idea:

"Even though the Vedic study is undertaken for the sake of memorization, it illuminates [its own meaning] by itself, like fire; therefore, it is intrinsically authoritative as long as it is not sublated. (263)

Recitation, study, and meditation—each accompanied by its respective fruit prescribed in the Śruti—do not obstruct the power of the word; how much less so, then, for the purpose of apprehending it? (264)

One who, by means of a particular application (*viniyoga*), denies the fact that the Veda has meaning as its primary purpose, is refuted by self-contradiction, because he subverts the cognition of the meaning derived from that very application. (265)
The injunction to study would either have the intended meaning as its purpose or it would not;
in the first case, there is the utterance [of the Veda], but in the latter case, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) cannot even arise. (266)
Furthermore, validity here cannot be established on the grounds that its fruit is the knowledge of the object;
for if it has that as its fruit, it is valid, and if it is valid, it has that as its fruit. (267)

If the injunction (*vidhi*), even when its meaning is a mandate (*niyoga*), accepts the status of being directed toward an object, then it would likewise be for the sake of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), since it possesses the same eagerness for its own accomplishment. (268)

The Veda is a self-evident knower (*nirapekṣavedaka*); that is to say, unlike the speech of a human being, it does not depend upon another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) that has become its source. Therefore, there is no room for suspicion regarding defects in its source, and thus no obstruction to its authority—this is the sense. The purpose (*prayojana*) here is the fourfold aim of human life (*caturvarga*). The objects possessing that [purpose] are the means thereto, consisting of ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*). Here, "the state of being a means of cognition" (*avabodhitva*) refers to the evident and undeniable capacity to produce a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*). With the intention that "nothing is impossible in what is observed," the word "from observation" (*darśanāt*) is used.

Even if [the Veda] were self-evident (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), one might argue that it need not be investigated because its purpose would already be established. To this he says: "Having perceived" (*gṛhītāt*). The connection is with the temporal qualification "having seen the objects as they are presented" (*arthān āpātato 'vagamyamānān dṛṣṭvā*). The intention is that the initial, superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*) itself is what is "seen"; therefore, the removal of doubt and so forth is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The first use of the word *artha* (object/purpose) serves to establish the authority of the Śruti by excluding the useless inquiry into such things as a crow's teeth. The latter [use], however, indicates that the superficial cognition acts as an impeller by generating an interest in investigating its own object. "Nothing whatsoever—whether already cognized or not yet cognized—should be investigated."
Thus, even the objection has been refuted by the statement that [the object] is known at the very first moment.

[Objection: But surely the superficial understanding [of the meaning] arises from the very nature of the word *yajati*; if that were so, it would occur even for those who have not mastered the language. Nor is there a rule here that such understanding belongs only to those who have mastered the language, because even in the case of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), where the injunction regarding the grasping of syllables ends as with the primary rite (*aṅgin*), that [understanding] is impossible. Furthermore, since the uniformity of the injunction applies equally to the study of the subsidiaries, there is no specific reason for the study of the subsidiaries to extend up to the comprehension of the meaning. To this we reply: For him, the refined language itself has been practiced since childhood. At that time, however, that superficial understanding of it would indeed arise for him spontaneously. (270)

If this is so even when studying the Veda without its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), how much more so when studying it with them? One who has attained an initial understanding of the meaning of the Vedic text should direct his attention toward an initial understanding of the meaning of the auxiliary sciences. (271)
And some wise men, having attained an initial understanding born from the words of those seeking their welfare, indeed proceed to engage in critical inquiry. (272)

Some, however, maintain that by grasping the syllables of the members [of the syllogism] in a form suitable for assisting the limbs, one practices the state of possessing knowledge of the meaning; they hold that this has a visible purpose and is easy to accomplish. (273)

Let it be granted that this is a superficial understanding; however, even if there were knowledge distinct from that, let it be established by other branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*). To this, the reply is given: "In its true nature," and so forth. The sense is that determining the specific form distinguished from what was stated in the opponent's position is the result here, which cannot be accomplished by others. By the phrase "consisting of the investigation of Vedic sentences," the body of Mīmāṃsā is manifested as being distinguished from other branches of learning. The statement that Mīmāṃsā consists of investigation is due to a metaphorical identification with it, or because the word "investigation" (*vicāra*) is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

The statement that "one has studied the Vedas" is intended to show that there remains no further duty regarding the sphere of ritual injunctions; it is also intended as a reason based on the fact that [the person] possesses a superficial understanding. The word "person" (puruṣa) contains a reason, namely, "because of the desire for a purpose. "By himself"—that is, by his own will independently of injunctions. For one who, when a superficially useful object appears, desires its definitive determination and proceeds toward the means to achieve it, an injunction is indeed unnecessary. (274)
That inquiry is established as the cause for determining one's own desired object through positive and negative concomitance; for even in that case, an injunction would be fruitless.
Upon perceiving treasures, jewels, and the like, those who desire them proceed toward the investigation of their true nature entirely without being prompted by another. (276)
Therefore, neither the inquiry nor its sequence is established here by scriptural injunction;
otherwise, the second [inquiry] would be justified merely through the perception of defects.

Even though one might engage [in study] spontaneously, this engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and relying upon them is intended to exclude independence from a teacher. Otherwise, there would be no fault in failing to act; but that is not so, because the very absence of the certainty dependent on him and the engagement in what is beneficial which relies upon him constitutes a fault. With this in mind, it is also said: "He who, having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, neglects inquiry, forgets his own exertion, and falls away from the goal."

[Objection: If inquiry (*vicāra*) were thus not sanctioned by scripture, how could one engage in *mīmāṃsā* when the opportunity for it is blocked by injunctions such as "having studied, one should bathe" (*adhītya snāyāt*), since withdrawal from residence in the teacher’s house—which consists of suffering—is already naturally obtained? For in this context, only immediate succession (*ānantarya*) would be the enjoined matter. [Reply: Not so. Here, what is enjoined is precisely the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of bathing accompanied by the observances and the return [from the teacher]. Otherwise, because the immediate succession following withdrawal is also naturally obtained, it too would be non-enjoined.

Furthermore, even if reflection (*vicāra*) were mandatory, how could there be any occasion for it? If you argue that it is because the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*, we say no; for even in the *śruti*, it is stated: "having studied" (*adhītya*) and "having returned home" (*abhisamāvṛtya*). If you claim that in those cases the intention is merely to express a common agent and immediate sequence, and not immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then why should it not be the same in the case of the *smṛti*? Nor can it be restricted that the word "studying" (*adhyayana*) in the *śruti* extends up to the comprehension of the meaning, while in the *smṛti* it extends only up to the grasping of the syllables.

If it is argued that this would be like the rule "that which has been studied," etc., we say no, because there is a distinction based on contradiction and non-contradiction. Suppose, then, that both Śruti and Smṛti merely restate the study [of the Veda] as being for the sake of understanding its meaning; in that case, the injunction for the ritual bath (*snāna*) would not obstruct the opportunity for the scripturally mandated inquiry (*vicāra*). If this is so, then the injunctions for the ritual bath and so forth—which, while prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), are nevertheless mandatory—would likewise not obstruct the opportunity for hearing (*śravaṇa*), just as they do not obstruct the acquisition of wealth necessary for one's own livelihood.
Those injunctions for the bath and other rites, which desire performance only after knowledge is attained, naturally embrace the very Mīmāṃsā pertaining to their own subject matter. (278)

Moreover, in this matter, those who do not know the specific measurements, the constituent parts, the sequence, the agent, and so forth, are not even capable of correctly understanding a single rule for ritual bathing. (279)
Out of necessity, one engages in study and such activities without prior deliberation;
however, since there is an alternative course regarding the ritual bath (snāna), that [necessity-based] course should not be adopted when another is available. (280)
And since it is authorized in all cases that one's own limb does not act as an intervention,
therefore, in this matter, the intervention by the Mīmāṃsā does not constitute a contradiction.

Alternatively, there is no contradiction even if the study and the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) follow immediately one after the other. If it is argued that there is a contradiction because for those who have not investigated the nature of *dharma*, the performance of subsequent rites would be impossible, we say no; for even after the ceremonial bath, as long as the investigation continues, the performance [of duties] is possible—just as it was for a religious student (*brahmacārin*) when his well-wishers urged him on. Nor does performance based on the words of well-wishers contradict the principle regarding "those who are not Śūdras" (*apaśūdra-naya*), because well-wishers incite one toward those specific duties appropriate to the individual, and because prohibitions such as "one should not teach him the *dharma*" are observed.

If it is argued that the study of Mīmāṃsā would be useless since the performance [of rituals] could be accomplished otherwise, that is not so; for its necessity is established by the possibility of doubt regarding the opposite [view], by the desire to know the source [of the texts], and by faith in such things as the authority of others, the lack of dependence on others, and the fame of the teacher. In this very way, the continuity of the tradition from predecessors to successors is established. If it is argued that someone might, out of laziness, rely solely on written documents and the like as the only means of knowledge, what of it? For others who are not lazy can still engage in the study of the scriptures.

If it is argued that for one who has completed his bath and is listening [to the Vedas], there might be an obstruction to his own duty (*svadharma*) due to activities for the sake of the teacher, we say: no; because those activities are prompted by the injunction for Vedic study and cease once that is accomplished. As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*:

"For this injunction is intended to prescribe the rules for the means of grasping the syllables; the Smṛti declares that the status of religious duties remains in force until that grasping is complete."
"After the Veda has been studied, the knowledge of its meaning arises spontaneously; however, that [spontaneous knowledge] is neither study itself nor a motivator for religious duties (*dharma*).

If this is so, for what purpose should the teacher teach Mīmāṃsā? Is it for the sake of gain and the like, or for the sake of *dharma*? For one who is occupied with the duties of a householder, what opportunity is there to listen? And what opportunity does the teacher have to speak? For him who seeks a livelihood, there is the time for acquiring wealth.

If this is argued, then hearing [the Veda] would also be like other activities for visible purposes that are permitted by injunction; moreover, even for a householder, there is some time for inquiry in the form of [listening to] histories (*itihāsa*) and so forth. At that time, Mīmāṃsā too would be employed as being conducive to its own purpose through those supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the Veda. Furthermore, they divide the study of the Veda (*vedābhyāsa*) in this way:
"First, the acquisition of the Veda, then inquiry, practice, recitation, and the giving of it to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold."

The time for hearing [the scriptures] is required even for someone who has acquired wealth and so forth through family lineage or by chance; for such a person, there must also be a specific time for that acquisition. Furthermore, householders and others who have not yet reflected upon their duties according to their caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*) are seen in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as listeners of those respective duties. Even for a householder, dwelling with a teacher for two months each year for the sake of superior knowledge has been authorized by some.

As it is restated: "When he has completed his residence [with a teacher], he should live for two months every year in the teacher's family with a concentrated mind, desiring further study," says Śvetaketu, adding, "For by this method, I studied more than before. Now, one might object: "But here there is a contradiction with those scriptures, for when the residence is completed, the obligatory duties are heard of, such as the *agnihotra* and guests," and so on—by which Āpastamba states his own view. True.

By that [statement] as well, only a continuous residence of two months in the teacher’s family (*gurukula*) at that time is prohibited; however, the opportunity for inquiry—which, like the case of the speaker, results in success for the listener—is not set aside.

Let it be granted that inquiry follows study and that it pertains to the entirety of the subject matter by virtue of natural inclination (*rāga*); nevertheless, if inquiry and its sequence were not prescribed by rule (*avaidhatva*), they would proceed according to one's own whim.
Because of the non-occurrence and the occurrence [of duality], it is said that "attainment occurs therein. || 282 ||
Because investigation is difficult to abandon, because simultaneity is contradictory, and because faults are seen in a deviation from the order, this sequence indeed follows the Sūtra. (283)

In this context, "in the Veda or in Mīmāṃsā" means when one proceeds according to one's own will. Here, "injunction regarding action" (karmavidhi) refers either to the impulsion toward optional rites (kāmyakarman) or the performance of such rites; or, because there is no distinction made, it includes obligatory rites (nityakarman) and so forth as well. By the term "essential nature" (svarūpa), it is indicated that the application [of the rite] as an auxiliary to the higher knowledge (paravidyā)—for one who has renounced its fruit—has not been considered here. For that indeed must be examined in the section on the means (sādhanalakṣaṇa); for upon its determination, one would understand that it culminates in an infinite and stable fruit.

Alternatively, the sense is that although the fact that mere actions yield results that are both meager and unstable has not been examined in some places; by the phrase "having been determined," the necessity of the determination of action having already occurred is intended. This has been elaborated upon in the *Tātparya-tūlikā*:
"In this regard, this obligatory action cannot be ignored;
for it follows a person in all states of existence."
Whether one desires worldly enjoyment or seeks liberation, whatever person may be taken as an example,
for all of them there is indeed the undertaking of manifold actions.
The obligatory daily rites, the occasional rites, and those that are prohibited must always be examined by everyone who desires to avoid the resulting transgression.
Those who do not fear sufferings should not engage in such deliberation;
however, it is clear that for others, this much action must indeed be examined.
But optional action (kāmya-karma) is capable of providing enjoyment even without Brahman;
however, Brahman does not attain the capacity for liberation without action.
For it will be stated later that "there is a requirement for all [stages of life], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth";
thus, even reflection on a single portion of the Veda is declared to be the motivator for the whole.
"Therefore, since it must necessarily be considered, karma alone is investigated first.

This means that having observed that the fruits of actions are minor and unstable, one determines this clearly through the meaning of those very scriptural passages. For, in defining the nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma, Agnihotra, and so forth, there would be a classification of the heaviness or lightness of the resulting heavens according to the means employed. Furthermore, once it is determined by the statement "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the Agniṣṭoma" that the Jyotiṣṭoma takes the form of the Agniṣṭoma, the determination of the spatial and temporal limitations of the heaven achieved thereby is made by such passages as "as much as one attains by the Agniṣṭoma."

In this regard, even the injunction for repetition is an indicator that the fruit is small for one who does not repeat [the rite]. Furthermore, regarding the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), a gradation of fruits according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life is recorded in traditional law (*smṛti*) for certain qualified persons, such as in the passage beginning, "The *prājāpatya* [fruit] belongs to Brāhmaṇas."

For once the nature of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices—the Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, and so forth—is understood, it is seen that the Vaiśvadeva and others have limited results, as indicated by such statements as: "This indeed is the measure of the Vaiśvadeva," "This is indeed the lowest of these; therefore, the subsequent ones become superior. Consequently, regarding the passage, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible," the intended meaning is understood to be merely that the fruit is to be enjoyed for a long time.

Although this quality of having inexhaustible fruit could be led to as a remote consequence by virtue of being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), nevertheless, because there is no intention to convey that meaning here, it is not so interpreted. Thus, only when the nature of the ritual action—which has limited fruits and consists of *soma* as its oblation—is determined, does the restriction [of the fruit] in passages such as "We have drunk the *soma*" arise from Smṛti texts such as "Immortality is the state [lasting] until the dissolution of all beings."

Furthermore, once the distinctions in the nature of the ritual acts that accomplish various fruits such as heaven (*svarga*) and self-sovereignty (*svarājya*) are established, the limited nature of that which is designated by the word "heaven" therein is also established. Moreover, the determination of the gradations among fruits—as seen in passages such as "whatever sacrifice one studies"—is derived solely from the ascertainment of the heavy or light nature of the ritual acts themselves. And because the nature of the ritual act that propitiates the object of worship is determined to be subject to origination and destruction, there is the perception of the instability of its results, such as union (*sāyujya*) with that deity.

Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating that the *Śārīraka*—whose subject matter is the inquiry into Brahman from which all obstacles have been removed—is a specific branch of *Mīmāṃsā* distinguished by its unique nature and fruit from other branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and for the sake of establishing the particularity of what is to be determined, the passage beginning with "furthermore, in the study... was stated. Here, the word "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) denotes the fruit known primarily through the end of the three Vedas (*trayyanta*); by this, there is an exclusion of the secondary fruits of the modern [Smṛtis], such as the possession of food, as well as the fruits of injunctions regarding meditations (*dṛṣṭi*) formed by other connections. It has been established that the immortality mentioned in the ritual section (*karmabhāga*) is merely relative.

However, because no contradiction is observed and because it is supported by certain portions of the Vedānta that have been determined to be consistent, this [view] is not like the former; with the intention of making this clear, it was stated: "because there is an initial cognition of an infinite and stable fruit. For here, it is not possible to postulate qualities such as being limited or unstable through inferences based on its being a "fruit" and so forth, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Because it is unconditioned (*anavaccheda*), the embodied one (*śārīra*) here is the one whose body is the universe; the scripture (*śāstra*) which proceeds with reference to him is called *Śārīraka*.

For it will be stated in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*: "That very [Self] is the unconditioned embodied Self (*śārīra-ātman*); for this reason, the scripture which proceeds with reference to this Supreme Brahman is designated by the learned as *Śārīraka*. Thus, that very [scripture] is the *Mīmāṃsā*, i.e., the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*; [the word *tatra* means] "in that [work]. The meaning is: "it occupies itself" (or "engages") with its own subject matter through the intent to understand it, but it does not occupy itself with some other preceding topic.

The sense is that once the immediate succession to the inquiry into Brahman is established by reasoning, the immediate succession to the scripture whose subject matter is that [Brahman] would also be established.

The fact that [the Veda] is to be grasped, its status as a fruit, its possession of meaning, and the investigation of its entirety arising from passion—all this has been stated here as unprecedented. (284)

And likewise, the Vedānta texts demonstrate that the fruit of mere ritual action is perishable, whereas the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is imperishable: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes. That becomes for him merely finite. For the impermanent cannot be attained through the impermanent. These forms of sacrifice are indeed frail rafts. Having examined the worlds acquired by action, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created."

To gain knowledge of that, one should approach a teacher alone, carrying fuel in his hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. To him, who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint, that wise teacher should fully declare that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence, by which one knows the Imperishable, the True Person.

The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; he does not see death again. He sees that One; as one who sees, he does not see death. He becomes the Lord of himself (*svarāṭ*). Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going. [He sees] the Self as distinct...

"And considering him the impeller, being favored by Him, he thereafter attains immortality," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of the meagerness of the fruits of action and the like, only an indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been seen; however, for the sake of strengthening a conviction that contradicts what is heard [in scripture], the attainment [of the fruit] must also be stated. Furthermore, the definition of the nature of action here is for the purpose of removing obstacles to spontaneous engagement. But the cause [for such engagement] is simply the immediate perception of infinite and stable fruits; from where does this arise? To this he says: "In that manner" (*tathā*). The meaning is: "so that this Sūtra may also have that same purpose, in accordance with the manner already described. The particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).

In this context, the mention of "wasting away" (*kṣati*) and "not wasting away" (*akṣayi*) is indicative of smallness and so forth. The citation of the passage beginning with "Just as... (*tadyathā*) serves to increase one's faith regarding another matter that is not explicitly stated, by means of a confirmed corroboration. "The world" (*loka*) means that which is to be seen (*lokya*), i.e., that which is to be experienced. If it were taken in the sense of a physical location, there would be no syntactical connection with the terms "here" (*iha*) and "thereafter" (*amutra*). "Accumulated through action" (*karmacitaḥ*) means obtained through worldly actions.

By the non-specific statement "one who has accumulated merit," [the author] says "it is finite" (antavat) in order to dispel the delusion that even that which is accomplished through the dharma of cessation is subject to decay. Since this follows from the meaning of the words already employed, and because the finitude of the nature of the action itself is not what is required to be stated here, the statement regarding its finitude is made by way of its result.

This is because of the preceding statement, "O Gārgī, he who, without knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years [is miserable]," and also because of the subsequent statement, "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable"; and once it is established that the term "finite" (*antavat*) refers to ritual action devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, it is easy to understand that the same reference applies to the phrase "those who have accumulated merit" (*puṇyacitaḥ*) and those that follow.

Just as there is a distinction in the fruits—such as heaven or self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)—among actions devoid of knowledge, so too there could be a distinction in the fruits of certain obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*). Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is prescribed] for all desires," one might argue that the cited passage refers only to the majority of cases. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). The meaning is: "by those which are unstable," that is, by those enjoined as means to unstable fruits. Through the connection with the portion of the sentence, "That is stable" (*dhruvaṃ tat*), the absence of the status of having a permanent fruit (*nitya-phala-arthatva*) is pervaded [established].

He confirms the absence of the attainment of a permanent fruit for those who possess the rule of returning, because it is impossible for them to uproot all karma—[stating], "The rafts... [They are] unstable, incapable of leading one to the further shore of darkness; in these [rafts], the eighteenfold inferior action is prescribed. "Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good, they surely return again to old age and death"—for here indeed is the flaw in the statement.

Now, the author states a passage that summarizes—both in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtras and by combining them—the fact that the certainty regarding the absence of eternal fruits as the result of ritual actions is a cause for world-weariness (nirveda), and that the knowledge of Brahman possesses infinite fruit: "Having examined... (parīkṣya).

This scripture has been explained in the *Sāra*: "A Brāhmaṇa—one devoted to the study of the Vedas—having examined through the inquiry into action (*karmamīmāṃsā*) the worlds acquired by ritual action as being perishable by nature because they are subject to decay, and having attained detachment, thinking 'The Uncreated—the eternal Supreme Person—is not attained through the created—namely, ritual action,' he should, for the sake of knowing That, approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a knower of the Upanishads (*vedāntavedin*), and established in Brahman."

[He is] one who has directly realized the nature of the Supreme Person. And that teacher, for him who has approached him properly, spoke—that is, he declared—that Brahma-vidyā by means of which specific knowledge one may know that Imperishable, True, Supreme Person. This is because there is no syntactic connection in the statements "he should approach the teacher alone" and "that wise man spoke to him," and because [the action] had not been previously established [as a duty]. Furthermore, the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is prescribed even in the context of an injunction, according to the rule: "In Vedic usage, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [may be used for all three times]."

In this context, regarding the portion that restates what is established by logic (*nyāya*), the word *brāhmaṇa*—though denoting a caste—is stated as "one devoted to the study of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsarataḥ*) in order to indicate that its scope extends to all three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*). This is achieved through a non-abandoning metaphorical indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), which conveys the sense of one who has studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*), thereby serving as a means for the examination of the subject matter at hand. They also etymologize the word *brāhmaṇa* as "one who breathes (*aṇati*) Brahman. The phrase "by virtue of being the object of worship" (*ārādhyakṣayitvena*) is an elliptical expression indicating the exhaustion of merit (*sukṛta*). The mention of "by means of the Mīmāṃsā of Action" (*karmamīmāṃsayā*) is a statement implied by the sense of the passage.

Because the word *akṛta* (uncreated) conforms to the masculine gender and by the power of the supplementary context (*vākyaśeṣa*), the Supreme Person is shown to be the substantive. Here, since it is impossible to negate the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the uncreated by means of the word "is not," and because [the phrase] does not connect with the word "by action" (*karmaṇā*), and because a negation of its origination is not required, the meaning is that this is for the sake of a clear understanding of that [nature]. In this context, "having fuel in hand" refers to Brahman.

Some say that [the statement] is for the purpose of hearing the Vidyā, for the sake of the intermediate rite of initiation (*upaneyana*), and for the sake of indicating the meaning of the inner [signs]. For it is said in the *Chāndogya* to Jābāla by Gautama: "A non-Brāhmaṇa is not fit to declare this; bring fuel, my dear, and I will initiate you. Others, however, say: since Jābāla was already uninitiated, the initiation is appropriate; whereas elsewhere, the mention of "having fuel in hand" is intended as an indication of having one's hands not empty.

For it is observed in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā: "They, with fuel in their hands, returned in the forenoon; having brought them near without yet initiating them (upanīya), he spoke this. And in the speech of Prajāpati, regarding the single Indra who returns with fuel in his hand amidst many questions, the phrase "he came again" is repeated. Indeed, a formal initiation (*upanayana*) is neither seen nor intended there on multiple occasions. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras will state only this much: "Because of the reference to the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*)."

Since one who has merely studied a single branch of the Veda is called a *śrotriya*, and since the mere study of one's own portion of scripture (*svādhyāya*) does not assist in the present context, the term *śrotriya* here is shown to refer to a *śrotriya* who is "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*), specifically one who knows the Vedānta. He states that the term *brahmaniṣṭha* (one established in Brahman) is intended to signify both the capacity for clear exposition and the highest degree of assistance through unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*): namely, "one who has directly realized the nature of the Supreme Person."

Because it is stated, "to one whose mind is tranquil" (*praśāntacittāya*), "tranquility" (*śama*) here refers to the cessation of the activities of the external organs. Here, tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) serve the purpose of providing the attentiveness necessary for hearing [the teaching]. However, in passages such as "one who knows thus, being tranquil and self-restrained," they serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*) for one who has already understood the meaning through hearing. Regarding the phrase "by which" (*yena*), since a change in gender would be forced, it indicates that the opening statement is general—namely, that it qualifies knowledge (*vidyā*).

And thus they employ [the following] as a refutation in that context: "Was there a sublation of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) or a sublation of external objects (bāhyārthabhaṅga), and so forth? With the intention of excluding Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña by means of the two terms "imperishable" (akṣara) and "real" (satya), which negate modification both in terms of essential nature (svarūpa) and intrinsic being (svabhāva), he says: "the Supreme Person" (paramapuruṣam). The qualification "in reality" (tattvataḥ) is used to cast aside speech that is subject to doubt or error, as well as speech that is incomplete.

The traditional authorities (smaranti) declare that even a teacher becomes a non-teacher if he desists from [imparting] what has been heard. To dispel the misconception regarding the meaning of the conduct (*vṛtta*), he says: "he should proclaim" (*prabrūyāt*). It is cumbersome to follow the grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*) by subverting the injunction perceived at the beginning through the word "should approach" (*abhigacchet*); therefore, with the intention that the word "proclaimed" (*provāca*) cannot be construed as referring to the past tense, he says: "He [should go] to the guru alone. The restrictive nature (*niyamavidhitva*) is indicated by the particle "alone" (*eva*). Regarding the word "proclaimed":

He states another reason for its being a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, "because it is not otherwise established" (*aprāptatvāt*). Although someone might engage [in this practice] out of passion due to a desire for gain and so forth, nevertheless, this is enjoined as a duty (*dharma*) for a teacher who is free from such motives with respect to a worthy disciple; thus there is no contradiction. He also mentions that the *liṭ* (perfect tense) specifically teaches the sense of the *liṅ* (optative/injunctive)—namely, "even in the case of an injunction" (*vidhāv api*).

Intending to show that the knowledge of Brahman, by virtue of leading to the attainment of Brahman denoted by the word "supreme," leads to the attainment of the eternal and unsurpassed bliss that is the subject of the context, he says: "the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). To dispel the suspicion that even one who has attained Brahman might return again—on the analogy of [attaining] heaven and so forth, or based on such passages as "these worlds"—he says: "not again. Here, "death" (*mṛtyu*) refers to dying; or it may refer to what is stated in such passages as "death is held by the wise to be delusion" (*moha*); etc.

The sense is that when evils are destroyed without remainder, nothing undesirable—characterized by death and so forth—would exist, and following the ways of the world would be a matter of one’s own choice. In this context, the vision of that [Self] alone is either the means or the fruit. This is because the statement, "There is no consciousness after departing," occurs within the section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).

By the words of the Elder, he dispels the suspicion that the liberated one might suffer a loss of knowledge and clarifies the cessation of death and its effects with the phrase "he does not see. Even though the liberated one may perceive the suffering of others at that time or his own past suffering, those two do not constitute adversity for him, because they lack the qualities of being inherent to himself or being present. For this is indeed observed even during the state of bondage. However, in that state, the experience of suffering due to the suffering of others and the grieving for what has passed are caused solely by the limiting adjunct of karma.

By the passage beginning, "He sees neither disease nor suffering; he sees everything," it is established that even when specific things are being seen, there is no perception of anything contrary to oneself. Here, the term *paśyaḥ* (the seer) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) who perceives Brahman, as is evident from the context of the same section where it says, "he sees that One. Furthermore, the term *paśyaḥ* can also apply to the Supreme Self based on its etymological derivation (*paśyati* = he sees), as seen in such usages as "the Seer sees the one being seen. Since everything is perceived as having Brahman as its essence, there is no contradiction between "seeing that One" and "seeing all."

It is not merely that there is a state of effortless omniscience; rather, other kings possess worlds subject to decay, rooted in the karma prescribed by tradition, and are dependent upon the Lord. Intending to show that one attains independent action through the cessation of such dependence on the Lord, he says: "He is self-ruling" (*sa svarāṭ*). For this very reason, the lexicographical statement that "self-ruling" (*svarāṭ*) means "independent" (*svatantra*) is not contradicted, even while remaining within the state of dependence on the Lord.

The scriptural denial of other means to immortality confirms that the statement regarding immortality being achieved through ritual action (*karman*) has another purpose; this is shown by the phrase "him alone" (*tameva*). Furthermore, because the reference here is to the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) as qualified by His attributes and manifestations, the position of the opponents—that liberation occurs for the individual soul (*jīva*) alone through the cognition of its own undifferentiated nature or through the cognition of another person—is refuted. He states "separately" (*pṛthak*) to show that the idea that the cognitions of identity or difference are the causes of immortality is rejected by the scripture itself.

The meaning is: "from that," namely from the meditation on separateness which consists of worship (*upāsana*). "Favored by him" (*tena juṣṭaḥ*) means made an object of affection by the Impeller. By this, it is stated that the stable grace of the Supreme is itself the gateway to the fruit. For it is also heard in scripture: "By the grace of the Creator. Now, one might object: here, the meditation on both "the Self" and "the Impeller" together has been taught; therefore, it appears that knowledge of something other [than the Self] is also a cause of liberation. True; however, that does not negate the primacy of the Impeller.

Even in passages such as, "A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned inward," the reference is to the vision of the individual soul (jīva) as a subordinate limb of the higher knowledge (paravidyā). The word "etc. is intended to reinforce what has been stated by other scriptural passages as well, according to the maxim that "the majority [of evidence] is stronger."

But surely, from the mere study of the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), it is already known that ritual acts have results such as heaven, that heaven and the like are perishable, and that the meditation on Brahman has immortality as its fruit. Consequently, one who desires liberation should proceed directly to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). What need is there for an inquiry into Dharma? If this were so, then one would not even proceed to the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (the Vedānta inquiry), since everything would be known through the study of the Veda with its auxiliaries alone. True.

If it is argued that while an initial intuition certainly exists, nevertheless, because only a sentence supported by reasoning (nyāya) determines the true meaning, even an intuitively grasped object does not transcend doubt and error; therefore, for the sake of its definitive determination, an inquiry into Vedāntic sentences must be undertaken—then please consider that for that very same reason, an inquiry into Dharma must also be undertaken.

Indeed, how can there be the possibility of ignorance, concealment, the perception of difference, bondage, its cessation, or the means of removal in Brahman—which is non-dual, eternally liberated, devoid of attributes, and whose very nature is the illumination of itself alone as the adversary of ignorance and the like? Furthermore, since bondage is produced by karma, according to the principle of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), it would be a specific karma alone that serves as the remover; and since there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating that "knowledge proceeds from that [karma]," the knowledge that removes [bondage] must also be accomplished through karma.

And how could action, which by its very nature is binding, be of use to one who desires liberation? From what source and of what kind is the impurity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and from what source and of what kind is its purity? Furthermore, while action is seen to be a cause for knowledge—which depends on the authority of the means of valid cognition—it is not observed to be a cause even for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is dependent upon the favorability of the object. If the duty of renunciation (*nivṛttidharma*) were not a cause of liberation, there would follow the consequence of the futility of the scriptural injunctions concerning it. Dispelling such spikes of doubt, [the author] demonstrates—both by summarizing what has been explicitly stated and what is implied—the intended meaning with the words "this" (*etad iti*).
The condensation of what has been elaborated, and the elaboration of what has been condensed—this is what is meant; there is no meditative concentration for one who is distracted. (294)

By the statement that it is "covering," its nature as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is indicated. For that very reason, it is possible for Brahman, when conditioned by it, to function as the material cause (*upādāna*). Because Brahman is slightly veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and the like are logically established. The term "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*) is used to indicate the similarity to the perception of distinctions such as other persons seen in a dream. In the phrase "the perception of distinction alone," the perception of distinctions such as agency, enjoyership, divinity, and humanity—even within the cognition of the identity of the body and the self—is included by implication.

By this, the doubt that "the knowledge of the self as distinct from the body alone is sufficient; what is the use of the knowledge of Brahman qualified by attributes such as non-agency? is dispelled. Furthermore, action itself does not possess inherent binding power, because it merely serves as a common instrumental cause for bringing about what is already perceived [through ignorance].
