Therefore, since even action—which is established through the delusion of difference—is ultimately unreal, and its binding nature occurs solely through the medium of the delusion of difference, the intended meaning of the restrictive statement here is that there exists nothing real whatsoever that binds which cannot be removed by knowledge.

To this, he replies with the words "And bondage... [in the verse], suggesting that in your own view, the establishment of the real from the unreal does indeed exist. The point is that as long as bondage remains unsublated, there is room for doubt regarding its reality or unreality, and it would contradict the eternal liberation of Brahman. To avoid the logical refutation based on the principle of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), he says "And that... [in the verse]; for the cessation of sin through virtuous action is established only through delusion.

Therefore, with the intention that the entire range from the root cause, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), up to bondage, is to be sublated solely by the non-dual cognition independent of ritual action—according to the analogy of the rope-snake which is independent of the mantra—it is said, "by knowledge alone" (*jñānenaiva*). To the objection that even if there is no combination of ritual action (*karma*) with the means of liberation, [the latter] might still arise due to the force of traditional scripture (*smṛti*), he says: "it is the remover" (*nivartakam*). The underlying thought is as follows: the subject under discussion is produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is a sublatively effective cognition, just like an uncontroverted one.

Alternatively, the probandum may be "not produced by karma. As for the Smṛti, it has another purpose. By the force of the reasoning stated by himself, the fact that [knowledge] is caused by the Veda follows by elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). With the intention that the application of karma mentioned by others is devoid of proof, he says: "Of this very [knowledge]," etc. "Of this" means of that which has non-duality as its object and possesses instruments other than karma along with their auxiliaries. "Of this very" means of that which is itself capable of subverting what is contrary to its own object.

The statement that [knowledge] is produced by the Vedic word (*vākya*) is intended to exclude other causes that possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He explains—by the words "in the desire to know" (*vividiṣāyām*)—that it is possible for sacrifices and the like to have distinct fruits due to their separate application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*), based on the scriptural text, "They seek to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*). The phrase "according to the literal text" (*yathāśrutāyām*) is intended as a restrictive emphasis.

In this context, the word "tu" (but) excludes the notion of being an immediate cause. The indirect interpretation—such as "he desires to kill with a sword"—is adopted only when a contradiction would otherwise arise. Now, he explains the turbidity of the mind and so forth, beginning with the words "And that" (*sa ceti*). For *dharma*, other effects such as the cessation of sin have been prescribed. Furthermore, the fact that *śraddhā* has another effect in the form of *sattva* is established by the scriptures. And the statement that *sattva* is a means to knowledge may be understood in a mediated sense. The increase of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are the roots of sin, constitutes the turbidity of the mind. Through *dharma*, these are dispelled, resulting in the purification and clarity of *sattva*.
For one whose mind is purified by actions, there arises a favorable inclination toward reality;
therefore, the desire to ascertain that reality would likewise be born of action alone. (295)

Now, the first word "iti" signifies "because"; the meaning is that [the means] is established in accordance with the natural sense of the Śruti along with its supporting texts (upabṛṃhaṇa). "Having intended this"—that is, having accepted it through another Śruti and Smṛti even though it is not explicitly stated in words—means that the injunction regarding the duties of renunciation (nivṛtti-dharma) achieves its purpose through such utility. With the intention that there is nothing further to be said regarding the purification of the means, he concludes with "ataḥ" (therefore).

The meaning is that there is no dependence on either action or its investigation for the purpose of acquiring or abandoning [the Self], because of the knowledge and the inquiry into that [knowledge]. Here is the summary contained in the *Tūlikā*:
"Because of contradiction, lack of authority, and the utility for the purification of the mind;
because of the scriptural statement of the cause being knowledge alone, and also by implication."
"Because it is traditionally taught that [knowledge] has tranquility (*śama*) and so forth as its constituent parts, there is no combination of knowledge and ritual action.
Knowledge born from the sentence [of scripture], awakened by the sequence of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, is the liberator.

This is because of contradiction—[the contradiction] being both in terms of essential nature and in terms of the result (as the remainder). Because of the lack of authority—because there is no evidence for ritual actions being the means to either knowledge or its fruit; or rather, because of the absence of authoritative proof [for such a claim]. By virtue of capacity—because knowledge alone is sufficient for the sublation of that which is illusory. "The combination of knowledge and ritual action" refers to the methods set forth in the three systems of thought. "Awakened" (*unnidra*) means being fully developed through the removal of obstacles.

The Shorter Conclusion (*laghusiddhānta*). Here it is said: As for what was stated—that liberation is indeed the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), and that this occurs only through the knowledge of Brahman—that is accepted. However, it must be investigated what the nature of the knowledge intended by the Vedāntic statements for the sake of removing ignorance is: is it merely the knowledge of the sentence-meaning arising from the sentence itself, or is it the knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*) rooted in that?

It cannot be the knowledge produced by the sentence, because that is established from the sentence alone even without an injunction, and because the cessation of ignorance is not observed through that much alone.
Because it is free from contradiction, well-known, and logically consistent, the objection that "the refutation must be stated against this position" is now addressed. (296)
The Refutation of the Duality of the Probandum and the Means of Proof.

Here, first of all, the refutation of the duality of the probandum and the means of proof is generally accepted through the passage beginning with "that which has been stated," in order to shatter the opposing position. Indeed, there remains a disagreement regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation, Brahman, and the knowledge thereof, due to specific differences in their respective modes. For in our own system, what is called the cessation of ignorance is the absolute eradication of that karma which obstructs the natural expansion of consciousness; and this [cessation] is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvāntara*). The aspect of the removal of the obstruction is what is described here as the "shattering of the undesirable."
The expansion of the intellect is accomplished by itself; for those who possess discernment, it is the attainment of their desired goal. (297)

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the restrictive statement (*avadhāraṇa*). Furthermore, since Brahman and its knowledge possess many aspects from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), we do not accept that there is an absence of causality for that knowledge, nor that it is combined with ritual action (*karma*), nor that it is merely assisted by such action in producing the fruit. With this intention, it was stated: "only from the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavijñānādeva*). If this is accepted, what is there to be refuted? To this, he states the disagreement regarding the mode of the knowledge that effects cessation, beginning with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

"Intended to be established" (*vidhitsitam*) means that which is desired to be enjoined as a means according to our own system, but which is intended to be produced [as a result] according to the opposing system. Thus, he analyzes what was stated in the *Tantra* with the words "of what form? (*kiṃrūpam*). The meaning is: is it as you have stated, independent of ritual action (*karman*), or as we have stated, as a subordinate member of ritual action (*karmāṅga*)? "To be discerned" (*vivecanīyam*) means that one must determine it by the elimination of one alternative through the remaining of the other alternative. He distinguishes the summarized point with the word "what? (*kim iti*).

The mention of "from the sentence" (*vākyāt*) is for the purpose of excluding that which is to be enjoined in the form of a memory whose object is the meaning of the sentence. Through connection with the sense organs, there may arise from the sentence a cognition of its own nature, as well as an inference regarding a son and so forth; to exclude those, the term "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*) is employed. The suffix *-mātra* expresses independence from means such as meditation (*dhyāna*). For another person, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is the realization of the identity of the individual self and the Supreme Self; for oneself, however, it is the cognition of the relationship between the attribute and the possessor of attributes. Therefore, the statement that [this knowledge] is the root [of liberation] is not contradictory.

The statement that [the knowledge] consists of meditation (*upāsanā*) is for the purpose of excluding [cognitive acts] such as mere reflection (*manana*). He refutes the position favored by others with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvad iti*). The meaning is: let other positions stand aside; this [position], however, is simply not the case. Intending to state the impossibility of the knowledge of the final sentence-meaning as conceived by the opponent, he reveals—indicated by the word *vidhitsita* (intended to be enjoined)—the consequence of the futility of injunctions such as "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), which would follow if the knowledge of the first sentence-meaning, accepted by everyone, were the means. This he does with the words "Of that" (*tasya iti*).

The intention [of the author] is as follows: others have indeed stated that an injunction (*vidhi*) is devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*) regarding the knowledge produced by words; for it has been said that knowledge arising from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is dependent on the object (*vastutantra*) and not dependent on the person (*puruṣatantra*), because it is impossible to perform, not perform, or perform otherwise. "From the sentence" (*vākyāt*) means, in short, from a sentence whose primary purport is its own nature (*svarūpapara*). The particle *eva* (only/alone) indicates both the independence from an injunction and the impossibility of sublated latent impressions (*bādhyavāsanā*) acting as an obstacle. "From the establishment" (*siddheḥ*) means from the production [of the knowledge].

In this context, the cognition produced by the sentence cannot be understood from that very sentence itself, because it does not enter [the meaning] either as a relation (*saṃsarga*) or as something related (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Nor can it be understood from other sentences such as "one should produce wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*), because that which is already established cannot be an object of injunction. Furthermore, its being taught as a means is unnecessary, since it is not admitted to have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because its status as a means is understood through its capacity once any imagined obstacle is removed. Therefore, the intention is that the injunction would be redundant. Nevertheless, the futility of such scriptural tradition (āmnāna) is difficult to avoid. The statement regarding the futility of injunctions also implies the futility of those scriptures which maintain that there is a category of things to be performed—such as the departure through the *brahmanāḍī* and the journey by the path of the gods (*devayāna*)—as well as those that prescribe the performance of the *ājyaprāya* and other rites.
This constitutes the refutation of the view that knowledge produced by verbal testimony is a means to liberation.

In this context, he also states the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) by saying "by that much alone" (*tāvanmātreṇa*). For a cognition that has arisen would not delay in removing ignorance by depending on anything else, such that non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) could remain unrefuted. And that [non-perception] is established for both oneself and others through perception and inference. Furthermore, what is contradicted by perception cannot be known through scripture (*śāstra*); nor is there a removal of ignorance from mere such consciousness alone, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not established—this is the intended meaning.

In this very context, Āpastamba has stated the contradiction with scripture: "The attainment of security once [the truth] is understood is contradicted by the scriptures. This means it is specifically prohibited; for a contradiction between two things of equal strength is not possible here. Furthermore, the contradiction with direct perception has been stated: "If the attainment of security occurs once [the truth] is understood, one would not experience suffering even in this world"; by this, the other [contradiction] is explained.

Nor should it be argued that as long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality has not been dispelled, the sentence does not produce the knowledge that removes ignorance; for even when such knowledge has arisen, the non-cessation of the cognition of duality for everyone all at once is no fault—just as the cognition of two moons does not cease even when the oneness of the moon is known. Furthermore, it cannot be said that what remains unceased, being cut off at its root, leads to bondage;

because it is impossible for knowledge not to arise when the causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) are present, and because we observe the arising of subverting knowledge through authoritative instruction, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, even when contrary impressions persist.

Having restated the two-fold response to the contradictions between scripture and perception, he refutes them with the words "And not... [na ceti]. To the question, "Why is there no arising of knowledge even before the hearing of the scripture that is endowed with logic, just as there is after it?", it is said: "Because of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference. The utility of the injunctions lies in the removal of obstructive latent impressions. For instances such as the confusion of directions, which do not cease through instruction or inferential signs, are eventually removed when the latent impressions are somehow severed; the sense is that it is the same in this case.

The phrase "the remover of ignorance" is stated for the purpose of excluding [the possibility that it is] a cognition of something currently being perceived; by the words "it does not produce," the contradiction with the non-perception of the cessation of ignorance is also resolved.

In this regard, the secret of the non-dual (advaita) tradition is as follows: initial knowledge does not remove ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is of an indeterminate nature. However, the cognition born of inquiry removes that portion of ignorance which generates the delusion of the reality of difference in the form of an indirect determination (*parokṣādhyavasāya*). Nevertheless, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) accumulated through the beginningless delusion of difference continues to produce such a delusion. That portion of ignorance which serves as its support is removed by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of non-duality.

Even when that [ignorance] has ceased, a certain portion of ignorance persists, supported by the karma whose effects have already begun (*prārabdhakārya*); they call that state "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). That portion also ceases either through the final experience of fruition or through self-realization. It is with reference to such distinctions in the portions of ignorance that it is said, "Indra, through his *māyās*, is perceived in many forms. Intending the cessation of the portions of *māyā* according to the sequence described, the Śruti declares: "And again at the end, there is the cessation of all *māyā*; being liberated, he is liberated. In this regard:

The second part here has been stated as belonging to ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, even by accepting that only knowledge in its indirect form (*parokṣa-rūpa*) is the remover [of ignorance], he avoids the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) by saying, "even when [knowledge] has arisen. Alternatively, it would not be logical for the all-knowing ones such as Sanaka and others to be without produced direct realization (*anutpanna-sākṣātkāra*) and yet possess ignorance; nor, for those who have produced direct realization, would there be the status of being teachers and so forth, since the appearance of disciples and the like would be impossible.

For one who possesses only indirect knowledge is not a teacher of the immediate; this is evident from the qualification, "The knowers of reality, who see the truth, will teach you knowledge. Therefore, since it is a rope with snares at both ends, [the text speaks of] the third ignorance.

He answers in accordance with the established position (*siddhānta*) by saying, "Even when [liberation] has occurred. For one who holds that there is only a single ignorance of Brahman and only a single individual soul (*jīva*), the objection might be raised: "If a single ignorance were to cease, how could there be the persistence of the delusion of difference—the locus of the term 'individual soul'—or the distinction between bondage and liberation? To indicate this restatement of the objection, the word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is used in accordance with the alternative view that manifestation is conditioned by the distinctions of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This should be construed with the phrase "all at once" (*sahasaiva*) following its cessation.

The intended meaning is that when the karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest is exhausted—being held back by a portion of residual ignorance—the delusion consisting of the perception of all duality ceases. This does not constitute a fault; for once ignorance is removed, the delusion must also cease, since it is impossible for an effect to persist without its cause.

Therefore, because delusion persists due to the presence of passion and other such views, ignorance (*avidyā*) has not ceased either; thus, there would be no contingency of knowledge lacking the power to remove [ignorance], since it is possible for that which has been sublated to continue to persist—this is the intended meaning. He makes his own position clear through the perspective of worldly experience with the word "moon" (*candra*). It should be understood that this refers to one who possesses the support of a finger-pointing gesture and so forth, even after the oneness of the moon has been known from a verbal statement.

This illustration is easily understood according to the theory of *anvāruhyavāda* (provisional acceptance). In other cases, however, the perceptual nature of the subverting cognition (*nivartakajñāna*) must be understood by taking it in its primary sense; for once the illusion of two moons has been subverted by perception, its recurrence is impossible. Or else, when an illusion has been subverted by perception due to a prior supporting condition, its recurrence is not observed even when another supporting condition, such as a finger, is applied. (Verse 298)

The error produced by ignorance, though sublated by both verbal testimony and direct perception, is reasonable to persist for a long time due to the remainder of its latent impressions (saṃskāra). (299)

[Objection: Is it not the case that even prior to the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*) alone is the root of bondage? Even after [that vision], if that [cognition] persists, then because passion (*rāga*) and so forth persist, bondage would not cease; for an effect does not proceed toward its own activity once its cause has ceased. And you yourself admit the persistence of a remnant of ignorance (*avidyā*). To this, he says: "It is not ceased. The word "even" (*api*) indicates a contradiction. Due to the cutting of the root, it would perish gradually according to the analogy of a severed creeper, and would not sprout again.

The statement that [the cognition] has its root cut refers to the intention that discriminative knowledge—stained by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the reality of its own objects—is the cause of passion and the like, since such is the case with things like statues or women. The analogy here intended is that of a burnt cloth or the illusion of a whirling firebrand. Having stated that it does not produce knowledge in this context, he now refutes that [objection] with the words "even when... (*satyām iti*). The word "sāmagrī" (assemblage) is used with the intention that a sentence whose words are well-understood, which is endowed with the consideration of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, and which lacks any other requirement, is what is meant.

The sense is that otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, according to the principle that "even a non-obstruction constitutes a causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) itself—being of the nature of the absence of the cause that consists in its own cessation—would constitute a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalya*). Or else, it may be that [the impression] acts as an obstructer by depriving even a complete causal complex of its power.

"Even when [the object] exists," he says. The meaning is this: if the contrary latent impression (*viparīta-vāsanā*) alone were the obstruction or the obstructing factor, then in a delusion such as that of a rope-snake where the latent impression has not been dispelled, a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-dhī*) would never arise; yet it does arise. Thus, through the method of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*tadviparyaya*), one observes a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*); therefore, the cessation of contrary latent impressions is not the cause here.

For even when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a snake in a rope persists, a sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) arises regarding the object indirectly through the authoritative statement "this is not a snake," as well as through signs such as motionlessness established by striking it with a staff. Similarly, even though the latent impression of two moons persists, once defects such as the pressing of a finger are removed, there also arises the direct perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣadhī*) of the oneness of the moon. Nor should it be argued that the cessation of contrary impressions is required for the production of immediate intuition from a verbal statement.

Alternatively, since a sentence whose power is not distinct [from other means of knowledge] would still entail a dependence on that [perception] even for the production of a cognition of an imperceptible object; furthermore, for one who asserts that the cessation of the latent impression of difference occurs through the latent impression of non-difference, there would be a logical circle (*cakraka*): the determination of non-difference arises from the cultivation of that [impression], by which the latent impression of difference ceases, and from that very cessation, the determination of non-difference [arises]. Moreover, the cessation of the latent impression is not required for the determination itself.

If it were not required even for direct realization, because there would be no distinction; furthermore, you yourself have stated that for one searching for the tenth person, the direct cognition "You are the tenth" is produced by the instruction, even while the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the absence of the tenth remains. Moreover, you yourself have declared that these two sentences—"That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) and "You are the tenth" (*daśamastvam asi*)—are identical in having the immediate Self as their object.

Nor can you maintain that even when there is knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, a trace of the cognition of difference persists due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for since these latent impressions, which constitute the causal complex for the cognition of difference, are themselves illusory in nature, they must cease at the very moment that true knowledge arises. If such an illusory impression were not removed even upon the arising of knowledge, it could never be removed, as there would be no other means to bring about its cessation.

To say that the cognition of duality—the effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—has had its root severed yet continues to persist is the talk of a fool. In cases such as the cognition of two moons, even when a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) is present, the false cognition does not cease because the cause of that false cognition—the ultimate defect of timira (ophthalmia) and the like—is not destroyed, since it cannot be sublated by cognition. Thus, the non-cessation of the false cognition is not contradictory; however, the effects such as fear and so forth do cease, as they are sublated by a more powerful means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is the refutation of the "persistence of the sublated" (*bādhitānuvṛtti*).

Now, intending to show the impossibility of the persistence of what has been sublated for one who wishes to avoid contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), he says: "Even though" (*satyapi*). "In part" (*mātrayā*) means not in its entirety; the sense is that while the determination of the reality of the difference between selves and so forth has ceased, the cognition of difference regarding external objects persists to some small degree. The word "for you" (*bhavate*) contains the reason why this is impossible; the sense is that you do not admit anything at all to be real apart from Brahman. He explains the reason: "in [the case of] difference" (*bhede*).

In this context, the word *sāmagrī* (the causal complex) indicates the fullness of the support provided by karma already set in motion. [The opponent asks: "How could the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of karma persist once ignorance (*avidyā*) has been destroyed? For when a mirage ceases, its waves and so forth do not continue to exist; therefore, the status of being a teacher and so forth would be untenable. This is the intended meaning. [The author replies: "But even though all errors are equally false, among those occurring with respect to a single substratum as opposed to those with different substrata, only some are sublated by some [other cognition]; it might be the same in this case. To this, it is said: "Precisely by the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*). [This means that the destruction of the causal complex occurs simultaneously with the dawn of knowledge.]

The sublating cognition (*bādhakadhī*) is that all things other than the Real are false; the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is incompatible with the arising of such a cognition. Nor can it be said that there is no contradiction because of some internal distinction within the impressions, for falsity has not been eliminated. Indeed, once it is understood that it is a rope, the cognition of any one of its [erroneous] aspects, such as a snake, cannot persist. Furthermore, according to you who claim that the sublating cognition arises only when the impression of difference has already been destroyed, how could that impression persist at the moment of its arising? And if some impression were to persist, by what would it be removed? If you say by another cognition;

That is not so, because there is no distinction [between them]. If it were argued that [the world] ceases upon the exhaustion of experience, then, since it would not be sublatable by knowledge (*jñāna*), it would be real; the same would apply to karma as well. Anticipating the consequence that liberation would be impossible if latent impressions (*vāsanā*) persisted even after the direct realization of non-duality (*advaita-sākṣātkāra*), he says: "Upon the arising of knowledge. The statement that [the world] is false in nature is intended to show that it is removable by knowledge alone.

The meaning is this: because there is no other means of cessation, those who fear the consequence of [the world] being real do not accept that it can be sublated by anything other than knowledge; for even when hundreds of cognitions—such as the experience of one's own imagined final enjoyment—arise, they cannot function as a sublater of those [prior cognitions], just like the previous cognitions themselves. Furthermore, the meaning of "this" is that it is difficult to be sublated even by a powerful cognition that sublates root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*); moreover, causeless destruction is not accepted anywhere by the followers of the scriptures (*naigamikaiḥ*).

Even if that [cessation] were admitted, since the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous cognitions and so forth would be established only as an illusion, the continuity of the stream of impressions would remain unavoidable due to the persistence of delusion; it is with this in mind that the phrase "even at any time" (*kadācid api*) was stated. For the cessation of impressions is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an existing entity, because it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor is it real as something distinct [from existence], for that would result in the collapse of non-duality (*advaita-bhaṅga*). If it is argued that even if non-existence (*abhāva*) were real, the non-duality of Being (*sad-advaita*) would still be established—[the author replies: no.

If difference were real in some cases, it would follow by the same principle that it must be real elsewhere as well; and even if other entities were real, just like that [difference], the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) would remain unimpaired. With the words "even though not removed," etc., he rebuts [the opponent] on the grounds of self-contradiction, saying "vāsanā. This is called "childishness" with the intention of showing that one who is ignorant of the contradiction in his own statement will know nothing else.

The intended meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "with its root severed," is "root" intended here to mean ignorance (*avidyā*), or rather the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*)? In the first case, since the root ignorance has been severed, the latent impression—which is of the same nature as that [ignorance]—is also sublated; therefore, it has been stated that the delusion of duality cannot be maintained. In the second case, how could its effect continue once the latent impression itself has been eradicated?

If an effect were to arise even in the absence of its cause, then those various effects would occur even without ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like—which are accepted by both our own and other schools—despite their being the intended causes. Therefore, this is not a logically sound statement. Regarding the example cited by the opponent for the persistence of a sublated [cognition], he says "the double moon," explaining that it is inconsistent because its root has not been severed.

The point is this: because the defect of *timira* (ocular disorder) and the like is not sublated even by hundreds of subverting cognitions due to its being real, you yourself have accepted it as having empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*); furthermore, even if it were unreal, the cognition of the oneness of the moon could not serve as its sublater, since it does not have that [defect] as its objective substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Indicating that, unlike in that example where the efficacy of the sublater lies in the cessation of fear and so forth, such would not be the case in what you desire, he refutes [the objection] with the words "by the powerful" (*prabalena*).

The meaning is: "because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition whose validity has been established. For this very reason, there is here an exclusion of fear and so forth produced by deception (*kuhaka*). In your position, however, since both cognitions—the sublated and the sublator—are known to arise from defects, the result of sublation (*bādhaphala*) is not established. The intention is that the result of the sublator is its serving as the cause for activity directed toward investigating the object as it truly is—a state which, in the world, lacks the fruit of confidence in either [cognition] due to the persistence of what was previously sublated. The mention of effects such as fear is in comparison with delusions regarding snakes and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), wonder and other such states are included.

[This is] the apprehension. Thus, with the intention that [the object] does not produce fear and so forth, it is stated in the *Nyāyatattva* that "knowledge during the state of the persistence of the sublated is indifferent (*udāsīna*) because it is ineffective. By the word "but" (*tu*), the distinction from what was stated by others is indicated: for here, when the causal complex of destruction is present, there is no existence of the thing to be destroyed; nor can an effect arise in the absence of its cause. [Objection: But even fear and so forth, being momentary like error, are not to be destroyed by a sublater.

Furthermore, the non-arising of a subsequent fear is already established prior [to the sublation], just like the non-arising of another delusion; so then, how can the cessation of fear and so forth be said to result from sublation? It is replied: when the sublater exists, there is a statement regarding the cessation of fear and so forth with reference to the continued non-arising of further fear due to the deficiency of the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalyāt*). Moreover, for those who maintain that the arising of knowledge occurs by means of the eradication of the latent impressions of difference (*bhedavāsanā*), the arising of knowledge will never be accomplished, because of the [persistence of] the latent impression of difference.

Because it has been accumulated since beginningless time, it is immeasurable; and because the cultivation of its opposite is slight, it is impossible for this [cultivation] to dispel it. Therefore, the knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta sentences is something other than the knowledge consisting in the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence, and is denoted by such terms as "meditation" (dhyāna) and "worship" (upāsana).

And thus say the Śrutis: "Having understood, one should exercise wisdom"; "Having discerned, one understands"; "Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone"; "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death"; "One should worship the Self alone as the world"; "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "That is to be sought; that is to be desired to be known"—and so forth. With a "lion’s glance" (looking back), he states another objection regarding the non-arising of knowledge—a position supported by many commentators—in order to demonstrate the weakness of the view that [knowledge arises] even after [the body] has been born: ...he says another refutation regarding the non-arising of knowledge...

"And even" (*api ca*) means: "even at some time"—that is, even after [the practice of] meditation, just as before it; the sense is that this holds true even after meditating for thousands of millions of *kalpas*. Now, one might object: "Just as those who desire the arising of knowledge seek to destroy the immeasurable impurities accumulated since beginningless time by means of limited rituals such as sacrifices, so too might knowledge arise through the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by means of hearing [the scriptures] and other practices. To this, he says: "Of the latent impression of duality" (*bhedavāsanāyāḥ*).

For here the principle that "even if [something] is remembered only once" and so forth does not apply; for if [ignorance] were removed by means of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), it would follow that the object to be removed is real. Nor can it be argued that, as in the case of what is removed by a mantra, its removal by an unseen potency is possible because it possesses empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*); for if the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) could be established in that same way, the search for a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-dhī*) would be rendered useless. However, if [the scripture] removes [ignorance] by its very nature, then since there is no evidence for such a diversity of powers, the relative strength or weakness of the means depends on factors such as frequency of repetition.

Furthermore, meditation (*bhāvanā*) is not an auxiliary cause for the sentence by its very nature, because—just as with indirect experience—it is not observed to have a positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with direct experience; nor is it accepted that it serves as an auxiliary through the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit). If such an auxiliary role were accepted, it would follow that the mind itself, acting as an auxiliary, could produce direct realization independently of the sentence. Therefore, the intention is that in no way whatsoever can a subverting perception arise from the sentence.
[This concludes the discussion on] the fact that the knowledge resulting from what is enjoined is the means to liberation.

With the words "What [is it]? and so forth, indicating other refutations of the two previously considered views that have already been criticized, he first states the remainder of his own position by means of a restrictive determination: "Therefore," etc. This refers to the logical and perceptual [grounds] for such things as the fact that knowledge produced by a sentence is neither something to be enjoined nor something to be negated.

The meaning is: "because it is contradictory to itself. Regarding the phrase "something other than the knowledge of the sentence-meaning," the intention is as follows: if one were to enjoin the mere cognition of the sentence-meaning as the means [to liberation], an insurmountable circularity would arise in its spontaneous engagement. For indeed, without knowing the nature of Brahman and the knowledge thereof, there could be no desire for that knowledge; and for one devoid of such a desire, there can be no engagement with the injunction regarding the means for that purpose. Furthermore, the realization of Brahman cannot be accomplished without the performance of those means.

[Objection: Let it be that one’s engagement [in practice] occurs through the instigation of well-wishers, just as in the case of the study of one’s own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*). [Reply: Not so; for even well-wishers would have to instruct [the seeker] thus: "Attain the knowledge of Brahman as the indeterminate, pure consciousness alone. For if such knowledge of Brahman were already present or absent, there would be no performance of its means [at all]. In our position, however, since Brahman is characterized by many forms, there is no contradiction with worldly experience regarding the engagement for the sake of a superior knowledge—characterized by repetition, continuity, and so forth—that is to be realized at a later time.

If one does not accept the processes established by worldly consensus, there would be a contradiction with one's own activity and so forth. Furthermore, for you—who maintain that there is an eternally perceived, featureless reality—it is impossible to attain a cognition superior to that [reality] through verbal testimony or any other means.

[Objection: But surely, the statement that [the knowledge of Brahman] is intended to be enjoined as a means to liberation is improper; for here, words of injunction are devoted to restating the knowledge produced by sentences which have human goals as their content, whereas meditation and the like are enjoined as being for the sake of that [knowledge]. Nor does everything else follow merely from the impossibility of another [explanation]. Furthermore, various kinds of knowledge are designated by such terms as "recollection" (smṛti) and "vision" (darśana). To this, he says: "And thus... (tathā ca).

The meaning is as follows: just as another means to liberation—distinct from the knowledge produced by [the study of] sentences—is enjoined by such injunctions as "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), and that [means], although expressed by various words such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and so forth, is established as being one and the same; so it is here. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction with the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Here, many such sentences are cited in order to clarify that words such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so forth refer to the specific states described by words such as "meditation," and to show the absence of any difference in meaning despite differences in prefixes, verbal roots, and the presence or absence of suffixes.

The word "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to the variety of types of sentences already mentioned. This word is used for the sake of establishing the commonality of those [sentences] in being intent upon injunctions (*vidhi*). The initial mention is made even regarding those not explicitly mentioned, for the purpose of applying the same logical principle (*nyāya-saṃcāra*).

Here, because of the unity of meaning with such passages as "one should meditate upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), and because the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—through such statements as "having understood, one discerns" (*anuvidya vijānāti*) and "having discerned, one should cultivate wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*)—is an aid to meditation, the words "having understood" (*anuvidya*) and "having discerned" (*vijñāya*) are restated (*anūdya*), and "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) and "one discerns" (*vijānāti*) are enjoined as meditation (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, the statement "it should be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) is also a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Since a person who has studied the Veda with the intent of grasping its meaning perceives that it provides knowledge of purposeful objects, he spontaneously engages in hearing (*śravaṇa*) for the sake of determining that meaning; thus, hearing is already established as a requirement. Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*) serves to stabilize what has been heard, the injunction "it must be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, meditation (*dhyāna*) alone is what is being enjoined. And the author will state later: "Repetition [is required], because of the repeated instruction."

In passages such as "one should exercise wisdom" (prajñāṃ kurvīta) and "he understands" (vijānāti), it does not appear that there is anything other than the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. With this in mind—referring to the principle *chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*—the author says: "In these [passages]. This means: "in those sentences heard [in the scriptures]"; the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). Here, "having a single purpose" (*aikārthya*) means having a single objective or a single subject matter. And that, in this context, consists of the relationship between the general and the particular, by way of the principle of reconciling different recensional branches (*śākhāntara-naya*).

This is established by logic. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), the passage beginning with "meditate" (*dhyāyatha*) is included; by the second, the passage beginning with "is to be sought to be known" (*vijijñāsitavya*). The statement regarding its being an aid to meditation is for the purpose of establishing the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the restatement (*anuvāda*) and for the purpose of connecting the restated subject with the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). And that [aid] consists in its presenting the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Now, one might object: in passages such as "having known" (*anuvidya*), let there be an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the case of "with curds" (*dadhnā*); for those who know the principles of interpretation hold that when a ritual action is heard along with an accessory, the sentence has that accessory as its primary purport, because enjoining a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) involves greater complexity (*gaurava*), whereas enjoining the action alone does not.

[The opponent argues: "Because the scriptural mention of the quality (*guṇa*) would otherwise be purposeless; however, the word denoting the action (*karmapada*) would be meaningful by providing a substrate for the enjoined quality, thereby serving as a reference to the act. [The author replies: Not so. For if, as in the case of the *homa*, the act whose purpose is knowledge were already established, then the quality could be enjoined by way of restatement (*anūdyā*). To refute the doubt that, in the absence of any other alternative, there must be an injunction of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it is stated: "by way of restatement" (*anūdya*). The point is this: if the word ending in *-ktvā* and the verb (*ākhyātānta*) were to have the same meaning, there would be a contradiction regarding their sequence (*paurvāparya*).

And what distinction could there be between one [action] and another? If it were merely a matter of practicing with similar types, it would suffice simply to say "one should practice knowledge"; furthermore, the difference in prefixes would be fruitless. If, however, they have distinct meanings—as in the case of *vijānāti* and so on—then since that which has not been previously established (the object) is mentioned later, like meditation (*dhyāna*), it is logical that its resolution lies in the meditation that is enjoined subsequently. But the cognition of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthadhī*) is not a subordinate element (*guṇa*) to be enjoined, because it is already established. For that very reason, hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other such acts are not for its sake; moreover, it is most appropriate to enjoin meditation as the primary element.

Nor should any other form of knowledge be suspected here as being enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). If, however, the sentence "he knows" (*vijānāti*) were to find its final rest in the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-jñāna*), then in the case of "having known" (*anuvidya*) and so forth, no other knowledge is seen that could be either enjoined or merely restated. Furthermore, meditation (*dhyāna*) cannot be enjoined as a subordinate quality to that [knowledge], because it has already been shown that it cannot possibly serve as a means toward the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, whether that knowledge be indirect (*parokṣa*) or direct (*pratyakṣa*).

Because the two passages occupy the same position [in the text], the reading of "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) is placed first in order to manifest its status as an injunction, even though it lacks the particle *iti* denoting an injunction. The success of the two prefixes (*upa* and *ni*) is due to the fact that meditation (*dhyāna*) is characterized by the clarity mentioned in the passage beginning with "having perceived" (*nicāyya*), and because it is characterized by the excellence attributed to the object of worship (*upāsya*). Furthermore, even in the case of these two restatements (*anuvāda*), the two prefixes express both the repetition and the clarity of the subject being restated.

Because the word *vijñānam* (in the phrase *avijñātam*, *vijñātam*) is read in place of *nididhyāsitavyam*, and because the word *anveṣaṇam* (inquiry) follows immediately after *mananam* (reflection), which occurs after *śravaṇam* (hearing), the term *vijijñāsitavyaḥ* (to be desired to be known) takes the place of *nididhyāsanam* (meditation). To the objection—"Why should general terms such as 'knowledge' (*vijñāna*), 'feeling' (*vedanā*), and so forth, which refer to means and objects, not find their final rest in the specific knowledge consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) expressed by the suffix *-tavya*?"—the author replies with the words "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*).

To the question, "How is the invalidation of the suffix *tavya* here without a cause? he says: "Of the private recitation (*svādhyāya*). The underlying point is this: the doubt that Mīmāṃsā need not be commenced—whether because the Śruti lacks the status of having a meaning to convey, or because there is no motivator for inquiry, or because there is no occasion for it—is dispelled. Furthermore, the verbal power (*śabdaśakti*) of the word "should be heard" (*śrotavya*) does not reside in the act of approaching a teacher and so forth; therefore, if it were intended to refer to the activity aimed at reaching a definitive conclusion, its meaning would already be established (*prāptārthatva*).

Is there not then an injunction for reflection (*manana*), which consists of the repeated cultivation of what has been commenced? And it would be appropriate to intend that very thing by the words "it must be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*); in that case, there might be a cessation of [the injunctions] such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so forth. To this he replies: "In hearing" (*śravaṇe*). Since hearing that is not firmly established does not assist meditation (*dhyāna*), the logical reflection (*manana*)—which is recited immediately after it and is required to establish that hearing—is [already] obtained through the persistence of passion and other factors. Therefore, the sense is that even that [reflection] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

By this, the logical contradiction of the claim made by some—that the triad of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is enjoined as a means to realization (*darśana*)—is demonstrated. Now, one might object: let it be that by the two injunctions "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*), only the hearing of the meaning accessible through the teacher's instruction is what is enjoined; for some have said that it refers to the hearing of the teachings of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and so on. To this, he replies: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This means: because of the distinction between what is already established and what is not yet established, or because of the [logical] conclusion reached by elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). The particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude hearing and reflection, as well as mere knowledge, and the desire denoted by the suffix *-san*.

Or, [the phrase] "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) may be intended to exclude the notion that it has a separate injunctive purpose, because it is merely a qualification of meditation (*dhyāna*). This is the underlying idea: since it is possible for the two [injunctions], "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*), to provide assistance that is well-known even without being scripturally enjoined, it is improper to assume the opposite. Furthermore, if "it is to be heard" and so forth were intended as injunctions for the fourfold process of hearing and the rest, a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result. Moreover, in this context, an option (*vikalpa*) is absolutely impossible—both because it is marred by the eight defects and because it would involve a choice between what is heavy and what is light—given that the assistance is to be realized sequentially.

Because there can be no combination of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth with the principal member of the compound, which is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) necessarily excludes any other alternative; because the nature of meditation (*dhyāna*) as being of the form of seeing (*darśana*) will be established in accordance with another scriptural passage (*śruti*); and for this very reason, even the root *dhyai* preceded by the prefix *ni* is indifferent here toward expressing the qualification of being of the form of seeing—which is already clearly conveyed by another word—especially since the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) is used in coordination with a restatement (*anuvāda*), thereby abandoning its natural inclination toward being a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).

Since it is untenable to assume that the passage is merely intended as a restatement of the result (*phalānuvāda*), and because even in the verse beginning with "It is to be heard from the Vedic texts" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyaḥ*), the mere statement that the triad of hearing and so forth is the cause for vision does not constitute a contradiction even if the goal itself were to be enjoined; therefore, meditation—characterized by the specific form of vision obtained through other injunctive words—is precisely what is to be enjoined here, preceded by hearing and the rest which are prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*).

Thus, by not accepting that the words "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth rest upon the specific injunctions stated by [the author] himself, he also indicates a contradiction with the Sūtras—introducing the phrase "and he will say. For the verb *dhyai* (to meditate), in the sense of "thinking," expresses a cognition that is repeated many times regarding a single object. Therefore, since "feeling" (*vedana*) taught in the context of meditation is indeed meditation itself, the point at hand is established. Likewise, "worship" (*upāsti*) is also included therein by such passages as "that which is within it is to be worshipped.
Consequently, the mention of "instruction" and so forth is subsumed under this very term, as it is consistent with the dependence on sacrifices and other such acts.

It is understood that this "knowing" (vedana), which is intended as a means to liberation, is actually "meditation" (upāsana); for we observe an interchange between the roots *vid* (to know) and *upās* (to meditate) in the opening and concluding passages. For instance, regarding the passage "One should meditate [upon] the mind as Brahman," it concludes: "He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge. Conversely, [the text says]: "He does not know; for this Self is incomplete; one should meditate [upon it] thus [as the complete Self]."

"He who knows what he knows has been told this by me; now, venerable sir, instruct me further regarding that deity whom you worship. And meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted stream of memory, like a flow of oil; it is "steadfast memory" (*dhruvā smṛtiḥ*). For it is heard that steadfast memory is the means to liberation, as in the statement: "Upon the attainment of memory, there is the loosening of all knots.
Thus, general terms such as "knowledge" (*vedana*) and so forth find their final resting place in the form of worship consisting of steadfast recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*).

He states the resting place of general terms such as "knowledge" (*vedana*) within the specific context of what was previously promised—namely, *upāsana* (meditative worship)—with the words "That" (*tat*). "That" refers to that which has been described without specifying its particular nature.
"This" (*idam*) refers to the specific [nature], because it is enjoined as having the character of a means to be accomplished through more weighty practices such as meditation (*dhyāna*).

In the context of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), it is fit to attain oneness with that [Brahman]. He clarifies its cause by stating: "intended as a means to liberation" (*apavargopāyatayā vidhitsitam*). The sense is that it is understood as "meditation" (*upāsana*) because it is designated by words such as "knowledge" (*vedana*) and so forth, which share the same subject matter within the same context. Regarding the reason provided in the Sūtra, "because of instruction" (*upadeśāt*), he states another specific reason found in the same context: "of *vid* and *upāsi*" (*vidyupāsyoh*). In passages such as "He should meditate on the mind" (*mana upāsitavyam*), the term *upāsi* (meditation) comes first, while *vid* (to know) comes at the end; however, in the passage "That which... (*yas tad...*), it is the reverse.

In the passage "He does not know," however, there is meditation on both [names and forms], because of the introductory statement: "Now, he who meditates on another deity" and "he who meditates on each one here. Thus, the "interchange" (vyatikara) here consists in the mutual occupation of positions. An objection is raised: "But here there is an injunction for the contemplative vision (dṛṣṭividhi) that 'the mind is Brahman'; moreover, the two other passages belong to distinct specific meditations (vidyā). How can the verbal application established in one place be transferred elsewhere? Anticipating this, it is stated in the Commentary: "Because it is seen even in similar cases. (300)

The phrase "he who knows thus" does not merely refer to the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture; for it would be improper to state the fruit of something unenjoined by way of restating another unenjoined thing, without first specifying the desired fruit of that which has been enjoined. [Objection: But at the beginning of the Bhūma-vidyā, a specific fruit was stated: "He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—so far as the mind reaches, there he has freedom of movement according to his desire. By that alone, the requirement for further specification would be satisfied.

Not so—because this [passage] belonging to the third *prapāṭhaka* belongs to a different section concerning meditative worship (*upāsanā*), and because a repetition would otherwise be purposeless; for once it is established that there is another thing to be enjoined, its connection with the result is appropriately understood through the result mentioned in close proximity. Therefore, in this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is proper to understand that meditative worship is restated by means of the verb "to know" (*vid-*) and that the injunction of its fruit follows. The principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice is intended here. Fame (*kīrti*) is renown produced by acts such as giving; glory (*yaśas*), however, is produced by valor and the like. He shines with fame and glory.

It should be construed as "he shines with Brahmanic luster" (*brahmavarcasena tapati*). In the intermediate sentence, the word "here" (*atra*) is not mentioned because of its proximity. Regarding the passage beginning with "He who that... (*yastad...*), the meaning is: "He who knows that Brahman, and he who knows that Brahman—he the knower is Raikva, and this Brahman which is to be known is that [which was mentioned]"; thus, a dyad has been stated to you. The omission of the word "and" (*ca*) is as in the case of expressions such as "the cow, the horse, the person, the world," and so forth. Because of its association with a neuter noun, the word "stated" (*uktam*) must be modified [to agree in gender]. Alternatively, it may be understood as: "He was stated [by me] as the knower with respect to that which is to be known."

Alternatively, the connection with the preceding passage is as follows: "Whatever that Raikva knows, another who knows that very same thing—whatever good deeds creatures perform—all that converges upon him. In the phrase "he was told this by me," the word *etad* (this) is an adverbial modifier of the action; thus, the meaning is "he was told by me in this manner. According to this interpretation, because it accords with the context, it is indicated that Jānaśruti must have been a disciple of Raikva. *Anuśādhi* means "instruct clearly" or "make known by distinguishing [the truth]."

Thus, it has been stated that "knowing" (vedana) is what is denoted by the term "meditative worship" (dhyānopāsana); however, it is not here being said that meditation itself is worship. This is understood from the statement "vidi and upāsi [are used] interchangeably," etc., as well as from the agreement with the sentence to be presented later, namely, "knowing would be worship. Here, the fact that the words "meditation" (dhyāna) and "worship" (upāsana) have the same referent, as well as the exclusion of meditation that is contrary [to the goal], are established by the very sense of the context.
If meditation were here specified by the word as being of the nature of worship (*upāsanā*), then the continuity would be broken when meditation is subsequently described in another form.

Now, it might be argued that the word *dhyāna* (meditation) denotes mere reflection (*cintā*) and could thus apply even to a continuous stream of memory (*smṛti-santāna*) that is interrupted, or that it is sometimes used for mere remembrance (*smṛti*). Furthermore, in the Sūtra, the words *dhyāna* and *upāsana* are said to refer merely to repeated practice. To address this, he states the specific scriptural meaning intended there—namely, that it consists of uninterrupted continuity—in the phrase: "And meditation... The word *santāna* (stream/continuity), accompanied by an illustrative example, is used to dispel the doubt that [the meditation] might be considered constant either by the logic of the lifelong *agnihotra* sacrifice, or by its own nature as something persisting over a long period of time.

Thus, it has been stated that rest is found in the excellence of *dhyāna*, which is common to both interrupted and uninterrupted perception; or rather, its exclusive characteristic of being uninterrupted has been established. This [point] he will indicate in its proper place with the words: "And from *dhyāna*, there is immovability, having regard for... The underlying principle (*tūlikā*) here is that, just as the word *upāsana* (meditative worship) has uninterrupted perception as its object, so too the word *dhyāna* is established here as having uninterrupted perception as its object. He establishes this by means of scripture with the word "firm" (*dhruva*).

The "steadfastness of mindfulness" (*smṛti-dhrauvya*) consists in a flow that is free from interruption by dissimilar cognitions; for it has been stated thus: "And there is a single continuity in the cognition of that form, which is indifferent to anything else," and so forth. Although it will be stated later that the unity of the knowledge (*vidyā*) does not follow merely from the unity of the connection with the fruit—as in the case [of the passage] beginning "though manifold due to the difference of sound and so on"—and although specific features such as being meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and steadfastness are mentioned in other contexts; [nevertheless, these do not preclude the identity of the knowledge here].

Nevertheless, since common terms such as "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth lack a specific referent, and since the fruit is devoid of gradation, there would be the difficulty of prescribing a distinction between heavy and light means. Furthermore, the inherent capacity of things (*vastu-sāmarthya*), characterized by the impossibility of alternative options regarding what is heavy or light, is more powerful than the context; therefore, the permanence of the Smṛti is established. With the intention that this [teaching], though heard in one place, is to be applied to all forms of knowledge, it is stated that it is the means to liberation (*apavarga*).

Thus it has been said. "Upon attaining mindfulness" (*smṛtilambhe*) means: when the aforementioned constant mindfulness (*dhruvānusmṛti*) has been accomplished through the sequence beginning with purity of diet (*āhāraśuddhi*). "Knots" (*granthayaḥ*) are those by which the field-knower (*kṣetrī*) is bound—namely, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), attachment and aversion (*rāga-dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and so forth, as well as the various transformations of the three *guṇas* brought about by karma. These are described in the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) as the knots of the noose of *māyā*. "Complete liberation" (*vipramokṣaḥ*) means: release after having analytically separated [the self from them] in an absolute manner. Now, one might object: "Bondage is universally accepted as being caused by error (*bhrānti*); how then can mindfulness, which is not a valid cognition (*apramā*), be its sublater?"

For that which is produced by action dependent on delusion cannot itself be established as an object of delusion. Even if bondage arises from error—just like fever caused by fear or the suspicion of poison—it is logical that such a remedial procedure is appropriate because of its reality; furthermore, even under the view that it is false, the principle of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth is not to be abandoned. Therefore, disregarding whether the object to be removed is real or false, or whether the remover is a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) or not, one must accept that [the ritual] achieves its own fruit because it has been enjoined.

And you yourself have stated that the memory in the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) is the destroyer of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference. Therefore, in this case, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of bondage as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; rather, its destruction occurs through memory or valid cognition (*pramiti*) according to the prescribed method. Nor is this memory invalid or non-conformable to reality (*ayathārtha*), because its object is not other than the object of the valid cognition that is its own cause. And it has been stated generally in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*: "Memory is a cognition produced solely from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience, having for its object that which was previously experienced. Its having a previously experienced object is not...

It has entered into the definition [of valid cognition]; however, this is for the purpose of making known its own cause, the cognition of the universal, regarding whether the object is real or unreal.
When that state has ceased, its reality should not be rejected on the grounds of memory as being in that same state, because of the sequence of cognitions concerning the past and the future. (301)

And when there is a lapse of memory, the object's state as it was does not appear; how then could there be non-correspondence with reality in that case, which is devoid of "that-ness" and "this-ness"? (302)

Therefore, following the root [cause] and according to what is observed, let it be accepted that memory—whether it corresponds to reality or does not correspond to reality—is like direct experience. (303)
Likewise, a view held elsewhere is considered to be the cause of the destruction of poison and so forth;
for even among the higher sciences (paravidyā), this [view] is sometimes adopted in certain respects. (304)

Therefore, this supreme knowledge, enjoined by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts and appearing in the form of traditional lore (smṛti), is being expounded as the atonement for the cycle of worldly existence.
And that memory has a form identical to direct perception:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed,
and one's karmas are exhausted when That, which is both high and low, is seen."

This is because they share this same purpose. This being the case, by the statement "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," the state of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) is enjoined as having a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*). And through the intensity of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), recollection (*smṛti*) indeed takes on the nature of direct perception;
that is, recollection possesses a form identical to direct perception.

[Objection: Is it not the case that [the statement] "meditation alone," etc., is incorrect? For even that [meditation] is said to be for the sake of *samādhi*, just like *dhāraṇā*. It is *samādhi* itself, consisting of vision, which is stated to be the cause of liberation in such passages as "one should see the Self. Furthermore, the perception of a yogin is not unaccepted, since it will be discussed in many places. To this, he says: "And that... This means "qualified by stability. The particle *ca* (and) is used for clarity to show that it is qualified by another form (*ākāra*) according to the method indicated by the Sūtra; or rather, it has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusively).

For that very same *smṛti* (recollection), due to its excellence of clarity, is designated as *samādhi*; it is not some other "vision" (*darśana*) that is the fruit of meditation (*dhyāna*), which would be what is enjoined in such passages as "one should see [the Self]" and so forth. The statement of their identity is intended to pacify the contradiction regarding *smṛti* being a form of vision; the sense is that even when indirect (*parokṣa*), it is metaphorically treated as direct (*aparokṣa*).
Recollection is twofold—indirect and direct—just like its own source (*mūla*).
Whether it be entirely indirect, or both [indirect and direct], in this case there is directness. (306)
In the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of another word is accepted when there is no other way to understand it;
for in the case of names such as *Śyena* and others used in reference to the *Darśa* and other sacrifices, a figurative (*gauṇī*) indication is indeed intended. (307)
And in the Vedic scripture, "One should measure half inside and half outside the altar," the middle region is thus indicated everywhere according to the specific requirements.
But surely, in this context, stability—not the nature of perception—is presented as the qualifier in one's own statement; for that reason, it is distinct from meditative absorption (samādhi).

To this he replies with the words "it is pierced. Here, the word *granthi* (knot) refers to objects distinct from the karma and other factors already mentioned; it refers to the knots of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which act as obstacles to the proper functioning of the heart, that is, the mind. Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is called *hṛdaya* because it occupies the location denoted by the word *hṛt*; or, by virtue of residing therein, the soul is indicated by that term. Its "knot" is the aforementioned category of transformations of the three *guṇas*. Or, the "heart" itself is the knot; this is an elliptical expression.

As for that which is explained in the *Chāndogya*: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its etymological derivation (*nirukta*): 'He is in the heart' (*hṛdy ayam*). Therefore, day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world. This refers to the Brahman that is the object of meditation. One must not, however, be deluded into thinking that the very same [Brahman] is what is denoted here by the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), because of the superimposition of contradictory attributes such as "knots" and "doubts. Here, "all doubts regarding all objects," or simply "all doubts"—the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) is also indicative of "error" (*viparyaya*).

The meaning is that they are severed because their causes are cut off, and thus they do not continue in a stream. "Actions" refers to both binding good deeds (*sukṛta*) and evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*). Since what is intended here is the destruction of those actions that obstruct attainment, there is no mutual dependence between the arising of knowledge and the cessation of karma. "High and low" (*parāvara*): "highness" (*paratva*) is the state of surpassing all others; "lowness" (*avaratva*) is due to qualities such as being the younger brother of Indra for the sake of accessibility. Alternatively, it refers to the bodies of high and low beings as mentioned in passages such as "the True Brahman is Brahman, [and] the slaves [are Brahman]."

"Parāvara" refers either to that which is both high and low, or distinct from the entire universe of highs and lows; or else, he whose lower state is itself supreme by virtue of his glory is "parāvara. The intended meaning here is as follows: in the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), the term "vision" (*darśana*) does not refer to the vision belonging to the state of liberation, because—like the term "constant remembrance" (*dhruvasmṛti*)—it pertains to the means for the loosening of the knots. Nor is there a conjunction of "remembrance" and "vision" toward liberation even when they pertain to the means, as in the case of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because of the nature of the copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Or rather, because the particle "ca" (and) is not perceived [in the text]. Furthermore, conjunction (*samuccaya*) is not possible here, because Brahman cannot be directly realized through the yoga that has been introduced; even if it were possible, simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is impossible, and there is no regulating factor for a sequence (*krama*). Nor can the earlier recollection of the Pole Star (*dhruva-smaraṇa*) and the later yogic perception (*yogi-pratyakṣa*) be conjoined as instruments, because since their purpose is already established by the presence of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the assumption of a conjunction is inappropriate.

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because if one were to assume that constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) is a remote means (*vyavahitasādhana*), there would be the consequence of abandoning what is directly stated in scripture (*śrutahāna*) and so forth. Furthermore, vision (*darśana*), which is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*), cannot be taken up in its own form such that it could be enjoined as a combined [practice]. [Objection: But this is the same even in the case of recollection (*smaraṇa*), whose fruit is the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

If it is argued that, according to the principle of the "inspection of the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa-nyāya*), the injunction to "see" here must have as its object a possible activity that serves as a means to that [vision], we say no. For if that were the case, there would be the consequence of redundancy between the two terms *draṣṭavya* (to be seen) and *nididhyāsitavya* (to be meditated upon) within a single sentence; because, ultimately, it is the instigation of the mind toward meditation—which is dependent on the person—that must be enjoined as the means to vision, and no other such means is perceived.

[Objection: Surely there is no tautology, since the single means to vision has been stated both generally and specifically by the two words [of the sūtra]; for, alas, if that were so, you would be abandoning the method of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and falling into our position, because by both [terms]—“it is to be seen” (*draṣṭavyaḥ*) and “it is to be meditated upon” (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)—only one and the same thing is enjoined. [Reply: But in our view, there is a distinction, in that meditation (*dhyāna*) is specified by its clarity. Nor is there a conjunction of the constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) with a different kind of meditation that has the same form as vision.

Because no other such [means] is observed, because postulating it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because it would entail the subversion of scriptural texts stating that constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) is an independent means;
furthermore, when liberation is the goal to be accomplished, one must not accept an option (*vikalpa*) between direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) and mindfulness that is corrupted by numerous defects.
The definition of the eightfold defect of an option is as follows: [it consists of four defects for each of the two alternatives].

They stated that there are eight defects in the two types of formal arguments, due to the sublation of conceptual cognition, its application, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), and its fruit, by means of the two extremes. (309)

The wise recognize two types of fallacies (prayoga) in each of these two [arguments]: from abandoning validity and accepting another, and from abandoning what was accepted and including what was abandoned. (310)

In this case, such [direct perception] is not possible due to the disparity between the heavy and the light; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), for it is observed that causality exists only among things of unequal results. Nor is there here the relationship of the "mediator and the mediated" (*dvāra-dvāritā*), as there is no evidence for it. For direct perception of the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—as mentioned by others—will be refuted in the *Śāstrayoni* section (Brahmasūtra 1.1.3), and because no such sequence or order is stated here. Furthermore, meditation is not seen to assist in producing direct vision in the same way that hearing and reflection assist in producing meditation. Nor is this [perception] heard of in scripture, since no such sequence and so forth are mentioned.

If it is argued that there is such a passage as, "Then, meditating upon Him, one beholds Him partless; through the practice of churning with meditation, one may behold the God as if hidden," and so forth—this is true; however, this vision is the fruit of meditation, and let it be another supernatural attainment (siddhi) like atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, but it is not the means [to liberation], for it is not stated as such.

In certain instances within the section on higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), the mention of that [vision] is for the purpose of demonstrating its respective power, as in the passages: "He, free from sorrow, beholds that purpose" and "he sees the Person dwelling in the city. Let such vision, described as being accomplished through meditation (*dhyāna*), belong to the liberated one (*mukta*). If, however, the vision described as accomplished through meditation belongs to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), it must be of the nature of a vivid meditation. For instance, since the word "vision" (*darśana*)—which is not applied to auditory cognition and the like—is primarily used for visual perception alone.

That [Self] is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech; however, it is rejected here [in the Upanishads] by such statements as "but by the purified mind" and so forth. Therefore, it must be said that the metaphorical designation of "seeing" (darśana) is applied to a specific kind of knowledge produced by the mind. This being the case, it is better to maintain that the metaphorical designation is applied to the very "constant remembrance" (dhruvānusmaraṇa)—which is explicitly stated as the means to liberation—with the intention of describing its such-like clarity.
