Now, it might be argued that the word "darśana" (vision/perception) qualifies memory by characterizing it as having the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). This is not so, because such a qualification is impossible in the case of memory; for even among those who believe it is possible based on the distinction between its source [the original experience], it is not established in the case of memory—which is accomplished through indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*). Furthermore, the statement that "samādhi is produced by meditation (*dhyāna*) performed with the mind" is due to the difference between the clear and the unclear [states].

And it has been stated by those who maintain that for this very [samādhi], there are two states—one being a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of yoga and the other being the principal limb (*aṅgin*)—that while it may be so here that the words "recollection" (*smṛti*) and "vision" (*darśana*) have the same meaning, nevertheless, let vision be figuratively designated by the word "recollection. This is not correct; for it has been established that the reversal [of the primary meanings] occurs precisely through the presence or absence of a contradiction regarding the primary sense. Furthermore, recollection would be praised by being described as clarity, whereas vision, by being described as recollection, would be deprecated.

Furthermore, even in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), one says "he shows the further shore of darkness" with the intention of expressing clarity (*vaiśadya*). In common worldly usage, we speak of one who "sees the further shore" (*pāradarśin*) or one who "sees from afar" (*dūradarśin*), and so forth. Now, how can there be a sublation (*bādha*) by indirect memory (*smṛti*) of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*), even though that memory is similar to perception? It cannot be so, because its falsity (*mithyātva*) has not been established. This is true even for that which is directly perceived.

The sublation (*bādha*) of such things as the oneness of the flame, the nature of the body as the self, and the duality of the moon by means of inference and other proofs has been observed and is accepted by everyone. Therefore, because clarity is attained for the memory concerning the means to liberation through the phrase "it being observed therein," that very [memory] in such a state is *samādhi*; thus, there is no consequence of omitting the eighth [limb].

Nevertheless, in response to the objection that—just as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), though implied by the power of meditation (*dhyāna*) in passages such as "it is to be seen," are understood to serve the purpose of meditation according to the principle of the "foremost" (*agryaprāya*), so too meditation itself might be understood as having the purpose of seeing, and thus the word "seeing" would not refer to something distinct from it—the author clarifies what is intended by the phrase "meditation alone" with the words "And this being so. This means that since it is established by another scriptural text (*śruti*) that *nididhyāsana* is distinguished not only by its identity with constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) but also by its similarity to "seeing."

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of removing doubt, or it serves to combine the logical argument that [the text] naturally pertains to injunction (*vidhi*) with the conformity to other clear scriptural passages (*śruti*). This is the intended meaning: if meditation (*dhyāna*), like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, were not something to be enjoined, then the attainment of the vision [of Brahman] would have to be postulated as resulting from sacrifices and the like alone through the medium of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). In that case, meditation in the interim would be fruitless, because there would be no such visible assistance [to the final result], given the impossibility of a perception produced by the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

If, however, [the suffix] denotes that which is to be performed (*vidheya*), then by the maxim that "when the meaning of a scripture has been determined in one instance, it is automatically established everywhere else," here too—just as in the case of the passage concerning the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*)—*nididhyāsana* must be qualified by its equivalence to *darśana* (seeing). Furthermore, if the opponent's view were correct—that the word "draṣṭavya" refers to the result—there would be an inconsistency regarding the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*). This is also evident from the preceding and following passages.

Since the fruit has already been stated in the passage, "By this I might become immortal; but there is no hope for immortality through wealth; verily, O dear one, immortality is only this much," that [description of the means] is not required here. However, its clarity is established elsewhere, and its presence here is dependent on the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, since it is possible for it to function as a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined—as in the expression "when that [Self] is seen"—it is appropriate to regard it as being subordinate to the means.

Because the combination of alternatives (*vikalpa*), their accumulation (*samuccaya*), or the abandonment of what has been heard (*śrutahāna*) and so forth is untenable; because, when it is possible for a single injunction to have the purpose of establishing a single qualified means toward a single result, a separate injunction for distinct results is not to be accepted; and because, as in the case of the word "with curd" (*dadhnā*), when there is an injunction following a restatement (*anūdyavidhāna*), a unity of the qualified object of injunction (*vidheya*) is possible—this sentence, beginning with "it should be seen that this is directed toward the injunction of meditation (*dhyāna*) qualified by clarity," must be understood as such. For this very reason, even the suspicion that this [sentence] simultaneously functions as both an injunction and a restatement is dispelled.

The objection—how can the vision of the Self, which consists in the direct realization of one’s own bliss and is itself desired, be something to be enjoined—is answered by the statement regarding the injunction for clear recollection (*viśadasmar-tividhāna*). By this, such passages as "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death," "When the seer sees the Golden-Colored One," and "By the knowledge of That, the wise perceive the immortal form of bliss which shines forth," are also appropriately established.

But in that case, the very perception of the yogi would be sublated; for even those words such as "seeing" found in various scriptural passages—which speak of the existence of the yogi’s perception—could be interpreted as referring to an object whose form is identical to that of [ordinary] perception. Nor can their existence be established by such arguments as "dharma and so forth are not perceptible to anyone because they are objects of knowledge," since this would result in proving something other than what was intended, namely, the perception of God (Īśvara).

Even when the formulation of the thesis is "perceptible by the senses," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because that which is known through scripture is also an object of the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, regarding the claim "to be directly perceived by the senses," this has already been answered by those who maintain that even supersensible things (*atīndriya*) are cognizable through reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), as this would result in proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*). If one intends to mean "directly perceptible in its own right" like pleasure and so forth, the necessary logical connection (*pratibandha*) cannot be established due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position. Otherwise, it would follow—just as for the Buddhists—that one could prove that even qualities such as *dharma* are visible to the eye.

For it is indeed possible for someone to employ such fallacious arguments as: "The eye is perceptible to someone, because it is an object of knowledge," and so forth. Furthermore, a counter-argument is easily available: "The sense organ of a yogin does not produce direct perception of dharma and the like, because it is a sense organ, just like the sense organs of people such as ourselves. Do not say this. For it was stated that the mention of "seeing" (darśana) in the context of the means to liberation is non-literal. Elsewhere, however, in the absence of any sublation, one should accept the term according to its literal meaning. (311)

For it is explicitly stated that those who have attained self-restraint possess knowledge of the past, the future, objects beyond the senses, and so forth. This is not memory, because its objects have not been previously experienced. For this very reason, there is no possibility of metaphorically designating it as "perception" (pratyakṣa) merely on account of its clarity. Nor is there any room for inference or other means of knowledge therein, since such possibilities are rejected by statements such as, "He perceives all that exactly as it is through the power of his dharma," and it is further described as being "like an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand."

The direct realization [of the Vedas] is proclaimed through various accumulations of dharma by those who have not studied the *sūkta*, *kāṇḍa*, or *mantra* sections; and it is well known from such statements as, "I give you divine vision. Therefore, there is no lack of proof, because the yogic perception of the external senses and the mind acquires extraordinary, supramundane excellence according to their respective merits through specific virtuous deeds. Nor is there an over-extension of the principle, because there is no reason to transgress what has been heard [in scripture], and because there is no subverting evidence against the contrary position in inference.

Nor can there be a sublation of what is heard (the Veda) by means of inference, because that [inference] is itself sublated by scripture; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, it may be argued that a treatise enjoins one to act within its own capacity; however, the similarity of memory to direct perception (*darśana*) is not dependent on the person, and even that [similarity] is not possible for it. Furthermore, what is impossible—just like the very nature of being a perception—cannot be grasped by an injunction. An injunction whose scope is restricted to the perceptible does not apply when a perceptible result is impossible. To this, he says: "it exists."

*Bhāvanā* is either the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by experience or the act of reflection itself. And that can be performed with devotion and without interruption; from that, the attainment of clarity in recollection follows. Here, a possessive *bahuvrīhi* compound based on a simile should be understood: "that which has a form like the form of perception. Examples such as the mental images of those who are terrified or those who are lustful should be cited here. Others also say: "Even an object previously perceived, when meditated upon though currently beyond the senses, attains the state of being directly present, [causing] afflictions such as desire."

In passages such as "I see [it] in every tree," the presence of error is dependent on a defect; however, here, because one reflects according to what is heard, there is no fault or sublation—this is the intended meaning.

If it were the case that memory becomes equal to direct perception through the intensity of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), what would be the need for ritual action (*karman*) here? It is not so, because both [perception and memory] are established by the mind (*mānasiddha*). (312)

The author of the *Vākya* has elaborated upon all this: "Knowledge (*vedana*) should be meditation (*upāsana*), because it is so heard in that context. In all the Upanishads, it is stated that knowledge—which is enjoined as the means to liberation—is indeed meditation. Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "one should perform the cognition only once, since the purpose of the word has been fulfilled, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings," he established the conclusion: "But [it is] meditation, on account of the word 'meditation' (*upāsana*). Thus, it was determined that knowledge, repeated many times, is the means to liberation.

"Worship (upāsana) would be constant recollection (dhruvānusmṛti), because of its being a vision and because of its etymology"—thus, the state of being constant recollection has been described for that very knowledge which takes the form of worship and is repeated. This recollection is established as having the nature of vision. And this "nature of vision" is the attainment of direct perception. Regarding the fact that recollection takes the form of vision, there is the approval of the author of the *Vākya* [Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya].

To strengthen the aforementioned group of principles, he states—“by the author of the *Vākya*”—that everything in the Sūtra, both literal and implied, has been examined and determined according to its primary distinctions by those who understand its intent. This is because [the term] is heard in that context; the meaning is that the word "knowing" (*vedana*) is used in place of the word "meditation" (*upāsana*) in one instance and in another section. To dispel the suspicion that what was stated here is merely incidental, he explains the *Vākya*: "In all," etc.
Even though it is stated in the injunction for a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭi*), namely, "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman."

Since the same logic applies to the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) as well, it is stated that [the term "knowledge"] is enjoined as a means to liberation for the sake of clarity—namely, to show that what is observed in one instance applies to all of them. By this, there is an exclusion of mere superficial understanding, hearing, reflection, and the resulting ascertainment. To dispel the doubt of the dull-witted—who might suspect that the statement "knowledge is worship" (*vedanam upāsanam*) is a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) due to its proximity to the subsequent sentence—the author says: "once" (*sakṛt*).

For an injunction (*vidhi*), impelling a person who is already naturally inclined toward action, would cause him to act only once even in this case—just as it does with the *prayāja* and other rites in the scriptures for the sake of its own fulfillment. It is with the intention that "the burden of repetition must indeed be endured only when there is a specific statement" that it was said: "because the meaning of the word has been accomplished. This means that the verbal root-meaning, which is the object of the injunction, is fully executed by that much alone. He states what was indicated by the word "but" (*tu*) located in the subsequent sentence: "having formulated the prima facie view" (*pūrvapakṣaṃ kṛtvā*).

He demonstrates the refutation of that [objection] with the words "it is established" (*siddham*). The meaning is that worship (*upāsana*) is established by means of reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*). Alternatively, "established" (*siddham*) means "the established conclusion" (*siddhāntaḥ*), because of the word "worship. The point is that the word "worship" does not have its conventional usage (*prakhyāti*) restricted to a single momentary cognition. He explains this sentence with the words beginning "knowledge" (*vedanam*). By the phrase "because of the word 'worship' and so forth," it is shown—through the recognition of the word—that even the sentence "knowledge is worship" has the status of a final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Although the constancy of *dhyāna* was not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, it was previously indicated by the symmetry of the reasoning and explained by [the author] himself. However, in the [present] statement, he adopts that same [constancy] for *upāsana*, which is non-different from *dhyāna*, saying "upāsanam. "Darśanam" refers to the natural worldly perspective. "Nirvacanam" refers to the scriptural passage cited earlier as providing the definitive determination (*nirṇāyaka*). Alternatively, "darśanam" refers to direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), while "nirvacanam" refers to the explanatory elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) consisting of a distinct, extracted statement.

The phrase "of that very [practice]" means of that which is prescribed as a means to liberation, and not of the cause of liberation favored by others; for since there is no application of the term *upāsanā* (meditation) to a single occurrence, the statement specifies that the word *upāsana* used in the sentence intends that which consists of repeated practice (*asakṛdāvṛtti*).

Now, it was previously stated that "all this has been explained in detail"; however, in that context, its nature as a form of vision (*darśana*) was not observed. Therefore, even though it was not explicitly mentioned there, [the author] restates it—saying "this very [meditation]"—in order to clarify that it follows the same logical principle as the two qualities already mentioned, namely repetition (*āvṛtti*) and constancy (*dhruvatva*), and for the purpose of prescribing another attribute. The meaning is that it is characterized by repetition through the qualities of being meditation (*dhyāna*) and worship (*upāsana*), and is further qualified by constancy as stated in another scriptural passage.

The meaning is that the author of the *Vākyakāra* has also implicitly stated that [this cognition] has the nature of perception (*darśana*). Alternatively, this was intended by us previously because of the symmetry of the underlying logic. Now, although it is impossible to establish the identity of one thing with another, and since memory and perception have distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), the unification of two heterogeneous types in a single instance is impossible elsewhere—even so, just as dream-cognition—which arises solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)—possesses the character of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) due to the auxiliary factor of a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*), here too, even though production by the eye is impossible, [the same may occur].

To the question, "Even though it is not directly perceived as being inseparable from that [object], why could the term 'vision' (*darśana*) not be applied figuratively to the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) simply because of its similarity in being a mere cognition? he says: "Because it has the form of vision. This refers to an attainment of perceptuality, but not direct perceptuality itself, because that is impossible. The intended meaning is this: even dream-cognition is not primary vision, due to the absence of the operation of the eyes.

However, when the functioning of the external senses has ceased, a vivid memory regarding previously experienced objects is produced by the mind—which does not wander elsewhere—due to the intensity of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). There is no lack of justification for this, as there is no other reason that could establish such a cognition. In this case, even though the memory is not produced by the eyes or other senses, the notion that it is so produced, as well as the notion of connection where there is none, is a mental error (*mānasabhrānti*) caused by a defect.

However, in accordance with the section on *saṃdhyā*, since [the cognition in question] lacks the quality of being produced by mere refinement (*saṃskāra*), its status as "seeing" (*darśana*) remains unmixed; therefore, it is not possible to establish the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) for the subject at hand by analogy with dream-vision. Furthermore, a metaphorical usage based merely on the similarity of "seeing" due to the common factor of being a cognition (*dhī*) is not appropriate when a specific distinction that accords with the most proximate praise of the subject can be established.

Thus, he distinguishes that *smṛti* which has become directly perceived and serves as the means for liberation: "This Self is not to be obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses him is He obtained; to him this Self reveals His own form. By this, having stated that mere hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are not the means for attaining the Self, it is said: "Only by whomsoever this Self chooses, by him alone is He obtainable. For only one who is most beloved becomes the object of choice.

He for whom this [Self] is the unsurpassed beloved becomes His most beloved; and as this most beloved one attains the Self, so does the Blessed Lord Himself exert effort—thus it has been said by the Blessed Lord Himself: "To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love, I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me."

Thus it is said: "For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me. Therefore, for one whose remembrance—which is of the nature of direct realization—is itself exceedingly dear because the object remembered is exceedingly dear, that very person becomes the one to be chosen by the Supreme Self; thus it is stated that the Supreme Self is attained by that [remembrance] alone.
It is precisely this worship in the form of constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) that constitutes the nature of devotion (*bhakti*).

Now, an objection is raised: in passages such as "This is not the Self," it was stated that after negating the triad of hearing and so forth, the attainment [of the goal] occurs solely through the unfathomable and independent grace [of the Lord]; therefore, according to the maxim, "I consider fate alone to be superior, while human effort is useless," everything previously stated is false. To this, he says "Thus" (*evam*), meaning that in the Sūtra and its commentary, what is intended by the term "meditation" (*upāsanā*)—which is defined by attributes such as constancy—is specifically the qualification of being of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*). Thus, he states: "Thus."

The meaning is: "by means of the method of resting in a specific [meaning], as stated in the Sūtras and elsewhere regarding general terms. The phrase "having attained perceptibility" is intended to indicate the formal similarity (*nyāyasāmya*) with the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) that will be discussed later. It is illogical for concealment (*āvaraṇa*) to be causeless; for if it had a beginning, it could not be causeless. If it were beginningless, it would follow that liberation (*mukti*) is also beginningless.

Because it would otherwise follow that the injunction regarding the means to liberation is futile, and because it would contradict sūtras such as those prohibiting partiality and cruelty—which are intended to negate specific distinctions in the form of the individual soul's (jīva) activity—it is stated that [the Self] "is the means to liberation. By this, the suspicion that the text is concerned with meditations for the sake of some other fruit is also dispelled; for it is the Supreme Self that is intended to be attained here. He qualifies this by saying: "it does not, however, set aside what is established by valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇa).
Otherwise, the injunction of other means would be purposeless.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the preceding and following passages, such as: "The wise man, having understood [this], does not grieve; he attains it through wisdom (*prajñāna*). Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "This is not the Self" (*nāyam ātmā*), the word *śruta* denotes hearing (*śravaṇa*). And the word *medhā* must have the sense of meditation (*dhyāna*), in accordance with the Vedic text: "May *medhā* and *manīṣā* enter me together for the attainment of what has been and what is to be. The *Nighaṇṭu* also states: "*Dhīḥ* is that which possesses retention; it is *medhā*. By process of elimination, the word *pravacana* refers to reflection (*manana*), which is mentioned alongside hearing and meditation.

It is called "manana" (reflection) based on the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*), meaning "that by which one reflects. Alternatively, it refers to the teacher’s instruction for the purpose of the disciple’s reflection; or, the effect (reflection) is metaphorically attributed to its cause (the instruction). Now, one might raise the objection: how can that which negates the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of something be an injunction for it? Furthermore, there is a doubt that in some cases it would be redundant because it negates what is already part of the means (*aṅga*) or the end (*aṅgin*), while in other cases there would be contradiction because it negates what has been enjoined. To this, while warding off the consequence of rendering hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest useless, he clarifies that the statement qualifies *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance) with the words "by this": "By this... [he says].

Just as in the case of the injunction "fire is not to be piled on the earth," where the purpose of the prohibition is to establish that the fire must be placed upon gold in order to avoid the deficiency of gold, so too here, since hearing and the other [means] must necessarily occur—either directly or through an appropriate indirect channel (praṇāḍī)—just as in the case of the earth, the word *kevala* (exclusive/only) intends to enjoin a specific degree of delight regarding all three [means] by way of prohibiting a deficiency of delight. Alternatively, the word *kevala* is read together with the prohibitions of non-participants, such as "not in the intermediate space" and "not in heaven."

The phrase "not on the earth" is a prohibition of what has been previously established; just as it rests upon the injunction of a specific qualification—namely, that gold must be placed [as a base]—by excluding the earth alone from being the locus, as is the case with the intermediate space and so forth; so too, the prohibition of meditation (*nididhyāsana*) together with hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), which are not themselves the means, results in an injunction of devotion (*bhakti*) as the essence [of the means], by way of stating that meditation alone, like hearing and so forth, is not the means.

The inclusion of the phrase "whomever" (*yameva*) is intended to exclude the suspicion of an arbitrary or independent choice according to one's own whim, and to clarify that the choice has a restricted object by the force of the subsequent statement. This is because a choice that is a friend to all, untainted by defects such as partiality, cannot possibly have a restricted object. Just as the verb *bhavati* in the sentence *yad āgneyaḥ*, the verb *vṛṇute* (chooses) must have its purport in enjoining the causal operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), implying that there must be one who possesses the causal operation of choosing what is to be obtained.

[Objection: Surely, just as gold placed upon a substrate must necessarily rest on the earth, so too, since no rule is observed for the connection between the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) and that specific quality which—suggested by the word *yat* in this sentence—is the cause of being desirable, that [remembrance] cannot attain distinction through it. To this, he says: "the most beloved" (*priyatama*). The use of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) is intended to exclude a semblance of devotion directed toward other fruits. The particle *hi* indicates that the nature of the Supreme and the Lower Persons is well-known from both scripture and common worldly experience.

[Objection: "Granted that by this much some other activity which brings about the state of being most beloved for the one to be chosen may be established; however, the specific nature of the constant remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti) has not been attained. To this he says: "Of whom... The meaning is: he alone—neither one possessing other meritorious deeds, nor one possessing mere constant remembrance, nor anyone who is merely a sincere devotee. "To him I am equal."

This means that he possesses the very nature described by [the Lord] himself in the passage beginning with "toward all beings" (*sarvabhūteṣu*). The underlying idea is this: since other activities that cause one's own pleasure lack the quality of being a cause for choosing [someone] for the sake of one's own attainment, only one who possesses absolute love fixed upon his own object—being the dearest to another—would be chosen for the purpose of attaining oneself.

And this state of consciousness, consisting of unsurpassed love, which is averse to both conceptual construction and mere accumulation [of merit], and which relies upon the constant mindfulness (dhruvānusmṛti) established as the means to liberation by the force of a unique and exclusive authority (*ananyagatika-pramāṇa*), distinguishes that [liberation]. Now, one might object: what is gained today for that which has been eternally acquired as one’s own remainder? And what is it to be "attained" now for that which is eternally present through its all-pervasiveness?

To clarify how it is established that "the Beloved alone is what is to be chosen" by this [devotee], he explains everything through the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (corroborative texts) with the words "Just as... and so on. This one—possessing unsurpassed love due to the manifestation of the state of being the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*) in the Lord without any limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)—therefore attains the Beloved, who is the Self; he rejoices in his own Self. To make clear that, unlike others, there is no dependence on another in granting to that [devotee] who has become gracious the yoga of the intellect (*buddhi-yoga*) and other means which are the immediate cause of liberation (*apavarga*), the word "himself" (*svayam eva*) is used.

Or rather, it may be indicated that He brings about inconceivable benefit for the worshipper—by the Lord Himself, as declared in the Śruti: "Whomever this one chooses" (*yamevaiṣa vṛṇute*), thus appearing as the agent of choice. By this, His status as the supreme authority (*paramāpta*) due to His innate omniscience is also revealed. The term *satatayuktānām* means those who desire constant yoga; the suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of a future possibility (*āśaṃsāyām*). Since the state of the worshipper’s intellect being characterized by love is established by the phrase "of those who are constantly engaged in devotion," the syntactical connection is: "I give with love. For the Supreme Lord, there is neither affection nor aversion caused by formal service or its neglect.
However, the view that the fruit of those two [the cause and the effect] arises through the power of the sign (nimitta) is devoid of logical principle.

Obstructing [the disciple], desiring to lead him upward, and desiring to lead him downward—these actions of the teacher are not prohibited because they are sanctioned by scripture, since they result in the attainment of the respective fruits of those specific deeds. (314)

He states—beginning with "For he is dear"—that the reason for someone being most beloved, which is the cause for being chosen (*varaṇīyatā*), and which is intended by the scripture and expressed by the word "ever-united" (*satatayukta*), has been explained right there. "Exceedingly" (*atyartham*) means beyond what can be expressed; the sense is that even I find it difficult to describe. In this context, "choosing" (*varaṇa*) refers to an unfailing resolve (*amoghasaṅkalpa*) such as, "May this person attain Me. Furthermore, the fact that He is obtainable in this regard is what is intended by the word "reveals" (*vivṛṇute*).

The meaning is that it has been stated, by implication, that [Brahman] is the object of unconditioned experience in which all obstacles have ceased. Here, the author clarifies what was not explicitly expressed—that constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is characterized as being of the nature of bliss—by means of scripture accompanied by its supporting texts (*sopabṛṃhaṇa*): "Therefore... This is done in accordance with common worldly usage and through the operation of the intended meaning of the cited scriptures and traditional texts.

This is the meaning. "Exceedingly dear" (*atyarthapriyā*) means that, by virtue of having a nature of extreme favorability, She manifests of Her own accord; even in an inappropriate state, She is made the object of a cognition in the form of love, according to the maxim: "For those lacking discrimination, there is love even [for what is] improper. The statement regarding Her being "exceedingly dear when remembered" is intended to show that, in all cases, the quality of being love itself and the state of being an object of love belong to the subject's cognition depending upon a particular object. Thus, it is shown that there is an implied exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the agent of choosing or revealing from that object of choice, as indicated by the word "by another" (*pareṇa*).

This very recollection of the Eternal (*dhruvānusmṛti*) of such a nature is designated by the word "devotion" (*bhakti*), because the word *bhakti* is a synonym for "worship" (*upāsanā*). For this very reason, it is stated thus in the Śruti and Smṛti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; only by knowing Him does one become immortal here. There is no other path for the journey. "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner as you have seen Me."
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna,
I who am of such a nature can be known and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.

"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion" (Gītā 11.54). Now, it might be objected: "It is well known from the Purāṇas and other sources that wisdom is of the nature of devotion; thus, the status of devotion as a means has been introduced. In the phrase 'expressed by words such as meditation (dhyāna), worship (upāsanā), etc.', the word 'etc. (ādi) was intended to include the word 'devotion' (bhakti) as well; however, that notion does not exist in the Śrutis cited here. Therefore, how can there be no contradiction? To this he replies: "Of such a form. This means it is qualified by the sequence of stages already described. To the objection that this is merely a formal proposition (pratijñā), he says: "In worship," etc.

The sense is that there is no occasion for contradiction, because although there is a difference in terminology—since *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance) is designated by the word "meditation" (*upāsana*) due to its nature as joy, and because it conforms to the definition that "devotion (*bhakti*) is meditation preceded by affection," and because "service," "devotion," and "meditation" are listed as synonyms—the identity of meaning is established; thus, there is no difference in what is to be enjoined.

He states "ataḥ" (therefore) to reinforce—by means of another logical argument consisting of the undesirable consequence that the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (the Purāṇas) and the *upabṛṃhaṇīya* (the Vedas) would mutually contradict each other—that words such as "knowledge" (*vedanā*) and so forth culminate in devotion (*bhakti*). This refers to the reason in the form of the result: the meaning is that since devotion alone is expressed by words such as "knowledge," "meditation" (*upāsanā*), and so on. The restrictive particle "eva" (alone) is used with the intention that otherwise there would be a mutual contradiction between the Śrutis and the Smṛtis, just as there is among the Śrutis themselves.
"In this way" (*evam*) means according to the manner already stated: that in the Śruti there is no final means other than knowledge, while in the Smṛti there is no final means other than devotion.

The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad has the Supreme Person as its subject matter. Now, an objection might be raised: the Śvetāśvatara statement, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," concerns Rudra because it is mentioned in conjunction with words such as "Śiva" and so forth; whereas the passage, "Knowing Him thus... concerns the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). Furthermore, in both that [passage] and this one, it is declared, "There is no other path for going. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction. To dispel this doubt of the dull-witted, both these passages are cited here.

The point is this: through the preceding passages such as "I know this great Puruṣa," and the subsequent passages such as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," there occurs a recognition—both by word and by meaning—of the Great Puruṣa described in the *Puruṣasūkta* as the one whose sole purpose is to impel *sattva*. Since it is therefore certain that words such as Śiva and Maheśvara must refer to Him, it is proper to abandon their conventional meanings (rūḍhi) in favor of this specific sense, according to the principle of the *aindrī* mantra.
Because of the recitation of the Lord's names as "Sarva," "Śarva," "Śiva," and "Sthāṇu," and because of the word "Śiva" itself—

Because [the term "Śiva"] is conventionally established at the beginning of auspicious rites; because, according to the method stated here, the excellence of its popular renown would otherwise be rendered fruitless; because the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the *Saubhāla-mahopaniṣad*, and other such texts—which cannot be explained otherwise—are more authoritative; and because, as in the case of the terms "eternal," "auspicious," and "imperishable," it must necessarily refer to the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). Therefore, since at the beginning of the passage "The auspicious one is all-pervading" there is recognition of attributes such as having a thousand heads in the verse "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings," and because of the word "Bhagavān" in the phrase "And the Blessed Lord is all-pervading," [it refers to Nārāyaṇa].

Because it establishes the state of being mounted upon the form of the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), and because the conclusion must be interpreted without contradicting that [establishment] as a supplement to the subject at hand, the disputed passage has as its very object that which is described in the Puruṣasūkta. In this regard:

The statement beginning with "I am not" (nāham) intends to show that the Vedas, austerities, and so forth lack direct status as means [to liberation]; thus, there is no contradiction with that [teaching]. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "but by unswerving devotion" (bhaktyā tvananyayā) intends to show that knowledge in the form of devotion—possessing distinct stages—is the means for achieving other forms of knowledge and so on; therefore, there is no contingency of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) or similar fallacies. Nor does the citation of the passage beginning with "That Person is the Supreme" (puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ) render the preceding [passage] redundant, because it elucidates what was not previously understood.

This is indeed the intended meaning here: that which was heard in the preceding statement, "He who knows Him thus—of solar hue, beyond darkness"—is precisely what is made recognized by the description of His having an inconceivable form and being of solar hue, beginning with the words, "He who should meditate on Him who is subtler than the subtle. Furthermore, what was stated as "the Ordainer in front" is shown to mean "the Ordainer of all. In that context, what was expressed by the verb *vid* (to know) in the Śruti is here explained by the verb *anusmaret* (should meditate upon). Moreover, he is immediately thereafter qualified by the phrase "endowed with devotion."

Therefore, it is understood that the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) in the form of devotion is enjoined by the Veda through the root *vid*. Although, in this context, it is more appropriate that it concerns the means for other human goals (*puruṣārtha*) due to the recurrence of the verbal suffix, nevertheless—by the same principle—it must be accepted that even the Vedic injunction for the sake of liberation finds its culmination in devotion. And in that very passage, with the words "that person is the Supreme" (*tatraiva ca puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ*), he reveals that even the Vedic injunction for the sake of liberation has that [devotion] as its specific goal.

"By whomsoever He is chosen, by him alone is He attainable"—this [truth], hidden within the encapsulation of the Śruti, is here revealed. For here, by means of the use of a qualifying attribute, not only is the existence of another object of attainment for the knowers (jñānins) excluded, as if there were another [attainment], but also another means of attainment is ruled out. Indeed, just as the identity of the object to be attained is established through the recognition (pratyabhijñā) expressed in the Śruti, the identity of the means is likewise logical. Therefore, in place of the word *vid* (to know), the root *bhaj* (to worship/seek refuge) is employed here as a qualifier, just as one uses *dhyai* (to meditate) or *upās* (to adore). "The Puruṣasūkta and the Bhagavadgītā are accepted as the most authoritative [scriptures].
They should not be subject to mutual contradiction; when they have the same meaning, there is no disregard for the Smṛti. (Verse 315)

[Objection: Is it not the case that in such passages as "By devotion he comes to know Me," the attainment of the Supreme is taught through knowledge produced by devotion? [Reply: Not so; for even there, in the phrase "Then he enters into Me," it is devotion itself that is referred to as the cause of attainment. Otherwise, the word "then" (*tataḥ*) would be redundant. Therefore, the meaning is the same as the statement "by devotion one enters."

It will be stated [in the Sūtras] that sacrificial rites and other such acts are the means for this kind of constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*), based on the scriptural mention of sacrifices and so forth, "like the horse. Although sacrifices and other acts are enjoined for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by the text "desiring to know," nevertheless, they serve that very knowledge which consists of meditation (*dhyāna*), which is performed day after day, which acquires excellence through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), and which continues until the moment of death.

Since they are the means for attaining Brahman, all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) must be performed throughout one's entire life for the sake of its arising. And the author will state this in such passages as: "Until death, for it is seen there as well," "But the Agnihotra and other rites are for that very purpose, because of scriptural evidence," and "And as auxiliaries," etc.
This constitutes the refutation of the position that the utility of rituals lies solely in their being the means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

One might object: "Since the natural import of the accepted Śruti and Smṛti texts suggests that devotion alone—without dependence on Vedic recitation, sacrifice, and so forth—is the means to liberation, it would follow that the inquiry into ritual action (karma) does not precede this [inquiry into Brahman]. To this, he says: "Of such a nature. This means: established by the statements of Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtra as possessing specific stages culminating in devotion, such as meditation and others, which depend upon previously performed merit (sukṛta).

With the intention of showing that the status of *śruti* and *sūtra* as having *vividiṣā* (the desire to know) as their subject matter is refuted both by context and by the sense of the words, the author says "of constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ*). The meaning is that this will be stated by the author of the *Sūtras* and will be established by us as well. In proximity to the word "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), a clear realization is enjoined in the passage "it is to be perceived by the mind alone" (*manasaivānudraṣṭavyam*); and it is praised in the passage "having known this very thing, one becomes a sage" (*etameva viditvā munirbhavati*). Therefore, there is a requirement for another injunction only with respect to that realization which is the object of the injunction and the praise here.

But this does not apply to a desire to know (*vividiṣā*) that is devoid of both [the desire for knowledge and the desire for action]. Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that [the sacrifice] is enjoined as a means to the desire to know. For when it is said, "one desires to go to heaven by means of a sacrifice," it does not follow that the sacrifice is the means to the *desire to go*; and here, in the absence of the desire for knowledge (*vedana*), the state of desiring to know (*vividiṣā*) cannot be established. If that [desire for knowledge] were already present, there would be no need for its means; moreover, the desire to know arises from the desire for knowledge, the desire to know leads to the performance of sacrifices and so forth, and that performance gives rise to the desire to know—this would result in a logical circle (*cakraka*).

In this context, some have asserted that there is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) due to the contraction of the stages (*parva*). However, this is not a case of an unknown principle regarding merit (*sukṛta*); for sacrifices and the like are accomplished through effort requiring great care. Therefore, as in the expression "he wishes to kill with a sword," there is no syntactical connection [of the means] as being the instrument of desire due to logical inconsistency.
Without a desire for the goal (*sādhya*), a desire for the means (*sādhana*) is never established anywhere.
Consequently, since it cannot serve the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), its purpose here is indeed knowledge (*vidyā*). || 316 ||
From the desire for liberation, the wish for its means is also established;
therefore, for one who desires knowledge, an injunction regarding its means is appropriate. (317)
In this context, devotion is perceived as the primary result, whereas the desire for that [result] is proclaimed as the qualification by means of the suffix. (318)

[Objection: Surely, it must be accepted that the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the cause of all worldly effects; otherwise, it would be impossible for the various desires that serve as the causes of unequal pleasure, pain, and so forth to arise at certain times and not arise at others. Therefore, if desire in general were merely something to be produced, then the desire to know would also be such, and its refutation would contradict all established systems (*sarvatantra*).

To this, it is replied in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*: "The arising of desire is possible from the cognition of the specific nature of an object, which is assisted by prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) awakened by the unseen merit/demerit of experience."

For even those effects that are not perceived for the sake of enjoyment, though unrequested by men, may bring forth their results because they reside within [the intellect] as the faculty of yielding fruit. || 319 ||

Therefore, in this context, the injunction regarding the performance of practice is: "One who desires the knowledge of Brahman in the form of devotion should cultivate that [Brahman] through sacrifices and other means accompanied by tranquility and the like. Now, one might object: "Even in the injunction for the means to achieve devotion, the aforementioned fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*) and so forth would still apply. This is not so—because that injunction is made with regard to the increase and the persistence of devotion. Likewise, there is no contradiction even in the injunction for the means to knowledge; for although [Brahman] is known in a general way, one proceeds [to practice] out of a desire to know it in its specific detail.

Nor should it be argued that even regarding a specific object, the conceptual distinction between the known and the unknown is untenable; for even according to you, one engages in debate and similar activities only when they involve the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and the posing of questions. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with both the common person and the investigator. If it is then claimed that for one who has thus developed the desire to know, there is an injunction regarding the means [to knowledge] out of a wish to continue that inquiry, we reply: even in that case, since there is no difference in the result, such a pursuit would follow from that very [desire], and because the "knowledge" asserted by others has already been refuted.

He states that the ritual action must be performed throughout one's life in order to maintain the desire for the realization characterized by the many forms he himself has described—this is expressed by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). However, if [the opponent] maintains the position that it is merely a means for the *vividiṣā* (desire to know) as stated by others, then the subsequent response must somehow be interpreted in accordance with the persistence of that *vividiṣā*. The phrase "of that very [desire]" (*tasyaiva*) refers precisely to the object of the *vividiṣā*. The statement that it takes the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) is made with the intention that this realization is not, like a sacrifice or like an *apūrva*, a means that is effective once produced or at intervals.

The expression "day after day" (*aharahar*) and so forth excludes both the notion that even a continuous practice could be accomplished in a single day—like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—and the notion that it could be accomplished with intervals between days. Furthermore, the statement regarding its continuation "until death" (*āprayāṇāt*) [establishes its lifelong duration].

This is for the purpose of excluding the notion that [the practice] must be performed every day for a period limited to a year or the like. By the phrase "an excellence to be produced through repeated practice" (*abhyāsādheyātiśaya*), it is indicated that there is also a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*). "For the sake of its arising" means for the sake of the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is intended as something to be accomplished through sacrifices and other means because it is desired as a continuous state. The word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) is to be distributed appropriately [with the various duties]. By the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), there is a rebuttal of what was previously stated, such as "for hundreds of future births" and so forth.

Even when the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has arisen, the abandonment of ritual action in the interim is not appropriate; for if the desire to know were interrupted, there would follow the interruption of knowledge itself. Indeed, the persistence of knowledge cannot be established by a single instance of the desire to know, just as the persistence of eating cannot be established by a single instance of hunger. Even if its continuation is possible through the abundance of past meritorious deeds, the intention is that one must still engage in practice to pacify potential obstacles. Previously, it was shown in the Sūtra that knowledge takes the form of meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and so forth.

Now, he states that there are sūtras regarding the necessity of following [the meditation] day after day until death, and likewise the continuation of its constituent rites, by saying: "And he will state... By these very sūtras, the scriptural passages concerning those respective topics are also indicated. By this, the contradiction with the sūtras and other authorities in the event of not accepting his own position is reinforced. For by the sūtra itself—"For it is seen even there until departure"—it is established that the performance of the rite must continue for as long as one lives.

Indeed, because the phrase "practicing in this manner for as long as life lasts" is intended to be expressed by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), and because the continuation of the duties previously mentioned—such as "in a pure household and in a pure place"—is restated here by the words "practicing in this manner," the mention of the *agnihotra* and other rites in the Sūtra is for the purpose of making known that even those obligatory rites, such as the *agnihotra*, are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). This is in accordance with the scriptural injunction: "One should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives."

Regarding the question of how ritual action—though described as a constituent part of the stages of life (*āśrama*) in the sūtra *vihitatvāccāśramakarmāpi*—can serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*), the sūtra portion *sahakāritvena ca* is cited to indicate the principle of "separate application" (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is a collection of sūtras indicating simultaneous performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*), such as *sarvathāpi ta evobhayaliṅgāt*, which show that those very same rituals serve both as constituents of the stages of life and as constituents of knowledge.

And the author of the *Vākyakāra* states that the attainment of constant mindfulness (*dhruvānusmṛti*) arises from discernment (*viveka*) and the other [means] alone: "Its attainment is possible through discernment, detachment, practice, virtuous action, lack of despondency, and lack of elation, according to both the derivation and the definition. He also explains the nature of discernment and the others: "Discernment is the purification of the body through food that is not defective in terms of species, source, or cause. The definition here is: "When there is purity of food, there is purity of the *sattva*; when there is purity of the *sattva*, there is constant mindfulness. Detachment (*vimoka*) is non-attachment to desires.

"One should worship with tranquility" is the etymological definition (*nirvacana*). Furthermore, "cultivation of the undertaking" means repeated practice. And the author of the Commentary has cited a Smṛti etymological definition: "Always permeated by that state. "Performance according to one's ability" refers to the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth; the etymological definition for this is: "This man of action is the best among the knowers of Brahman," and "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know him through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting."

Truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, charity, non-violence, and freedom from covetousness constitute the auspicious discipline (*nīti*). Its etymological definition is found in such passages as: "He is to be attained through truth," and "For them alone is that stainless world of Brahman. Dejection (*avasāda*) is the lack of luster in the mind, born of depression due to unfavorable place and time, and the recollection of objects of grief. Its opposite is non-dejection (*anavasāda*). Its etymological definition is: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength. Exultation (*uddharṣa*) is the satisfaction born from the opposite of that [dejection]. Its opposite is non-exultation (*anuddharṣa*).

The meaning is that excessive contentment is an obstacle. The scriptural definition is also "one who is tranquil and self-controlled. Thus, it is stated that for one endowed with such restraints (*niyama*), the perfection of knowledge (*vidyā*) occurs precisely through the performance of the duties prescribed for one's stage of life (*āśrama*).
This refers to the sevenfold means beginning with discrimination (*viveka*), as taught by the author of the *Vākya*.

Now, he also refutes the arguments of the prima facie position—such as "because of contradiction" and "because of lack of authority"—by means of the words of those who know the intention of the author of the Sūtras, beginning with the verse: *vākye* (In the sentence...). By the word *eva* (only), it is made known that there is no contradiction between [the requirements of] tranquility (*śama*) and so forth and sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth, and that there is agreement with what has been stated by himself. Alternatively, the meaning is: not by the fourfold means, nor by any one of the [means] such as discrimination (*viveka*), nor by action alone, nor by tranquility and so forth alone. "For one who has desisted from prohibited, optional, and fruitless actions, the engagement in the limbs of knowledge appropriate to his own stage of life (*āśrama*) is not contradicted by tranquility and the rest. (320)

In order to show that [the means] function as a single instrument when combined without contradiction, he cites the sentence: "The attainment of that" (*tallabdhi*). Here, the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is indicated by the phrase "of constant recollection" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ*); for it refers back to what was under discussion there, namely, that "constant recollection would be meditation" (*upāsana*).

The suspicion of some—that it might be possible to establish a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) for the seven [factors] beginning with *viveka* (discrimination) based on their mutual dependence in a single effect through their conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*), such that they function equally in both engagement and withdrawal according to the different stages of life (*āśrama*)—is also refuted. This is because of their "possibility" (*sambhavāt*), meaning there is no contradiction in their coexistence within a single locus due to their respective capacities; and because of "definition" (*nirvacanāt*), meaning from a definitive statement (*niṣkṛṣṭa-vacana*) which serves as a means of certain knowledge regarding supersensuous matters, that is to say, from scripture (*āgama*) accompanied by reasoning (*yukti*). Here, this is intended to establish that knowledge (*vidyā*) is produced by action (*karman*).

Regarding the question of what these [qualities] such as discernment (*viveka*) are, and how they are not in conflict with one another, the author of the *Vākya* states that this has already been explained by him: "of discernment and the others. This means both their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the specific characteristics that distinguish them from one another. "Defiled by genus" (*jātiduṣṭa*) refers to garlic and the like; "defiled by source" (*āśrayaduṣṭa*) refers to the food of a Śūdra and the like; and "defiled by cause" (*nimittaduṣṭa*) refers to that which is contaminated by hair and so forth.

Discrimination (*viveka*) is the separation, by means of purification, of the body along with its senses from impure food—food which has been distinguished from what is impure by being free from such defects—through the manifestation of *sattva* that is devoid of the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*. He states the illustrative sentence: "Born... (*jāti-*, etc.). Here, the commentary says this is the "etymological derivation" (*nirvacana*). In the etymological derivation, "purity of food leads to purity of *sattva*" (*āhāraśuddhau sattvaśuddhiḥ*), *sattva* refers either to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or the quality of *sattva*. The mention of the "body" (*kāya*) in the sentence is intended as an illustration for all things that require purification.

That [sattva] is also characterized by the group of instruments (karaṇa). Longevity, vitality, and so forth, as well as pure and impure food, have been described. Here, the word "liberation" (vimoka) refers to desire, anger, and likewise greed.

The intention is that the statement "non-attachment to desires" (*kāmanabhiṣvaṅga*) is an expression of a "blow to the root," as it aims at the non-contact with the aforementioned group of things to be abandoned. Here, "desire" (*kāma*) is that which is produced by the most intense attachment (*saṅga*), in accordance with the teaching: "From attachment, desire is born. By this, "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*) refers to persistent and firm grasping; in its absence, the cessation of the sequence described in such passages as "from desire, anger is born" follows. In the phrase "one who is tranquil should meditate" (*śānta upāsīta*), the word "tranquil" (*śānta*) refers to the absence of desire and the like by way of the cessation of the activity of the senses.

The "support" (*ārambhaṇa*) is a beautiful object of refuge serving as a mental focal point for one desiring to ascend the path of yoga. In the *Vivaraṇa*, however, it is stated that one should worship the object of knowledge (*jñāna*). Its "cultivation" (*saṃśīlana*) is the practice of it in a manner conducive [to progress]. The phrase "again and again" is to be connected with the time of rising from sleep, based on the context of the ancillaries (*aṅga*) and the Smṛti passage beginning with "even by a mind occupied [with other things]. For this very reason, there is no suspicion of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). And this [practice] is for the purpose of accumulating impressions (*vāsanā*) favorable to yoga and for the purpose of removing the impurities (*kaṣāya*).

The statement from the *Smṛti* is made with the intention of showing an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the Vedic definition—"Having become disillusioned with both childhood and scholarship, one then becomes a sage"—because its meaning is not explicit. Here, the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is the teacher Dramiḍācārya, who is the expounder of the *Vākyakāra* (Brahmanandin). By him, scripture (*śruti*) was cited in other instances, but here it is *Smṛti*. Alternatively, in other cases the *Vākyakāra* himself cited scripture, whereas here the *Bhāṣyakāra* himself cites *Smṛti*.

Although the phrase "whatever [being] he remembers" (*yaṃ yaṃ vāpi smarann*) introduces a general principle—as seen in the words "always" (*sadā*) and so forth—nevertheless, because it refers to the specific subject at hand in accordance with the subsequent sentence, "Therefore, at all times remember Me," that [specific object] is what is understood here. The mention of the "five great sacrifices" (*pañcamahāyajña*) is for the purpose of indicating the Smṛti teaching that even a householder is liberated. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the duties belonging to the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are also included. Although in the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the inclusion of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is required;

Nevertheless, the phrase "according to one's ability" (*śaktitaḥ*) is stated here with the intention that, as expressed in this teaching, performance according to one's capacity is sufficient. For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Performing that [duty] according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. Furthermore, because there is no use of the desiderative suffix (*san*) in the passage "this performer of rites is the best among the knowers of Brahman," the connection of ritual acts with knowledge is made explicit; thus, even the term *vividiṣanti* ("they desire to know") is thereby regulated. And this statement has as its purport that action, as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), is a cause for the full perfection of knowledge.

But this does not indicate the existence of one who knows the inactive Brahman, because it has been stated that ritual action persists as long as life lasts; or rather, by taking the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) to mean "abundance," it is intended to exclude those who know Brahman but are incapacitated (such as the blind and others). For they are inferior because they possess only the duties of their social class (*varṇadharma*). Therefore...

However, it is established by the sūtra, "But the other [is] superior, because of the indicative mark" (*liṅgāt*). In this regard, the scriptural passage beginning with "In these mantras are the rituals... and ending with "...perform them constantly, O you who desire truth," should also be considered. The phrase beginning with "this very one" (*tam etam*) is employed to exclude the mere concentration of the mind and so forth from the word *kriyā*. By the term *anāśakena*—meaning by non-eating—the word *tapas* (austerity) is restricted here according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Alternatively, it means "by something other than that which causes destruction."

Even sacrifices and the like, if performed for the sake of enjoyment, are established by the Śruti and other authorities as leading only to destruction, which is of the nature of saṃsāra. Truth (*satya*) is speech that is beneficial to living beings and consistent with reality. Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the uniformity of the three instruments [of body, speech, and mind]. Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to dispel the suffering of others, independent of one's own interest. Generosity (*dāna*) is the bestowing of wealth acquired through righteous means upon a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rules; by this, the cessation of greed is manifested. Alternatively, based on the verbal root *daip* in the sense of "purifying," it may mean the purification of one's own side and so forth.

Regarding the root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*), this refers here to the shattering of the egoism of others, according to the Smṛti: "One should subdue those who revile the deities and gurus to the best of one's ability. This is because the injunction "one should not engage in contentious debate" (*na vigṛhya kathāṃ kuryāt*) pertains to matters of personal whim. Here, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) consists in the avoidance of causing harm to living beings contrary to the scriptures, as established by the statement: "Not harming any living beings, except at sacred sites" (*ahiṃsan sarvabhūtānyanyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*). Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the thought of doing harm to others.

For in the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like, the prefix *abhi-* signifies hostility, or constant remembrance of harm done by another, or false attachment, or the notion that another's property should be seized; the cessation of these is non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*). In this way, the mention of a few [virtues] serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others as well, such as those recited together with straightforwardness (*ārjava*), compassion (*dayā*), and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), there is an inclusion of such qualities as freedom from pride (*amānitva*), freedom from ostentation (*adambhitva*), compassion toward all beings, patience, and lack of envy.

Thinking that non-dejection would follow as a matter of course, he provides a statement with its reason regarding the nature of its opposite: "Place," etc. A "thing of sorrow" (*śokavastu*) is an object that causes grief; alternatively, the word *śoka* may be derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*), meaning "that by which one sorrows. The word "etc. refers to the cause of fear. Sorrow and fear are forms of suffering consisting of cognitions directed toward undesirable things past or yet to come. These two connect with the phrase "the mind's lack of luminosity due to imperfection and recollection" (*vaiguṇyād anusmṛteśca*).

Non-luminosity (*abhāsvaratva*) is either the absence of luminosity or its opposite. That which is produced by that [absence] is "non-luminosity born thereof. When there is a requirement for a further explanatory sentence to manifest its nature, another sentence—"depression born thereof"—is inserted in the middle. Depression is non-luminosity born therein, or born in that mind; the meaning is the incapacity to manifest what has been employed. Alternatively, it should be construed that both the non-luminosity of the mind and the depression produced by it constitute "despair" (*avasāda*).

*Tajjam* means "born from such a specific kind of compassion. For men, there exists a dejection of the mind—such as being pained by the suffering of others—which is contrary to luminosity (*bhāsvaratva*); and from that [dejection] arises grief and so forth. This is how it should be understood. Here, *bhāsvaratva* refers to the quality of illumination (*prakāśakatva*); its absence is [the state of non-luminosity]. Regarding the statement that dejection born from that is "despair" (*avasāda*), the commentary (*bhāṣya*) supplies the ellipsis: "the opposite of that is non-despair" (*anavasāda*). However, this is not stated explicitly in the aphorism (*vākya*) in order to cultivate the students' power of inference (*ūha-śakti*).

"By one who is weak"—the meaning is "by one devoid of mental strength," as described by the term "steadfast" (*dhīra*) who is equal in pain and pleasure. "Born from its opposite" means born from the qualities of place and so forth, from the notion that there will be happiness in the past or future, and from the happiness derived from kinsmen. Although "exultation" (*uddharṣa*) was mentioned previously, its opposite, "non-exultation" (*anuddharṣa*), should be inferred as before; thus, though not explicitly stated in the verse, it is shown in the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Anticipating the objection that this contradicts such passages as "content with what comes spontaneously" (*yadṛcchālābhasaṃtuṣṭaḥ*), "the constant yogi," and "self-study, purity, and contentment," he says:

Regarding the term *atisantoṣa* (excessive contentment): the meaning is that, like discontent (*asaṃtoṣa*), excessive contentment is also an obstacle because it causes one to engage in other sense-objects. This is indicated by the prefix *ud-* in the word *uddharṣa*. Furthermore, its status as an obstacle is well-known from various accounts, such as those concerning "one intoxicated by the pride of power" (*aiśvaryamadamatta*) and so forth. As for the word *api* in the phrase *nirvacanam api*, it serves to include possible alternative etymologies; this should be understood to apply to the previous etymologies as well.

He concludes—by the word "evam" (thus)—the application of action to its natural state and its integration without contradiction through the aspect of cessation, which is established by the synthesis of the principles intended in the words of the Sūtras. The particle *eva* (only/just) indicates that this is not desired by others, or it excludes sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Thus, here the [objections regarding] the non-application of action and the absence of evidence for contradiction have been refuted.
And the phrase "and knowledge" refers to the meaning of the scriptural passage from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*.

And so says another Śruti: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he attains immortality through knowledge. Here, that which is denoted by the word "ignorance" (avidyā) is action (karma) prescribed for the various castes and stages of life. "By means of ignorance"—that is, by means of action—"having crossed over death"—meaning having dispelled past karma which is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge—"through knowledge"—that is, through wisdom—"he attains immortality"—meaning he reaches Brahman. This is the meaning of the verse from the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad beginning with "knowledge and [ignorance]."

Now, he states—beginning with "tathā" (so it is)—that the scripture, which was otherwise interpreted by the Mṛṣāvādin and the Samuccayavādins, actually reveals the very method we have described; the word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, or the construction may be understood as "and another scripture [also] says so."

The word *antara* (internal) distinguishes this statement from the previously cited passage by clarifying its meaning through its lack of the suffix *-san*, by indicating the gateway for the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the production of the whole (*aṅgin*), and by teaching that the culmination of the supreme human goal occurs when ritual actions (*karman*)—along with their specific injunctions (*vidhyanta*)—are established as being directed toward the cultivation of the fruit (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is the direct knowledge of the Veda. Furthermore, the phrase "and [he who knows] knowledge" (*vidyāṃ ca*) means one who, according to the scripture, knows both the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) and the lower knowledge consisting of ritual action (*karmarūpāvidyā*) as things to be practiced.

The two *ca*s have the sense of collecting (*samuccaya*) what has been stated. However, if they serve to indicate what has not been stated, they include the specific subsidiary procedures (*itikartavyatā-viśe�a*), as well as the respective fruits of knowledge (*vidyā-phala*) to be attained and the obstacles to the means of attainment. In the phrase "both together" (*ubhayaṃ saha*), what is intended is the simultaneity of the two things to be performed—whose relationship as primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitā*) will be established in the third chapter—as they arise in the mind; it does not mean that they are to be undertaken simultaneously. For "togetherness" (*sahabhāva*) is said with respect to being known (*vedyatva*); it is not that they are known together.

For indeed, the coexistence of knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*karman*) is impossible both at the stage of origination and at the stage of the removal of opposing factors. In this context, the passages beginning with "They enter into blind darkness" and "Into a darkness greater than that" are intended to express a specific censure of each [taken individually]. One should not be misled by the fact that the particle *ca* and the word *saha* establish a simultaneous conjunction; for these are established otherwise. The phrase "those who are devoted to knowledge" means those who possess the enthusiasm for the arising of knowledge through disregard for ritual action.

For those devoted to ritual action (*karman*), the very nature of action—which is independent of knowledge (*vidyā*)—is indeed accomplished; however, liberation does not result from that alone. For those devoted to knowledge, since the cause [of action] is absent, knowledge itself does not arise; how much less, then, can there be liberation? This is the intended meaning of the word "furthermore" (*bhūyas*). He establishes, by means of the context, that the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) here refers to ritual action, but not everywhere.

In such passages as "dwelling in the midst of ignorance" (*avidyāyāmantare vartamānāḥ*) and "the perishable is indeed ignorance, [it is] the notion of self in what is not-self," the term *avidyā* is used in other senses. However, here, by means of the phrases "he perceives only the Self" (*ātmanyevānupaśyati*) and "performing actions here" (*kurvanneveha karmāṇi*), knowledge (*vidyā*) and its constituent action (*karma*) are the subjects under discussion. That very same thing is here restated by the word *avidyā* for the purpose of making known the utility of knowledge. In order to sever doubt and misconception—which have been explained in the commentary on the previous [section]—he clarifies the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence with the words "by ignorance" (*avidyayā*).

The statement that [ignorance] is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge is made for the following reasons: first, so that it may be understood by the word "death" (mṛtyu) either through its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) or through a secondary sense (*gauṇī*), since evil is a cause of misfortune; second, to exclude the possibility that sacrifices and the like merely remove obstacles to the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); and third, to distinguish it from the attainment of worldly results—which, though established by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts as being removable by enjoined knowledge—is here shown to be an obstacle to the very arising of that knowledge. By this, the interpretation of Yādavaprakāśa is also refuted. For if the "crossing over death" (*mṛtyutaraṇa*) here were liberation itself, how could anything else be accomplished by knowledge?
Furthermore, the use of the gerund suffix *-ktvā* would be untenable, as it is impossible for something to be prior to itself.

If the cessation of the contraction of the intellect is [effected] by the karma known as ignorance, then the expansion of the intellect is that very same thing; thus, there is no possibility of another goal to be accomplished. || 321 ||
If the removal of obstacles is accomplished through ignorance, then the attainment of immortality would be established by itself, without requiring any other unseen means. (322)
The Lord of living beings is naturally inclined toward instilling self-experience;
for those whose obstacles have been stilled, He is indeed the independent cause.

Although the word "death" (mṛtyu) may have a common application [to ignorance], it cannot refer to something that is opposed to attainment and is to be removed by knowledge, on the strength of numerous clear scriptural and traditional texts such as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death. Furthermore, since in that context the phrase "there is no other path" excludes other means, it is impossible for ritual action (karman) to be combined with knowledge as a means to liberation; for the status of action as a means to knowledge has already been established by the scriptures themselves. Therefore, in this instance, the term refers specifically to that kind of action which is opposed to the means [of knowledge].

The inclusion of the word "ancient" (*prācīna*) is because, unlike knowledge, action lacks the capacity to oppose subsequent evil. The interpretation offered by others—that the meaning of the word *tīrtvā* is "having reached and remained," which requires abandoning its natural sense—is incorrect due to its forced nature and the necessity of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the attempt to explain that one "crosses over" action—which is denoted by the word *mṛtyu*—because sacrificial and other good deeds are opposed to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), is refuted by the fact that such an application contradicts the injunction regarding the purpose of the desire for knowledge.

In passages such as "This is the bridge," since there is no motion [involved], the intention is that the root *tṛ* (to cross) signifies "attainment"; with this in mind, he says "having cast aside. Since the word *vidyā* is used for scriptures and so forth as well, he clarifies that its scope here is the knowledge of Brahman under discussion by saying "by means of knowledge. In accordance with scriptural passages such as "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman" and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," he says "the immortal Brahman."

Objection: Is it not the case that you have previously accepted the opponent's view that liberation is simply the cessation of ignorance, and that this occurs solely through the knowledge of Brahman? Yet here, by the statement "The knower of Brahman attains [it]," it appears that another goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is admitted in this scripture.
