Response: Not so; since by the term "cessation of ignorance" the cessation of the contraction of knowledge is intended, that very attainment of Brahman is identical to it according to the principle that "the absence of one thing is the presence of another. Thus, the meaning is the same.

Because of this, and in accordance with the natural meaning of the word "liberation" (mokṣa), if one intends to speak of the cessation of the binding karma described as "ignorance" (avidyā), then that alone is what is to be accomplished through meditation. Upon the cessation of the cause of the contraction of the intellect, the expansion of the intellect occurs spontaneously through the will of such a Lord, according to the principle of the flow of a stream when a dam is broken.

Therefore, by the statement "through knowledge one attains immortality," since the removal of obstacles is established through knowledge, the experience of Brahman—which will accrue spontaneously—is what is being described; thus, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following passages. Furthermore, although the attainment of Brahman is desired as the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), the means for removing its obstacles is designated as entirely distinct from the category of things to be desired.
For all duties of cessation (*nivṛttidharma*), which remove obstacles to the attainment [of the goal] and its means, are situated within the domain of occasional duties (*naimittika*). (Verse 324)

Here, by means of the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*) and the words "action" (*karman*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it is indicated—by way of reinforcing the clear meaning—that the ripening of the *kaṣāya* consists of actions, whereas knowledge is the supreme goal; that is, when the *kaṣāya* has been ripened by actions, knowledge then proceeds. By this, it is established that the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) here refers to that which is opposed to the means [to liberation], that the connection of "Vedic recitation" (*vedānuvacana*) and so forth is with the root-meaning in the phrase "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), and that the doctrine of the combination [of action and knowledge] (*samuccayavāda*) is refuted.

The "cooking" (*pāka*) refers to the ripening of impurity (*kaṣāya*), which is evil, or of the passion and so forth produced by it; that by which something is cooked is the "instrument of cooking" (*pāka-nimitta*); and that by which one goes is the "path" (*gati*). From that [ripening], knowledge arises—not the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), nor liberation (*mukti*). The meaning is that it comes to possess an excellent function toward its appropriate object. The fact that merit (*puṇya*) has the nature of evil (*pāpa*) means that both merit and demerit are to be removed by *dharma*. Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is understood as the means for crossing over death, is simply that which is other than knowledge (*vidyā*), namely, prescribed ritual action (*karma*). As it has been said:

"He too, taking refuge in knowledge, performed many sacrifices, having established himself in the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), in order to cross over death by means of [the practice of] avidyā.

Let this context stand. With the intention that, in this very statement, there exists a reason—consisting in the natural force of the matter (*vastusāmarthya*)—which is unimpeded and attains its own inherent fitness (*svārasya*), regarding the fact that ritual actions are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) and the determination of the meanings of the common terms such as *avidyā* as stated by us, he says: "in crossing over death. The word "perceived" (*pratīte*) contains a reason. The phrase "other than knowledge" (*vidyetarat*) is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term *avidyā* used here.

With the intention that, according to the logic of terms such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), it is appropriate for a word to function by excluding others when it refers to something proximate within the context, he stated, "the action prescribed. This implies a restriction conveyed by the two words [of the verse], namely that it is neither unprescribed action nor knowledge of Brahman and the like. By this, although the word "action" (*karman*) in the passage "only performing actions here" is general in nature, its scope is restricted to the appropriate subject; for optional rites and the like are not to be performed throughout one's entire life. He states that the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence in his own interpretation have been stabilized by corroborating them with the aforementioned scripture: [The text continues: "By this, even though the word 'action' in the passage 'only performing actions here' is common to all types of action, its application is restricted to the proper context; for optional rites and the like are not to be practiced for the duration of one's life. By providing a commentary on the cited scripture, the meaning of the individual words and the meaning of the sentence in my own statement have been made firm."

"Yathoktam" (as stated) means: "relying on knowledge," that is, established in the knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*); "having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman"—the meaning is, having intended to bring about the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) consisting of devotion, which is produced by discrimination (*viveka*) and the like. For it is precisely these two types of knowledge introduced here—namely, that arising from scripture and that from discrimination—which have been clarified in this context. Therefore, the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) here refers to the obstacle to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Furthermore, [the interpretation of *yajña* as] "having performed" is incorrect; for that [performance] is not mentioned as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because the fulfillment of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is already established by the very phrase "having resorted to the knowledge of Brahman. Moreover, by the statement of the purpose, "to cross over death," any suspicion that the word "having crossed" (*tīrtvā*) implies the sense of "attaining" is also dispelled. And precisely what was expressed by the word *avidyā*, which indicates the Vedic terms to be supplemented, is made manifest by the word *yajña*. The meaning is: "he performed sacrifices"—that is, he carried them out.

Action, consisting of both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*), is an obstacle to knowledge. Because it obstructs the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and because its fruit is undesirable, both are designated by the term "demerit" (*pāpa*). Furthermore, this action's status as an obstacle to knowledge is mediated by the increase of *rajas* and *tamas*, which oppose the pure *sattva* that serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge. That demerit obstructs the dawn of knowledge is understood from the Śruti: "It is He who makes him perform evil action, whom He wishes to lead downward."

The Lord himself has established that *rajas* and *tamas* are obstacles to the knowledge of reality as it is, while *sattva* is the cause of such knowledge—as stated in the passage beginning, "From *sattva* arises knowledge. Therefore, for the production of knowledge, sinful action must be eliminated. And the elimination of that [sin] is achieved through dharma performed without desire for its fruits. Thus says the Śruti: "By dharma one drives away evil."

Now, it may be objected: "It is heard in scripture that only evil (*pāpa*) is to be removed by *dharma*, yet here, by speaking of 'prior karma' without distinction, how can it be said that even merit (*puṇya*) is crossed over? To this, he clarifies what was stated as being removable in the scripture to be cited later, beginning with the words "In knowledge" (*jñāne*). To the question, "How can merit be removable by *dharma*, and why is it denoted by the word 'evil' (*pāpa*)?", he replies with the words "Brahman" (*brahma*). The statement "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*) is intended as an illustration, referring to the fact that they are combined with what is disagreeable (*vigīta*) and what is not disagreeable (*avigīta*). Here, "being denotable" (*abhidheyatvam*) means "being cognizable" (*bodhyatvam*).

The statement in the *Vivaraṇa*, "one should observe," is made by way of its full significance (*vaibhava*). This is the intended meaning: it is recorded in the Smṛti that "that very same thing is dharma and that very same thing is adharma, depending upon each particular person. Therefore, even that which is established as a meritorious intention becomes sinful during the stage of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

Due to the distinction between the stages of desiring liberation and not desiring liberation, a single action for a ritual performer attains the status of both sin and merit, even though the object to be accomplished remains the same. (325)
The dual nature of the enjoined hawk-sacrifice and others arises from two types of scriptural injunctions;
if this exists for a single act at one and the same time, how much more so when there is a difference in time? (326)

For even merit (*puṇya*), which is the sole means for attaining heaven—the nature of which is preeminent pleasure—obstructs the knowledge of Brahman, whose nature is unconditioned bliss, in order to achieve its own fruit: attachment to objects that are censured by the terms "obstacle" (*antarāya*) and "hell" (*niraya*). Therefore, it is logical that the dharma of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*) must be dispelled by the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛttidharma*). Furthermore, the definition of sin (*pāpa*) is that which is known through scripture as a means to an undesirable result for the agent. [As it is said: "Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [cross it]."

Furthermore, in the Śruti passage, "All evils turn back from here," although the word *pāpman* (evil) used in the concluding statement is taken figuratively to mean grief and so forth, its primary sense must be accepted because it is possible for it to refer to good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) as well. Even in the view that there is a single figurative application throughout according to the "umbrella-bearer" maxim (*chatrinyāya*), there remains a distinction of degree. Nor is it the case that [good and evil deeds]...

One might suspect that, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *pāpman* here refers to a specific subset of *duṣkṛta*, as is the case with the words *duṣkṛta* and *pāpa*. However, this is untenable because both terms are equally pervasive, making such a distinction impossible—just as one cannot distinguish between the words *haya* and *turaṅga*. Furthermore, the qualification by the word "all" (*sarva*) would otherwise be redundant. Moreover, the immediately following passage, "For this world of Brahman is free from evil," is naturally intended to proclaim the cessation of all things to be abandoned that have been under discussion.

Therefore, in this context, it is appropriate that the two words *pūrva* (prior) and *aparapāpman* (subsequent evil) have the same meaning without restriction. This being so, the word "evil" (*pāpa*) applies to a specific kind of merit because the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical. Now, it is accepted that *rajas* and *tamas* are opposed to knowledge; but does this [opposition] occur through conjunction with "evil," through alternation (*vikalpa*), or by some other cause? Since there is no determining factor, the opposition of "evil" to knowledge is difficult to ascertain. Therefore, one might think that its nature is simply to be a means to suffering. To this, he says: "Of this... (*asyeti*).

"Pure *sattva*" here refers to that *sattva* in which *rajas* and *tamas* have been overcome, and which produces illumination and the other qualities when employed. Even at the stage of the arising of knowledge, because the three *guṇas* persist for persons, the word "increase" (*vivṛddhi*) is used to indicate the specific manifestation [of *sattva*] in distinction from the other *guṇas* present at that time. Through such statements as "the *guṇas* are subject to karma," it is established that the *guṇas* serve as the means [to the results]; the sense is that the fact that sin is a cause of suffering is not established by the exclusion of anything else.

Regarding the question of how the relationship of "mediator and mediated" can be postulated when there is no evidence for both being equally opposed to knowledge, he states the evidence for the mediator's opposition in the words beginning with "of sin. In the scriptural passage beginning with "This very one," the phrase "desires to lead downward" does not mean desiring to lead [the person] to hell; for in this context, the desire to lead upward does not have heaven and so forth as its object. Indeed, in the passage "whom He desires to lead up from these worlds," it is understood by the natural sense of the words that the leading upward is from all the worlds, including heaven and the rest.

Therefore, in this context, "unrighteous action" (asādhukarma) must be that which leads downward, being the opposite of what brings about liberation; and its means is prescribed here in such passages as "Worship Me. Furthermore, at the beginning of that [passage], it is established that "the most beneficial" (hitatama)—in the sense of being the immediate means to liberation—is that which you consider most beneficial for a human being. That very thing is what is grasped here by the term "righteous action" (sādhukarma), even though it is a general term, due to the force of proximity.

Furthermore, His role as the instigator [of that action] has been specifically stated in such passages as, "I give him that yoga of discernment" (Gītā 10.10). And the action that is opposed to this [discernment] by way of obstructing its arising is the action that causes aversion toward the Lord; for when there is favor toward Him, there is no possibility of falling into an inferior state. That unwholesome action is the primary cause of the downward fall has been made clear in the passage beginning with, "But those who hate Me, cruel... and ending with, "...therefore they go to the lowest state" (Gītā 16.18–20).

Alternatively, the term "good action" (*sādhukarma*) here refers to the subsidiary elements required by the means under discussion. Furthermore, the status of action as a means to liberation—expressed by the word "leading upward" (*unnayana*)—is not direct (*advāraka*); for scripture and other authorities establish that it is mediated (*sadvāraka*). Therefore, "bad action," which stands in opposition to action as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), is precisely what is contrary to the arising of knowledge. Moreover, the Lord's role as the instigator of good and bad actions here does not occur independently of the prior karma of the individual soul (*jīva*), for that would entail the faults of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*).

Nor is there a state of being an impeller, as in the case of wind, water, and so forth; for that would entail the consequence of the scriptures becoming useless and would contradict such statements as "the bestowing of intelligence. Therefore, the phrase "whom he wishes to lead downward" (Yama 3.1.6), by way of restating the condition of a certain person, reveals his status as a perpetrator of sin which serves as the cause for the desire to lead him downward. Furthermore, when one begins a subsequent sin while still possessing a prior sin, the loss of knowledge and the resulting contrary knowledge rooted therein serve as the means [for descent]. This is corroborated by such passages as, "To whomsoever the gods grant [sin], it destroys his wisdom," and so on. Although this was stated generally regarding all gods and all sins, it applies here [specifically] as well.

It is unimpeded; and it is especially sung [in scripture]: "I hurl them incessantly," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that sin is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge. Now, one might object: "Let knowledge be obstructed by the two kinds of sin mentioned in the Śruti, and let it arise through the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti-dharma); there is no need for the qualities of *prakṛti* to act as intermediaries in both cases. To this he says: "Rajas," etc.

The inclusion of the term "of the *sattva*" here is for the purpose of ascertaining that *sattva* is the cause of knowledge through its pervasive concomitance with the exclusion of *rajas* and *tamas*, for the purpose of demonstrating the gateway of virtuous action, and for the purpose of establishing what was stated—that it is the pure *sattva* which is the cause of the arising of knowledge. The sense is that since it is improper to abandon either [cause] when both are established by *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and since an option (*vikalpa*) is inadmissible when another alternative exists, it is logical that here there is a relationship of means and end (*dvāra-dvāritva*).

But surely, by the statement "greed is from rajas," its status as a cause for erroneous cognition is also established, because greed for an unattained object is a cause of delusion; this is made explicit by the verse beginning with "by which one regards dharma as adharma," and so forth.

To dispel the doubt that—on the basis of such Smṛti texts as "Action is not exhausted without being experienced"—knowledge might only be accomplished at the conclusion of the experience of the fruits of action, and that dharma’s status as a means to the happiness denoted by the word *dhṛti* (fortitude) would thus be established, [the author] concludes the two points already stated, determining their nature as that which is to be removed and that which removes it, through the distinct application of the scriptures on expiation (*niṣkṛti*). He does so with the words: "Therefore... (ataḥ).

It must be dispelled—the sense being that while infinite sins continue to accumulate, there is never an occasion for their complete cessation through experience alone; therefore, their removal must be effected solely by means of the expiation prescribed in the scriptures. Even so, one might argue that expiation is impossible for such immeasurable sins; to this he replies with the words "of that" (*tadi*). The intention is that its removal is possible through the majesty of the *nivṛtti-dharma* (the path of renunciation) when performed without attachment to other fruits, according to the maxim beginning with "even a small portion of this dharma."

In passages such as "He who knows this thus," the declaration of a fruit for the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture is intended as praise, or may be understood as indirect (paramparayā), or according to the distinction of qualified practitioners (adhikāribheda). Therefore, performance is primary; with the intention that for those who abandon it, the effect is absent due to the absence of its cause, it is said: "by [the rite] being performed."

He cites a scriptural passage that clarifies how words such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and others, when occurring in the context of what has been previously acquired, possess their intended meanings, and that even sin can be removed without the experience of its results: "In the same way... (*tatheti*). In that passage, although the word *dharma* refers specifically to expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), it also includes the "dharma of cessation" (*nivṛttidharma*) because there is no distinction made; this is due to the proximity of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), as seen in the phrase "from [the knowledge of] Brahman comes bliss, the source of Brahman," and so forth. Even the other fruits perceived in the acts of giving and so on, which are recited together with those [expiations], such as the subjugation of enemies, are indeed conducive to the accomplishment of the knowledge of Brahman. This is the fruit of the auxiliary part (*aṅgiphala*).

And here [in the Upanishads], it is clearly stated: "O wise one, do not undergo death again. Therefore, by means of the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), the cessation of both worldly merit and demerit—both of which are designated by the term "demerit" (*pāpa*)—is established as that which is to be removed. Thus, the study of ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) must precede. Consequently, knowledge, which is the means for attaining Brahman, depends upon the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, the knowledge of the nature of those required duties, as well as the knowledge that mere rituals yield only limited and impermanent results, is to be understood through the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*. Hence, that very [study] which is required by the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*) must be declared as its prerequisite.

To the question, "What follows from this? he says "That" (*tad iti*), intending that the knowledge consisting of meditation—which is the root of that [liberation]—is established as being dependent on action. "That" means by the force of the aforementioned scriptures, traditional law (*smṛti*), aphorisms (*sūtra*), logical reasoning (*upapatti*), and oral tradition (*sampradāya*). "In this way" means by the manner in which selfless actions (*niṣkāma-karma*) serve to remove obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Granted that meditation, which is the object of inquiry, requires the performance of its own constituent parts (actions), how does the inquiry into that [meditation] require an inquiry into all actions? To this, he confirms the point already established by means of a conclusion (*nigamana*): [The text continues: "Therefore, since the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas is preceded by the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*), the inquiry into the meaning of the Upanishads (*vedānta-mīmāṃsā*) is preceded by the inquiry into ritual action. This is because the inquiry into the meaning of the Upanishads is preceded by the inquiry into ritual action, due to the dependence of the former upon the latter. This is so because the inquiry into the meaning of the Upanishads depends on the inquiry into ritual action for the purpose of determining the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of the seeker, as well as for the purpose of ascertaining the nature of the fruit (*phala*) through the removal of obstacles. Furthermore, it is because the inquiry into the meaning of the Upanishads depends on the inquiry into ritual action for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of the Self (*ātman*) by means of the removal of the misconception of agency (*kartṛtva*) regarding the body and other such things, which arises from the study of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) concerning ritual action. "—*ataḥ* (therefore). This means that it is impossible for the knowledge (*vidyā*) which is the means to liberation to be independent of the duties of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*). By the phrase "knowledge of the nature of the required ritual acts," it is shown that—just as with rice and other grains through the linguistic usage of elders—the specific nature of the ritual objects such as the *yajña*, along with their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*), must be known specifically through the *Mīmāṃsā* of rituals. Since an application (*viniyoga*) depends on the nature of that which is enjoined by an injunction, according to the maxim of "not apprehending a qualified object when the qualifier is not apprehended" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*), there is a desire to know [the ritual] precisely as it is endowed with its own constituent parts, because it is the means to the fruit achieved through those very parts.

Even though the worship is inconceivable, it is indicated that the action can nevertheless be conceived. And the statement beginning with "exclusive" (*kevala*) was spoken with the intention that the encouragement toward knowledge (*vidyāprarocana*)—which occurs through the censure of actions that are not auxiliary to knowledge—depends upon such knowledge of action. It should be understood as "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). Here, "investigation" (*mīmāṃsā*) means deliberation (*vicāra*).

With the intention that—for those investigating the meaning of the scriptures on meditation, which include both what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—the determination of the true nature of both is inevitable and must necessarily be accomplished through the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*; therefore, it is appropriate to state that [the knowledge of Brahman] is preceded by that [investigation of ritual action], as it has not been previously established by you. By this, the claim that [the inquiry into Brahman] ultimately depends upon an examination of ritual action, as well as the statement regarding the occurrence of the three-fold suffering (*tāpatraya*), is refuted. Alternatively, the word "only" (*eva*) implies the exclusion of the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). This is the refutation of the view that the fourfold prerequisites must precede [the inquiry into Brahman].

Moreover, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities and so forth cannot be accomplished without hearing the Mīmāṃsā, because the nature of ritual action, its results, their permanence or impermanence, and the eternity of the Self are difficult to comprehend without a definitive determination of the specific fruit, the instrument, the procedure, and the qualified agent. Furthermore, their status as means of knowledge is to be understood through application (*viniyoga*), and application is derived from direct statement, indicative mark, and other criteria; and that [application] belongs to the third book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras].

It is not merely that what we have stated is logical; rather, with the intention of showing that there is also a fault in what you have stated, he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*). Therein, he exposes the circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*) by saying, "In the case of the eternal" (*nitye*). The word *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tu*), indicating the reversal of the sequence of what is yet to be discussed from what has already been discussed. Here, the word *mīmāṃsā* refers to both parts [of the Mīmāṃsā system], because of the inclusion of the eternity of the self and so forth. And the word *śravaṇa* (hearing) extends up to *vicāra* (investigation).

The point is this: what is intended here by the word *viveka* (discrimination)—is it certain knowledge (*niścaya*), or is it a superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*)? It cannot be the first, because that which is established by the entire Mīmāṃsā system cannot logically be a prerequisite for the inquiry into Brahman; indeed, the eternality of the Self and other such matters will be determined in the section concerning Brahman. Nor can it be the second, because since such a superficial cognition is common to both the sections on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*) and Brahman, it is inappropriate to mention it specifically here. Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no reason to bypass the primary alternative [the first option].

Nor is that [knowledge] the cause of detachment from other fruits and so forth, since the notion of the attainment of immortality and the like is established in both cases. Nor is there a distinction [to be made] by means of the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others, because it is stated that their opportunity is barred by the sequence beginning with Vedic study; and because you yourself agree that in those systems there is a manifold perversion of discrimination regarding liberation and its means. For this very reason, they will be refuted. As for the supplementary passages such as "The world is not eternal," these must serve the purpose of discrimination precisely by following the Śruti.

But not independently; otherwise, what would be the need for the *Śārīraka*? If you argue that this is because doubt and other such states arise elsewhere than there [in the *Sāṅkhya*], then in that case, the establishment of discrimination (*viveka*) does not occur therein. As for what was stated here by Vācaspati—beginning with "The eternal and the non-eternal dwell together, thus it is the 'eternal-non-eternal entity'; its properties are the 'discrimination of the eternal and the non-eternal entities,' meaning the discrimination between the two substrates, the eternal and the non-eternal, and their respective properties"—and continuing until: "Eternality is truth; that which possesses it is eternal and true, and thus it is the object of one's reliance."

Impermanence is unreality; that which possesses this quality is impermanent and false. Thus, it is said to be an object of non-reliance. That which is real is established as permanent and blissful, and will therefore be an object of reliance; whereas that which is impermanent and unreal, being encompassed by the three types of suffering, will be abandoned. This is what is called "the discrimination between permanent and impermanent entities. This too is weak, because even that which is impermanent will be established as real by virtue of its being non-sublated.

Nor is it the case that the engagement of those engaged in ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*) in the inquiry into karma and so forth proceeds from the thought that "eternal happiness is not to be pursued"; rather, it proceeds either from the delusion that it is achievable through ritual action, or from the perception of its extreme rarity. Furthermore, mere eternality and the like are not the cause for such pursuit; rather, pursuit arises precisely from being an end of man (*puruṣārtha*) and a means thereto, while non-pursuit arises from the opposite of these two. And both [the state of being an end and the state of being a means] may apply to the eternal and the non-eternal as appropriate.

For even one who investigates must renounce impermanent pleasure, according to the principle that such things are impossible to achieve, lead to miserable ends, and yield results equal to the effort expended; or else, it would be accepted through satisfaction derived from obtaining a superior pleasure. In the absence of that [superior pleasure], even a very small amount of pleasure is adopted. Furthermore, if even that which is eternal were of the nature of suffering or neutral, how could it be worthy of reliance? This is because the subject under discussion is characterized by its excellence as pleasure.

If it is argued that [the goal] is well-known (*pratītatva*); that recognition is not established through pervasion (*vyāpti*), because such a relation is never observed. Nor is it established through scripture (*śruti*), because the superficial understanding based on its source would be common to all [systems], leading to difficulty; and because certainty is seized by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, it has been shown that the traditions (*smṛti*) of other systems do not prove this. Moreover, the desire to acquire [the goal] is based on the possibility of eternal bliss, which is common to all; and the impossibility of such bliss in other systems is very clear.

The passage beginning with "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*) and so forth is difficult to understand for those who have not investigated the portions concerning ritual action (*karma*) and Brahman, because such [notions] are refuted in the *Pramāṇa-adhyāya* and the *Tarka-pāda*. Therefore, it is also impossible to maintain that the impossibility of an eternal fruit is established here in the first sūtra and elsewhere for the sake of the subject at hand, since you yourselves have not stated the meaning of the words of the sūtras in this manner. Furthermore, there is here only a mere possibility of eternal happiness.

Furthermore, the impermanence of the happiness of heaven and so forth could not be established by another scripture or by inference, because the opposite could just as easily be asserted by those very means—for instance, the argument "the happiness of heaven is impermanent because it is happiness" would be sublated by scriptural texts such as those concerning immortality (*amṛtatva*). Moreover, the determination of the secondary meaning (*anyaparya*) of such texts depends upon that very ascertainment [of the truth]. Otherwise, the undesirable consequence would follow that even the happiness of liberation is impermanent because it is happiness. And the avoidance of that consequence depends upon the determination of the meaning of the Upanishads (*trayyantārtha*), which in turn depends upon those [scriptures]; thus, there is a circular dependency.

Therefore, it is the inquiry into action (*karma*) alone that is required here. As for the discernment of tranquility, self-control, and so forth as being means (*sādhana*), or their mere nature (*svarūpa*), it is said to have been "already established" (*vṛtta*). It cannot be the former, because that is to be accomplished in the section defining the means (*sādhanalakṣaṇa*) by the rule, "He should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth. Nor can it be the latter, because those forms of attention and so forth which are merely conducive to hearing (*śravaṇa*) are common to all scriptures; thus, it is inappropriate to speak of them specifically here. However, regarding those forms such as the restraint of the external and internal organs which are conducive to *yoga*—for the purpose of hearing the meaning of the final portion of the Vedas (*trayyantārtha*)— [The text continues: ...it is appropriate to speak of them here specifically. But even there, since they are already well-known from other sources, it is not necessary to state them again. Therefore, what has been "established" is the inquiry into action, which is the cause of the desire to know Brahman. This is because the desire to know Brahman arises only when one perceives that the fruit of actions is impermanent and that the Self is distinct from the body and its adjuncts. Consequently, since the inquiry into action is the prerequisite for the inquiry into Brahman, the inquiry into action is indeed the "prior" (*pūrva*) inquiry. Thus, the statement "the prior [inquiry] has been established" is made with reference to the inquiry into action. Furthermore, the inquiry into action is called "prior" because it is the cause of the desire to know Brahman, and because it is the means for attaining the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the inquiry into Brahman. Because [the means] were not previously enjoined, and because it is stated that "one who knows thus is peaceful and self-controlled" (*śānto dāntaḥ*)—which indicates that the knowledge of Brahman comes first. Furthermore, do the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*) and so forth exist as cause and effect, or otherwise? In the former case, the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) must also be studied together [with the inquiry into Brahman], since, through the sequence beginning with "having examined the worlds," there is a causal relationship leading ultimately to the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*). Otherwise, only the desire for liberation alone would need to be studied.

What is the purpose of mentioning the "fourfold" (catuṣka)? Even in the second case, there is a contradiction with one's own admission, because others have explained the sequence as "from discrimination comes dispassion," and so forth. Here, he explains what was stated [in the verse], "without hearing the Mīmāṃsā," by saying "in the result" (phale), etc. In the *karmabhāga* (the section on ritual action), the results are heaven and so forth; the means are sacrifice and so forth, as well as the preparatory rites (*prayāja*) and so forth; and those who desire enjoyment are the agents. In the *brahmabhāga* (the section on Brahman), however, the results are liberation and meditation; the means are tranquility (*śama*) and so forth; and those who desire liberation are the agents. Their "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) consists of their form as excluded from that stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), as well as their mutual differences.

In this context, there is no lack of distinction between the subject matter (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) in the statement that explains the nature of action and so forth through the determination of the fruit, the instrument, and other factors. This is because, in those various topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), the meaning of the great sentence—composed of mutually connected specific elements—is explained subsequently through the determination of the respective intermediate sentence-meanings (*avāntaravākyārtha*), which are based on the meanings of individual words (*padārtha*). Furthermore, it is because the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*), which is the root of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the other [means], has as its purpose the instruction included within the determination of the fruit, the instrument, and so forth.

The mention of "action" (*karma*) here is intended to indicate meditation (*upāsti*) as well; alternatively, the term "action" encompasses both by virtue of the fact that both are performed. Furthermore, the word "action" is used even for meditation in the Sūtra itself: "And light [arises] from the practice of action" (*prakāśaśca karmaṇyabhyāsāt*). Regarding this, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "In the action consisting of meditation. Elsewhere too, it is said that action consists of sacrifices and the like, as well as meditation. Moreover, the designation of "mental action" is seen in the Smṛtis and other texts.

Some maintain that here, considering the word *karman* to refer exclusively to [rites] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, this is an imitation of the method of determining its permanence or impermanence, and not of the method of [its] ascertainment. Here, the intention of what is being stated by way of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that reveals the incongruity is as follows: how can there be an understanding of ritual action (*karman*), which consists of a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) with three components, without the ascertainment of the three required factors—such as the fruit—namely, "what," "by what means," and "how"?

And how can there be the certainty that the referent of words such as "heaven," which are connected to a qualification specified by "living" and so forth, belongs to another body and another place? And in the absence of that [certainty], how can there be the determination of a self that persists through prior and subsequent bodies—the very core of the refutation of the Lokāyata and Buddhist positions on transmigration? Furthermore, since the perception of pleasure in the self is established otherwise [than by its being the self], how can the scriptural statement regarding its nature as pleasure be taken in its primary sense without [this] declaration? In the absence of such a determination of the self, for one who considers the body alone to be the self—

How can there be detachment from fruits pertaining to this world? Even for an eligible seeker who has established that the fruit of active religious duty (*pravṛttidharma*) is entirely impermanent—consisting of limited sensory enjoyments—while the fruit of abstinent religious duty (*nivṛttidharma*) is supreme and eternal, how can there be a desire to abandon impermanent fruits such as heaven, and how can there be an attraction toward the eternal fruit known through the Vedānta? Therefore, in the doctrine concerning the occurrence of the fourfold means, one must accept an inquiry into both sections [of the Veda], based on specific discernment and the like as their root.

And thus, there is a dependence upon an inquiry into karma; furthermore, there is the additional fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the nature of knowledge and bliss is intended. He states the specific defect regarding the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth with the words "of these" (*eṣām*). This means: of those [means] mentioned in the injunctive statements such as "one who is tranquil, self-controlled," and so on. "Injunction" (*viniyoga*) is the communication of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgitva*); however, the *Nyāyasudarśana* uses the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*).

For when it is understood that tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities serve as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), their status as means (*sādhana*)—though not explicitly stated—is established by implication. To the question "What follows from this?", [the author] states "application" (*viniyoga*), which depends upon the definition of the means of knowledge established by the definition of the auxiliaries (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. To the objection that "the application of these means of knowledge should be considered in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* itself," he replies with the word "sa" (that). That [application] belongs to the third [chapter]; it was stated in the third chapter of the *Karmakāṇḍa* according to the sequence of connection previously mentioned. Here, however, in this third [chapter], merely the raising of objections and their resolution will be performed by means of those very [means] already established earlier for the sake of brevity. The sense is that one should observe here as well the reliance upon the logic (*nyāya*) of other chapters.
This is the consistency regarding the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth.

The meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, although intended for the success of ritual action (*karma*), consist in the vision of Brahman and thus depend upon the knowledge of Brahman; they must therefore be considered here [in this work] itself. Furthermore, since those very rituals—when performed without desire for their fruits—are means for generating the knowledge of Brahman, these meditations, which bring about their excellence, are all the more appropriately connected here. And it is universally agreed that these meditations depend upon the comprehension of the nature of the rituals themselves.

Now, demonstrating another line of reasoning, [the author] establishes the sequence of the inquiry into ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman here itself—due to its primary connection as being unfit for other locations—by means of the discussion on the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth, beginning with the words "In the *udgītha*. By the phrase "even those for the sake of the success of ritual action," the doubt is raised that while there was utility in the previous section, there is none here; this is then resolved by the statement regarding the success of ritual action: "That very [action] becomes more powerful" (*tadeva vīryavattaram*).

The statement in the Śruti implies that there is no obstruction by powerful karmas to that which consists of the fruits of the qualities. The phrase "consisting of the vision of Brahman" contains a reason: they depend upon the knowledge of Brahman—for one who does not know the nature of the object to be superimposed elsewhere can never effect its superimposition anywhere, since views such as the "indescribable" (anirvacanīya) will be refuted later. Furthermore, the intention here is that the knowledge of Brahman is to be accomplished through the first two sections. He resolves the objection that these meditations on [Brahman as] visions are not useful for the primary goal by showing their utility through an indirect means, with the words "those [meditations]."

This means that the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth are to be set aside or discarded. Furthermore, the word "api" (*also*) here indicates the contradiction superimposed by others. Alternatively, having accepted the lack of utility in the preceding section, the connection [of this section] was established through the mere application of similar examples and by stating that there is no other way to resolve the expectancy. Here, however, it is suggested that there *is* utility. "Those whose fruits are not intended" means they are devoid of the volition for results that lead to bondage. The knowledge of Brahman is what is desired here. "Excellence" refers to the very prosperity mentioned previously.
But there is no cessation of deficiency; rather, [the causes] are those that produce the perfection of karma which brings about that [result].
From the excellence of karma arises [excellence] born of karma, and from the excellence of knowledge arises that [excellence];
therefore, there is no contradiction, as this is established through the distinction between individual instances. (327)

"Sutarām" (all the more so)—the sense is that both with respect to itself and with respect to higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). Here, just as non-connection (*ayoga*) is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*), so too is connection with anything else (*anyayoga*) excluded.
However, in the case of meditations such as viewing [something] as Brahman (*abrahmadṛṣṭi*), there may be a single primary purpose;
yet here, it is desired because of the logic of the means to knowledge (*vidyā*) and the reasons for such meditative views. || 328 ||
In this way, there would be no over-extension [of the rule], because the recitation follows immediately after the study;
furthermore, the connection with other [words] that is somehow intended here is not precluded. (329)

To the objection that false perception (mithyādṛṣṭi) is well-known to occur when the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) is not correctly understood, he replies with the words "of these" (teṣām). For this is not merely a case of false perception; rather, it is the superimposition of something else upon that which has been correctly understood. Consequently, for one who does not know the constituent part of the ritual action—which serves as the substrate—correctly, it is impossible to conceive of an injunction regarding the perception of something else in its place.

"Agreed by all"—even those who deny everything find it impossible to refute when confronted by an investigator; the sense is that there is no disagreement regarding the mere existence of reality (*sanmātra*). Now, one might object: even optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) have a requirement for these [virtues], which—though not constituent parts of the rites themselves—render them more potent; and since the performance of those [optional rites] requires both ritual action and knowledge, let the inquiry into that [reality] take place within the Ritual Section (*karmakāṇḍa*) due to this mutual requirement. This is not so; for it has already been stated that such inquiry is impossible for one who does not know Brahman.

For this very reason, its study occurs only within the Upaniṣads. As for the previous objection raised—that for one who has studied the Vedānta, reflection on that alone is possible—it is incorrect; for the injunction to study compels the study of the whole [Veda] in its proper order. Nor can the inquiry into the Vedānta now seek a prerequisite based on a study of the final portion of the Veda alone, undertaken either by transgressing the injunction or due to some emergency.

By this, the view that "due to an excellence of dispassion determined by specific past merits (*prācīna-sukṛta*), there may be both the study and the investigation of only a single portion [of the Veda]" is also refuted; for even that would involve an improper transgression of the injunction to study the entire Veda. Furthermore, it has already been stated that for one who has not mastered the ritual actions (*karman*), the acquisition of the knowledge that constitutes their auxiliary parts (*karmāṅga-vidyā*) is impossible to investigate. Moreover, to attempt to fill in the deficiencies later through an indistinct preliminary examination is a laborious and strained approach.

If it is argued that for one intent upon the contemplation of Brahman, there should be comprehension of the constituent rituals of knowledge through the mere instruction of the teacher, then by that same logic, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) itself should not take place. Therefore, the pure path is this: for one who has studied the entire text according to rule, a specific stage of conduct (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) is established for the remaining portion of the inquiry, just as it was previously.

The conduct of the Lord of Ascetics—characterized by the thievery of impure behavior that drags away the body of his scripture-crown—seemed as if it had shattered the twenty-fold discipline; yet he restored it.
Thus ends the Laghusiddhānta.

Because the ritual action known through the first part of the Mīmāṃsā yields results that are meager and unstable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman—which is to be understood from the subsequent part—yields infinite and imperishable results, it is stated that after the knowledge of ritual action as previously presented, for that very reason, Brahman must be known. Thus says the author of the Vṛtti: "After the mastery of ritual action as previously established, there arises the desire to know Brahman."

And he will state the unity of the two systems of inquiry—into ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) and into Brahman (*brahma-mīmāṃsā*)—in the words: "This *Śārīraka* [Mīmāṃsā] is joined with the sixteen-chaptered [work] of Jaimini; thus is the unity of the scripture established."

In this work, *Tātparyadīpikā*, it appears as if the author intends to address the account previously stated by Yādavaprakāśa and his establishment of the point that the inquiry into Sāṅkhya and other systems is not to be commenced. Setting aside that view, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Mīmāṃsā. This word is derived either from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*), with the suffix *naṅ* applied as a nipātana (irregular formation), or from the root *mān* in the sense of "reverence" (*pūjāyām*), according to the rule *mānbadha-* etc., forming a desiderative (*nicchā-sannanta*) without the addition of *i*. The grammarians’ statement that it is derived from *māni* in the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) is accepted here because it is not far removed from the intended meaning.

For when the investigation (*vicāra*)—which is prompted by a specific desire to know (*jijñāsā*), is honored, and is connected to that [desire]—is understood as a praiseworthy method (*nyāya*) due to its usage by the elders, the primary power (*śakti*) of the word *mīmāṃsā* is extracted from it. And they have said: "All reasoning designated as *mīmāṃsā* originates from the Veda," and so forth. However, when the word *mīmāṃsā* refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) whose nature consists of such a compendium of methods, the term is used in a secondary sense (*bhākta*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in describing the two parts [of the work] as "already known" and "to be understood" through their division into earlier and later sections. Here, the construction of the sentence begins with "pūrvavṛttāt" (from what has preceded); the remainder is the justification for the causal portion found therein.

The sequential instruction on investigation is based on the Sūtra; however, in this context, the unity of the treatise and its sequence are explained here as intended by the author of the Sūtras. (208)

By the two terms "prior portion" (*pūrvabhāga*) and "subsequent portion" (*uparitanabhāga*), the unity of the treatise—which consists of an exposition following a fixed sequence—is indicated. The basis for this is the sequential nature of the Veda, which is to be explained; this is shown in the word-connection (*padayojanā*) by the term "together with the head" (*saśiraska*). There is no tautology between the explanations of the words and the sentences, as their intended meanings (*tātparya*) differ. "Of that which is known" means of that which has been determined. "Of that which is to be understood" means of that which is to be determined because it resides in an uncontradicted initial cognition. "Of the knowledge of Brahman" means of the meditation upon Brahman (*brahmopāsana*).

Because, when the intention is merely to express the nature of Brahman, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is superfluous here; because it is more appropriate to grasp a specific result by placing it on the same level as "the action already known" (*jñātasya karmaṇaḥ*); because it is improper to speak of knowledge—whether in the form of inquiry or in the form of ascertainment—as something to be attained; and because [such knowledge] is not enjoined with respect to the result being indicated.

Therefore, here, according to the principle of coordination (*samanvaya*), although Brahman is to be known as the primary object because it is itself the infinite and imperishable fruit, it must also be known as its object because it is the means for attaining that infinite and imperishable fruit through its own worship; thus, its mention as a subordinate element is also perfectly consistent. However, by the statement "Brahman is to be known," its primacy is manifested. In this context, the reason for being an object of inquiry is the presence of a preliminary cognition (*apātadhī*) regarding it as possessing a purpose.

However, for that [inquiry] which occurs subsequent to the inquiry into karma, there is dependence on it once obstacles have been stilled; and as for "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), it is the absence of any other such requirement. Therefore, with reference specifically to the particular inquiry that culminates in the fulfillment of *nirveda* as stated in the scripture, [the sūtra says] "from that very [karma]."

Thus it has been said. Here, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended to exclude the deficiency of a reason, for it is impossible to negate a reason that is already accompanied by a restriction. Some, however, say: "Since the investigation of Brahman might otherwise follow from other causes—leading to the consequence that it would not be necessary or that Śūdras would be eligible—this teaching is intended to show disregard for any cause other than the knowledge of ritual action (*karmadhī*). In this view, there would be much impropriety, as the primary thesis, its reason, and the reason for a further thesis would not have been stated.

By the very exclusion of the impossibility of the specific probandum (sādhya) being preceded by the intended reason, the rejection of other reasons and so forth is established by implication; however, it is logical that this is explicitly stated. "To be known" (jñātavyam) means "to be investigated" (vicāryam). It will be stated later that "investigation is to be performed. Here, the kṛtya suffix is used in the sense of fitness (arha). Furthermore, in the phrase "from the knowledge of karma," "knowledge" (jñāna) likewise refers to investigation.

By stating "Brahman is to be known" (*brahma jñātavyam*), [the author] indicates, through its natural sense and by means of reasoning, that the meaning of the sentence is "Brahman alone is to be known," thereby refuting those who hold otherwise. For this Sūtra is intended to remove the notion that [Brahman] is not an object of inquiry. Since the knowability of Brahman has not been established prior to this, the restriction that "that alone is to be known" does not arise. Furthermore, how can one speak of the knowability of a specific established entity without first proving the possibility of words having established entities as their referents?

The proof for that [non-exclusion] follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*; moreover, a syntactical connection involving expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa-yojanā*) is not tenable. Here, as in the case of the *Codanā-sūtra*, it is also untenable to claim that there is both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with another (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*) by virtue of both the word and the meaning, and that there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because a mere thesis (*pratijñā-mātra*) that is irrelevant is illogical. Furthermore, the claim that "increasing faith in Brahman" and "the negation of others" are useful for the subject at hand is weak; even if that were asserted, the reason (*hetu*) for it must still be inferred here.

However, if that were inferred, it would be redundant, as its proof has already been established by the sections beginning with *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* up to the end of the *Tarka-pāda*. Furthermore, how can those who assert that parts not mentioned in the *Śārīraka* are to be understood through Sāṅkhya and Yoga now deny them here? As for the point that portions contrary to the Vedas are to be disregarded, this was already established prior to the *Virodha-adhikaraṇa*; yet, while strengthening his own stated positions regarding word-meanings and sentence-meanings, he demonstrates the agreement between his work and their treatises by following their system, saying: "Thus he says."

The author’s intention is also that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) serves as a cause [for the inquiry into Brahman] by virtue of its being established as preceding [the latter] in an invariable manner. Here, "attainment" (*adhigama*)—defined as that by which something is attained—is the inquiry itself. The mention of "desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) is to be understood in the same way as the mention of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*).

To establish the meaning of the sūtra he himself has stated, he also confirms the unity of the scripture (*śāstraikya*) which was indicated [earlier], saying: "He will state. This is a future reference to another section of the work that is yet to be explained. By the expression "being joined together" (*saṃhitatva*), he intends to show that the unity of the scripture here consists not merely in belonging to the same branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), but rather in forming a single continuous composition (*aikaprabandhya*).

The meaning is that once the unity of the investigation into the nature of the entire Veda’s meaning has been established, the two sections—the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *brahmakāṇḍa*—are joined together according to the maxim of the lost horse and the burnt chariot (*naṣṭāśvadagdharathanyāya*), because each is incomplete in itself and thus possesses a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Furthermore, this commentary indicates the causes for the misconception of a division in the scripture and their respective resolutions: by using the term *Śārīraka*, which shows that [the subject] concerns all embodied beings (*sarvaśarīrin*), it makes known the difference in subject matter; and by pointing out with his very finger the difference between the purpose and the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), as well as the manifestation of the non-contradiction of the subject matter. This is indicated by the phrase "by Jaimini's [work]."

This indicates a suspicion of division. The resolution, however, is that it is "by means of the sixteen characteristics," that is, by the two sections consisting of twelve chapters. Regarding this, that [system] concerning ritual action (*karma*), the deities, and Brahman appeared in three ways from the author of the Sūtras: from the sage Jaimini, from Kāśakṛtsna, and from Bādarāyaṇa, respectively. Thus ends the *Tattvaratnākara*.

Furthermore, because of the mention of "him" (*tam*) and because of the context, any apparent contradiction should be understood as being resolved through metaphorical usage. By employing the counter-argument regarding the "sixteen characteristics," it is shown that differences in intermediate subject matters and so forth do not contradict the unity of the treatise. By the very phrase "by the follower of Jaimini," it is indicated that the suspicion of a contradiction in meaning arises from a lack of understanding regarding the intended purport of the Sūtras; for [Bādarāyaṇa] will indeed demonstrate agreement with Jaimini on many points concerning the subject matter of the Śārīraka.

In passages such as "Jaimini [says] dharma is for the sake of removing delusion" (*vyāmohaśāntyai*), there is both the statement of a disagreement and its subsequent refutation. In cases such as "Jaimini [holds] the absence of the *naiṣṭhika* and other stages of life," although Jaimini did not actually compose a sūtra to that effect, it was certainly stated—and later restated and rejected—for the purpose of preventing those with desires from turning away from the duties of the householder. Otherwise, it would be inconsistent to speak of agreement with Jaimini regarding the prohibition of falling away from the *naiṣṭhika* and other stages of life, as seen in passages such as "But for one who has become that [ascetic], there is no returning to the other state, even according to Jaimini."

Jaimini [asserts] non-qualification [for the study of the Upanishads] because of the impossibility [of the ritual elements] in the Madhu-vidyā and others; yet Jaimini also maintains that there is a positive intention [regarding qualification], as there is no statement contradicting the unity of the scripture even in cases such as the option [of different paths]. This is because a slight difference in expression does not contradict [the unity of the teaching], just as there are differences in the explanations given by oneself. By the mention of "being joined together" (*saṃhitatva*), it is demonstrated that the difference or non-difference of authors does not necessarily entail the difference or non-difference of the treatise, according to what is observed. For when there is a connection of meaning, it is logical for a joining to occur through the intention of either one or the intention of both. [This is established] through the firmness of the dialogue with Brahmā, since there is no contradiction with the primary subject matter.
However, a contradiction with a non-primary element is set aside by virtue of the intended meaning (tātparya). || 209 ||

Or rather, just as in the case of filling out what remains after removing the portions obstructed by a palace imagined by another, here too the possibility of speaking of "connection" (saṃhitatva) arises. || 210 ||

Therefore, the distinction between the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās is based on the difference in the objects intended to be explained, just as there is a distinction between the six sections (ṣaṭka) and the distinction between the chapters (adhyāya). The Mīmāṃsā-śāstra begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and ends with "Non-return, because of the scriptural statement; non-return, because of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), following a specific sequence determined by particular logical connections.

To the unreflective inquiry, "Whence then is the manifestation of that difference? Or, even if there were a difference, how could there be a unity of the continuum? [the author] clarifies what is intended by the second commentary with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). This means: "from the authoritative tradition supported by reasoning. By stating that this is "what he intends to explain," it is indicated that although the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) and others in the *Karmakāṇḍa* are devoted to establishing the excellence of ritual action for those who lack a definitive ascertainment of the true nature of the deity, they have no underlying intent (*tātparya*) regarding the refutation of the deity's corporeal form (*vigraha*) and so forth.

For it is stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "Just as for the venerable Jaimini, the presentation of the fruit of ritual action was intended to increase one's faith in ritual action. And this has been explained in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "In the section concerning the deities (*Devatādhikaraṇa*), hyperbolic statements (*ativādāḥ*) were made so that those who have not heard the Vedānta might not lose faith in ritual action. Hyperbolic statements are expressions intended for another purpose. The intention is that even by that much, the suspicion regarding the lack of authority of the Śruti—based on reasons such as its connection with impermanent things as asserted by outsiders—is dispelled; and from that very fact, one's own desired goal is established.

Moreover, in this way, in the first pāda of the ninth [book], among the two topics under consideration—the fruit and the deity—concerning which it was stated in the sūtra *na codanāto hi tādguṇyam* that "there is no such quality [of the fruit] because of the injunction," we shall now explain those sūtras relating to the deity, beginning with *devatā vā prayojayet*. [The view is: the substance to be given by means of dedication to the deity should not be prompted by the deity. Why? Because, as in the case of agriculture and the like, it is logical that the action itself, being the means to the fruit, is the prompter.

To this he replies: "Or rather, the deity should impel [the person], because the eating is for its sake, like [the treatment of] a guest. The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the doubt. The deity, who is the intended recipient of the oblation (*havis*), should impel the seeker of fruit toward its own propitiation. Why? Because the eating is for its sake; that is, because the eating of the oblation and the offering of it are for the sake of that [deity], being subordinate to it. For the deity, as the recipient (*sampradāna*), being primary, impels the substance and its offering toward its own purpose.
Even though the deity is subordinated in sentences where the action is primary, [it remains the goal].
By the power of its respective mantra and so forth, it possesses the predominance of the intended meaning. || 211 ||

Nor should it be argued that the deity is not an agent because of the absence of the fivefold attributes such as a physical body (*vigraha*); for its existence [as such] is established by uncontradicted evidence consisting of traditional texts (*smṛti*), figurative usage (*upacāra*), and the observation of other scriptural passages (*anyārthadarśana*). Therefore, just as a guest possessing a physical body and so forth is to be worshipped and, for his own sake, employs the ritual service toward his desired end, so too does the deity. Furthermore, regarding the term *ārthapatya*: "artha" means prosperity (*vibhūti*) which is either attained (*aryate*) or sought after (*arthyate*). Consequently, one should not suspect that the deity is unworthy of worship due to the absence of such [prosperity], or that it is ineffective because it does not grant what is desired.

The Supreme Deity indeed rules over everything, while another [deity] appointed by Her exercises various powers according to their respective jurisdictions. Nevertheless, that independent Deity is pleased with nothing and does not please anyone; therefore, how can She be the motivator? To this he says: "And thus, there is a connection through That."

Therefore, even in the absence of [the deity's] dependence, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the connection between the one performing the service and the desired fruit is established through the very grace of the deity—who, though indifferent, is attended upon with a devotion characterized by compassion and generosity according to the principles of human and divine ethics—by means of such things as recollection (*smṛti*) and ritual application (*upacāra*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word 'śara', the sacrificial act (*yajña-karma*) should be primary. Here, the phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates a partial acceptance while setting aside the previous position.

Although the fivefold attributes of a deity, such as its physical form and so forth, are difficult to deny; although the recipient (saṃpradāna) is primary in relation to the substance and other factors; and although sacrifice (yāga), being synonymous with the propitiation of a deity, has that deity as its purpose; and although in established scriptural passages we learn the essential nature and other details of both the higher and lower deities for their own sake—nevertheless, in the injunctions regarding what is to be performed, ritual action in the form of sacrifice and the like is primary because it is enjoined as the means to achieve results such as heaven. Thus, by appearing as something to be accomplished, it motivates the person toward action, while the deity and all else remain subordinate to the ritual act.

[Objection: "But surely we have heard in scripture that the deity who bestows the fruit possesses primacy by virtue of being the object of worship. To this, he says: "The scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate. For we hear in scripture that the deity is subordinate with respect to the offering of the oblation (*havis*). The deity—presented through mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)—is understood as the means for the fruit arising at a later time for the enjoined action, which is itself momentary; this deity is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) consisting of the deity's satisfaction. Therefore, although the deity possesses actual primacy, it becomes subordinate to the action, just like [the primacy] expressed by words that incite one desiring the fruit.

"It is not the primary motivator. If that is so, how then does the guest function as the motivator? He explains it thus: "In the case of a guest, there would be a predominance of him [and] an absence of [independent] action. The predominance of the guest with respect to hospitality is established; otherwise, because there would be no motivator for the action intended for his sake, that action would be absent. If it is argued that the very injunction for the ritual service of him is the motivator, he replies to that: "Because it is a response to him.
For the injunction for the act of hospitality is indeed prompted solely as a response to the arrival of the guest.
The deity, invoked by a person engaged in ritual action, becomes present for the sake of that person's desired object; it does not, however, derive its agency from that person.
But when a guest arrives of his own accord, he should fulfill his own desired purpose; by complying with that desire, one is prompted to perform service for him. (213)

Therefore, the statement regarding the preeminence of the guest is based on a distinction between what has been attained and what has not yet been attained. Just as there is never any harm, but rather a gain of its true nature, in the performance of service toward a guest even if that guest possesses a physical body and so forth, likewise we see no success in refuting [the reality of] the deity even if it possesses such [corporeal] attributes. If it is asked, "What is the fruit even in establishing [the deity's] subordinate status? [the answer is: it serves to increase devotion to ritual action even among those who have not determined the actual preeminence [of the deity].
Thus, in these Sūtras, regarding the prior and subsequent positions:
This indicates that [the teachings on] possession by deities and so forth are not to be rejected. || 214 ||

Regarding the unity of the deity and other matters asserted in the prima facie argument of the Śabara-bhāṣya, their refutation does not appeal to those who recognize the intrinsic validity [of scripture]. (215)

Through the application of memory, through other scriptural observations, and because it was spoken by himself, that which he uttered cannot be denied by those who are not nihilists merely on the basis of words alone. (216)

If the meanings of what has been heard are denied on account of non-perception and fallacious reasoning, then by falling into the views of the Cārvākas and others, the subversion of everything becomes possible. (217)

The claim that the grammatical compounds and so forth heard in scripture are merely figurative is born of delusion; for you, however, there is the burden of postulating the non-existence of the powers and other properties of what has been heard. (218)
When considering what the gateway to the fruit might be for that which is momentary, it is better here to accept the scriptural formulation of the gateway as a distinct entity. (219)

The fact that the deities have action as their purpose, and that ritual acts have them as their purpose, is established through different aspects; therefore, they do not deserve to contradict one another. (220)
By establishing the meditations on the sun and other deities within the sacrificial fire, Bādarāyaṇa indicated that the preeminence of the deities is established by the very nature of the matter.
Furthermore, the perception of the form of a deity that has not been accomplished is not applicable elsewhere;
nor should a procedure based on such a perception be postulated for every uncontradicted case. (222)
Nor is it contradictory for deities to engage in ascetic practices and the like,
because such activity is logically justified as being undertaken for the purpose of pleasing their own superior Lord.
And for the ruler who seeks to establish dharma by means of punishment,
there shall be the practice of various dharmas according to the influence of past karma.
The qualities and actions of animals, stationary beings, and insentient things, as well as their remedies,
are also heard [taught] by the deities through their continuous intention.
The bestowal of different fruits occurs according to the differences in the sacrificial offerings;
and through prohibited acts, provocation arises, following the logic of the "king and so forth" (rājādinyāya). || 226 ||
If the nature [of deities] in relation to the oblation and other offerings is in accordance with scripture, then it is appropriate that each respective deity’s nature be accepted as such. 227.
Even when the meaning of a mantra is established through an explanatory passage (arthavāda), if no sublation is observed therein,
then the Smṛti rooted in that [mantra] is also not subject to sublation, just like its own source.

The conceptualization of distinct deities occurs both through synonyms and through specific attributes, by means of their respective designations, in order to establish them as the objects of reference. (229)
Those nihilists who, failing to recognize their own dullness, have spoken of dullness among the believers here, are to be pitied by those of subtle vision. (230)

Even when the substance and the deity are common [to two mantras], the substance is more powerful, because it is established by means of valid cognition whether it be perceptible or imperceptible. || 231 ||
The sacrificial nature of a substance established through perception is the domain of scripture;
likewise, the nature of the deity and its status as a dharma [are established] through distinction. (232)
Because it depends upon perception and other means of knowledge, cognition derived from scripture is delayed;
for that reason, there is a relative weakness even among the [six indicators] such as direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga).
The disparity between the substance and the deity does not arise from a difference in their reality or unreality;
for if the deity were false, how could it possess attributes such as differentiation? (234)
Whether its nature consists of words connected with meaning, or whether it consists of mere sound, or even as it is grasped exactly as heard, the deity is indeed truly real. (235)
Success through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, is accepted as being taught;
why then is that which is innate at birth not also accepted among the gods? (236)

It is not appropriate to assume [the existence of] both the object and another location here, as in the case of the injunction regarding the vision of Deva, because the injunction for the nature [of the object] is well-established. (237)

And by the rule of the *Rātrisatra* and other such [Vedic] precedents, in accordance with the requirement of injunctions, the deities are established as bestowers of fruits because they themselves constitute the fruit. (238)
Thus, by this ancient method, the view that there is no divine being has been refuted;
the remainder will be addressed in the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "tadupari" (above that). 239.

The author of the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya* has also stated: beginning with "the form of the Creator of the universe is indeed manifest," [he says] "for the form of a formless deity is not taught, since the scripture speaks of things as they truly are. Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not previously stated that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi*), whereas in the *Samanvaya* section it was otherwise? How, then, is there no contradiction? It is thus: because the two proceed by way of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*). And this is observed in other scriptures and in other sections of the same work.

In this same manner, contradictions imagined through false views (*kudṛṣṭi*) elsewhere must also be pacified. The phrase "like the division of the *Ṣaṭka*" serves as a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) regarding the *Karmakāṇḍa*, while "like the division of the chapters" applies to all three *kāṇḍas*. The word "and" (*ca*) here includes the unmentioned divisions such as the *pādas*. Furthermore, the separate treatment of the *Śārīraka* from the *Devatākāṇḍa* is established by way of a counter-argument based on that very separation. Now, he clarifies—on the basis of what is established in the *Vṛtti*—the removal of the notions that [this work] lacks a sequential order (*vinnakrama*) or constitutes a disjointed composition (*bhinnaprabandha*), by stating: "The Śāstra of Mīmāṃsā."

The meaning is: "by a specific connection," that is, by a relationship such as that of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). And this [connection] is explained in the *Viṃśatilakṣaṇī* as the state of being accomplished by a single effort due to the accomplishment of a single purpose. This is for the sake of manifesting the unity of the work as a single treatise (*ekaprabandhya*). "Specific order" means a fixed order; the intention is that, unlike in other scriptures, there is no sequence here based merely on the occasion (*avasara*) or similar factors. Regarding this, the distinction is stated: "In this system, study is established as occurring prior to inquiry (*vicāra*) because of the injunction.
Therefore, inquiry by one who has not studied the Veda is prohibited by the Śruti. (240)
The sequence of the twenty characteristics is not based on scriptural injunction (vaidha), but rather is logical (yauktika);
therefore, any consideration of a different order reveals its impropriety.

By the word "beginning with" (*ārabhya*), the promise to investigate the entire meaning of the Veda is indicated in the *Dharmajijñāsā-sūtra*, because the term "dharma" includes all things—whether established or to be accomplished, superior or inferior, and the cause of the support [of the world]. The promise regarding the ritual portion alone may also be established therein either by implication (*tantrataḥ*) or by repetition (*āvṛttyā*). It is for this reason alone that the statement in the *Sāra* that the purpose is the investigation of ritual action is made. From the two promises concerning the two portions, the general promise is understood, just as in the *Nyāya-sūtra* the general category of *pratidharmasama* is inferred from the mention of *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama*.
