All of this has been stated in the *Saṅgatimālā*.

Nor should it be argued: "Since the entire matter is established by the initial proposition alone, what is the purpose of the specific propositions? For it is appropriate here as well—just as in the preceding chapters—to include them for the sake of purposes such as removing specific doubts. Furthermore, this opening [sūtra], beginning with *athāto dharmajijñāsā*, does not have an irrelevant subject matter; the intent is that just as elsewhere there is a fixed sequence due to logical connection (*saṅgati*), so it is here. For in this context, since that which lacks a means of knowledge cannot be defined, the first [section] was devoted to the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Once the authority of the Veda as a whole was established, and since no distinction exists among its constituent parts, it would be impossible for any factor such as subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) to apply; therefore, immediately after the investigation into the means of knowledge (*māna*), the investigation into the distinctions among the meanings of the scriptures (*śāstrārtha*) proceeded. Some say this is the "investigation into the distinctions among the scriptures" (*śāstrabheda*). In that regard, once the distinction [of actions] is established through difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*), the definition of the subsidiary (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*) proceeds by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and title (*samākhyā*).

In the fourth [book], there is an inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), so that the remaining [subsidiaries] may be employed by those who possess the primary purpose; some say this is an investigation into "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which consists in the requirement of an injunction (*vidhyapekṣā*). Once [the subsidiaries] have been enjoined, the order of sequence (*krama*) is set forth in the fifth [book] by means of direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual position (*pāṭha*), performance (*pravṛtti*), and the principal section (*mukhyakāṇḍa*). When the meaning of the scripture has been established as possessing a specific order, the agent who performs it is declared in the sixth [book]. Thus, once the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been taught, the general principle of extension (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) is established in the seventh [book]. In the eighth [book] as well, the specific details connected to that [extension] are treated.

In the ninth [book], there is a manifold discussion regarding the modification (*ūha*) of mantras and other elements that have been extended by analogy (*atideśa*). In the tenth [book], there is sublation (*bādha*), occurring when—among those things obtained through extension—there is an absence of purpose, or when it is obtained from another source, or due to an explicit prohibition. In the eleventh [book], there is the principle of common performance (*tantra*), which applies when both [the primary and secondary acts] possess the capacity for separate performance, yet share identity in place, time, and so forth. In the twelfth [book], there is the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), which occurs when one act falls within the course of another and depends upon that other's performance.

They summarized this as follows: "By means of [the sections on] Dharma, Intellect (Buddhi), Non-difference, Limbs, Application, Order, and Agent; and by means of [the sections on] Beginning, Specific Place, Exception, Sublation, and Tantric Connection. Thus, once the ritual action had been deliberated upon in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa* consisting of four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*), the very deity to be worshipped through each respective rite was extracted (*nirakṛṣyata*) according to the distinctions of essential nature, attributes, and excellence.

And at its conclusion, because of the vision of Him as Hari, the elders who know the truth state that [the final portion] was added as an introduction to what is about to be investigated: "They call Him Brahman; they call Him Brahman. Therefore, in the final section (kāṇḍa), the Supreme Deity—who is to be worshipped through all the duties taught in the twelve chapters (the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras) either directly or through intermediaries, and whose body comprises all deities as determined by the immediately preceding four chapters—is intended to be examined.

In that regard, the first chapter establishes the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all causal statements with Brahman by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "By setting aside [the objections] regarding the lack of subject matter and the subject matter being something other [than Brahman], the concordance of sentences with Brahman is demonstrated here through the first chapter. In the second chapter, the removal of suspected contradictions is treated.

By those two [chapters], the establishment in Brahman is shown; by the third and fourth, the excellence of the means and the fruit according to the order of origination (*utpatti-krama*). Thus, the specific sequence of the twenty chapters has been indicated merely in outline. Now, one might ask: "In this case, how is the priority of the group of four [chapters] concerning the sixteen-fold [breath-control] established? For even if there were a reversal of order, it would not matter."

There is no contradiction; for although the authority of the Vedas and so forth must be accepted as a prerequisite (*upajīvya*), they can be established in their proper place within the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], or one might engage in the inquiry into Brahman after having heard only that much. This is not so; for regarding the three aims of life (*trivarga*) practiced since time immemorial, the agent first becomes attached to them until he perceives their defects—this is the sequence of meaning.

Although there is no difference between the two cases regarding the immediate perception of limited or unlimited fruits, according to the maxim "if one can find honey in the mud," it is better to first undertake the contemplation of karma—which, while independent of knowledge, yields fruits equal to that [knowledge] once its conceptual fluctuations have been shaken off—rather than the exertion of knowledge which is dependent on ritual action. Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of sentences pertaining to the constituent parts of that [knowledge] depends upon the understanding of the categories such as sacrifice (*yajña*). In the various types of knowledge, the investigation into injunctions for viewing sacrifices and their components as specific meditative objects (*dṛṣṭi*) likewise depends upon the determination of the qualifiers of those specific views.

Furthermore, the cognitions regarding the analogies such as the piling of bricks (*iṣṭakacita*) depend upon the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*). Consequently, it is logical that the sequence of inquiry follows the sequence of study, which—regarding the portion of the Veda abounding in *karma* and *brahma*—is fixed by the time-honored tradition of study. And this [sequence] here is indeed the "order of the principal" (*mukhyakrama*), because of the order of the arising of the subsidiaries and the primary rites consisting of ritual action (*karma*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*). Thus it has been stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "Since the relationship of cause and effect is accepted between the knowledge of ritual action and [the knowledge of] Brahman, the priority of ritual action is established, and the posteriority of the other."

And because those two [offerings] occur in a sequence, their investigations likewise follow that same order; this must be so according to the principle of "principal order" (*mukhyakrama*), just as in the case of the subsidiaries of the Sārasvata offerings. For instance, regarding the two sacrifices arising from the pair mentioned in the passage, "The two Sārasvatas exist; this indeed is the divine couple," when there is no determination as to which of the two has priority among the subsidiaries, the priority of the sacrifice to Sarasvatī is established by its *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. Consequently, it is stated that the priority of its subsidiaries follows that sequence, according to the rule: "Or rather, the order of the subsidiaries follows the order of the principal, because they exist for its sake. This is because the principles well-known in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) are here being summarized.
Remember also that the section on Brahman would be in vain, as it was in the preceding chapters. (242)

The explanation of things not previously understood, as well as their establishment by means of refutation, and in some cases an exception—by these, the meaningfulness of this work is established. (243)

Now, if the Mīmāṃsā concludes with "Non-return [is established] from scripture, non-return from scripture," then—given that the Śārīraka accepts that only those who are dispassionate have the qualification [for its study], and given the certainty therein of a faultless and infinite fruit—no one would succeed in performing the means for results such as heaven. Consequently, the injunctions regarding optional rites (kāmya-vidhi) would suffer invalidity characterized by their non-performance.

It is not so. For those who, out of delusion or due to obstacles, have rested after merely investigating ritual action; or those who, desiring only fame, gain, honor, and the propagation of their teachings, might contemplate the meaning of the Upanishads; or those whose dispassion has later subsided due to the force of destiny—even these, though they have heard the *Śārīraka*, would abandon the dharma of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*).
Even a wise man, when afflicted by illness, may indulge in unwholesome things;
why then should that which is desired not likewise occur even in a person of intelligence regarding forbidden acts? (244)
Even great beings are said to possess a dual cultivation [of both paths] due to desire;
for some, gradual liberation is likewise taught. (245)

For instance: first of all, by the injunction "one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," the grasping of the collection of syllables called the Veda—denoted by the term *svādhyāya*—is prescribed by the act of study itself. The phrase beginning with "for instance" (*tathā hi*) is stated for the sake of establishing the sequence and the logical consistency of the present subject matter: the inquiry into Brahman and the undertaking of the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*). (146)

Anticipating the objection that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) might occur even before the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), [the author] sets forth the following dilemma in his mind: does he intend for it to precede even the study [of the Veda], or does he mean it should precede the investigation of ritual action for one who has already studied the Veda? Having thus formulated the alternative, he negates the first position with the word "first" (*prathamam*). The commentary (*vivaraṇa*) explains that the word "first" (*tāvat*) demonstrates that immediate succession to the study [of the Veda] is universally accepted.

By this, it is indicated that—just as inquiry occurs immediately after study—the subject matter to be explained possesses the nature of a single continuous composition with a fixed sequence, being the object of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of study established by a single injunction; that study, by the force of the injunction, has the entirety of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) as its scope; and consequently, the inquiry into it likewise has that same scope. This is difficult for anyone who reflects upon ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman to deny. Alternatively, the word *tāvat* may be used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

And by that very [injunction], since there is no opportunity for other treatises due to the mandatory study preceded by the training in rules of purity (*śaucācāra*) immediately following the initiation (*upanayana*) at eight years of age, any prior occurrence such as the "four means" (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*)—which might otherwise be presumed to be its root—is excluded. By adopting its own injunction, "One's own Veda is to be studied," the application of that [study] is intended. By the phrase "the acquisition of a mass of syllables through study," the attainment of the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) is indicated. Here, the particle "eva" (only/alone) illuminates the fact that the restriction (*niyama*) is the resulting consequence.

Although this injunction for study is obligatory because of the sin incurred by non-performance and because no specific occasion (*nimitta*) is mentioned, nevertheless, since a visible fruit cannot be abandoned, when the mass of syllables is acquired through study undertaken for the sake of attaining that fruit, there is no room here for any other cause of acquisition. Even for one who asserts that study is for the sake of the mandatory injunction (*niyoga*), the reading from books and so forth must be precluded by implication; for this very reason, there is even a censure of those who read from written texts.

By the three [verses] beginning with "That which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*," it is indicated that neither a mere portion of one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*) nor the meaning of the Veda is what is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*; the sense is that study according to the traditional succession (*paramparā-prāpta*) and in the prescribed order is what is sanctioned by the injunction. "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is enjoined and understood as the fruit; the meaning is that while other means might be possible, this fruit is restricted to this specific means. For a restriction (*niyama*) applies precisely where the particle *eva* (only) occurs, and not elsewhere.

Although there is no restriction regarding the essential nature of grasping the syllables, since that can be accomplished by other means as well, nevertheless, the restriction is justified because the utility for recitation and so forth applies only to what has been acquired through formal study (*adhyayana*). Those who maintain a restriction regarding the knowledge of the meaning are likewise saved by this same argument.

In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of that study is and how it is to be performed, the following are prescribed through such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brahmin boy at eight years of age and teach him," and through specific instructions regarding vows and observances such as: "Having performed the *upākarma* ceremony on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months according to the rule. Thus, those requirements are established.

Surely, by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), one understands only that one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied. By that much alone, there is no obstruction to the opportunity for other scriptures which serve as causes for the attainment of the fourfold qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth; for it is possible to study [those others] even after that. Whether one studies them without the preliminary rites or having studied one's own Veda once, let one practice another scripture—this is what is expressed here by the word "that" (*tat*), clarifying the nature, time, and qualification for the study: the meaning is that this refers to the initial study established by the universally accepted obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*).

Of what form? Does it mean an independent recitation like that of *japa* and so forth, or an unrecited [mental] repetition; or is it based on a different principle like the study of the *Gauḍa* [Veda], or like the *pārāyaṇa* (non-repetitive), or like *avaghāta* (repetitive)? By the word "form" (*rūpa*), the inclusion of the fruit is intended; thus, even for the *Tūlikā*, the intent is that the form consists of repetition as long as the [fruit] is being attained. "How? refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

With the intention of showing that there must necessarily be a distinction and a state of uniformity (*aikarasya*) between those supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇas*) which are accepted as being for the purpose of study—though they might be suspected of being for the purpose of teaching—and those [other] supplementary texts, he makes this separate mention by saying "and by these instructions. The statement "having performed the *upākarma*, one should study" establishes the intent of the revealed scripture (*śruti*), which is that "one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) should study"; for it is precisely for the sake of the study of one who has been initiated that the *upākarma* and other rites are prescribed. "Diligent" (*yuktaḥ*) means attentive, or else, engaged in the observances (*vratas*) and so forth.

"Those for whom the fifth is half" means *ardhapañcamāḥ*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included such previously mentioned statements consistent with the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), such as: "But from this point forward, one should regularly recite the Vedic hymns (*chandas*) during the bright fortnights; and one should recite all the auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*) during the dark fortnights. The "specific vows" (*vrata-viśeṣāḥ*) are those accompanied by initiatory rites (*sopākṛti*), such as the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, and others.

The "specific observances" (*niyama-viśeṣāḥ*) concern the distinctions in the time for reciting the limbs and the main body of the Veda, divided according to the bright and dark fortnights, the half-month, the five-month period, and so forth; they also concern matters of place and so on, such as the rule that "one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra."

Thus, it is understood that study (*adhyayana*) consists in the grasping of the mass of syllables through the repetition of what is uttered by a teacher who is a knower of the Vedas, endowed with self-qualities such as steadfastness in good conduct born of a lineage of virtuous ancestors, and who has initiated the student with specific vows and observances.

One might object: "If the Vedic injunction *upanayīta tam adhyāpayet* (‘He should initiate him and teach him’) prescribes the duties of the teacher, how can it be a rule required for the student’s own study? And how, by this very scriptural statement, is the prevention of opportunities for other [worldly] treatises established? To this, he says: *evam* (‘in this manner’). This means: by the method of enjoining the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), which is established by one’s own injunction supported by the aforementioned Śruti and Smṛti; [and] by [the qualifications of] the teacher, such as being well-born and endowed with knowledge, etc.

Because of the mention of qualities (*guṇa*), one should not suspect that the injunction is primarily concerned with the act of teaching itself; rather, this is based on the principle of the "mention of the qualities of the officiating priest" (*ṛtvigguṇoktinyāya*). With this intention, the statement beginning with "in a lineage of the virtuous" (*satsantāne*) is made. Here, the words "composed" (*samāhita*) intend both proper conduct (*ācāra*) and personal qualities (*ātma-guṇa*). The phrase "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) clarifies the state of being fully endowed with knowledge. Furthermore, teaching by an unqualified person is prohibited, and when such qualities are lacking, it is rectified. Thus, the loss for the student is described in passages such as, "He indeed enters from darkness into darkness."

The fact that these qualities belong to the student is evident from such statements as "he should seek out a preparer" and "in him alone [the teacher should impart] the end of knowledge and action. Just as for those who maintain that the injunction to teach is the primary rule, the qualifications of the student—such as being eight years old—are for the sake of the teacher, so too the qualifications of the teacher are for the sake of the student. To indicate this parallelism, the phrase "endowed with specific vows and observances" and so forth has been cited; for by means of the two words ending in the genitive case, the qualified person (adhikārī) is also shown to be a specific observance, and because one who is initiated at eight years of age is already governed by the injunction to study.

By the phrase "repeating after the utterance of the teacher" (*ācāryoccaraṇānūccāraṇam*), independent utterance and the suspicion that reflection might enter into the meaning of the scripture of study are excluded. Just as, according to another view, the presence of a pupil suitable for instruction is considered a helpful factor for the teacher because it serves as a visible result of the initiation (*upanayana*), so too, in this view, there is a proximity conducive to repeating after the teacher. And such is the intended sense.

In this first chapter, disregarding specific details such as "once," "not once," "twice," or "thrice" according to the logic of threshing (*avaghātanyāya*), he states—"the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables"—with the intention that the purpose of repetition is established by the attainment of the result. By this, it is also implied that the desire to grasp the syllables is a qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) of the seeker.
Even though it is accepted as the fruit, its status as such is like the state of being husked (which is a means to the grain).
Furthermore, the utility of even such grasping in rituals like sacrifice is difficult to deny. (247)

For one who desires the knowledge of the meaning here as the fruit, whether through injunction or by permission, it is difficult to maintain that its status as a compulsory duty (*nitya*) would be lost due to the connection with a fruit. (248)

However, those who—regarding the injunction for the compulsory study (*nityādhyayana*) as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—postulate heaven as the fruit because it is not distinguished from anything else according to the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice, and who [hold] the knowledge of meaning as the fruit in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), are also refuted by this: for it is logical that the apprehension of syllables, which is a visible result, should be a fruit terminating in happiness, even though it is distinct from happiness itself, just like the knowledge of meaning and so forth.

Thus, both the non-omission [of the syllables] and the grasping of the collection of syllables constitute the fruit; by these two, the nature of the meaning of the first study—which was desired to be known as being of what form—is demonstrated. And so is the commentary: "For the function of a verbal root (*dhātu*) consists in a collection of momentary actions delimited by a single result, as in 'he cooks rice'; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the collapse of the designation of the present tense. For the meaning of the word 'present' is that which has begun but is not yet completed."

However, if action—which is momentary—were the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then because the moment of action known prior to the utterance of the word has already perished, and because the subsequent moment is yet to come, and because a simultaneous moment cannot be known and thus is not an object of the word, it would follow that even though it is perceptible by the eye, its beginning and completion could not be established due to its destruction at every moment and the impossibility of defining a beginning, middle, or end. Therefore, he states that the word "study" (*adhyayana*) applies to a collection of action-moments delimited by the fruit of grasping [the text].

The statement that study consists of the non-simultaneous recitation performed by one who has been initiated by a teacher clarifies that both injunctions—“he should initiate him” and “he should teach him”—prescribe that [the act of study] must be preceded by initiation and other rites performed by the teacher.

[Objection: But surely, the statement "one should teach" must have the purpose of restricting the means of livelihood (to teaching). [Reply: Not so; for since one observes that even those who have not been initiated (anupanetṛ) may teach for that purpose, the injunction for initiation would be rendered useless. Nor is there a restriction regarding sequence, such as "one should teach only one who has been initiated," because that would result in the statements such as "a Brāhmaṇa of eight years" being unnecessary. Furthermore, it is entirely inconsistent to claim that the instruction on that [initiation] here is for some other purpose. Nor can a restriction regarding initiation be suspected here, as no other source is seen that establishes it. If it is argued that a Smṛti text is observed [as the source], we say no, because the mention of "eight years" and so forth would then be of no use.

O King, there is no statement here regarding two means of livelihood (*vṛtti*), because initiation (*upanayana*) is not enumerated as one of those means. Even if that were the case, the impossibility of a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) has already been stated due to the absence of a source for its application, and this is further because a response has already been given. Therefore, this is simply an injunction required by the act of study (*adhyayana*). And in this context, the injunction would be one of instigation (*prayojaka*), like the command "one should cause [another] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). For teaching (*adhyāpana*) also, being established as a means of livelihood just like officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), is not itself something to be enjoined.

Therefore, in this context, an eight-year-old Brahmin, desiring to acquire the Veda (*svādhyāya*), having been initiated by a teacher according to the aforementioned manner, should approach him and study while observing the vows and rules as prescribed. This establishes the meaning of the scriptural injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) along with its supporting arguments. For this very reason, it is incorrect to assume that the performance [of study] is prompted by something else simply because no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is heard in the injunction for study; for such an assumption would apply equally to both cases, since no such person is heard in the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) either. Nor can such an assumption be made here.

The requirement [of study] is established by merely changing the case endings in passages such as "a Brāhmaṇa," from "one desiring offspring" and so forth; furthermore, this is supported by the Smṛti rule, "A Brāhmaṇa should study. If it is argued that because a child lacks knowledge of his own entitlement (*adhikāra*), he cannot be prompted by a Vedic injunction, we say no: the performance of the rite is possible through others who are knowledgeable about it, according to the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* (the chief of the Niṣādas). Indeed, those seeking the welfare of children and others who do not know their own entitlement perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) themselves, as they understand their utility. As for Vedic study, however, it is appropriate for a child to engage in it even through the instigation of authoritative persons, since its efficacy can be inferred therefrom.

For those who maintain that constant study is prompted by desire, how can there be in that case the characteristic of a niyoga (an injunction) having the performance of the action as its intended object? 249.
If it is held that for those who are enlightened [the means] is by their own rule, while for the unenlightened it is otherwise,
then in the postulation of such a distinction in application, there would be the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya).

And as for the claim that, in the case of a student who has completed the hardship of study, the knowledge of meaning—which is perceived prior to reflection—is accepted as the purpose by virtue of being the object to be accomplished, so that the injunction to study may find its completion in its qualification [for the rite]; that too is weak, because once the study is established from another source, it is improper to postulate a further purpose for it through an effect that is already established without being its motivator; for, like other obligatory rites (*nitya*), this too can be shown to have the mere performance of the injunction (*niyoga*) as its sole purpose.

If it is argued that something other than the visible result is also permitted [by the injunction], we say no; for then there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting even incidental gains such as profit and honor, since these too would be permitted by the injunction here. Nor can it be said that the injunction permits only the knowledge of meaning because it is useful for the performance of Dharma, and nothing else; for wealth and so forth are also useful for that purpose, and thus they too would obtain permission. While it may be possible for the knowledge of meaning to assist all injunctions, one does not disregard other visible results on the basis of this much distinction. (251)

If you argue that wealth and the like provide assistance through their own inherent power, then knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda] would likewise be so; it would not be subject to the authority of injunctions. (152)
In its true sense, that [injunction] is authorized and manifested by the very power of the word;
let it be relied upon by the injunctions of sacrifice, giving, and so forth, which are themselves dependent [upon it]. (253)
Moreover, a single [action] would incur a dual nature because it consists of both an injunction and a permission;
this would also apply in the case of primary and subordinate actions. (254)

Therefore, it is a matter of common experience even in your own villages that at the very time of beginning the study, teachers and others, intending the welfare of the boy—either by their own intelligence or having been instructed by others—act as the motivators for him. No one is seen engaging in such activity with the thought, "I must assume the role of a teacher for another. And those who wish him well, while instructing him, point out to the child the future results [of his learning].

And in the *Chāndogya*: "I shall dwell as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) with the Blessed One; I would approach the Blessed One," thus Jābāla said to Gautama. And he replied: "Bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you," and so forth. Therefore, the teacher proceeds solely for the sake of the disciple; it is established that the gift (*vara*) and other such things are to be obtained by him [the disciple]. For this very reason, the claim made by some—that study is motivated by the attachment of the teacher who is greedy for the acquisition of wealth and the like—is refuted.

This is established in order to show that even if its own injunction (*svavidhi*) cannot be the motivator, the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*) cannot be the motivator either. For it is not possible to compel a boy to act without first making him understand his own purpose; otherwise, the teacher would be acting out of sheer force. Therefore, in the injunction for the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅgādhyayanavidhi*), the Brahmin and others—who are explicitly mentioned—become qualified by aiming for their own welfare; thus, there is no motivation from any other source.

By this, the argument raised by some—that if one does not accept the impulsion (*prayukti*) of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), then since the impulsion of the ritual injunctions (*kratuvidhi*) must necessarily be resorted to, even Śūdras and others desiring those respective fruits would have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to study—is refuted; for the study is impelled by its own injunction, which has a fixed agent, just like the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). Furthermore, the objection regarding the lack of an entitlement in the injunction for study is also refuted by stating that the result is the acquisition of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), which is a visible effect similar to the threshing of grain (*vaituṣya*).

The Smṛti passage beginning with "upanīya" (having initiated) also does not enjoin teaching (*adhyāpana*), nor does it take the status of being an *ācārya* as its result; for it is intent upon deriving the meaning of the word *ācārya* by way of restating a specific form of teaching already established elsewhere, just like the derivation of words such as *upādhyāya*. Indeed, there is no reason here to assume an intention distinct from that. Nor is there a single, separate kind of *ācārya*-ship [distinct from the mere act of teaching], as there is no evidence for it. If it is argued that such a distinction is postulated because no other basis for the term is observed, we say no.

This is because we observe that the cause for the application of the term [‘Ācārya’] is the conjunction of the restriction of the initiation (*upanayana*), the instruction, and the absolute exclusion of non-application. For this very reason, the usage of the word ‘Ācārya’ is justified even at a time subsequent to the initiation and so forth, following the logic of the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*) and others. However, previously, due to the difficulty of anticipating the future, there was no usage [of the term] because of doubt regarding the knowledge of the cause and its manifestation. Furthermore, if the Smṛti here were intended merely to derive the meaning of the word, its basis is seen to be simply the linguistic usage of the elders.

If, however, [the injunction] were for the purpose of the rule regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), then one would have to assume that it is rooted in a scriptural text (*śruti*) concerning a non-worldly matter; and when there is a conflict between what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what is to be assumed (*kalpya*), the established alone should be accepted. Furthermore, the scriptural mention of the suffix *-ktvā* and so forth here—such as in the case of "having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—is compatible even if [the acts] are not auxiliary parts (*anaṅga*), provided there is merely the commonality mentioned in the Sūtra, such as having a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). [Objection: But surely, because of the natural force of the single-agent construction and because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), the relationship of principal and auxiliary (*aṅgāṅgitva*) would be established through a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*). [Reply: That is not so; for the scriptural mention of *-ktvā* resides in Smṛti, and it may also be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
In this case, the indicative mark (liṅga) residing in the Vedic text is indeed stronger, for it is without delay.

The *upanayana*, which is heard in the Veda as being for the sake of the single refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the boy—designated by the term "Brāhmaṇa"—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study (*adhyayana*) performed by the initiated boy, due to its status as an internal mark (*antaraṅga-liṅga*) because it resides within the ritual action itself. This is so even though it stands in proximity to both the fruit-bearing activities of studying and teaching, insofar as they consist of the operations of the one who is prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*). If it were for another purpose, there would be a mediated connection (*praṇāḍyā*). Thus, since it is enjoined for study based on the scriptural mark (*śrauta-liṅga*), any assumption that it is an auxiliary to teaching would involve the contradiction of enjoining what has already been enjoined (*viniyuktaviniyoga-virodha*).

For a scriptural indication (*liṅga*) based on a *smṛti*—which is not directly heard in the Veda—is not capable of subverting a directly stated (*śrauta*) indication; this is because it is obstructed by a double delay: first, the *smṛti* depends upon its own source (the Veda), and second, a subsequent statement depends upon a prior one.

[Objection: But surely, from the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by the rule "svarita... etc., the act of initiation (*upanayana*) would be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the teaching residing in the initiator. [Reply: It would not be so, because it is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with "sammānana... (Pāṇini 1.3.36).

The Grammarians (Śābdikas) maintain that this [present] undertaking is for the purpose of expressing what is not intended for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). They argue that "intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*) means the connection of the result with the agent alone, whereas "not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāyatva*) is simply the absence of such a restriction. If this is argued, it is not so; for even in the case of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by rules such as *svarita-jitaḥ* etc., as in the example *ādadhīta*, the result is connected to both [the agent and another]. Nor is it the case that the fruit of the action cannot be connected to two conscious beings; for that is observed even in the passage, "The husband and wife should establish the sacred fires" (*jāyāpatī agnimādadhīyātām*). Furthermore, the claim that the connection must be with a conscious being other than the agent is also refuted.

From the perspective of authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika*), in all scriptural matters, since there are scriptural declarations of results consisting of joy toward one who is not the agent but the object of worship, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of losing the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) endings in cases such as *ādhāna*. Furthermore, in passages such as *abhicaranyajeta* ("one performing sorcery should sacrifice"), a result appropriate to that [act] is admitted even for the enemy (*bhrātṛvya*). And in the case of *ṛtvijo vṛṇīte* ("he chooses the priests"), the result is established even for those being chosen. Since the term "result of the action" (*kriyāphala*) is intended to refer to the immediately following result, its connection with the agent constitutes "being for the benefit of the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*).

As for the argument that the *Sammānanādi-sūtra* is intended to establish the connection of the agent with a remote result (*vyavahita-phala*), this too has already been answered: because there is a deviation [in the rule] in cases such as "one should establish the fires" (*ādadhīta*). For in this case, the result—namely, the status of being one who has established the fires (*āhitāgnitva*)—belongs to the establisher, even though it is mediated by the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire. Now, one might object: "The result for the establisher is simply the accomplishment of the consecrated fire, which serves as the basis for future obligatory and optional sacrifices; thus, there is no connection with a remote result. Do not say so.

In this case as well, the result for the initiator (*upanetṛ*) is simply the accomplishment of the student who has been consecrated by the initiation rite (*upanayana-saṃskṛta*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering the sūtra beginning with "honoring" (*sammānanādi*) superfluous. If it is argued that both sūtras serve a purpose because the immediate result is either desired or undesired by the agent, we say no; for even an initiator who desires the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) cannot be said to be indifferent to the consecration of the one being initiated. Therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here is used solely to establish the connection of the result with the agent. Likewise, by the expression "he should teach," the result does not accrue to the agent. Thus, in this manner, study is not prompted by another injunction.

And as for reflection (*vicāra*), is it enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*)? Not the first, because the authorization of its subject matter and fruit has already been refuted. Not the second, because it does not exceed the limits of what is reasonable;

for once the teacher has caused [the student] to grasp the *svādhyāya*, he too may desist. However, if it is prompted by compassion and the like, then it remains established that this was already the case previously. (256)
Therefore, thinking that the entire system of Mīmāṃsā would fail under the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), those who wish to establish the original position have rejected it. (257)

And study (*adhyayana*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*); for from the injunction "the sacred text is to be studied," it is understood that the sacred text is the object (*karman*).

Although, in this way, the opportunity for other treatises is blocked once the grasping of the syllables has been accomplished, there may still arise the doubt that such [study] could occur even after the syllables have been grasped. To prevent this even subsequently, he clarifies—by means of the phrase "adhyayanam" (study)—that study is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text), a point previously indicated by rejecting the view that study is the object of an injunction (*niyoga*). The particle *ca* serves to dispel that doubt; alternatively, it is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*), serving to conjoin the nature of being a refinement with qualities such as being repeated many times.

By those who maintain that "purification through mantras, sprinkling, and so forth is intended for the person alone," it is accepted that even the purification of study (*adhyayana-saṃskāra*) belongs to the agent alone. To dispel the doubt that [the definition of *svādhyāya*] would thus fail to establish the intended meaning, he says: "svādhyāya" (one's own Veda). And it has been stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "In the enumeration of purifications, the purification of the syllables is indeed appropriate; for *svādhyāya* is clearly an action, and it is that which is directly purified.
As for those who hold that the infusion of excellence into the person occurs through sprinkling and other such rites—
They too did not abandon their status as conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and karma in each respective case. || 258 ||
The impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by various specific actions resides in the person;
for it is certain that, when conjoined with those [actions], it brings about the respective effects. (259)

In this context, since study (*adhyayana*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), its status as an object (*karman*) serves as the reason; thus, there is no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This is the intended meaning: for here, no other meaning for the suffix *tavya* is possible. Consequently, whether the accusative case-ending or the suffix *tavya* itself denotes the object, there is no distinction; and although grammatical factors (*kārakas*) exist for the sake of an action, because a verbal root whose sense is directed toward an entity (*bhāva*) is for the sake of that entity, the principle of [the threshing of] rice and so forth is appropriate here.

Furthermore, it is established that the acts of threshing and so forth are *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites) directed toward their respective substances, as stated in the section defining "difference" (*bhedalakṣaṇa*): "These [actions] are twofold, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*). By the phrase "of one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyasya*), the impossibility of [the Veda] being something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth is indicated; for it is certainly not something to be produced, since its sequence is established from time immemorial, and because there is no conventional usage of constructing a sentence [anew] during a prior recitation. Nor is it something to be modified (*vikārya*), since no change of state is observed, as would be the case with milk turning into curd and the like.

Nor does it consist merely in being something to be attained, for that would be incompatible with its having other functions [such as recitation]. Therefore, the understanding of its status as an object (*karman*), supported by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), is the reason for its being something to be refined (*saṃskārya*).

For "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) indeed means the production of fitness for another purpose. And it is logical that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is something to be refined, because it provides knowledge of the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as well as their means; and because it serves as a means to those ends even in its own form through practices such as silent recitation (*japa*).

Now, one might ask: even if it is understood to be an object (*karman*), how can the Veda (*svādhyāya*)—which has not been enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) and the like for any specific purpose and is not itself a material substance (*adravya*)—be something to be refined (*saṃskārya*)? To this he says: "For [the word] *saṃskāra* [is used] in the sense of a well-known [fact]. The particle *hi* indicates what is well known; the word *nāma* expresses the excellence of that fact up to the point of being accepted by others. Here, the statement regarding the production of fitness for another function is intended to refer to a refinement that, once produced in the Veda, is useful for a future result. Alternatively, the definition of refinement (*saṃskāra*) here is: "the imparting of an excellence (*atiśaya*) to something that already exists."

[This has been] explained. Consequently, even though [the *paridhi*] is already in use, one must somehow apply the term "fitness for another effect" (*kāryāntara-yogyatā*) here with the intention of expressing a use that conforms to that [other effect], by way of figurative usage (*bhākta*). For it is heard in scripture that even when they have been employed as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), they remain fit for another effect in that very same form, namely, the form of assisting the sacrificial fire (*bhūtopakāra*). This is the underlying point: it is not the case that something cannot be consecrated simply because it has not been previously enjoined; for even in the absence of a specific injunction, its status as an object of consecration is possible precisely through the observation of its utility.

Furthermore, there is an application (viniyoga) both generally and specifically through such [scriptural] statements as "The Hotṛ priest acts with the Ṛgveda"; nor is it the case that it cannot be the object of a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) because it is not a substance, for there is no contradiction provided it has been acquired through study as previously described. Moreover, the fact that it is an object of apprehension is universally admitted even in the case of qualities and so forth.

Even though the excellence (*atiśaya*)—consisting of the Lord’s grace—which is to be accomplished by the action enjoined, does not reside in the Veda itself, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because that very excellence, being acquired through study and apprehended as an object of worship, is restricted by the scripture to the subsequent action appropriate to it. Whether or not an imperceptible excellence arises in the rice and other materials through acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the aforementioned principle applies universally.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in such instances as "one offers groats" (*saktūñ juhoti*) and "gold is to be worn" (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*), even though there is an understanding of the object (*karman*) as being devoid of the status of something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) does not have the purpose of [merely] the substance? Likewise, in injunctions for recitation (*japa*) such as "the Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) and "one should study the Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhīyīta*), the understanding of the object is no different. Therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that regard; or else, in those cases too, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the object being something to be purified (*saṃskārya*). To this, he says: "The status of being something to be purified... (*saṃskāryatvam*).

The point is this: because it is impossible for groats (*saktu*) and the like to have utility either in the past or the future; because repetition (*japa*) and the like necessarily must have the syllables as their object; because of the complexity involved in postulating multiple latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); because no other utility is observed that could be accomplished by the latent impressions produced by repetition and so forth; and because a fruit is explicitly heard [in the scriptures], one abandons the notion of a latent impression in those cases. However, it would not be so here, since the status of these as ritual actions (*karman*), once understood, remains uncontradicted.

On this very point, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states: "We maintain that the first study [of the Veda] is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), because it is measured as an action and because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is useful [for other purposes], even though no specific fruit is heard [in the case of the first study]. If it were claimed that even recitation (*japa*) and the like are purificatory rites, then the first study would not be a purificatory rite, because it is not useful for the entire Veda. Consequently, the status of being an action would apply everywhere, which would result in the sublation of the Veda's status as a purificatory object. Therefore, the first study is a purificatory rite, while the others are actions for a purpose (*arthakarman*)."

In this case, the fruit must be that which is mentioned in the explanatory passages (arthavāda), as in the case of the Rātrisatra sacrifice. Here, the wise maintain that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is an unintended object (*anīpsita-karma*), whereas in the first [case], it is considered an intended object (*īpsita-karma*), and the action is regarded as being for its sake. If even recitation (*japa*) and the like were merely purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), then the only useful application of the Veda—which is the object of all such purifications—would be the comprehension of its meaning. Since that [comprehension] would be useless regarding those portions of the ritual not authorized for one's station (*anadhikṛta-karmabhāga*) and regarding interjections like *hum* and so forth, all studies of the Veda would consequently become purposeful actions (*arthakarma*).

In that case, the status of *svādhyāya* as an object of action (*karman*) would be destroyed; therefore, the first study alone is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). But [an objection may be raised]: even here, since no utility is observed, the argument remains untenable; for if utility is postulated solely on the basis of its being a thing to be purified (*saṃskārya*), there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). And they say: "A rule prescribing a purification does not enjoin the thing to be purified; rather, a rule of purification culminates in the purification only when its utility is already established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it does not itself conceive the purpose of the thing to be purified. To this, he replies: "For the sake of dharma and artha. For it is because no utility is observed that the scriptural injunction regarding the act (*karma-śruti*) is set aside in the case of *saktu* (barley flour) and similar instances.

The point is that since various purposes—both seen and unseen—are observed for the study of one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya*), it is not logical to regard it as something not to be refined (i.e., not requiring preparation), just as in the case of *saktu* (barley meal) and other such items. Here, the statement that the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are to be known through the Veda is intended to show that the entire [Veda] is to be investigated, by demonstrating a commonality of purpose that runs through all its parts; furthermore, it is intended to show that those [aims] taught in non-Vedic scriptures are not to be trusted. Even though some objects of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*), along with their means, are established in the world, it is appropriate that wealth and pleasure in the form of sovereignty over the three worlds, etc., and their means, are to be known through the Veda.

The operation of the scripture is established even regarding worldly ends and desires (*artha* and *kāma*) through means such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice. However, while *dharma* may be perceptible in the form of substances and so forth, it is grasped by the scripture specifically as a means to stability (*dhṛti*). As they say: "For their status as means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda; and since its nature as *dharma* consists in that [status], it is therefore not within the range of the senses."

Furthermore, liberation (mokṣa) is not perceptible to people like us. As for arguments such as "the self is at some time devoid of all specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), because it possesses non-eternal specific qualities, like a jar," they do not constitute valid inference because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka) against the contrary case (vipakṣa). If one were to state a subverting argument against the contrary case by relying on the scriptures that aim at liberation, then the inference would be rendered futile. However, since liberation consists in the experience of Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss, there is no possibility of the application of a logical reason [to prove its absence]; indeed, if one were to attempt to prove the opposite of that, it would contradict scripture (āgama-bādha).

Furthermore, it can also be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is never devoid of all its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because it possesses the nature of self (*ātmatva*), just like the Lord (*īśvara*). In this context, just as the object itself, dharma is also a means for achieving the desired goal since it is the means for attaining the human aim (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, it too is designated by the term "means" (*sādhana*). Furthermore, it should be understood that both the *mantras* and the *arthavādas* appropriately convey the four aims of life (*caturvarga*) or assist in conveying them.

Even in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others such as the *vajra*, there is no injunction toward what is harmful (*anartha*), because they merely instruct on the means for achieving desired ends, such as the destruction of one's enemies. (Verse 260)
And from other terrible means, one may obtain protection here; for they declare that even malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) can be overcome by a light expiation. (261)
Furthermore, it is taught that "one who does not practice sorcery shall fall into the six [hells]";
by this, they understand that killing an *ātatāyin* (aggressor) is consistent with dharma.

But surely, the quality of making known extraordinary human goals and the like exists even in the Smṛtis and other texts; therefore, if the purpose is to be accomplished by other means, what is the use of the Veda’s refinement? Furthermore, there is no comprehension of meaning in cases such as the *hum* and other ritual interjections. Moreover, in the case of portions that have not been mastered or intended for performance by a particular person, even if such comprehension were present, it would be of no use because it does not extend to the point of actual performance. Thus, in this context:

Because the utility of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is obtainable through other means, because it is impossible for the act of recitation (*adhyayana*) to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the entire Veda, and because a purificatory rite applied to only a portion [of the Veda] is not supported by the words [of the scripture],—and since, in the absence of its being a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāravidhi*), the view that it has the purpose of a mandatory obligation (*niyoga*) would otherwise follow—it is said: "by means of recitation (*japa*), etc. By the word "etc.," memorization (*dhāraṇa*) is included. "Even in its own form" means not only by way of the knowledge of the meaning; or else, teaching (*adhyāpana*) is what is grasped by the word "etc."

Then, even by its own nature—that is, by its mere shaken-off nature—according to the Smṛti passage beginning with "the wise man, upholding the Ṛgveda. The intended meaning is this: knowledge is accomplished solely through the Vedic study (svādhyāya) acquired by formal recitation.

The ritual injunctions (*vidhi*) are that which must be relied upon; however, the explanatory supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) do not possess the capacity to be independent means for achieving *dharma* and so forth. Furthermore, there is a scriptural text (*śruti*): "By constant study of the Vedas, by truth, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. Such well-known purposes as the recitation of mantras (*japa*) and the like, which cannot be accomplished by any other means, establish the necessity of purification (*saṃskāra*) even in those portions of the text that are purposeless, not intended for qualified persons, or not desired to be performed. Thus, their status as objects of purification is logically justified.

Furthermore, the rule for recitation (*japa*), even when its object is mere vocalization, does not contradict the fact that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) has meaning as its primary purpose; for if it did, there would be the consequence of self-contradiction by subverting all other injunctions. Nor is there a conflict regarding the distinct application (*viniyoga*) [of the Veda] to both purposes, since there is no multiplicity of purposes in a single form. Thus, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states: "In its own form, it serves the purpose of recitation and so forth; by its own power, it conveys the meaning. There is no contradiction due to the difference in forms, just as fire possesses both burning and illuminating."

The intended meaning is this: since the possibility of infinite purposes arises from the Veda once it has been refined by study, who would exert themselves in other scriptural pursuits without first undertaking its investigation?
Thus, the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables, just like the rules governing the recitation of mantras.

One might object: "Surely, by one who has understood the utility [of study], the knowledge of the meaning must also be accepted as the fruit of the injunction; however, by one who has not understood the utility, even the grasping of the syllables cannot be recognized as a fruit. Therefore, since the knowledge of the meaning is directly useful for performance, it should be considered a perceptible fruit of the injunction to study, just like the grasping [of syllables]. He refutes this objection under the guise of a summary of the topic at hand with the word "evam" (thus). This means: by the method of determining the nature of the injunction, its fruit, and so forth.

The possession of mantras and the possession of observances (niyama) reside in the non-deficient pronunciation; they are metaphorically attributed to their fruit when that fruit is grasped. "Mantras" refers to those that are constituent parts of the *kāṇḍavrata* and so forth, as well as those to be recited during the period of study, such as "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*) and others. "Observances" refers to those previously mentioned. Some maintain that the phrase "as with mantras" is an illustrative statement: just as the study enjoined regarding a mantra is accepted as culminating merely in the grasping of the syllables, so it is here as well.

Others, however, maintain that it should be understood as follows: just as in the case of the rites to be performed at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), such as for one who has merely been initiated regarding the mantras for placing fuel on the fire (*samid-ādhāna*) and so forth, so it is here as well. Others say it is "like *hum* and so forth," meaning like specific mantras used for neutralizing poison and the like. By the words "merely" (*mātra*) and "conclusion" (*paryavasāna*), the cessation of the injunction both before and after the grasping of the syllables is negated.

The intended meaning is as follows: the word "study" (*adhyayana*) does not denote the knowledge of the meaning, because such a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) does not exist, and because in expressions such as "one becomes a Brāhmaṇa after having studied something," it is impossible for it to have that meaning as its primary referent. Furthermore, with respect to study as the object of an injunction, there is observed a result that is an immediate goal, pervasive, and unavoidable.

If one were to postulate that something other than that [knowledge] is its fruit, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate that even a remote goal (*sādhya*) is the fruit, it would follow that the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) which is itself produced by that knowledge would also be so designated, just like the knowledge itself. Moreover, the state of being required without intervention by a subsequent injunction is equal for both the grasping of the text and the knowledge of its meaning. If the knowledge of the meaning were indeed enjoined as having the ritual action as its object, then there would be a conviction in it even when it is non-pervasive or remote; however, this is not the case. Therefore, the knowledge of the meaning must be accepted solely on account of its utility.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, according to the logic of the *Samanvaya* section, it is proper to establish that the knowledge of meaning alone is the fruit by virtue of its being an end in itself? [Reply: It is not so; for that [logic] was stated only with respect to those portions of scripture that propound Brahman as unsurpassed bliss, whereas here we are considering the fruit of the study of the entire [Veda], and thus a discordant determination is inappropriate. [Objection: But in such cases as "Listen to the words of the elders," it is observed in common experience that the injunction to hear the sentence culminates in the knowledge of its meaning. [Reply: No; for that is because there is a purpose in instructing one to hear a particular sentence that serves as a guide to a path—such as the location of a tree—and it is also observed that this is not the case in other instances.

Furthermore, in some cases, the instruction consisting of hearing a sentence must, out of necessity, be taken as being for the sake of the meaning; however, this is not the case here, as it is observed in common worldly practice. [Objection: But surely, by such scriptural passages as "He who, indeed, with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity (*daivata*) are unknown... and by such Smṛti passages as "That which is recited without knowing the seer and the meter," the knowledge of the meaning has been established as something that must necessarily be accomplished, since faults are stated in the contrary case.

It is stated that in the absence of that [knowledge], study is fruitless, whereas in its presence, the attainment of all human goals occurs: "This man is a mere pillar, a bearer of burdens, who having studied the Veda does not understand its meaning; he who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness and, with his sins shaken off by knowledge, goes to the world of Brahman. Therefore, the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas is mandatory. This is not so;

Just as for one who has attained passion (*rāga*), a fault is incurred by not performing acts such as approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), while the attainment of progeny and so forth is recorded in the Smṛtis as the fruit resulting from performing them according to the injunctions—so too should it be here. Therefore, the statement "one should know these [ṛṣis, etc. in each mantra" is intended for the recollection of the ṛṣi and other details known for each individual mantra at the time of its ritual application. For this very reason, the prohibition against using a mantra whose ṛṣi and other attributes are unknown refers only to that much.

Therefore, since the spontaneous inclination toward study is encouraged by the praise of the knowledge of meaning through such passages as, "He who has studied [the Veda] is a mere wooden post," and "He who deliberates upon the sacrifice [without knowing its meaning]," and since this knowledge of meaning is necessarily required, one should not assume that the injunction for study extends as far as that [knowledge], even though it is an injunction; for [study] is independent [of other goals], because an injunction remains indifferent toward what is already established by other means, and because, even if it were to extend that far, it would not by itself culminate in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

As for what is argued by some: since the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) culminates in the knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda], as evidenced by such scriptural passages as, "Having studied the Veda in the teacher’s house, and having performed the duties for the teacher according to rule with the remainder of one's life, having returned home, studying one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) in a pure place within the family, one should establish virtuous sons," and so forth; and by such Smṛti texts as, "Having studied, one should bathe" (*adhītya snāyāt*), the knowledge of the meaning—which consists of the Self—is also employed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent of ritual action, because it serves the purpose of that action; therefore, [the Self] is "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) and "to be heard" (*śrotavya*).

Since the Self—declared as the object of inquiry in such passages as "It is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon; that is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known"—is established as a subsidiary element of ritual action (karma-śeṣa) by not contradicting its inherent fitness for refinement (*saṃskāryatva*), just like rice-grains to be pounded; and since texts such as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman" declare that even one subject to karma is indeed Brahman; and since universal authorship (*viśvakartṛtva*) is logically possible through the medium of karma; and since, when there is a conflict between what is already established and what must be postulated, it is proper to adopt the established; and since the individual soul (*jīva*), having attained the status of agent in rituals, is fit for refinement for their sake—therefore, this being the case, the Vedānta texts are concerned with the individual soul.

Since there is no possibility of a scripture whose subject matter is an Īśvara distinct from that [Veda], for what could this single scripture and its sequential order be postulated? That argument is also refuted by the fact that [the Vedic texts] terminate merely in the acquisition of the syllables. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras, by using such expressions as "having studied" (*adhītya*) and "having returned home" (*abhisamāvṛtya*), does not enjoin the knowledge of meaning as a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of ritual action; for the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* rests merely upon the identity of the agent and so forth. Even if such an injunction were granted, meditation (*upāsanā*) is something entirely different from the knowledge of meaning required for the performance of rituals.

The knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts consists of this very nature [of Brahman]. Furthermore, the Self to be meditated upon is established by Scripture itself as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), and is not merely a conceptual construct. Moreover, the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the individual soul and Brahman—just like the coordination between the insentient and Brahman—is for a purpose other than [denoting] identity, since such identity is contradictory. Let the injunction of such knowledge stand aside; nevertheless, there is no contradiction.

Since the object of worship, like the agent, must be investigated as being for the sake of the ritual action (*karman*), and since that [object] is established by scripture (*śruti*) as being distinct from that which is subject to *karman*, it is established that there exists a separate section (*kāṇḍa*) and so forth for the purpose of investigating it. Even though, in this case as well, the knowledge of the meaning is subordinate to the performance of the rite, the conclusion reached is that it may also, according to its respective portion, be subordinate to the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the Supreme Brahman.

Nevertheless, since the objection is rooted in the necessity of striving for the knowledge of the meaning, and because it is improper to overlook the grave offense committed at the very outset of the first section, the word "mātra" (only) in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya is intended to convey that one must not resort to a mere tentative argument (*anvāruhyavāda*), but must rather cut off the root of the error itself.

Since it is observed that the Vedic study acquired through formal instruction possesses by its very nature the capacity to bring about an understanding of a purposeful meaning, a person who has completed his studies of the Veda spontaneously engages himself in listening to Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the investigation of Vedic sentences resulting in the determination of the specific nature and mode of the purposeful meanings understood from that studied Veda—upon seeing those purposeful meanings presented in a preliminary manner.

In this regard, once the nature of ritual action has been determined, one observes that the fruits of actions are limited and unstable; yet, upon hearing certain Upaniṣadic passages—a portion of the Veda acquired through study—one gains an initial understanding that immortality constitutes an infinite and stable fruit. Consequently, such a person qualifies for the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, which consists of an inquiry into the Vedānta passages aimed at reaching a definitive conclusion regarding that fruit.

Now, an objection: if the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of syllables, then even though the meaning of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic text) is perceived when it has been studied for another purpose, that meaning cannot be the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*) and thus is not to be investigated. Consequently, the Veda would be meaningless; the injunction for study would not culminate in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); and since there would be no subject matter, and because the opportunity [for inquiry] is blocked by the traditional rule "having studied, one should bathe," the Mīmāṃsā itself could not be commenced.

Dispelling the doubt as to how there could be identity [between them] and demonstrating the unity of the scripture—which consists of the Veda as the subject matter and its commentary as the exposition—by way of having a single object, [the author] also indicates the meaning of the opening sūtra of Mīmāṃsā: "In the study... Here, by the words *adhyayana* (study), *svādhyāya* (one's own Veda), *nirṇaya* (determination), and *vicāra* (investigation), which denote one who has studied the Veda, the unity of the subject matter, the fruit, the nature, and the qualified person (*adhikārin*) of Mīmāṃsā is manifested. By the word *gṛhītasya* (of that which has been grasped), the cessation of the operation of the injunction is stated.

The statement that [the Veda] shows a purposeful meaning is for the sake of making known that it culminates in human goals (*puruṣārtha*). "By its very nature" means without depending on the operation of an injunction; the phrase "by one who has mastered the meanings of words and their relations" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This is the intended sense:

"Even though the Veda was undertaken for the purpose of being memorized, it illuminates [its own meaning] by itself, like fire; therefore, it is intrinsically authoritative, provided it is not sublated. (263)
Recitation, study, and meditation accompanied by their respective fruits as prescribed in the Śruti do not obstruct the power of the word; how much less so its capacity for apprehension? (264)

One who, by means of a specific application (*viniyoga*), denies the fact that the Veda has meaning as its primary purpose, is refuted by self-contradiction, because he subverts the cognition of the meaning derived from that very application. (265)
The injunction to study would either have the intended meaning as its purpose or it would not;
in the first case, there is the utterance [of the Veda], but in the latter case, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) cannot even arise. (266)
Moreover, validity here is difficult to establish on the grounds that it has the knowledge of the object as its fruit;
for if that [knowledge] is its fruit, then it is valid, and if it is valid, then that [knowledge] is its fruit. (267)
If the injunction (*vidhi*), though having *niyoga* as its primary meaning, were to accept a focus on the external object,
then it would likewise have the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) as its meaning, being equal in its eagerness for its own establishment.

The Veda is a self-evident knower (*nirapekṣavedaka*); the meaning is that it does not depend on another means of knowledge that has become its root, as is the case with human statements. For this very reason, there is no room for suspicion regarding defects in its source, and thus there is no obstruction to inquiry—this is the intended sense. The purpose here is the fourfold aim of human life (*caturvarga*). The objects possessing that [purpose] are the means thereto, consisting of ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*). Here, "the state of being made known" refers to the evident and undeniable capacity to produce a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*); and since nothing is impossible in what is directly perceived, the word "from observation" (*darśanāt*) has been used with this intention.

Even if [the Veda] were self-evident (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), one might argue that there is no need for inquiry because the object to be established (*sādhya*) is absent; to this he says: "Having perceived" (*gṛhītāt*). The connection is with the temporal qualification "having seen the objects as they are presented" (*arthān āpātato 'vagamyamānān dṛṣṭvā*). It is the initial, superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*) itself that is "seen"; therefore, the intention is that the removal of doubt and so forth is what remains to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The first use of the word *artha* (object) is for the sake of establishing the authority of the Śruti by excluding the mention of things like a crow's teeth. The latter [use], however, indicates that the superficial cognition acts as an impeller by generating an interest in investigating its own subject matter. Nothing whatsoever—whether already known or unknown—should fail to be investigated.
Thus, even the objection has been refuted by the statement that [the object] is known upon first encounter.

[Objection: But surely, since it is the very nature of the word *yajati* (to sacrifice), there would be an initial comprehension even for those who have not mastered the linguistic convention (*avyutpanna*). [Reply: It is not the case that the injunction for that [study] applies only to those who have mastered the convention; for even in the case of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), when the injunction regarding the grasping of the syllables is completed just as it is for the primary rite (*aṅgin*), such [initial comprehension] is impossible. Moreover, if the injunction were uniform, there would be no specific reason for the study of the subsidiaries to extend up to the comprehension of the meaning. To this we reply: For one whose refined language (*saṃskṛtabhāṣā*) has been practiced from childhood, that initial comprehension (*āpātamatir*) would indeed arise for him in that regard. (270)

If this is so even when studying the Veda without its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), how much more so when studying it with the auxiliaries? An initial comprehension of the meaning of the Veda should lead to an initial comprehension of the meaning of the auxiliaries. (271)
And some wise men, having attained an initial understanding born from the words of those wishing them well, indeed proceed to engage in investigation. (272)
However, some maintain that because the syllables of the constituent parts are grasped in a form suitable for assisting the limbs [of the body], they possess meaningful knowledge;
yet they consider the state of having a visible purpose to be more concise. (273)

Let it be granted that such is the superficial understanding; however, even apart from that, let knowledge be accomplished through other branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*). To this, the reply begins with the words "But its own nature... and so forth. The sense is that the ascertainment of its distinct nature—differentiated from what was stated regarding the opposing view—is the result here, which cannot be achieved by others. By the phrase "consisting of the investigation of Vedic sentences," the specific form of Mīmāṃsā is distinguished from the other branches of learning. The statement that Mīmāṃsā consists of investigation (*vicāra*) is due to a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the two, or because the word "investigation" is derived in the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*).

The statement that "the Veda has been studied" is intended to show that there is no further remainder of duty (*kṛtya-śeṣa*) regarding the sphere of injunctions (*vidhi-viṣaya*), and it is also intended as a reason based on the fact that [the person] possesses a superficial understanding (*āpāta-dhī-mattva*). The word "person" (*puruṣa*) contains a reason, namely, "because of the desire for a purpose. "By himself" means by his own will, independent of injunctions. For one who, when a subject useful to himself appears even superficially, seeks its definitive determination and proceeds toward the means thereto, an injunction is indeed unnecessary. (274)
That investigation is established as the cause for determining one's own desired object through positive and negative concomitance; for even in that case, an injunction would be fruitless.
Upon seeing treasures, jewels, and the like, those who desire them proceed toward the investigation of their true nature entirely without being prompted by another. (276)
Therefore, neither the investigation nor its sequence is established here by injunction;
