otherwise, the second [investigation] would be justified simply through the perception of defects.

Even if one were to engage [in inquiry] spontaneously, one would still act in order to hear [the scriptures] and rely upon them, so as to eliminate the possibility of independence from a teacher. If one were not to do so, there would be no fault; yet that is not the case—because the very absence of certainty dependent on him, and the absence of engagement in what is beneficial which depends on him, constitutes a fault. It is with this intention that it is also said: "He who, having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, neglects inquiry and forgets his own exertion, shall fall away from his purpose."

[Objection: If inquiry (*vicāra*) were thus not sanctioned by scripture (*avaidha*), how could one engage in *mīmāṃsā* when the opportunity for it is blocked by injunctions such as "having studied, one should bathe" (*adhītya snāyāt*)? For the cessation from residing in the teacher’s house—which consists of suffering—is already established by its own nature; therefore, only the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be the object of the injunction here. [Reply: Not so. For in this context, what is enjoined is precisely the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of bathing accompanied by the specific rules of the *samāvartana* (the return ceremony). Otherwise, since even the immediate sequence following [the study] would be established by its own nature, it too would become non-injunctional.

Furthermore, even if inquiry (*vicāra*) is mandatory, how can there be an occasion for it? If you argue that it is because the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*, we say no; for even in the *śruti*, it is stated: "having studied" (*adhītya*) and "having returned home" (*abhisamāvṛtya*). If you claim that in that case the intention is merely to express a common agent and a prior temporal sequence, and not immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then why should it not be the same in the *smṛti*? Nor can it be restricted that in the *śruti* the word "study" extends up to the comprehension of meaning, while in the *smṛti* it extends only up to the grasping of the syllables.

If it is argued that [the injunction for bathing] would be like the statement "that which has been studied," etc., we say no, because there is a distinction based on contradiction and non-contradiction. Suppose it is granted that both Śruti and Smṛti enjoin study as a means to the knowledge of meaning; if that were so, the injunction for bathing would not obstruct the opportunity for the scripturally mandated inquiry (vicāra). If this is the case, then the injunction for bathing and others, which are prompted by natural inclination (rāga), would likewise not obstruct the opportunity for hearing (śravaṇa), just as the acquisition of materials required for one's own use does not.
Those injunctions for bathing and so forth, desiring performance after having gained knowledge, naturally embrace the very Mīmāṃsā pertaining to their own respective subjects. (278)

Moreover, in this matter, those who do not know the specific measures, the constituent parts, the sequence, or the performer [of the rite] are not even capable of correctly understanding a single rule for ritual bathing. (279)
Out of necessity, one engages in study and the like without prior reflection;
however, since there is an alternative course regarding the ritual bath (snāna), such a course [of action] cannot be considered a lack of alternatives.
And since it is authorized everywhere that one's own limb does not act as an obstruction,
therefore, in this case, the intervention of *mīmāṃsā* does not constitute a contradiction.

Alternatively, there is no contradiction even if the study and the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) follow immediately after one another. If it is argued that there is a contradiction because for those who have not yet investigated the nature of *dharma*, the performance of subsequent rites would be impossible, we say no; for even after the ceremonial bath, as long as the investigation continues, the performance [of rites] is possible—just as it was for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) while he was still under the care of his preceptor. Nor does performing [rites] based on the words of well-wishers contradict the principle regarding the exclusion of *Śūdras* (*apaśūdranaya*), because well-wishers merely incite them toward those duties appropriate to their respective stages, and because prohibitions such as "one should not teach him the *dharma*" are observed.

If it is argued that the study of Mīmāṃsā would be useless since the performance [of rituals] could be accomplished otherwise, we say no; for its utility is established by the desire to investigate the source when doubts about the opposite arise, as well as by faith in the authority of the teacher’s instruction, fame, and so forth. In this very way, the continuity of the tradition from predecessors to successors is secured. If it is argued that someone might, out of laziness, accept only written documents and the like as authoritative in every respect, what of it? For others who are not lazy can still engage in the study of the scriptures.

If it is argued that for one who has completed his bath and is listening [to the Veda], there might be an obstruction to his own duty (*svadharma*) due to activities on behalf of the teacher, we say: no; for those duties are enjoined by the injunction for study and cease once that is accomplished. As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*:

"For this injunction is intended to establish the rules regarding the means of grasping the syllables; the Smṛti declares that the status of religious duties persists until that grasping is complete."

"After the Veda has been studied, the knowledge of its meaning arises spontaneously; however, that [spontaneous knowledge] is neither study itself nor a motivator for the performance of religious duties (*dharma*).

[Objection: For what purpose, then, should the teacher teach Mīmāṃsā? [Reply: Is it for the sake of gain and so forth, or for the sake of *dharma*? For one who is occupied with the duties of a householder, what opportunity is there to listen? And what opportunity does the teacher have to speak? For him who seeks his livelihood, there is the time for acquiring wealth.

If this is argued, then hearing (*śravaṇa*) would also be [permitted], just like other activities for visible purposes authorized by injunctions. Furthermore, even for a householder, there is some time for inquiry when [he engages] with the purpose of the *itihāsas* and so forth. At that time, Mīmāṃsā too would be employed as being conducive to its own goal through those supplements to the Veda (*vedopabṛṃhaṇa*). And they divide the study of the Veda (*vedābhyāsa*) in this way: "First, the acquisition of the Veda; then inquiry, practice, recitation, and the giving of it to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold."

For some, such as those who have inherited wealth through family lineage or obtained wealth by chance, even the time for its acquisition must be awaited; yet, the time for hearing [the scriptures] is required. Furthermore, householders and others who have not yet reflected upon the duties pertaining to their specific caste (*varṇa*) and so forth are seen in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as listeners to those respective duties. Moreover, for the sake of attaining superior knowledge, the residence with a teacher for two months every year has been permitted by some even for a householder.

As it is restated: "When he has settled [in a household], he should live for two months every year in the family of his teacher, concentrated in mind, desiring further hearing of the scriptures"—thus said Śvetaketu, "for by this practice, I studied more than before. Now, one might object: "Is this not contradicted by those scriptures? For when one has settled [in a household], the obligatory duties are prescribed, such as the Agnihotra and hospitality to guests," and so on; thus Āpastamba states his own view. True.

By this [statement] as well, only an uninterrupted residence in the teacher's house for two months is prohibited at that time; however, the opportunity for inquiry—which, like the case of the speaker, leads to the hearer’s success—is not set aside.

Let it be granted that inquiry follows study and that, by natural inclination (*rāgataḥ*), it has the entire [Veda] as its object; nevertheless, since inquiry and its sequence would lack scriptural authority (*avaidhatva*), they would proceed according to one's own whim.
Because of the non-occurrence and the occurrence [of duality], it is said that "attainment occurs therein. || 282 ||

Because investigation cannot be abandoned, because simultaneity is contradictory, and because a fault is seen in deviating from the sequence, this sequence [of the means of knowledge] indeed belongs to the Sūtra. (283)

In this context, "there" refers to either the Veda or the Mīmāṃsā; or the meaning is: when one proceeds according to one's own will. Here, "injunction regarding action" (karmavidhi) means either the impulsion toward optional rites (kāmyakarman) or the performance of such rites; or, since no distinction is made, it includes obligatory rites (nityakarman) and others as well. By the word "essential nature" (svarūpa), it is indicated that the application [of the rites] as auxiliary elements to the higher knowledge (paravidyā) for one who has renounced the fruits was not considered here; for that indeed must be examined in the section on the means (sādhanalakṣaṇa). For, upon its determination, one would understand that [the rites] culminate in an infinite and stable fruit.

Alternatively, the sense is that although the fact that actions performed alone yield results that are meager and unstable has not been examined in certain places; by the phrase "having been determined," the necessity of the determination of action having already occurred is intended. This has been explained in detail in the *Tātparya-tūlikā*: "In this regard, this obligatory action cannot be neglected, for it follows a person in all states of existence."
Whether one desires worldly enjoyment or seeks liberation, whatever person may be taken as a subject,
for all of them there is indeed the undertaking of many actions.
The obligatory daily rites, the occasional rites, and those that are prohibited must always be examined by everyone who desires to avoid the resulting transgression.
Those who do not fear sufferings should not engage in deliberation;
however, it is clear that for others, this much action must be deliberated upon.
Desirable action is capable of providing enjoyment even without Brahman;
however, Brahman does not attain the power for liberation without action.
For it will be stated [in the Sūtras] that "there is a dependence on all [duties], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth";
thus, even reflection upon a single portion of the Veda is declared to be the motivator for the whole.
"Therefore, since it must necessarily be considered, action itself is examined first.

This means that having observed the limited and unstable fruits of actions, one determines—by the very words of the scriptures themselves—their nature with clarity. For, in defining the essential nature of rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnihotra, there would be a classification of the heaviness or lightness of the resulting heavens according to the means employed. Furthermore, once it is established through the statement "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the Agniṣṭoma" that the Jyotiṣṭoma takes the form of the Agniṣṭoma, the determination of the spatial and temporal limitations of the heaven achieved thereby is made by such passages as "as much as one attains by the Agniṣṭoma."

In this regard, even the injunction for repetition is an indicator that the fruit is small for one who does not repeat [the rite]. Furthermore, regarding even the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), a gradation of fruits according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life is recorded in traditional law (*smṛti*) for certain qualified persons, such as in the passage beginning, "The Prājāpatya [fruit] belongs to Brāhmaṇas," and so forth.

For once the nature of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices—the Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, and so forth—is understood, it is seen that the Vaiśvadeva and others yield limited results, as indicated by such statements as: "This indeed is the measure of the Vaiśvadeva," and "This is the lowest of these; therefore, the subsequent ones become superior. Consequently, regarding the text "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible," the intended meaning is understood to be merely that the results are to be enjoyed for a long time.

Although this state of having inexhaustible fruit could be led as a remote consequence by virtue of being an ancillary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*), nevertheless, because there is no intention to convey that meaning here, it is not so interpreted. Thus, only when the nature of the ritual action—characterized by the *soma* oblation and yielding limited results—is established, is there a restriction [of its fruit] by such Smṛti texts as "We have drunk the *soma*" and "Immortality is a station lasting until the dissolution of all beings."

Furthermore, once the distinction in the nature of the ritual acts that accomplish various fruits such as heaven (*svarga*) and self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) is established, the limited nature of that which is designated by the word "heaven" therein is proven. Moreover, the determination of the gradations of fruit in passages such as "Whatever sacrifice one studies... is based precisely on the ascertainment of the heavy and light natures of the ritual acts. And because the nature of the ritual act—which consists of pleasing the object of worship—is determined to be subject to origination and destruction, there is the perception of the instability of its results, such as union (*sāyujya*) with that [deity].

Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating that the *Śārīraka*—whose object is the inquiry into Brahman from which all obstacles have been removed—is a specific portion of *Mīmāṃsā* distinguished by its unique nature and fruit from other branches of knowledge, and for the sake of establishing the particular subject matter to be determined, the passage beginning with "furthermore, [the study of]... was stated. Here, the term "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) denotes the fruit known primarily through the end of the three Vedas (*trayyanta*); by this, there is an exclusion of the secondary fruits such as the attainment of food and so forth belonging to those of recent times, as well as the fruits of injunctions regarding meditations (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*) formed by other types of connection. It has been established that the immortality mentioned in the ritual section (*karmabhāga*) is merely relative.

However, because no contradiction is observed and because it is supported by certain portions of the Vedānta that have been determined to be consistent with experience, this [work] is not like the former; it is intended to convey that it is for the most part established as such. With this in mind, it is said: "because there is an initial cognition of an infinite and stable fruit. For here, it is not possible to postulate qualities such as being limited or unstable through inferences based on its being a "fruit" and so forth, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Because it is unconditioned (*anavaccheda*), the embodied one (*śārīra*) here is the one whose body is the universe (*sarva-śarīra*); the scripture that has proceeded with reference to him is the *Śārīraka*.

For he will state in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*: "That very [Self] is the unconditioned embodied Self (*śārīra ātmā*); for this reason, the scripture which proceeds having taken that Supreme Brahman as its subject is designated by the learned as *Śārīraka*. It is the *Mīmāṃsā* of that [scripture], hence *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*; [the word *tasyām* means] "in that [work]. The meaning is: it "pertains to" (*adhikaroti*) [Brahman] because one becomes intent upon it with the thought that it is one's own object, and not because it pertains to some other preceding matter.
The sense is that once the immediate succession to the inquiry into Brahman is established by reasoning, the immediate succession to the scripture whose subject is that [inquiry] is also established.

The fact that [the Veda] is apprehended, that it is a fruit [of knowledge], that it possesses meaning, and that its investigation is undertaken out of passion—all these are unprecedented points asserted here regarding the scripture. (284)

And thus the Vedānta texts demonstrate that the fruit of mere ritual action is perishable, whereas the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is imperishable: "As here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes; for that becomes for him only finite. Indeed, the impermanent cannot attain the permanent. For these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts. Having examined the worlds acquired by action, let the Brāhmaṇa arrive at detachment, realizing: 'There is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created.'"

To gain knowledge of that, one should approach a teacher alone—who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman—with fuel in hand. To him who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint, that wise teacher shall declare in truth that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the Imperishable, the True Person.

The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; he does not see death again. He sees that One; as a seer, he does not see death. He becomes his own light. Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going. [One should perceive] the Self as distinct...

"And considering him the impeller, being favored by Him, he thereafter attains immortality," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of the meagerness of the fruits of action and the like, only an indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been seen; however, for the sake of strengthening a conviction that contradicts what is heard [in scripture], the actual attainment must also be stated. Furthermore, the definition of the nature of action here is intended to remove obstacles to spontaneous engagement. As for the reason, it is simply the immediate perception of infinite and stable fruits; from where does this arise? To this he says: "In that manner" (*tathā*). The meaning is: "so that this Sūtra may also have that same purpose. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Here, the mention of "woundedness" (*kṣati*) and "perishability" (*akṣayi-tva*) is indicative of smallness and so forth. The citation of the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as) serves to increase faith regarding another matter that is not explicitly stated, by means of a confirmed analogy. "Loka" means that which is to be seen (*lokya*), i.e., that which is to be experienced. If it were taken in the sense of a place, there would be no syntactical connection with the terms "here" (*iha*) and "there" (*amutra*). "Accumulated by action" (*karmacitaḥ*) means obtained through worldly actions.

By the non-specific statement "the accumulation of merit," [the author] says "it is finite" (antavat) in order to dispel the delusion that even that which is accomplished through the dharma of cessation is subject to decay. Since this is consistent with the meaning of the previously cited passages, and because the finitude of the nature of the action itself is not what is intended to be stated here, the statement regarding its finitude is made by way of its fruit.

This is because of the preceding statement: "O Gārgī, he who, without knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years [is miserable]," and because of the subsequent statement: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable. Once it is established that the term "finite" (*antavat*) refers to ritual action devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, it is easy to understand that its reference applies to the phrase "those who have accumulated merit" (*puṇyacitaḥ*) and those that follow.

Just as there is a difference in fruits—such as heaven or self-sovereignty—in ritual acts devoid of knowledge, so too there might be a possibility of a difference in fruits for certain obligatory rites; furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for all desires," one might think that the cited passage refers only to the majority of cases. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). The meaning is: by those [acts] enjoined as means to unstable fruits (*adhruvaiḥ*). Through the connection with the phrase "That is stable" (*dhruvaṃ tat*), the absence of the status of having a permanent fruit (*nityaphala*) is pervasively established.

He confirms the absence of the attainment of a certain fruit for those who possess the rule of returning, because it is impossible for them to uproot all karma—[stating] "rafts" and so forth. They are "unstable," meaning they are incapable of leading one to the further shore of darkness (*tamas*). "Those fools who rejoice in this inferior karma, which is said to consist of eighteen [elements], they surely return again to old age and death. For in this regard, there is a flaw in the statement.

Now, the author states a passage that summarizes both the fact that the certainty regarding the absence of eternal fruits as the means of action—consistent with the meaning of the scriptures—is a cause for world-weariness (*nirveda*), and the fact that the knowledge of Brahman has infinite fruit: "Having examined... (*parīkṣya*).

This Śruti has been explained in the *Sāra*: "A Brāhmaṇa—one devoted to the study of the Vedas—having examined with the help of Karma-mīmāṃsā the worlds acquired through action (*karmacitān*) as being perishable by nature because they must eventually decay, and having attained detachment (*nirveda*), thinking, 'The Uncreated (*akṛtaḥ*)—the eternal Supreme Person—is not attained through the created (*kṛtena*)—that is, through ritual action,' he should, for the sake of knowing That, approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—a *śrotriya* who knows the Vedānta and is established in Brahman."

[He is] one who has directly realized the nature of the Supreme Person. And that teacher, for him who had approached him properly, spoke—that is, he declared—that Brahma-vidyā by means of which specific knowledge one may know that Imperishable, the True, the Supreme Person. [This is so] because there would be no syntactic connection in the passage "he should approach the teacher alone; to him that wise man spoke," and because [the verb form used] is not otherwise applicable. Furthermore, the *liṭ* (perfect) tense is prescribed even in the context of an injunction, according to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses may be used]."

In this context, regarding the portion that restates what is established by logic (*nyāya*), the word *brāhmaṇa*—though denoting a caste—is stated as "devoted to the study of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsarataḥ*) in order to indicate that its scope extends to all three castes (*traivarṇika*) through *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), thereby providing for those who have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*), which is useful for the examination of the subject matter at hand. They also etymologize the word *brāhmaṇa* as "one who breathes (*aṇati*) Brahman. The phrase "by virtue of being the object of worship" (*ārādhyakṣayitvena*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the destruction of merit (*sukṛta*). The mention of "by means of the Mīmāṃsā of Action" (*karmamīmāṃsayā*) is a statement implied by the sense.

In accordance with the masculine gender of the word *akṛta* and by the power of the supplementary context (*vākyaśeṣa*), the Supreme Person is shown to be the substantive. Here, because it is impossible to negate the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the uncreated by means of the word "is not," and because [the phrase] would not connect with "by action" (*karmaṇā*), and because the negation of its origination is not required, the meaning is that this is for the sake of a clear understanding of that [nature]. In this context, "having fuel in hand" refers to Brahman.

Some say that [the statement] is for the purpose of hearing the Vidyā, for the sake of the intermediate rite of initiation (*upaneyana*), and for the sake of indicating the meaning [of the term]. For it is said in the *Chāndogya* to Jābāla by Gautama: "A non-Brāhmaṇa does not deserve to speak thus; bring fuel, my dear, and I will initiate you. Others, however, say: initiation was appropriate for Jābāla because he had not been initiated before; in other cases, however, the mention of "having fuel in hand" is intended as an indication of having one's hands not empty.

For it is seen in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā: "They, with fuel in their hands, approached him in the forenoon; having brought them near, even without the formal initiation (upanayana), he spoke this to them. And in the speech of Prajāpati, regarding the single Indra who returns with fuel in his hand for many questions, the phrase "he returned" is repeated. For in that case, a formal initiation (upanayana) is seen neither there nor is it intended. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras will state only this much: "Because of the reference to the purificatory rites (saṃskāra)."

Since one who has merely studied a single branch of the Veda is called a *śrotriya*, and such a person who has only mastered his own portion of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*) does not assist in the present context, the term *śrotriya* here is shown to refer to a *śrotriya* who is "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*), specifically one who knows the Vedānta. He states that the term *brahmaniṣṭha* is intended to signify both the capacity for clear exposition and the highest degree of assistance through unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), by describing him as "one who has directly realized the nature of the Supreme Person" (*sākṣātkṛtaparamapuruṣasvarūpa*).

Because it is stated, "to one whose mind is tranquil" (*praśāntacittāya*), "tranquility" (*śama*) here refers to the cessation of the activity of the external organs. In this context, tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*) are for the sake of attentiveness conducive to hearing (*śravaṇa*). However, in passages such as "therefore, one who knows thus is tranquil and self-controlled," they are for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*) for one who has already understood the meaning through hearing. Regarding the phrase "by which" (*yena*), since a change in gender would be forced, it indicates that the opening statement is general—this is shown by the term "qualifying knowledge" (*vidyāviśeṣaṇa*).

And thus they employ [the following] refutations therein: "Is there the destruction of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), or the destruction of external objects (bāhyārthabhaṅga)," and so forth. With the intention of excluding Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña by means of the two terms *akṣara* (imperishable) and *satya* (real), which negate modification both in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherent character (*svabhāva*), he says: "the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣam*). The qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is used to cast aside speech that is subject to doubt or error, as well as speech that is incomplete.

The traditional authorities (smaranti) declare: "Even a teacher becomes a non-teacher if he neglects the sacred learning. To dispel any doubt regarding the meaning of the conduct (*vṛtta*) and its purpose, he says: "he should proclaim" (*prabrūyāt*). It would be cumbersome to follow a reversal of the word order by overriding the injunction perceived from the opening phrase "he should approach" (*abhigacchet*); therefore, with the intention that there is no syntactic connection for the word "he spoke" (*provāca*) as a statement of past fact, he says: "He [should go] to the teacher alone" (*sa gurum eva*). The restrictive nature (*niyamavidhitva*) of the rule is indicated by the emphatic particle "alone" (*eva*). As for the word "he spoke": [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly here.]

He states another reason for its being a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) with the words "because it is not [otherwise] obtained" (*aprāptatvāt*). Although someone might engage [in this practice] out of passion due to a desire for gain and so forth, nevertheless, this is enjoined for the sake of dharma in the case of a teacher who is independent of such motives regarding a worthy disciple; thus there is no contradiction. He also states that the *liṭ* (perfect tense) specifically teaches the sense of the *liṅ* (optative/injunctive) with the words "even in the case of an injunction" (*vidhāv api*).

Intending to show that the knowledge of Brahman leads to the attainment of the eternal, unsurpassed bliss that is the subject of the context—by virtue of its capacity to bring about the realization of Brahman indicated by the word "para" (the Supreme)—he says: "brahmavid" (the knower of Brahman). To dispel the suspicion that even one who has attained Brahman might return again to these worlds—as suggested by the logic of [attaining] heaven and so forth, or by such passages as "these worlds"—he says: "na punaḥ" (not again). Here, "mṛtyu" (death) refers to dying; or it may refer to what was stated in such passages as "Death is considered by the seers to be delusion."

The sense is that when evils are destroyed without remainder, nothing undesirable—characterized by death—shall remain, and following the ways of the world would be a matter of one's own choice. In this context, "the vision of That alone" is either the means or the fruit. This is because the statement, "There is no consciousness after departing," occurs within the section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).

By means of the words of the Elder (*sthavākya*), [the text] dispels the suspicion that knowledge might be lost for one who is liberated, and it clarifies the cessation of death and its effects with the words "he does not see" (*na paśyati*). Even though the liberated one may perceive the suffering of others at that time or his own past suffering, those two do not constitute a source of aversion toward him, because they lack the qualities of being dependent upon him and being present. For this is indeed observed even during the state of bondage. However, in that state, the experience of suffering due to the suffering of others and the grieving for what has passed are caused solely by the limiting adjunct of *karman*.

By the statement, "The seer sees neither disease nor suffering; he sees everything," and so forth, it is established by way of distinction that even when things are being seen, there is no perception of anything adverse to oneself. Here, the term "seer" (*paśya*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) who perceives Brahman, as is clear from the context of the passage, "He sees that One. Furthermore, the term can also apply to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) through the etymological derivation of "seeing" (*paśyati*), as evidenced by such usages as "the Seer sees the one who sees. Since everything is seen as having Brahman as its essence, there is no contradiction between seeing that One and seeing all things.

It is not merely a state of effortless omniscience; rather, other kings possess worlds subject to decay, rooted in the karma prescribed by tradition. With the intent that there should be freedom from dependence on another and the capacity for independent action through the cessation of such dependence, he says: "He is self-ruling" (*sa svarāṭ*). For this very reason, even while remaining under the sovereignty of the Lord, the statement of the lexicographers—that he is "self-ruling" (*svarāṭ*) and "independent" (*svatantra*)—is not contradicted.

By means of the scriptural texts that negate other means for attaining immortality (*amṛtatva*), he confirms that the statement regarding immortality being achieved through ritual action (*karman*) has another purpose—namely, "Him alone" (*tameva*). Furthermore, since this refers to the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) as qualified by His attributes and manifestations (*guṇavibhūti*), the position of the opponents—that liberation occurs for the individual soul (*jīva*) alone through the cognition of its own undifferentiated nature or through the cognition of it as distinct from the Supreme Person—is refuted. He states "separately" (*pṛthak*) to show that the idea that the cognitions of identity or difference are the causes of immortality has been rejected by the Scripture itself.

The meaning is: "from that," namely from the meditation on distinctness which consists of worship. "Favored by him" means made an object of affection by the Impeller. By this, it is stated that the stable grace of the Supreme is itself the gateway to the fruit. For it is also heard in scripture: "By the grace of the Creator. Now, one might object: since here the meditation on both "the Self" and "the Impeller" is taught in conjunction, it appears that knowledge of something other [than the Self] is also a cause of liberation. True; however, that does not diminish the primacy of the Impeller.

In passages such as, "A certain wise man beheld the inner Self, with his eyes turned away, desiring immortality," the reference is also to the vision of the individual soul (jīva) as a constituent part of the higher knowledge (paravidyā). The word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to reinforce what has been stated by other scriptural passages as well, according to the maxim that "that which is supported by a greater number [of authorities] is stronger."

But surely, from the mere study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), it is already known that ritual actions have results such as heaven, that heaven and the like are perishable, and that the meditation on Brahman has immortality as its fruit. Consequently, one who desires liberation should proceed directly to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). What is the need for a prior inquiry into Dharma? If this were so, then one would not even proceed to the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (the inquiry into the embodied soul), since everything would be known through the study of the Vedas and their auxiliaries alone. True; yet—

If it is argued that while an initial impression certainly exists, nevertheless, because a sentence aided by logic (*nyāya*) is what determines the meaning, even an initially perceived meaning does not transcend doubt and error; therefore, for the sake of its definitive determination, an inquiry into the Vedānta texts must be undertaken—then please consider that for that very same reason, an inquiry into Dharma must also be undertaken.

Now, how can there be the possibility of ignorance, concealment, the perception of difference, bondage, its cessation, and the means of that cessation, in a Brahman that is non-dual, eternally liberated, devoid of distinctions, and whose very nature is the illumination of itself alone as the adversary of ignorance and the like? Furthermore, since it is a principle that the expiation for a bondage produced by karma must be through a specific karma, the knowledge that effects such cessation would also be accomplished by karma, according to the traditional teaching that "knowledge proceeds from [the performance of] karma."

And how could action, which is by nature a bond, be of any use toward liberation? From what source and of what kind is the impurity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and from what source and of what kind its purity? Furthermore, while action is seen to be a cause for knowledge—which depends on the authority of the means of valid cognition—it is not observed to be a cause even for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is dependent upon an inclination toward the object [of knowledge].

If the duty of renunciation (*nivṛttidharma*) were not a cause of liberation, there would be the undesirable consequence of its scriptural injunctions being useless; thus, uprooting such thorns of doubt, he demonstrates [the solution] by synthesizing both the explicit and the implied intentions, stating: "This... [referring to the following verse].
The condensation of what has been elaborated, and the elaboration of what has been condensed—this is what is meant;
concentration is not for one who is distracted. (294)

By the statement that [ignorance] is "concealing," its positive nature (*bhāvarūpatva*) is indicated; for it is precisely because of this that the possibility of its being the material cause (*upādānatva*) of that which is conditioned by it is established. Since Brahman is slightly veiled by ignorance, the occurrence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and so forth upon it is logically consistent. The term "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*) is used to indicate the similarity to the perception of distinctions such as other persons seen in a dream. In the phrase "the perception of difference alone," the perception of distinctions such as agency, enjoyership, divinity, and humanity—even within the cognition of the identity of the body and the self—is included by implication.

By this, the doubt that "the knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body alone is sufficient; what is the use of the knowledge of Brahman qualified by attributes such as non-agency? is dispelled. Furthermore, action itself does not possess the power to bind, because it is merely a common instrumental cause that brings about what is already perceived [in the form of the body]. Therefore, since action—which is established through the delusion of difference—is itself unreal, and since its binding power functions solely through the medium of that delusion of difference, the intended meaning of the restrictive statement (*avadhāraṇā*) here is that there exists nothing real whatsoever, other than knowledge, that can act as a binder.

Now, [the opponent] objects: "In your view, the establishment of the real from the unreal exists. To this he replies: "And bondage... The point is that doubt regarding whether something is real or unreal arises only when bondage is not sublated; otherwise, it would contradict the eternal liberation of Brahman. To avoid the application of the logic of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), he says: "And that... For the cessation of sin through virtuous action is established only by way of error.

Therefore, with the intention that the entire range from the root cause, ignorance (*avidyā*), up to bondage is to be sublated solely by the non-dual cognition independent of ritual action—according to the analogy of the rope-snake which is independent of the mantra—it is said, "by knowledge alone" (*jñānenaiva*). To the objection that even if there is no combination of ritual action (*karma*) as a means to liberation, it might still arise [as a requirement] due to the authority of Smṛti, he says: "it is the remover" (*nivartakam*). The underlying thought is this: the subject under discussion is produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is a sublatively effective cognition, just like a non-contested [cognition].

Alternatively, the probandum may be "not produced by karma. As for the mention of memory (*smṛti*), that is intended for another purpose. By the force of the reasoning stated by himself, he concludes through elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the cause is the sentence (*vākya*). With the intention that the application of karma mentioned by others is devoid of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-śūnya*), he says: "Of this very [knowledge]," etc. "Of this" refers to that which has non-duality as its object and possesses instruments distinct from karma along with their auxiliaries. "Of this very" refers to that which is itself capable of subverting what is contrary to its own object.

The statement that [knowledge] is produced by the Vedic word (*vākya*) is intended to exclude other causes that possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He explains how it is established that sacrifices and the like have distinct fruits through their distinct application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*), based on the scriptural text, "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), with the words "in the desire to know" (*vividiṣāyām*). The use of the restrictive particle "as it is heard" (*yathāśrutāyām*) is intended to emphasize this point.

In this context, the word "tu" (but) excludes the notion of being an immediate cause. Just as in the expression "he desires to kill with a sword," the figurative sense is established when there is a contradiction [with the literal meaning]. Now, he explains the turbidity of the mind and so forth with the words "And that" (*sa ca*). For *dharma*, other effects such as the cessation of sin have been prescribed. Furthermore, the fact that faith has purity of *sattva* as its effect is established by the scriptures. And the statement that *sattva* is a means to knowledge would be only through a mediated succession. The increase of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are the roots of sin, constitutes the turbidity of the mind. By removing those through *dharma*, the purification of *sattva*—that is, clarity—is attained.
For one whose mind is purified by actions, there arises a favorable inclination toward reality;
consequently, the desire to ascertain that reality would likewise arise from action itself. (295)

Now, the first word "iti" is used in the sense of "because"; the meaning is that this is established in accordance with the natural import of the Śruti along with its supporting texts (upabṛṃhaṇa). "Having intended this"—that is, having accepted it through another Śruti and Smṛti even though it is not explicitly stated in words—meaning that there is a fulfillment of the injunction regarding the duties of renunciation (nivṛtti-dharma) due to such utility. With the intention that there is nothing further to be said regarding the clarification of the means (upāya), he concludes with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).

The meaning is that there is no dependence on either action or reflection upon it for the purpose of either adopting or abandoning [the means], because of knowledge and its reflection. Here is the summary contained within the *Tūlikā*:

"Because of contradiction, because of lack of authority, because of the utility for the purification of the mind, because of the scriptural statement regarding the cause being knowledge alone, and also by implication."
"Because it is traditionally taught that [knowledge] has tranquility (*śama*) and so forth as its constituent parts, there is no combination of knowledge and ritual action.
Knowledge arising from the sentence [of scripture], awakened by the sequence of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, is the liberator.

This is because of contradiction—meaning contradiction both in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and result (*phala*). "Because of the lack of authority" means that there is no evidence for ritual actions being the means to knowledge and its fruit; or alternatively, because they lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "By virtue of capacity" means that knowledge alone is sufficient for the sublation of that which is false. "The combination of knowledge and ritual action" refers to the modes described in the three systems of thought. "Awakened state" (*unnidratva*) refers to fullness through the removal of obstacles.
The Shorter Conclusion (*Laghusiddhānta*).

Here it is said: As for what was stated—that liberation is indeed the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*), and that this occurs solely through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavijñāna*)—that is accepted. However, it must be investigated what the nature of the knowledge intended by the Vedāntic statements for the purpose of removing ignorance is: is it merely the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence arising from the sentence itself, or is it the knowledge consisting of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) which has that [sentence] as its basis?

It cannot be the knowledge produced by the sentence, because that is established by the sentence alone even without an injunction, and because the cessation of ignorance is not observed through that much alone.
Because it is free from contradiction, because it is well-known, and because it is logical, the objection that "a refutation must be stated against this position" is now being addressed. (296)
The Refutation of the Duality of the Probandum and the Means of Proof.

Here, first of all, the refutation of the duality of the probandum and the means of proof is generally accepted through the passage beginning with "that which was stated," etc., for the purpose of shattering the opposing position. Indeed, there remains a disagreement regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation, Brahman, and the knowledge thereof, due to their respective specific modes. For in our own system, what is called the cessation of ignorance is the absolute destruction of that karma which obstructs the natural expansion of consciousness; and this [cessation] is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvāntara*). The aspect of the removal of the obstruction is here declared as the elimination of the undesirable.
The expansion of the intellect is accomplished by itself; for those who possess discernment, this is the attainment of their goal.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Furthermore, since Brahman and its realization possess many forms from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), we do not accept that there is an absence of causality for that realization, nor that it is combined with ritual action (*karman*), nor that it is merely assisted by such action in producing the fruit. With this intention, it was stated: "only from the realization of Brahman" (*brahmavijñānādeva*). If this is accepted, what is to be refuted? To this, he states the disagreement regarding the mode of the knowledge that brings about cessation, beginning with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

"Vidhitsitam"—that which is intended to be enjoined as a means according to our own system (*svamata*), but which is intended to be established [as such] according to the opponent's system (*paramata*). Thus he analyzes what is stated in the *Tantra*: "Of what nature?"—the meaning is: is it as you have stated, independent of ritual action (*karman*), or as we have stated, as an auxiliary to ritual action? "Is to be discerned" (*vivecanīyam*) means that by the rejection of one alternative, it is to be determined as the other remaining alternative. He distinguishes the summarized point: "What? and so forth.

The mention of "from the sentence" (*vākyāt*) is for the purpose of excluding that which is to be enjoined in the form of a memory whose object is the meaning of the sentence. Since cognition of the nature of that [Self] might arise from the sentence due to its connection with the senses, as well as inference based on the son and so forth, the inclusion of the term "meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*) is intended to exclude those. The suffix "-mātra" expresses independence from means such as meditation (*dhyāna*). For another person, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence consists in the realization of the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme; for oneself, however, it is the cognition of the relationship between the mode and the possessor of the mode. Therefore, the statement that [this knowledge] is the root is not contradictory.

The statement that [meditation] consists of *upāsana* (devotional meditation) is intended to exclude mental reflection (*manana*) and other such activities. He refutes the position favored by others with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvad iti*). Let other positions be set aside for the moment; the meaning is simply that this [position] is not tenable at all. Intending to explain the impossibility of the knowledge of the final sentence-meaning as conceived by the opponent, he reveals—indicated by the word "intended to be enjoined" (*vidhitsita*)—the consequence of the futility of injunctions such as "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), which would follow if the knowledge of the sentence-meaning of the first verse, accepted by all, were the means. He does so with the words "Of that" (*tasya*).

The intent is that others have themselves stated that an injunction (*vidhi*) is devoid of function (*nirvyāpāra*) regarding the knowledge produced by words; for it has been said that the knowledge arising from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is dependent on the object (*vastutantra*) and not dependent on the person (*puruṣatantra*), because it is impossible to perform, not perform, or perform otherwise [at will]. "From the sentence" (*vākyāt*) means, that is to say, from a sentence whose primary purport is its own nature (*svarūpapara*). The word "only" (*eva*) indicates independence from an injunction and the impossibility of sublated latent impressions (*bādhyavāsanā*) acting as an obstacle. "Establishment" (*siddheḥ*) means origination (*utpatti*).

In this context, the knowledge produced by the sentence cannot be understood from that very sentence itself, because it does not enter [the cognition] either as a relation (*saṃsarga*) or as something related (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Nor can it be understood through other sentences such as "one should produce wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*), because that which is already established (*siddha*) cannot be an object of injunction (*avidheya*). Furthermore, its being understood as a means (*sādhana*) is unnecessary, since it is not admitted to have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because its status as a means is understood through its inherent capacity once any imagined obstacles are removed. Therefore, the intention is that the injunction would be redundant.
If it is argued that there is no redundancy because the nature of the injunction follows from the [contextual] injunction;

Nevertheless, the futility of such scriptural tradition is difficult to avoid. The statement regarding the uselessness of injunctions also implies the futility of those scriptures which advocate for the necessity of performing rituals such as the *āghāra* and *praṇayana*, as well as those which teach about exiting through the *brahmanāḍī* and traveling by the path of the gods (*devayāna*).
This constitutes a refutation of the view that knowledge produced by sentences is the means to liberation.

Here he also states the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) by saying "by that much alone" (*tāvanmātreṇa*). For a cognition that has arisen would not delay in removing ignorance by depending on anything else, such that non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) could serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*). And that [non-perception] is established for both oneself and others through perception and inference. Furthermore, what is contradicted by perception cannot be known through scripture; nor is there a removal of ignorance from mere such consciousness alone, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not established—this is the sense.

In this very context, Āpastamba has stated the contradiction with the scriptures: "The attainment of security once [the truth] is known is contradicted by the scriptures. The meaning is that it is specifically prohibited; for a contradiction between two things of equal strength is not possible here. Furthermore, the contradiction with direct perception has been stated: "If the attainment of security occurs once [the truth] is known, one would not experience suffering even in this world"; by this, the subsequent [state] is explained.

Nor should it be argued that as long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference has not been dispelled, the sentence does not produce the knowledge that removes ignorance; for even when such knowledge has arisen, the non-cessation of the cognition of difference for everyone all at once is not a defect, just as the cognition of two moons does not cease even when the oneness of the moon is known. Furthermore, it cannot be said that what remains unceased fails to lead to bondage because its root has been severed;

for it is impossible for knowledge not to arise when the causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) are present, since we observe the arising of subverting knowledge through authoritative instruction, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, even when contrary impressions persist.

Having restated the two-fold response to the contradictions with scripture and perception, he refutes them with the words "And not... [na ceti]. To the question, "Why is there no arising of knowledge even before [hearing the scripture], just as there is after hearing it when it is endowed with reason?"—it has been stated: "Because of the latent impression of difference" (*bhedavāsanāyām*). The utility of the injunctions lies in the removal of obstructive latent impressions. For instances such as the delusion regarding directions, which do not cease through instruction or inferential signs, are eventually removed once the latent impressions are severed by some means or another; the sense is that it is the same in this case.

The phrase "the remover of ignorance" is stated in order to exclude the knowledge of things that are currently being perceived. By the words "it does not produce," the contradiction with the non-perception of the cessation of ignorance is also resolved.

In this regard, the secret of the non-dual (Advaita) tradition is as follows: initial knowledge does not remove ignorance because it lacks the nature of certainty. However, the cognition born of inquiry removes that portion of ignorance which produces the delusion of the reality of difference in the form of indirect determination (*parokṣādhyavasāya*). Nevertheless, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) accumulated through the beginningless delusion of difference continues to produce such a delusion. That portion of ignorance which serves as its support is removed by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of non-duality.

Even when that [ignorance] has ceased, a certain portion of ignorance remains, supported by the karma whose effects have already begun (*prārabdhakārya*); they call that state "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). That portion also ceases either through the final experience of fruition or through self-realization. With reference to such distinctions among portions of ignorance, it is said: "Indra, by means of his powers of illusion (*māyā*), is perceived in many forms. Intending the cessation of the portions of *māyā* according to the sequence described, the Śruti declares: "And again, at the end, there is the cessation of the entire *māyā*, and the liberated one is liberated. In this regard:

The second part here has been stated as pertaining to ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, even by conceding that only knowledge in its indirect form (*parokṣa-rūpa*) possesses the power to remove [ignorance], he avoids the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) by saying, "even when [knowledge] has arisen. Alternatively, it would be improper for those who know all things, such as Sanaka and others, to be without the arising of direct realization (*anutpanna-sākṣātkāra*) and yet still possess ignorance (*avidyāvat*); for those in whom direct realization has arisen, there could be no status as a teacher and so forth, since the appearance of disciples and the like would be impossible.

For one who possesses only indirect knowledge is not a teacher of the immediate; this is evident from the qualification, "The knowers of reality, who see the truth, shall teach you knowledge. Therefore, in this case—where it is said that the rope has a noose on both ends—the third [type of] ignorance is [implied].

He provides the answer in accordance with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) by saying, "Even though [it has arisen]," and so forth. For one who holds that there is only one ignorance of Brahman and only one individual soul (*jīva*), the objection would be: "If a single ignorance were removed, how could there be the persistence of the delusion of difference—the locus of the term 'individual soul'—or the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation? To indicate the restatement of this objection, the word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is used in accordance with the alternative view of manifestation conditioned by the distinctions of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The phrase "all at once" (*sahasā*) should be construed with "by its removal."

The sense is that, upon the exhaustion of karma whose fruit has already begun and which was seized by a portion of ignorance, there occurs the cessation of the delusion consisting in the perception of all distinctions. This is not a fault—for when ignorance ceases, the delusion must also cease, since it is impossible for an effect to exist without its cause.

Therefore, because delusion persists through the view of passion and so forth, ignorance (*avidyā*) has not ceased; thus, there would be no contingency of knowledge lacking the power to remove [ignorance], since even that which has been sublated can continue to persist—this is the intended meaning. He makes his own position clear by means of a worldly illustration: "The moon," etc. It should be understood that this refers to one who possesses the support of a finger-pointing and so forth, even after the oneness of the moon has been known from a verbal statement.

This illustration is easily understood when following the theory of *anvāruhyavāda* (provisional acceptance). In other cases, however, the perceptual nature of the sublating cognition (*nivartakajñāna*) must be understood by taking it in its primary sense; for once the delusion of two moons has been sublated by perception, its recurrence is impossible. Or rather: "When a delusion has been sublated by perception due to a prior supporting condition, its recurrence is not seen again due to another supporting condition, such as the pressing of a finger. (298)
The error produced by ignorance is sublated by verbal and perceptual cognitions;
however, its continued recurrence is logical due to the persistence of residual mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (299)

[Objection: Is it not the case that even prior to the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), the very cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*) is the root of bondage? And even after [that vision], if that [cognition] persists, then because passion (*rāga*) and so forth persist, bondage would not cease; for an effect does not proceed toward its own function once its cause has ceased. Furthermore, you yourself admit the persistence of a remnant of ignorance (*avidyā*). To this he says: "not ceased" (*anivṛttam*). The word "even" (*api*) indicates a contradiction. [Reply: Due to the cutting of the root, it would perish gradually according to the analogy of a severed creeper, and would not sprout again.

The statement that [the cognition] has its root severed is made with the intention that discriminative cognition—stained by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the reality of its own objects—is the cause of passion and so forth, because such is the case with images of women and the like. The maxim of the "whirling firebrand" or the "burnt cloth" is intended here. He first refutes the claim that [the cognition] does not produce knowledge, stating: "Even when... The word *sāmagrī* (causal complex) is used with the intention that a sentence whose words are well-formed must be accompanied by the consideration of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, while being devoid of any other required factors.

The sense is that otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, according to the principle that "even a non-obstruction constitutes a causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) itself—being of the nature of the absence of the cause that consists in its own cessation—would constitute a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalya*). Or rather, it might act as an obstructer by depriving even a complete causal complex of its power.

"Even when [the object] is present," he says. The meaning is this: if the contradictory latent impression (*viparīta-vāsanā*) alone were the obstruction or the obstructing factor, then in a delusion such as that of a rope-snake where the prior impression has not been discarded, a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-dhī*) would never arise; yet it does arise. Thus, through the method of reductio (*prasaṅga*) and its inversion (*tadviparyaya*), one observes a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*); therefore, the cessation of the contradictory latent impression is not the cause here.

For even when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a snake in a rope persists, a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) arises regarding the object out of sight through the authoritative statement "this is not a snake," as well as through signs such as immobility established by striking it with a staff. Similarly, even when the latent impression of two moons persists, a direct perception of the oneness of the moon occurs once defects such as the obstruction of a finger are removed. Nor should it be argued that the cessation of contrary impressions is required for the arising of immediate intuition (*aparokṣabuddhi*) from a verbal statement.

Otherwise, even though a sentence possesses an undifferentiated capacity for producing a cognition of the imperceptible, it would follow that it still requires [external] dependence. Furthermore, for one who asserts that the cessation of the latent impression of difference occurs through the latent impression of non-difference, there would be a logical circle (*cakraka*): the determination of non-difference depends on the cultivation of that [impression], by which the latent impression of difference ceases, and from that very cessation follows the determination of non-difference. Moreover, the cessation of the latent impression is not required for the determination itself.

If it were not required even for direct realization, there would be no distinction [between the two cases]. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that for one searching for the tenth man, the direct cognition "You are the tenth" arises through instruction—even while the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the absence of the tenth still persists. You have also asserted that these two sentences, "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) and "You are the tenth" (*daśamastvam asi*), are identical in having the immediate Self as their object.

Nor can you maintain that even when there is knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, the cognition of difference persists to some degree due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for since the latent impression—which constitutes the causal complex for the cognition of difference—is itself illusory in nature, it ceases at the very moment that knowledge arises. If that illusory latent impression were not removed even upon the arising of knowledge, then, in the absence of any other means of removal, there would never be an end to this latent impression.

To say that the cognition of duality—which is the effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—has had its root severed yet continues to persist is the talk of a fool. In cases such as the cognition of two moons, even when a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) is present, the false cognition does not cease because the cause of that false cognition—the ultimate defect of ophthalmia or the like—is not destroyed, since it cannot be sublated by cognition. Thus, the non-cessation of the false cognition is not contradictory; however, effects such as fear and so forth do cease, because they are sublated by a powerful means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is the refutation of the "persistence of what has been sublated" (*bādhitānuvṛtti*).

Now, intending to show the impossibility of the persistence of what has been sublated for one who wishes to avoid contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "Even though" (*satyapi*). "In part" (*mātrayā*) means not in its entirety; the sense is that while the determination of the reality of the difference between selves and so forth has ceased, the cognition of difference regarding external objects persists to some small degree. The word "to you" (*bhavate*) contains the reason why [such persistence] is impossible; the sense is that you do not admit anything at all to be real apart from Brahman. He explains the reason: "In the case of difference" (*bhede*).

In this context, the word *sāmagrī* (the causal complex) indicates the fullness of the support provided by the karma already set in motion. [The opponent objects: "How could the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of karma persist once ignorance (*avidyā*) has been destroyed? For when a mirage ceases, its waves and so forth do not continue to exist; therefore, [if ignorance were destroyed], the impossibility of being a teacher and so forth would follow. This is the intended meaning. [The author replies: "But even though falsity (*mithyātva*) is common to all, why is it that among delusions—whether they have a single substratum or different substrata—only some are sublated by something specific? To this, it is said: "By the very arising of knowledge (*jñāna*). [This means that sublation occurs through the power of the specific cognition that removes the particular error.]

The sublating cognition (*bādhakadhī*) is that all things other than Reality are false. The persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is incompatible with the arising of such a cognition. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction because of some internal distinction among the impressions, for their falsity has not been removed. Indeed, once the rope is known [to be a rope], the cognition of anything else—such as a snake—cannot persist. Furthermore, according to you who claim that the sublating cognition arises only when the impression of difference has already been dispelled, how could that impression persist at the time of its arising? If it were to persist, by what would it be sublated? If you say by another cognition; [then the same question applies].

That is not so, because there is no distinction [between them]. If it were argued that [the world] ceases upon the exhaustion of experience (*bhoga*), then it would be real, since it would lack sublation by knowledge (*jñāna*); the same would apply to karma as well. Anticipating the undesirable consequence that liberation would be impossible if latent impressions (*vāsanā*) persisted even after the direct realization of non-duality (*advaita-sākṣātkāra*), he says: "Upon the arising of knowledge. The statement that [the world] is illusory in nature is for the purpose of establishing that it can be removed by knowledge alone.

The sense is this: because there is no other means of cessation, those who fear the consequence of [the world] being real do not accept that it can be sublated by anything other than knowledge; for even when hundreds of cognitions—such as the experience of the final enjoyment imagined by them—arise, they cannot function as a sublater of those [prior cognitions], just like the previous cognitions themselves. The meaning of "of this" is: of that which is difficult to sublate even by powerful knowledge that sublates root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Furthermore, causeless destruction is not accepted anywhere by the followers of the scriptures (*naigamikaiḥ*).

Even if that [cessation of the stream of impressions] were admitted, since the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous cognitions and so forth would be established only through delusion, and because error would thus persist eternally, the continuity of the stream of impressions would remain unavoidable; it is with this in mind that the phrase "not even at any time" was stated. For the cessation of impressions is not the very nature (*svarūpa*) of an existing entity, as it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor is it real if it is distinct [from the entity], for that would result in the collapse of non-duality (*advaita*). If it is argued that even if non-existence (*abhāva*) is real, the non-duality of Being (*sad-advaita*) remains established, we say no.

"If difference were real in some cases, it would follow by no distinction that it must be so elsewhere; likewise, even if other entities were real, there would be no loss of the non-duality of Brahman. With the words "even though not ceased," etc., he rebuts [the opponent] by pointing out his own self-contradiction: "The latent impression (*vāsanā*)," etc. This is called "childishness" with the intention of suggesting: "What else will one who is ignorant of the contradiction in his own statement understand?"

The intended meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "whose root is severed," is ignorance (*avidyā*) intended by the word "root," or is it the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*)? In the first case, it has been stated that when the root-ignorance is severed, the delusion of duality cannot be maintained, because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is equally sublated by that [ignorance], is also sublated. In the second case, how could its effect continue once the latent impression has been eradicated?

If an effect were to arise even in the absence of its cause, then those various effects would occur even without ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like—which are accepted by both our own and other schools—despite being devoid of them. Therefore, this is not a logically sound statement. Regarding the example cited by the opponent for the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), he says "the double moon," explaining that it is inconsistent because its root has not been severed.

The point is this: because the defect of *timira* (ophthalmia) and the like is not sublated even by hundreds of sublating cognitions due to its being real, you yourself have accepted it as having "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*); furthermore, even if [the double moon] were unreal, the cognition of the oneness of the moon could not serve as its sublater, since it does not have that [double moon] as its objective substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, pointing out that—unlike in the aforementioned example where the sublater is successful through the cessation of fear and so forth—it would not be so in your desired case, he refutes [the objection] with the words "by the powerful" (*prabalena*).

The meaning is: "because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition whose own validity has been established. For this very reason, there is here an exclusion of fear and so forth produced by deception (*kuhaka*). In your position, however, since both cognitions—the sublated and the sublator—are known to arise from defects, the result of sublation is not established. The intention is that the result of the sublator is its capacity to serve as the cause for activity aimed at investigating things as they truly are—a capacity which lacks the fruit of trust in either [cognition] due to the persistence of what was previously sublated in worldly experience. The mention of effects such as fear is made in comparison with delusions regarding snakes and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), astonishment and other such states are included.

[This is] the apprehension. Thus, with the intention that [the object] does not produce fear and so forth, it is stated in the *Nyāyatattva* that "knowledge during the stage of the persistence of the sublated is indifferent because it is ineffective. By the word "but" (*tu*), a distinction from what was stated by others is indicated: for here, when the causal complex of destruction is present, there is no existence of the thing to be destroyed; nor can an effect arise in the absence of its cause. [Objection: But even fear and so forth, being momentary like an error, cannot be destroyed by a sublater.

Furthermore, the non-arising of subsequent fear is already established beforehand, just like the non-arising of other delusions; so, how can it be said that the cessation of fear and so forth occurs through sublation (*bādha*)? It is replied: when a sublatant exists, the expression "cessation of fear and so forth" is used with reference to the continued non-arising of further fear due to the deficiency of its causal conditions (*sāmagrīvaikalya*). Moreover, for those who maintain that the arising of knowledge occurs by means of the eradication of the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*), the arising of knowledge will never be established, because of the [persistence of] the latent impression of duality.

Because it has been accumulated since beginningless time, it is immeasurable; and because the cultivation that opposes it is minimal, it is impossible for this [cultivation] to dispel it. Therefore, the knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts is something other than the knowledge consisting in the comprehension of the meaning of sentences, being designated by such terms as "meditation" (dhyāna) and "worship" (upāsana).

And thus say the Śruti texts: "Having understood, one should exercise wisdom"; "Having discerned, one understands"; "Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone"; "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death"; "One should worship the Self alone as the world"; "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "That is to be sought; that is to be desired to be known"—and so forth.

In order to demonstrate the weakness of the position that [liberation occurs] even when [the body] has been born, he states another objection regarding the non-arising of knowledge—a point agreed upon by many commentators—using the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokita) method: ... [text continues] ... [Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.]

"And also" (*api ca*) means: even at some time—meaning even after [the practice of] meditation, just as before it; the sense is that this holds true even after meditating for thousands of millions of *kalpas*. Now, one might object: "Just as those who desire the arising of knowledge through sacrifices and the like expect it by destroying immeasurable impurities accumulated since beginningless time through their limited nature, so too might the arising of knowledge occur through the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) via hearing [the scriptures] and other means. To this, he says: "Of the latent impression of duality" (*bhedavāsanāyāḥ*).

For here the principle that "even if remembered only once [it removes ignorance]" does not apply; because if [ignorance] were removed through an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), it would follow that the object to be removed is real. Nor can it be argued that, as with things removed by mantras, its removal by an unseen potency is possible because of its empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*); for if the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) were established as being removable by an unseen potency in that very same way, the search for a sublating cognition (*bādhakadhī*) would be useless. However, if [the scripture] removes [ignorance] by its very nature, then since there is no evidence for such a diversity of powers, the relative strength or weakness [of different means] must be determined by their frequency and other such factors.

Furthermore, meditation (*bhāvanā*) is not an auxiliary cause for the sentence by its very nature, because—just as with indirect experience—it is not observed to have a positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with direct experience either; nor is it accepted that it acts as an auxiliary through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). If such an acceptance were made, it would follow that the sentence could be disregarded, since meditation itself, acting as an auxiliary to the mind, would suffice to produce direct realization. Therefore, the intention is that in no way whatsoever can a subverting perception arise from the sentence.
[This concludes the discussion on] the fact that the knowledge resulting from what is enjoined is the means to liberation.

With the words "Why? (*kimiti*) and so forth, indicating further refutations of the two previously debated positions that have already been criticized, he first states the remainder of his own view by means of a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*), beginning with "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). [This is done] because the knowledge produced by the sentence possesses qualities such as being an injunction or a negation, [as established] through reasoning and perception.

The meaning is that it is contradictory to itself. "It is indeed something other than the knowledge of the sentence-meaning"—this is the underlying thought: if one were to enjoin the mere understanding of the sentence-meaning as the means [to liberation], a difficult circularity (*cakraka*) would arise regarding its spontaneous engagement. For, without knowing the nature of Brahman and the knowledge thereof, there could be no desire for that knowledge; and for one devoid of such a desire, there can be no engagement with the injunction regarding the means to that end. Furthermore, the realization of Brahman cannot be accomplished without the performance of those means.

[Objection: But surely, let there be engagement [with the scriptures] through the prompting of those who desire one's welfare, just as in the case of the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*). [Reply: Not so; for even those who desire one's welfare must instruct: "Attain the knowledge of Brahman, which is pure consciousness without distinctions. For if such knowledge of Brahman were absent or present, there would be no performance of its means [of attainment]. In our position, however, since Brahman is characterized by many forms, there is no contradiction with worldly experience regarding the engagement for the sake of a superior knowledge—characterized by repetition, continuity, and so forth—that is to be realized at a later time.

If one does not accept the procedures established by worldly consensus, there would be a contradiction with one's own activity and so forth. Furthermore, for you who maintain that there is an eternally perceived, attributeless reality, it is impossible to have a cognition superior to that [worldly] regarding its object—whether through verbal testimony or any other means.

[Objection: But surely, the statement that [knowledge] is intended to be enjoined as a means to liberation is improper, because the words of injunction here are intent upon restating the knowledge produced by the sentence—which is already a human goal—whereas meditation and so forth are enjoined for the sake of that [knowledge]. Nor does everything else follow merely from the impossibility of [the stated] alternative. Furthermore, various types of knowledge are designated by terms such as "recollection" (smṛti) and "vision" (darśana). To this, he says: "And thus... (tathā ca).
