The meaning is as follows: just as another means to liberation—distinct from the knowledge produced by verbal testimony—is enjoined by such injunctions as "it is to be seen," and that [means], although expressed by various terms such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and so forth, is established as being one and the same; the particle *ca* (and) serves either to indicate this through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) or for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Here, the inclusion of so many sentences is intended to clarify that terms such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so on refer to the specific states described by terms like "meditation," and to show that there is no difference in meaning despite differences in prefixes, roots, or the presence or absence of suffixes.

The word "śabda" (scriptural statement) refers to the variety of types of statements already cited. The word "evaṃ" (thus) is used for the sake of establishing their commonality in being intent upon injunction (*vidhi*). The initial mention is made even regarding those not yet cited, for the purpose of applying the same logical principle (*nyāya-saṃcāra*).

Here, because of the unity of meaning with such passages as "one should meditate upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), and because the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—through such statements as "having understood, one discerns" (*anuvidya vijānāti*) and "having discerned, one should form wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*)—is an auxiliary to meditation, the words "having understood" (*anuvidya*) and "having discerned" (*vijñāya*) are restated (*anūdya*), and meditation is enjoined by the phrases "one should form wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) and "one discerns" (*vijānāti*). Furthermore, the statement "it should be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) is also a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Since a person who has studied the Veda with the intent of understanding its meaning sees that it provides knowledge of purposeful matters, he engages in hearing (*śravaṇa*) himself in order to determine that meaning; thus, because hearing is already established, and because reflection (*manana*) serves to stabilize what has been heard, the injunction "it must be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, meditation (*dhyāna*) alone is what is being enjoined. And the author will state later: "Repetition [is required], because of the repeated instruction."

In passages such as "one should exercise wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) and "he understands" (*vijānāti*), no distinctness from the knowledge of the sentence-meaning appears; with this in mind, [the author] says "here," intending the principle that "it is the goat [that is sacrificed], because of the wording of the mantra. This means "in those sentences heard [in the Upaniṣads]. The locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). Here, "having a single purpose" (*aikārthya*) means either having a single aim or having a single object. And that [single purpose] here consists of the general and the particular, by way of the rule regarding different recensional branches (*śākhāntara-naya*).

This is established by logic. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of passages such as "meditate" (*dhyāyatha*); by the second, there is the inclusion of passages such as "it is to be sought to be known" (*vijijñāsitavya*). The statement regarding its being an aid to meditation is for the purpose of establishing the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the restatement (*anuvāda*) and for the purpose of connecting the restated subject with that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). And that [aid] consists in its presenting the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Now, one might object: in this context, in passages such as "having known" (*anuvidya*), let there be an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the case of "with curds" (*dadhnā*) and so forth. For those who know the principles of exegesis hold that when a ritual action accompanied by an accessory is heard, the sentence has that accessory as its primary purport, because enjoining a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) involves greater complexity (*gaurava*), whereas enjoining the action alone is simpler.

[The opponent argues: "Because the scriptural mention of the quality (*guṇa*) would otherwise be purposeless; however, the word denoting the action (*karmapada*) would be meaningful by providing a locus for the enjoined quality, thereby serving as a reference to the act itself. [The author replies: Not so. For if, as in the case of the *homa* (oblation), the act of knowing were already established [as a primary injunction], then the quality could be enjoined by way of restatement (*anūdyā*). To refute the doubt that, in the absence of any other alternative, one must resort to an injunction of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the author says "by way of restatement" (*anūdya*). The underlying point is this: if the suffix *-ktvā* and the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) were to have the same referent, there would be a contradiction regarding their temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*).

And what distinction could there be between one [action] and another? If it were merely the repetition of the same kind, it would suffice simply to say "one should practice knowledge"; furthermore, the difference in prefixes would be fruitless. If, however, they have distinct meanings—as in the case of *vijānāti* ("he discerns") and so forth—then since these refer to objects not previously established, it is logical that they find their rest (*viśrānti*) in meditation (*dhyāna*), which is mentioned later as the subsequent thing to be enjoined. The cognition of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthadhī*), however, being already established, is not an attribute to be enjoined. For that very reason, hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the like are not for its sake; moreover, it is most appropriate to enjoin meditation, which has that [cognition] as its primary object.

Nor can any other form of knowledge be suspected here as being enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). If, however, the sentence "he knows" (*vijānāti*) were to culminate in the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-jñāna*), then in the passage "having known" (*anuvidya*), no other knowledge—whether to be enjoined or merely restated—is observed. Nor can meditation (*dhyāna*) be enjoined as a subordinate quality of that [knowledge], because it has been shown that it cannot possibly serve as a means toward either indirect or direct knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.

Because they occur in the same location, even though they lack a prescriptive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*), the reading of "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*) is placed first in order to manifest its status as a prescription. Since meditation (*dhyāna*) is characterized by the clarity mentioned in the passage beginning with "having perceived" (*nicāyya*), and since it is characterized by the excellence expressed by the object of worship, the two prefixes (*upasarga*) are rendered purposeful. Furthermore, even in the case of two restatements (*anuvāda*), the two prefixes manifest both the repetition and the clarity of that which is being restated.

Regarding the phrase "it is to be sought to be known" (*vijijñāsitavyaḥ*), since the word *vijñāta* (known) is read in place of *nididhyāsitavya* (to be meditated upon), and because it follows immediately after the word *anveṣaṇa* (searching), which is the object of *manana* (reflection) occurring after *śravaṇa* (hearing), this [term] takes the place of *nididhyāsana*. To the question, "Why should general words such as 'knowledge' (*vijñāna*) and 'feeling' (*vedanā*), which refer to the means and the object, not find their rest in that specific knowledge consisting of *śravaṇa* denoted by the suffix *-tavya*? he says: "It is to be heard" (*śrotavya*).

Regarding the question, "How is there here a sublation of the suffix *tavya* by the absence of a cause?", he says: "Of the private recitation (*svādhyāya*). The underlying intention is as follows: the doubt that Mīmāṃsā need not be commenced—whether because the Śruti lacks a focus on meaning, or because there is no impetus for inquiry, or because there is no occasion for it—is thereby dispelled. Furthermore, the verbal power of the word "is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) does not reside in approaching the teacher and so forth; therefore, if it were intended to refer to an activity aimed at reaching a definitive conclusion, its meaning would already be established (*prāptārthatva*).

Is there not, indeed, a further duty consisting of reflection (*manana*) in the form of the repeated cultivation of what has been commenced? And it would be appropriate to intend that very thing by the injunction "it must be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*), so that there might be a final rest in knowledge (*vedana*) and the other stages. To this he replies with the words "in hearing" (*śravaṇe*). Since hearing that is not firmly established does not assist meditation (*dhyāna*), the logical reflection (*manana*)—which is recited immediately after it and is required as its support—is [already] obtained through the persistence of passion and other defects; therefore, the sense is that even this is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*).

By this, the contradiction with reason regarding the claim made by some—that the triad beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*) is enjoined as a means to realization (*darśana*)—has been demonstrated. Now, one might object: let it be that by the two [injunctions] "he is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) and "he is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*), only the hearing of the meaning accessible through the teacher's instruction is what is enjoined; for some have said that it is the hearing of the instructions of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and so forth. To this he replies: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*)—meaning, by the exclusion of what is already established or what is not yet established, or by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). The particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude hearing and reflection, as well as mere knowledge, and the desire denoted by the suffix *-san*.

Or, the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) may be intended to exclude the view that it constitutes a separate injunction, because it functions as a qualification of meditation (*dhyāna*). This is the underlying point: since it is possible for the two [injunctions] "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) to provide assistance through well-known non-scriptural means, it is improper to assume the opposite. Furthermore, if "it is to be heard" and so forth were intended to enjoin the fourfold process of hearing and the rest, this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Moreover, in this context, an option (*vikalpa*) is absolutely impossible, as it is tainted by eight defects and concerns matters where there is a disparity between what is heavy and what is light; thus, the assistance must occur in a sequential order.

Because there is no possibility of a combination [of means] with hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which constitute the constituent parts of the principal element, namely *samādhi*; because there is no other way to account for the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*); because the nature of meditation (*dhyāna*) as being of the form of seeing (*darśana*) will be established in accordance with another scriptural passage (*śruti*); and precisely because the root *dhyai*, even when preceded by the prefix *ni*, is indifferent to the expression here of its distinction from seeing—which is explicitly conveyed by other words—therefore, even though the term "is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) occurs in coordination with a restatement (*anuvāda*), one must abandon its natural inclination toward being a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).

Since it is untenable to assume that [the text] is merely intent on restating the result (*phalānuvāda*), and because even in the verse beginning with "It is to be heard from the Vedic texts" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyaḥ*) there is no contradiction in the fact that the triad of hearing and so forth is stated only as the cause for vision (*darśana*) in its proper sequence—even if the goal itself were to be enjoined—it follows that what is enjoined here is meditation (*dhyāna*) characterized by the specific form of vision, which is obtained through other injunctive words following upon hearing and the rest, which are prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*).

Thus, by not accepting that the words "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth rest upon the specific injunctions stated by [the author] himself, he also indicates a contradiction with the Sūtras—introducing the phrase "and he will say. For the root *dhyai* has the sense of "thinking" and denotes a cognition that is repeatedly applied to a single object. Therefore, since "feeling" (*vedana*) taught in the context of meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed meditation itself, the point at hand is established. Likewise, "meditation" (*upāsti*) is also included therein by such passages as "that which is within it is to be meditated upon.
Consequently, the teaching and so forth, which are consistent with the dependence on sacrifices and other rites, are subsumed by this very term.

It is understood that this "knowing" (vedana), which is intended as a means to liberation, is in fact "meditation" (upāsana); for we observe an interchange between the roots *vid* (to know) and *upās* (to meditate) in the opening and concluding passages. For instance, regarding the instruction "One should meditate [upon] the mind as Brahman," it is said: "He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of Brahman. Conversely, [the text says]: "He does not know; for this Self is incomplete; one should meditate [upon it] as 'This indeed'."

"He who knows what he knows—him I have instructed thus. To this [the disciple replied], "Venerable sir, please instruct me further regarding that deity whom you worship. And meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted stream of memory, like a continuous flow of oil; it is "steadfast memory" (*dhruvā smṛtiḥ*). For it is heard in scripture that steadfast memory is the means to liberation: "Upon obtaining memory, there is the loosening of all knots.
Thus, general terms such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so forth find their final rest in the form of worship consisting of steadfast recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*).

He states that the general terms such as "knowledge" (*vedana*) and so forth find their ultimate rest in the specific [practice] called "meditative worship" (*upāsana*), which was previously promised—namely, the word *tat* (that), which refers to what was stated without specifying a particular detail;
and the word *idam* (this), which refers to the specific [practice], because it is enjoined as the means to be accomplished through more weighty practices such as meditation (*dhyāna*).

In the context of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), it is subject to the consequence of becoming identical with that [vision]. He clarifies its cause by stating: "intended as a means to liberation. The sense is that it is understood as "meditation" (*upāsana*) because it is designated by words such as "knowledge" (*vedana*), which have the same object and occur in the same context. Regarding the reason provided in the Sūtra, "because of instruction," he states another specific reason found within the same context: "of the two, *vid* and *upāsi*. In passages such as "the mind," *upāsi* occurs first and *vid* at the end; however, in the passage "he who that," the order is the reverse.

In the passage "He does not know," however, there is meditation on both [the self and the deity], because of the introductory statement: "Now, he who meditates on another deity... he who meditates on each one separately. Thus, here "interchange" (*vyatikara*) refers to the mutual overlapping of positions. An objection is raised: "But here there is an injunction for the contemplative view (*dṛṣṭividhi*) that 'the mind is Brahman'; moreover, the two other sentences belong to distinct specific meditations (*vidyāviśeṣa*). How can the verbal function established in one place apply elsewhere? Anticipating this, the commentary says "because it is seen even in similar cases" (*tattulye'pi darśanāt*). 300.

The phrase "he who knows thus" does not merely state the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture; for it would be improper to state the fruit of something not enjoined by way of restating another thing that is not enjoined, without first specifying the desired fruit of what has been enjoined. [Objection: But at the beginning of the Bhūma-vidyā, a specific fruit was stated: "He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—so far as the mind reaches, there he has freedom of movement according to his desire. By that alone, the requirement for further specification should be satisfied.

Not so—because this [passage] belongs to the third chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) and thus falls within a different context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), and because a repeated scriptural statement would otherwise be purposeless; furthermore, since it is established that there is another thing to be enjoined, its connection with the result is appropriately understood through the very result mentioned in proximity. Therefore, in this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is logical to restate meditative worship by means of the verb *vid* (to know) and then enjoin its fruit. The principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice is intended here. Fame (*kīrti*) is renown produced by acts such as giving; glory (*yaśas*), however, is produced by valor and the like. He shines with both fame and glory.

It should be construed as "he shines with the splendor of Brahman" (*brahmavarcasena*). In this middle sentence, the word "here" (*atra*) is not mentioned because it is so close [to the context]. Regarding the passage beginning with "He who that... (*yastat*), the meaning is: "He who knows that Brahman, and he who knows that which is Brahman—that knower is Raikva, and this Brahman is the object to be known (*vedya*); thus, both have been stated by you. The omission of the word "and" (*ca*) is as in the case of "the cow, the horse, the person, the world," and so on. Because of its association with a neuter noun, the word "stated" (*uktam*) must be modified [to agree in gender]; or else, it may be understood as "he was spoken of as the knower in relation to the object to be known."

Alternatively, the connection with the preceding passage is as follows: "Whatever that Raikva knows, another who knows that same thing—whatever good deeds people perform—all that converges upon him. In the phrase "he was told this by me," the word *etad* (this) is an adverbial modifier of the action; the meaning is, "he was told by me in this manner. According to this interpretation, because it accords with the context, it is indicated that Jānaśruti must have been a disciple of Raikva. *Anuśādhi* means "instruct clearly," that is to say, "make it known through detailed explanation."

Thus, it has been stated that the act of knowing (vedana) is denoted by the term "meditation-practice" (dhyānopāsana); however, it is not here being asserted that meditation itself is practice. This is understood from the statement, "The roots *vid* and *upās* [are synonymous]," and because it will be shown later that "knowing would be practice. Here, the fact that the words "meditation" (dhyāna) and "practice" (upāsana) refer to the same object, as well as the exclusion of meditation from its opposite (pratikūladhyāna), are established by the very context.

If meditation were here specified by the word as being of the nature of worship (*upāsana*), then the continuity of the sequence would be broken upon the subsequent mention of another form of that meditation.

Now, one might object that the word *dhyāna* (meditation) denotes mere reflection and could thus apply even to a succession of memories separated by intervals, or that it is sometimes used for memory alone; furthermore, since the Sūtra repeatedly uses the terms *dhyāna* and *upāsana* (worship), it might be thought to refer merely to repeated practice. To address this, he states the specific scriptural meaning intended there—namely, that it consists in uninterrupted continuity—with the words "And meditation... (*dhyānaṃ ca*). Furthermore, to dispel the doubt that steadiness might be understood either through the analogy of the lifelong Agnihotra sacrifice or simply as lasting for a long duration in its own nature, he employs the term "succession" (*santāna*) along with an illustrative example.

Thus, it has been stated that the distinction of *dhyāna*—which is common to both interrupted and uninterrupted perception—rests upon its specific nature; or rather, its exclusively uninterrupted character has been established. He will set forth this point in its proper place in the Sūtra: "And from *dhyāna*, [there is] immovability, with reference to [the former]. The underlying principle (*tūlikā*) here is that just as the word *upāsana* (meditation) has uninterrupted perception as its object, so too the word *dhyāna* is established here as having uninterrupted perception as its object. He demonstrates what has been stated by means of scripture: "Steadfast," etc.

The "steadfastness of mindfulness" (*smṛti-dhrauvyam*) consists in a flow that is uninterrupted by dissimilar cognitions; for it has been stated thus: "And there is a single continuity regarding the cognition of that form, which is indifferent to anything else," and so forth. Although it will be stated later that the unity of knowledge does not follow merely from the unity of connection with the fruit—as in the case [of the passage] beginning, "Even though they are manifold due to the difference of sound and so on"—and although specific features such as being meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and steadfastness are mentioned in other [sections on] knowledge;

Nevertheless, since common terms such as "feeling" (*vedanā*) lack a specific referent, and since the fruit is devoid of gradation, there would be the difficulty of prescribing a distinction between heavy and light means. Furthermore, the inherent capacity of a thing (*vastusāmarthya*), characterized by the impossibility of heavy and light alternatives, is more powerful than the context; therefore, the permanence of the Smṛti is established. With the intention that what is heard in one place is to be applied to all meditations (*vidyā*), [the text mentions] its being heard as the means to liberation (*apavarga*).

Thus it has been said. "Upon attaining *smṛti*"—the meaning is: when the aforementioned constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is accomplished through the sequence beginning with purity of diet and so forth. "Knots" (*granthayaḥ*) are those by which the field-knower (*kṣetrī*) is bound—namely, dharma, adharma, attachment, aversion, delusion, and so on, as well as the various transformations of the three *guṇas* brought about by karma. And these are declared in the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) to be the knots of the noose of *māyā*. "Complete liberation" (*vipramokṣaḥ*) means being released from them through total and final separation. Now, one might object: since bondage is universally accepted as resulting from error (*bhrānti*), how can memory (*smṛti*), which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramā*), serve as its sublater?

Since that which is produced by action dependent on delusion cannot itself be established as an object of delusion; and because bondage—even if arising from error—is real, like fever caused by the fear of poison, this method of counteraction is appropriate. Even under the view that it is false, the principle of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth is not to be discarded. Therefore, disregarding whether the object to be removed is real or false, or whether the remover is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not, one must accept its capacity to produce its own result because it has been enjoined.

And you yourself have stated that the memory in the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) is the destroyer of the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*). Therefore, in this case, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of bondage as in the case of "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"; rather, its destruction occurs through memory or valid cognition (*pramiti*) according to the prescribed method. Nor is this memory invalid or non-conformable to reality (*ayathārtha*), because its object is not other than the object of the valid cognition that is its own cause. And it has been stated generally in the *Śrīmad-Gītā-Bhāṣya*: "Memory is a cognition produced solely from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience, having as its object an entity previously experienced. This [memory] does not lack the quality of having a previously experienced object.

[The cognition] has entered into its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇapraviṣṭa*); however, this is for the purpose of making known the specific cause-cognition regarding whether the object is real or unreal.
When that state has ceased, its reality as such [a past state] must not be rejected in memory, because of the sequence of cognitions regarding what was past and what will be. (301)

And when there is a lapse of memory, the object's state as it was does not appear; how then could there be non-correspondence with reality (*ayāthārthya*) in that case, which is devoid of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*)? (302)
Therefore, following the root [cause], let it be accepted according to what is observed:
that memory, like direct experience, may be both true to the object and not true to the object. (303)
Likewise, a view held elsewhere is considered to be the cause of the destruction of poison and so forth;
for even among the higher sciences (paravidyā), this [view] is sometimes adopted in certain respects. (304)
Therefore, this supreme knowledge, enjoined by hundreds of Śrutis and Smṛtis, is being expounded in the form of a Smṛti; it is the atonement for the cycle of worldly existence.
And that memory has a form identical to direct perception;
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when That, which is both high and low, is seen."

This is because they share this same purpose. This being so, by the statement "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," the state of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) having a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*) is enjoined. And through the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), recollection (*smṛti*) indeed takes on the nature of perception;
that is, recollection possesses a form identical to direct perception.

[Objection: Is it not the case that [the statement] "meditation alone," etc., is incorrect? For even that [meditation] is said to be for the sake of *samādhi*, just like *dhāraṇā*. It is *samādhi* itself, consisting of vision, which is stated to be the cause of liberation by such [scriptural passages] as "one should see the Self. Furthermore, the perception of a yogin is not unaccepted, since it will be discussed in many places. To this, he says: "And that... The meaning is that it is qualified by the attribute of "steadiness" (*dhruvatva*). The particle *ca* (and) is used for the sake of clarity to indicate that it is also qualified by another form according to the method suggested by the Sūtra; or, it has the sense of *eva* (only/itself).

For that very *smṛti* (remembrance), due to its excellence in clarity, is designated as "samādhi"; it is not some other fruit of meditation such as "vision" (*darśana*) that is to be enjoined in passages like "he would see," and so forth. The statement regarding their similarity is intended to dispel the contradiction between *smṛti* and "vision. The sense is that even though [the object] is remote (*parokṣa*), there is a figurative usage of "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*).
Remembrance is of two kinds: remote and immediate, according to its own source.
It may be entirely remote, or both [kinds] here possess immediacy. (306)
In the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of another word is accepted when there is no other way [to understand it];
for in the case of names such as *Śyena* used for the *Darśa* and other sacrifices, a figurative (*gauṇī*) indication is indeed desired. (307)
And in the Vedic scripture, "One should measure half inside and half outside the altar," the middle region is thus indicated everywhere according to the specific requirements.
But surely, in this context, stability—not the nature of perception—is presented as the qualifier in one's own statement; for that reason, there is a distinction from meditative absorption (samādhi).

To the objection that [the knot] might be avoided, he says: "it is pierced. Here, the word *granthi* (knot) refers to objects distinct from the karma and other factors already mentioned; the knots are attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, which act as obstacles to the proper functioning of the heart, that is, the mind. Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is called *hṛdaya* because it occupies the place denoted by the word *hṛt*; or, by virtue of residing therein, it is indicated by that term. Its "knot" is the aforementioned group of transformations of the three *guṇas*. Or, the "heart" itself is the knot; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

As for that which is explained in the *Chāndogya*: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its etymological derivation (*nirukta*): 'He is in the heart' (*hṛdi ayam*); therefore, day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world. That [passage] refers to the Brahman that is the object of meditation. One must not, however, be deluded into thinking that the very same [Brahman] is what is denoted here by the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), because of the superimposition of contradictory attributes such as "knots" and "doubts. Here, "all doubts regarding all objects," or "all doubts whatsoever"—the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) in this context also implies "error" (*viparyaya*).

The meaning is that they are cut off because their causes are severed, and thus they do not continue in a stream. "Actions" refers to both binding good deeds (*sukṛta*) and evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*). Since what is intended here is the destruction of those actions that obstruct attainment, there is no mutual dependence between the arising of knowledge and the cessation of action. "High and low" (*parāvara*): "highness" (*paratva*) is the state of surpassing all others; "lowness" (*avaratva*) is due to qualities such as being the younger brother of Indra for the sake of accessibility. Alternatively, it refers to the bodies of high and low beings as described in passages such as "the existent Brahman, the Brahman, the slaves," and so forth.

"Parāvara" means either that which is both high and low, or distinct from the world of highs and lows; or else, he whose lower state is itself supreme through his glory is "parāvara. The underlying intention here is this: in the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), the term "seeing" (*darśana*) does not refer to the vision belonging to the state of liberation, because—like the term "constant remembrance" (*dhruvasmṛti*)—it pertains to the means for loosening the knots of bondage. Nor, even if it pertains to the means, is there a conjunction of "remembrance" and "vision" toward liberation, as in the case of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because of the nature of the dual compound (*dvandva*).

Or rather, because the particle *ca* (and) is not perceived [in the text]. Furthermore, conjunction (*samuccaya*) is not possible here, because Brahman cannot be directly realized through the yoga that has been introduced; even if it were possible, simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is impossible, and there is no regulating factor for a sequence (*krama*). Nor can the prior recollection of the Pole Star (*dhruva-smaraṇa*) and the subsequent yogic perception be conjoined as instruments, because since their purpose is already established by the act of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the assumption of a conjunction is inappropriate.

Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); furthermore, if one were to postulate that constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) is a mediated means [to the goal], there would be the fault of abandoning what is directly stated in scripture (*śrutahāna*) and so forth. Moreover, the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*), which is vision (*darśana*), cannot be taken up in its own form such that it could be enjoined as something to be combined [with other means]. But surely this same [objection] applies even to recollection (*smaraṇa*), the fruit of which is the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

If it is argued that, according to the principle of the "inspection of the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), the injunction to "see" here must have as its object a feasible activity that serves as a means to that [vision], we say no. For if that were the case, there would be the consequence of redundancy between the two terms *draṣṭavya* (to be seen) and *nididhyāsitavya* (to be meditated upon) within a single sentence; because, ultimately, it is the instigation of the mind toward meditation—which is dependent on the person—that must be enjoined as the means to vision, and no other such means is perceived.

[Objection: But surely, since the single means to vision has been stated both generally and specifically by two words, there would be no tautology. [Reply: Alas! If that were so, you are abandoning the doctrine of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and falling into our position; for by both [terms]—"it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) and "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*)"—only one and the same thing is enjoined. In our view, however, there is a distinction: meditation (*dhyāna*) is specified by its clarity. Nor can there be a conjunction of constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) with another kind of meditation that merely resembles the form of vision.

Because no other such [means] is observed, because postulating it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because it would entail the subversion of scriptural statements that declare constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*) to be an independent means;
furthermore, when liberation is the goal to be accomplished, one must not accept an option (*vikalpa*) between direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) and mindfulness that is corrupted by numerous defects.

The definition of the eightfold defect of an option is as follows: [it consists of four defects for each side: the acceptance of the first alternative entails abandoning the second, and vice versa; likewise, the acceptance of the second entails abandoning the first, and vice versa.]

They have stated that there are eight defects in the two types of formal application (prayoga), due to the sublation of conceptual cognition, its performance, the unseen merit (apūrva), and its fruit, by means of the two alternatives (koṭi). (309)

The wise recognize two types of fallacies (*prayoga*) in each of these two cases: [the first] from abandoning the validity [of one's own position] while accepting another, and [the second] from rejecting what has been accepted while including what has been rejected. (310)

In this case, such [sequential causality] is impossible due to the disparity between the heavy and the light; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), for it is observed that causality exists only between things of unequal results. Nor is there here a relationship of primary and secondary means (*dvāra-dvāritā*), as there is no evidence for it. Indeed, unlike the way hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) assist meditation (*dhyāna*), meditation’s assistance to direct perception (*darśana*) is not observed. As for the direct perception born of the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) mentioned by others, that will be refuted in the *Śāstrayonitva* section. Furthermore, it is not stated here [in the scripture], since no such sequence or the like is mentioned.

If it is argued that there exists such a passage as, "Then, meditating upon Him, one sees Him partless; through the practice of churning with meditation, one may see the God as if hidden," we reply: True, but this vision is the fruit of meditation; let it be another supernatural power (siddhi) like atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, and not the means [to liberation], for it is not stated as such.

In the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), the mention of that [vision] in certain places is for the purpose of demonstrating its respective power, as in the passages: "He, free from sorrow, beholds that purpose" and "He sees the Person dwelling in the city. Let such vision, described as being accomplished through meditation (*dhyāna*), belong to the liberated one (*mukta*). If, however, this vision described as being accomplished through meditation belongs to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), it must be of the nature of a vivid meditation. For instance, since the word "vision" (*darśana*)—which is not applied to auditory knowledge and the like—is primarily used for visual perception, it follows that here too it refers to a clear mental visualization.

But that [seeing] is not grasped by the eye nor even by speech; rather, it has been rejected here by such statements as "but by the purified mind" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8). Therefore, one must say that the term "seeing" is used figuratively for a specific kind of knowledge produced by the mind. This being the case, it is better to maintain that the figurative use of the term applies to the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmaraṇa*) itself—which is explicitly stated to be the means to liberation—intended to express its possession of such clarity.

One might object that the word "darśana" (vision/perception) qualifies memory by characterizing it as having the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). This is not so, because such a qualification is impossible in the case of memory; for even among those who imagine it possible based on differences in the original source, it is not established in the case of memory—which is accomplished through indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*). Furthermore, the statement that "samādhi is produced by meditation (*dhyāna*)"—meaning that samādhi is accomplished by the mind through meditation—is due to the distinction between the clear and the unclear.

And it has been stated by those who maintain that for that very [concentration], two states exist—one being a limb of yoga and the other being the principal—regarding concentration: "Let it be so that the two statements concerning memory (*smṛti*) and seeing (*darśana*) have a single meaning here; nevertheless, let 'seeing' be figuratively designated by the word 'memory'. To this we reply: no, because the reversal [of the meanings] has been established precisely on the grounds of whether the primary sense is sublated or not. Furthermore, memory would be praised by being described as clarity, whereas seeing, by being called memory, would be deprecated.

Furthermore, in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), one says "it shows the further shore of darkness" with the intention of expressing clarity (*vaiśadya*). In common worldly usage, we speak of one who "sees the further shore" or "sees from afar," and so on. Now, how can there be a sublation (*bādha*) by indirect memory (*smṛti*) of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is directly perceived, even though that memory is similar to perception? Not at all; for its falsity (*mithyātva*) is not established. This is true even for that which is directly perceived.

The sublation of such things as the oneness of the flame, the nature of the body as the self, and the duality of the moon by means of inference and other proofs has been observed and is accepted by everyone. Therefore, because clarity is attained for the memory concerning the means to liberation through the phrase "it being seen in that," such [memory] itself is samādhi; thus, there is no contingency of violating the eighth [limb].

Nevertheless, in response to the objection that—just as in passages such as "it is to be seen," hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), though implied by the power of meditation (*dhyāna*), are for the sake of meditation, yet by the logic of "the principal [is included] in the secondary" (*agryaprāya-nyāya*), meditation itself might also be understood as being for the sake of seeing, and thus the word "seeing" (*darśana*) would not refer to that [meditation]—the author clarifies what is intended by the phrase "meditation alone" with the words "And this being so. The meaning is: since it is established by another scriptural text (*śruti*) that *nididhyāsana* is qualified not only by its identity with constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*), but also by its similarity to seeing (*darśana*).

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of removing doubt, or it serves to combine [the present argument] with the reasoning that [the texts] naturally possess the status of injunctions, in accordance with other clear scriptural passages. This is the intended meaning: if meditation (*dhyāna*) were not something to be enjoined—just like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—it would have to be assumed that the realization of the vision [of Brahman] is accomplished solely through sacrifices and the like by means of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). In that case, meditation in the interim would be fruitless, because there would be no such visible assistance [to the sacrifice], since a perception produced by the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) is impossible.

If, however, [the suffix] denotes that which is to be performed (*vidheya*), then by the maxim that "once the meaning of a scripture has been determined in one instance, it is automatically established everywhere else," here too—just as in the passage concerning the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*)—*nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection) must be qualified by its equivalence to *darśana* (vision). If, on the other hand, the opponent's view were accepted that the word "draṣṭavya" (to be seen) refers to the fruit, there would be a syntactical inconsistency (*vaighaṭya*) of the suffix. Furthermore, this is so in light of the preceding and following passages.

Since the fruit has already been stated in the passage, "By which I might become immortal; but there is no hope for immortality through wealth; verily, O dear one, this much alone is immortality," that [statement regarding the means] is unnecessary here. However, its clarity is established elsewhere, and its inclusion here is dependent on the force of the expectation [of the context]. Therefore, since it is possible for it to function as a qualifier of the injunction—being subordinate to the means, like the phrase "when it is seen"—[the statement is appropriate].

Since the combination of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), their accumulation (*samuccaya*), or the abandonment of what has been heard (*śrutahāna*) and so forth is untenable; since it is possible for the sentence to have the purport of enjoining a single qualified means for the sake of achieving a single result, making it improper to accept a separate injunction for distinct results; and since, by treating [the object] as a restatement—as in the case of "with curd" (*dadhnā*)—there is the possibility of a single qualified thing to be enjoined, this sentence "He should see" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*) and so forth should be understood as being primarily an injunction for meditation (*dhyāna*) qualified by clarity. For this very reason, even the suspicion that this [sentence] simultaneously functions as both an injunction and a restatement is dispelled.

The objection—how can the vision of the Self, which consists in the direct realization of one’s own bliss and is itself already desired, be something to be enjoined—is answered by the statement that it is an injunction for the production of clear recollection. By this, such passages as "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death," "When the seer sees the golden-colored One," and "By the knowledge of That, the wise perceive the immortal form of bliss which shines forth," are also appropriately established.

But in that case, the perception of yogis would indeed be sublated; for even those statements in various scriptures that speak of the existence of yogic perception—using terms such as "seeing" (*darśana*) and so forth—could be interpreted as referring to objects that have a form identical to that of [ordinary] perception. Nor can its existence be established by arguments such as "dharma and the like are perceptible to someone because they are objects of knowledge" (*prameyatva*), since this would result in proving something other than what is intended, namely, the perception of God (*īśvara*).

Even if the formulation of the thesis were "cognizable by the sense-faculties" (*indriyagrāhya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because that which is known through scripture is also an object of the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, regarding the claim that they must be "directly perceived by the sense-faculties" (*indriyasākṣātkartavya*), this has already been answered by the fact that for those who maintain that even supersensible things (*atīndriya*) are cognized by reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), the argument results in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). If one intends to mean that they are directly perceived in a primary sense, like pleasure (*sukha*) and so on, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, as there is no subverting counter-argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position. Otherwise, one would face the absurd consequence of having to prove that even dharma and other such factors are visible to the eye, as the Buddhists do.
For it is possible for someone to employ a disputed argument such as: "The eye is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it is an object of knowledge," and so forth.

Furthermore, a counter-argument is easily available: "The sense-faculty of a yogin does not produce direct perception of dharma and the like, because it is a sense-faculty, just like the sense-faculties of people such as ourselves. Do not say this. For in the context of the means to liberation, the non-primary status of the term "vision" (darśana) has been stated. Elsewhere, however, in the absence of any sublation, one should accept the term according to its literal meaning. (Verse 311)

For it is explicitly stated that those who have attained self-restraint possess the knowledge of the past, the future, objects beyond the senses, and so forth. Nor is this [knowledge] mere recollection, because its objects have not been previously experienced. For this very reason, there is no possibility of metaphorically designating it as "perception" (pratyakṣa) based merely on its clarity. Furthermore, there is no room for inference or other means of knowledge therein, since such possibilities are rejected by statements such as, "He perceives all that correctly through the power of his dharma," and it is further indicated by the phrase, "as if an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand."

The direct realization [of the Vedas] is proclaimed through various means of accumulating merit, such as the recitation of *sūkta*, *kāṇḍa*, and *mantra*; and it is well known from such statements as, "I give you divine vision. Therefore, there is no lack of proof, because the yogic perception of the external senses and the mind is endowed with supramundane excellence according to their respective fitness through specific meritorious deeds. Nor is there an over-extension [of this principle], because there is no reason for transgressing what has been heard [in scripture], and because there is no subverting evidence against the inference in the contrary case.

Nor can there be a sublation of what is heard (śruta) by means of inference, because that [inference] is itself sublated by scripture (āgama); otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Now, it may be argued that scripture enjoins one to perform what is possible; however, the similarity of memory to direct perception (darśana) is not dependent on a person, and even that [similarity] is not possible for it. Furthermore, that which is impossible—just like the very nature of being a perception—cannot be grasped by an injunction. An injunction does not function with respect to a perceived capacity when a perceived result is impossible; to this, he says: "it exists."

*Meditation* (*bhāvanā*) is either the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by experience or simply the act of reflection itself. And that can be performed with devotion and without interruption; from that, the attainment of clarity in recollection follows. Here, a possessive *bahuvrīhi* compound based on a simile should be understood: "that whose form is like the form of perception. Examples such as the mental images of one who is afraid or one who is in love should be cited here. Others also say: "Even that which was previously perceived, when meditated upon though now beyond the senses, attains a state of direct manifestation, becoming a source of affliction such as desire and the like."

In passages such as "I see [it] in every tree," the mixture with error is dependent on a defect; however, here, because one reflects according to what is heard, there is no defect or sublation—this is the intended meaning.

If it were the case that memory becomes equal to direct perception through the intensity of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), what would be the role of ritual action (*karman*) in this regard? It is not so, because both are established by the mind. (312)

The author of the Vākya has elaborated on all this: "Knowledge (*vedana*) must be worship (*upāsana*), because it is so heard in that context. In all the Upaniṣads, it is stated that knowledge—which is enjoined as the means to liberation—is indeed worship. Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "one should perform the cognition only once, since the purpose of the word has been fulfilled, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings," he concludes: "But it is established from the word 'worship' (*upāsana*)," thereby determining that knowledge, when repeated, is the means to liberation.

"Worship (upāsana) would be constant recollection (dhruvānusmṛti), because of its nature as seeing and because of the etymological derivation"—thus, the state of being constant recollection has been described for that very knowledge which takes the form of worship and is repeated many times. This recollection is established as having the nature of seeing. And this "nature of seeing" is the attainment of direct perception (pratyakṣatā).
Regarding the recollection's nature as seeing, there is the approval of the author of the Vākya.

He says "by the author of the Vākya" to establish the firmness of the group of principles already stated, indicating that everything—both literal and implied—has been examined and determined according to its primary distinctions by those who know the intended meaning of the Sūtra. This is because [the same] is heard regarding that subject; the meaning is that the word *vedana* (knowing) is used in place of the word *upāsana* (meditation) in one context and in another context as well. To dispel the suspicion that what was stated here is merely incidental, he explains the sentence with the words "in all," for even though it is stated in the injunction of a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭi*) such as "one should meditate on the mind as Brahman," [it applies universally].

Since the same logic applies to the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) as well, it should be applied there too; however, to clarify that this [rule] is observed in one specific instance among them, it is stated that [knowledge] is "enjoined as a means to liberation. By this, the distinction from mere superficial understanding, hearing, reflection, and ascertainment is made. To dispel the doubt of the dull-witted—who might suspect that what was stated as "knowing is worship" (*vedanam upāsanam*) is merely a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) due to its proximity to the subsequent sentence—he says: "once" (*sakṛt*).

For an injunction (*vidhi*), impelling a person who is already inclined toward action for its own sake, would cause him to act only once even in this case—just as it does with the *prayāja* and other subsidiary rites in the scriptures—so that the injunction itself may be accomplished. It is with the intention that "the burden of repetition must indeed be endured only when there is a specific statement" that it was said: "because the meaning of the word has been fulfilled. This means that the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), which is the object of the injunction, is fully accomplished by that much alone. He states what was indicated by the word "but" (*tu*) in the subsequent sentence: "having formulated the prima facie view" (*pūrvapakṣaṃ kṛtvā*).

He demonstrates the refutation of that [objection] with the words "it is established" (*siddham*). The meaning is that worship (*upāsana*) is established by logical reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*). Alternatively, "established" means "the final conclusion" (*siddhānta*). This is because of the word "worship"; for the word "worship" is not commonly known to denote a single act of cognition—this is the intended sense. He explains this sentence with the words beginning "knowledge" (*vedanam*). By the phrase "from the word 'worship' and so forth," it is shown through the recognition of the word itself that even the sentence "knowledge is worship" has the status of a final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The permanence of *dhyāna*, although not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, was previously indicated by the symmetry of the underlying logic and explained by [the author] himself. In this passage, however, he adopts what has been said regarding *upāsana* as well, since it is non-different from *dhyāna*: "Upāsana... "Darśana" refers to the natural worldly perspective. "Nirvacana" refers to the Vedic statement cited earlier as providing a definitive explanation. Alternatively, "darśana" refers to direct scriptural revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), and "nirvacana" refers to the derivative explanation (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) that provides a precise definition.

The phrase "of that very [practice]" means precisely that which is prescribed as the means to liberation, and not that which others desire as the cause for the means to liberation. Since there is no application of the term *upāsanā* (meditation) when it occurs only once, the statement specifies that the word *upāsana* used in the sentence is intended to mean that which consists of repeated practice (*asakṛdāvṛtta*).

Now, it was previously stated that "all this has been explained in detail"; however, in that context, the nature of [meditation] as a form of seeing (*darśana*) was not observed. Therefore, even though it was not explicitly mentioned there, he restates it—saying "this very [meditation]"—in order to clarify that it follows the same logical principle as the two qualities already mentioned, namely repetition (*āvṛtti*) and steadiness (*dhruvatva*), and for the purpose of prescribing another kind [of meditation]. The meaning is that it is characterized by repeated recurrence through the states of *dhyāna* and *upāsana*, and is distinguished by the steadiness mentioned in another scriptural passage.

"Established"—the sense is that the author of the *Vākyakāra* has also stated, by implication, that [perception] possesses the nature of a vision (*darśana*). Alternatively, this was intended by us as previously stated due to the symmetry of the underlying logic. Now, although it is impossible to enjoin the identity of one thing with another, and since memory and perception have distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it is impossible for two things of contradictory natures to be identical elsewhere; nevertheless, just as dream-cognition—which arises solely from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—possesses the form of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) through the assistance of a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*), so too here, even though production by the eye is impossible, [the same may occur].

To the question, "Even though it is not directly perceived as being inseparable from that [object], why could the term 'vision' (*darśana*) not be applied figuratively to the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) simply because of its similarity in being a mere form of cognition (*dhītva*)," he says: "The nature of vision" (*darśanarūpatā*). This refers to the attainment of the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*), but not direct perception itself, because that is impossible. The intended meaning is this: even dream-cognition is not primary vision, since there is no activity of the eyes.

However, when the functioning of the external senses has ceased, a vivid memory is produced regarding previously experienced objects by means of the mind—which does not wander elsewhere—due to the intensity of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). There is no lack of other established reasons for postulating a cognition distinct from that [memory]. In this case, even though it is not produced by the eyes and so forth, the notion that it is so produced, as well as the notion of connection where there is no connection, is a mental error (*mānasabhrānti*) caused by defects.

However, in accordance with the section concerning the twilight (sandhyādhikaraṇa), since [the cognition in question] lacks the property of being produced by mere refinement (*saṃskāra*), its nature as "seeing" (*darśanatva*) is unmixed; therefore, it is not possible to establish the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) for the subject at hand on the basis of the example of dreaming. Furthermore, a metaphorical usage based merely on the similarity of "seeing" due to the commonality of being a cognition (*dhītva*) is not appropriate when a specific distinction—consistent with the immediate praise of the subject—is established.

Thus, he qualifies the *smṛti* (sacred tradition), which has become directly perceived and serves as the means for liberation: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. By this, having stated that mere hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are not the means for attaining the Self, it is said: "Only by whomsoever this Self chooses, by him alone is He attained. For only one who is most beloved becomes the object of choice.

He for whom this [Self] is the unsurpassed beloved becomes His dearest; and as this dearest one attains the Self, so does the Blessed Lord Himself exert effort—thus it has been said by the Blessed Lord Himself: "To those who are ever steadfast and who worship with love, I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me."

Thus it is said: "For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me. Therefore, for one whose remembrance—which is of the nature of direct realization—is itself exceedingly dear because the object remembered is exceedingly dear, that very person becomes the one to be chosen by the Supreme Self; thus it is stated that the Supreme Self is attained by that [remembrance] alone.
It is precisely this meditation (*upāsana*) in the form of constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) that constitutes the nature of devotion (*bhakti*).

Now, an objection is raised: in passages such as "Not this, not this" (neti neti), the triad of hearing and so forth is negated, and it is stated that [the goal] is attained solely through the independent choice of the Unquestionable One. Therefore, according to the maxim, "I consider fate alone to be superior; human effort is useless," everything previously stated is false. To this, he replies with the words "Thus" (evam), stating that what is intended there is specifically the qualification of being of the nature of devotion (bhakti-rūpatva), which is meant by the term "meditation" (upāsana) for the remembrance (smṛti) qualified by "steadfastness" (dhruvatva) and other attributes in both the Sūtra and the scriptural passage. Thus: "In this way, having first described the nature of the Self as characterized by the qualities of steadiness and so forth, he enjoins meditation upon It as the means to attain that very Self. By the word "thus" (evam), he indicates that the aforementioned characteristics of the Self are established by the scriptures and reasoning. By the phrase "having first described," he shows that the description of the Self's nature is the cause for the subsequent injunction of meditation. By the phrase "as characterized by the qualities of steadiness and so forth," he indicates that the Self is the object of meditation, and that the qualities of steadiness and so forth are the means for Its attainment. By the phrase "he enjoins meditation upon It," he shows that the act of meditation is the means for attaining that Self. By the phrase "as the means to attain that very Self," he shows that the attainment of the Self is the result of that meditation. Thus, the meaning is that one should meditate upon the Self, which is characterized by the qualities of steadiness and so forth, as the means to attain that very Self. This is because the scripture declares: "The Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9). And from the Smṛti: "By single-minded devotion, one may know Me in truth and thus become one with Me" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.55). Therefore, it is established that the Self, characterized by the qualities of steadiness and so forth, is to be meditated upon as the means to attain that very Self. This is the conclusion. || 1.1.12 || Now, an objection is raised: since the scripture says, "The Self is to be known through hearing, reflection, and meditation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), and since the Sūtra states, "But that [Self] is to be meditated upon as described in the scriptures" (sūtra 4.1.1), it follows that the Self is to be meditated upon.
