The meaning is: "by means of the method of resting upon a specific [meaning], as stated in the Sūtras and other texts regarding general terms. The phrase "having attained perceptibility" is intended to indicate the logical equivalence with the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) that will be discussed later. It is illogical for concealment (*āvaraṇa*) to be causeless; for if it had a beginning, it could not be causeless. If it were beginningless, it would follow that liberation (*mukti*) is also beginningless.

Because it would otherwise follow that the injunction regarding the means to liberation is futile, and because it would contradict the Sūtras and other texts—such as those prohibiting partiality and cruelty—which are intended to negate specific distinctions consisting of the individual soul's (jīva) activities; with this intention, it is stated that [the Self] "is the means to liberation. By this, the suspicion that [the text] is concerned with meditations for the sake of some other fruit is also dispelled, for it is the Supreme Self that is intended to be attained here. He distinguishes [it from the individual self]: the meaning is that it does not set aside what is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Otherwise, the injunction of another means would be purposeless.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the earlier and later statements: "The wise one, having realized [it], does not grieve" and "One should attain it through wisdom" (*prajñāna*). In passages such as "This is not the Self," the word *śruta* denotes hearing (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, the word *medhā* must mean meditation (*dhyāna*), in accordance with the Vedic text: "May *medhā* and *manīṣā* enter me together for the attainment of what has been and what is to be. The *Nighaṇṭu* states that *medhā* is "retentive intelligence" (*dhāraṇāvatī dhīḥ*). By process of elimination, the word *pravacana*, mentioned alongside hearing and meditation, refers to reflection (*manana*).

It is called *manana* because of its derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning "that by which one reflects. Alternatively, it refers to the teacher’s instruction for the purpose of the disciple's reflection; or, the effect is metaphorically attributed to its cause, namely the instruction. Now, one might object: how can that which negates the essential nature be an injunction for it? Furthermore, in some cases there is futility due to the negation of both the subordinate and the principal, while in others there is contradiction due to the negation of what has been enjoined. Anticipating this doubt and avoiding the consequence of rendering hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means futile, he clarifies that the statement qualifies *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance) with the words "by this" (*anena*).

Just as in the case of the injunction "fire is not to be piled on the earth," where the purpose of the prohibition is to ensure the avoidance of a deficiency in gold, and thus the intended meaning lies in the injunction that [the fire] must be contained within gold; so too here, since hearing and the other [means of knowledge] necessarily occur—either directly or through an appropriate indirect channel—just as they do with the earth, the word *kevala* (exclusive/only) is used by one who intends to enjoin a specific excellence of pleasure (*prīti*) regarding all three [means], by way of prohibiting a deficiency in that pleasure. Alternatively, the word is read together with the prohibitions against non-participants, such as "not in the intermediate space" and "not in heaven."

The phrase "not on the earth" is a prohibition of what has been previously established; just as it rests upon the injunction of a specific qualification—namely, that gold must be used as a base—by excluding bare earth from being the locus, as is the case with the intermediate space and so forth; likewise, the prohibition of meditation (*nididhyāsana*) when accompanied by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), which are not themselves the means, results in an injunction that meditation is of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*), by way of stating that bare meditation, like hearing and so forth, is not the means.

The inclusion of the word "whichever" (*yameva*) is intended to exclude the suspicion of an unrestricted, arbitrary, or independent choice, and to clarify that the choice has a restricted object by the force of the subsequent statement (*yadvṛttānūkti*). This is because a choice made by one who is a friend to all, untainted by defects such as partiality, cannot possibly have a restricted object. Just as the verb *bhavati* in the sentence *yad āgneyaḥ*, the verb *vṛṇute* (chooses) must have its purport in enjoining the causal activity (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), since there must be one who possesses the causal activity for the choice that is about to be obtained.

[Objection: Just as gold placed upon it must necessarily rest on the earth, so too, since no rule is observed for the connection between the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) and that specific quality which is the cause of being desirable—implied by the relative pronoun *yat* in this sentence—that [remembrance] does not attain its distinction through it. To this, he says: "the most beloved" (*priyatama*). The use of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) is intended to exclude a semblance of devotion aimed at other fruits. The particle *hi* indicates that the nature of the Supreme and the Lower Persons is well-known from both scripture and common worldly experience.

[Objection: "Granted that by this much some other activity may be established which brings about the state of being most beloved for one who is to be chosen; however, the specific nature of the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) has not yet been attained. To this, he says: "Of whom... The meaning is: he alone—not one possessing other meritorious deeds, nor one possessing mere constant remembrance, nor anyone who is merely a sincere lover [of the Lord]. "To me, he is equal."

The meaning is as follows: by the words "toward all beings" and so forth, [the Lord] is indicated as having the very nature described by Himself. This is the intended sense: since other activities that cause one's own pleasure lack the quality of being a cause for choosing [someone] for the sake of one's own gain, only he who possesses absolute love fixed upon his own object—being the dearest to another—would be chosen for the purpose of attaining oneself.

And this state of the intellect, consisting of unsurpassed love, which is averse to both the alternatives and their combination regarding the production of liberation, relies upon the *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant mindfulness) established as the means to liberation by the force of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that admits no other recourse, and thus it distinguishes that [mindfulness]. Now, one might object: "What is gained today by the covering (*varaṇa*) of that which is eternally possessed as one's own? And what is there to be obtained now of that which is eternally attained due to its all-pervasiveness?"

Regarding the question of how it is known that "the Beloved alone is to be chosen by him," the author clarifies all of this through the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (corroborative scriptural passage), beginning with the words "Just as... (*yathā*). "This one" refers to one who possesses unsurpassed love for the Blessed Lord due to the manifestation of His absolute state of being the object of enjoyment (*nirupādhika-bhogyatā*). For this very reason, he attains the Beloved—the Self—and rejoices in his own Self. To clarify that, unlike others, He has no dependence on another in bestowing upon such a person the yoga of the intellect (*buddhi-yoga*) and other means which are the immediate cause of liberation (*apavarga*), the word "Himself" (*svayam eva*) is used.

Or rather, it may be indicated that [the Lord] performs an inconceivable benefit for the worshipper—by the Blessed One Himself, as the one who chooses, as heard in the scripture: "Whomever He chooses" (*yamevaiṣa vṛṇute*). By this, His status as the supreme authority (*paramāpta*) due to His innate omniscience is also revealed. "For those who are constantly united" (*satatayuktānām*) means for those aspiring to constant yoga; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of aspiration (*āśaṃsāyām*), according to the rule "as if already accomplished. Since the state of the worshipper's intellect being of the nature of love is established by the phrase "for those who are constantly united and devoted," the syntactical connection is: "I give with love. For the Supreme Lord, there is neither love nor hatred based on favors or offenses.
But the fruit of those two arises through the power of the sign; thus, [the view] that abandons this principle is rejected. || 313 ||

Obstructing, the desire to lead upward, and the desire to lead downward are not prohibited for the Teacher because they are [traditionally] heard [in scripture], since he bestows the fruits of those respective actions. (314)

He states that the reason for being most beloved—which is the cause for being chosen—and which is intended by the Śruti and expressed by the word "ever-devoted" (satatayukta), has been explained in that very same place: "For he is dear... (*priyo hi*). "Exceedingly" (*atyartham*) means beyond what can be expressed; the sense is that even I would find it difficult to describe. Here, "choosing" (*varaṇa*) refers to the unfailing resolve: "May this person attain Me. And the fact that He is obtainable is what is intended by the word "reveals" (*vivṛṇute*) in this context.

The meaning is that it has been stated, by implication, that [Brahman] is the object of an unconditioned experience in which all obstructions have ceased. Here, the author clarifies—through the word "ataḥ" (therefore)—the fact that the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is specified as being of the nature of bliss (*prītyātmakatva*), even though this was not explicitly manifested in the cited scripture along with its supplements (*sopabṛṃhaṇa*). This is done by following worldly usage and by means of the operation of the intended sense of the cited scriptures and traditional texts.

This is the meaning. "Exceedingly dear" (*atyarthapriyā*) means that, by virtue of having a nature of extreme favorability, she manifests of her own accord; she is the objectified by another cognition in the form of love, according to the maxim: "Even in an improper state, there is love for those who lack discrimination. For it is intended that, in all cases, the state of being love itself and the state of being the object of love belong to the subject's cognition depending upon a particular object. Thus, the statement regarding her being "exceedingly dear when remembered" is made. By the words "by another" (*pareṇa*), the contextual exclusion of the agent of the acts of choosing and revealing, as well as the object of those acts—the one to be chosen—is demonstrated.

This very recollection of the eternal (*dhruvānusmṛti*) of such a nature is designated by the word "devotion" (*bhakti*), because the word *bhakti* is a synonym for "worship" (*upāsana*). For this very reason, it is stated thus in the Śruti and Smṛti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; only by knowing Him does one become immortal here. There is no other path for the journey. "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner as you have seen Me."
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna,
I who am of such a nature can be known and seen in truth, and entered, O scorcher of foes.

"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone. Now, it may be objected: "It is well known from the Purāṇas and other sources that wisdom is of the nature of devotion (bhakti), and thus the status of devotion as a means has been introduced. In the phrase 'expressed by words such as meditation (dhyāna) and worship (upāsanā),' the word 'etcetera' (ādi) was intended to include the word 'devotion' (bhakti) as well; however, this notion does not exist in the Śrutis cited here. Therefore, how can there be no contradiction? To this he replies: "Of such a form" (evam-rūpā). This means it is qualified by the sequence of stages already described. To the objection that this is merely a formal proposition (pratijñā-mātra), he says: "In worship" (upāsane).

The sense is that there is no occasion for contradiction because, although the words differ, they are established as having the same meaning; for (1) constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is qualified by its nature as joy and its being denoted by the term "meditation" (*upāsana*); (2) it conforms to the definition of devotion (*bhakti*) as "contemplation preceded by affection" (*sneha*); and (3) "service" (*sevā*), "devotion" (*bhakti*), and "meditation" (*upāsti*) are listed as synonyms. Thus, since there is no difference in the object to be enjoined, no conflict arises.

He says "ataḥ" (therefore) to strengthen the point that words such as *vedanā* (realization) and so forth culminate in *bhakti* (devotion), by means of another argument consisting of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (the Purāṇas) and the *upabṛṃhaṇīya* (the Vedas) would mutually contradict one another. This [word "therefore"] refers to the reason in the form of the result: the meaning is that since devotion alone is expressed by words such as *vedanā* and *upāsanā*, otherwise there would be a mutual contradiction between the Śrutis and the Smṛtis just as there is between the Śrutis themselves; this is the intention behind the restrictive particle (*eva*). "In this way" means according to the manner already stated: that in the Śruti there is no final means other than *vedanā*, whereas in the Smṛti there is no final means other than *bhakti*.

The *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* has the Supreme Person as its subject matter. Now, an objection might be raised: the statement in the *Śvetāśvatara*, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," refers to Rudra because it occurs in proximity with words such as "Śiva" and so forth; whereas the passage, "Knowing Him thus... refers to the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). Since both of these passages declare, "There is no other path for going," there is a mutual contradiction. To dispel this doubt of the dull-witted, both of those passages are cited here.

The intended meaning is as follows: through the preceding passages such as "I know this great Puruṣa," and the subsequent passages such as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," there occurs a recognition—both by word and by sense—of the Great Puruṣa who is described in the Puruṣasūkta as being solely devoted to the impelling of *sattva* and who is the "great Lord, the Puruṣa, the impeller of *sattva*. Since it is therefore certain that words such as Śiva and Maheśvara must refer to Him, it is logical to abandon their conventional meanings (based on the *aindrī-nyāya*).
Because of the recitation of the Lord's names as "Sarva," "Śarva," "Śiva," and "Sthāṇu," and because of the word "Śiva" [itself].

Because [the term "Śiva"] is conventionally established as auspicious at the beginning [of a work], because the excellence of its renown is rendered fruitless here according to the method stated, because the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, *Saubāla-mahopaniṣad*, and other such texts are more authoritative as they cannot be explained otherwise, and because—as in the case of the terms "eternal," "auspicious," and "imperishable"—it must necessarily refer to the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa); therefore, since at the commencement of the passage "The auspicious one is omnipresent" there is recognition of the thousand-headedness and so forth in the verse "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings," and because of the word "Bhagavān" in the phrase "And the Blessed Lord is all-pervading."

Because the status of being established upon the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) is affirmed, and because the conclusion must be interpreted without contradicting that [status] as it is supplementary to the subject at hand, the disputed passage has as its sole subject matter that which is declared in the Puruṣasūkta. In this regard:

The statement beginning with "not by [Vedic study] etc. intends to show that the Vedas, austerity, and so forth are not direct means [to liberation], and thus there is no contradiction with that [other teaching]. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "but by unswerving devotion" intends to show that knowledge in the form of devotion—which possesses distinct stages—is the means for achieving other forms of knowledge and so on; therefore, there is no risk of circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*). Nor does the citation of the verse beginning with "That Supreme Person... render the preceding [passage] redundant, because it demonstrates what was not previously established.

This is indeed the intended meaning here: that which was heard in the preceding statement, "He who knows Him thus—of solar hue, beyond darkness"—is precisely what is made recognizable by the description of His inconceivable form and solar hue, starting from the words, "he who should meditate on Him who is subtler than the subtle. Furthermore, what was stated as "the Ordainer in front" is shown to mean "the Ordainer of all. In that context, what was expressed by the verb *vid* (to know) in the Śruti is here explained by the verb *anusmarati* (he should meditate/remember). Moreover, he is immediately qualified as "endowed with devotion."

Therefore, it is understood that the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) in the form of devotion is enjoined by the Veda through the verb *vid*. Although, in this context, it might seem more appropriate that it refers to the means for attaining other human goals based on the recurrence or non-recurrence of the verbal suffix, nevertheless, by the same principle of analogy, one must accept that even the Vedic injunction for the sake of liberation finds its culmination in devotion. And in that very passage, with the words "In Him alone is the Supreme Person," etc., [the author] reveals that even the Vedic injunction for the sake of liberation has that specific [devotion] as its ultimate purpose.

Here, that which was hidden within the encapsulation of the Śruti—“He is attained by whomsoever He chooses”—has been revealed. For here, by means of a statement containing specific qualifications, not only the various objects to be attained by the knowers of truth (jñānins), but also the various means of attainment, have been set aside. Indeed, just as the identity of the object to be attained is established through the recognition (pratyabhijñā) expressed in the Śruti, the identity of the means is likewise logical. Therefore, in place of the term ‘vid’ (to know), the roots ‘dhyai’ (to meditate) and ‘upās’ (to worship) are employed here with the sense of ‘bhaj’ (to devote), serving as specific qualifiers.

Regarding the Puruṣasūkta and the Bhagavadgītā, which are both accepted as the highest authorities: they should not be subject to mutual contradiction; for when they share a single purpose, there is no reason to disregard the Smṛti. (Verse 315)

[Objection: Is it not the case that in such passages as "By devotion he comes to know Me," the attainment of the Supreme is taught through knowledge produced by devotion? [Reply: Not so; for even there, in the words "Then he enters into Me," devotion itself is referred to as the cause of attainment. Otherwise, the word "then" (*tataḥ*) would be redundant. Therefore, the meaning is the same, as both state that one enters [the Supreme] by means of devotion.

It will be stated [in the Sūtra] that "sacrifices and other rites are the means for this kind of constant recollection (dhruvānusmṛti), because of the scriptural mention of sacrifices and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Although sacrifices and other rites are enjoined for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by the text "they desire to know," nevertheless, they serve that very same knowledge—which is of the nature of meditation, which is practiced day after day, which attains excellence through repeated practice, and which continues until death.

Since they are the means for attaining Brahman, all duties pertaining to the stages of life (*āśrama*) must be performed throughout one’s entire life in order to bring that [knowledge] into being. And the author will state this in such passages as: "Until death, for it is seen there too," "But the *agnihotra* and so forth are for the sake of that very [result], because it is so seen," and "And as auxiliaries," etc.
This is the refutation of the position that the utility of ritual actions lies solely in their being the means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

One might object: "Surely, based on the natural force (*svārasya*) of the accepted Śruti and Smṛti, devotion alone—without dependence on Vedic recitation, sacrifice, and so forth—should be the means to liberation; consequently, the fact that [the inquiry into Brahman] follows upon the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) would not be established. To this he replies: "Of such a nature" (*evam-rūpāyāḥ*). This means: [of devotion] which is established by the statements of Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtra as possessing specific stages ending in meditation and other practices that depend upon well-performed merit (*sukṛta*).

With the intention that the status of the *śruti* and the *sūtra* as having *vividiṣā* (the desire to know) as their subject matter has been refuted both by context and by meaning, he says "of the constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ*). The sense is that this will be stated by the author of the *sūtras* and will be established by us as well. In proximity to the phrase "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), a clear realization is enjoined in the words "it is to be perceived by the mind alone" (*manasaivānudraṣṭavyam*); and it is praised in the words "having known this very [Self], one becomes a sage" (*etameva viditvā munirbhavati*). Therefore, it is only for this realization—which is the object of both injunction and praise—that there is a requirement for another injunction here.

But this does not apply to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) which is devoid of both [the desire for knowledge and the desire to perform sacrifices]. Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that [sacrifices] are enjoined as the means to the desire to know. For when it is said, "one desires to go to heaven by means of sacrifice," it does not follow that sacrifice is the means to the *desire* to go; and here, in the absence of the desire for knowledge (*vedana*), the state of desiring to know (*vividiṣā-kāmatva*) cannot be established. If that were possible, there would be no need for its means; moreover, the desire to know arises from the desire for knowledge, the desire to know leads to the performance of sacrifices and so forth, and that performance produces the desire to know—thus there would be a circular argument (*cakraka*).

In this context, some have asserted that there is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) due to the contraction of the stages (*parva*). However, this is not a case where the rule of merit remains unknown, for sacrifices and the like are accomplished through effort with full awareness. Therefore, as in the expression "he wishes to kill with a sword," there is no syntactic connection [of the means] with the desire [itself] due to logical inconsistency;
for nowhere is a desire for a means established without a desire for the end.
Consequently, since it cannot serve the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), its purpose here is indeed knowledge (*vidyā*). || 316 ||
From the desire for liberation, the desire for its means is also established;
therefore, for one who desires knowledge, an injunction regarding its means is appropriate. (317)
In this context, devotion is perceived as the primary result, whereas the desire for that [result] is declared to be the qualification by means of the suffix. (318)

Now, it must be admitted that the unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the cause of all worldly effects; otherwise, it would be impossible for the various desires that serve as the causes of unequal pleasure, pain, and so forth to arise at certain times and not arise at others. Therefore, if desire in general were merely something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then the desire to know (*vedanecchā*) would also be such, and its refutation would contradict all established systems (*sarvatantra*).

To this, it is replied in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*: "The arising of desire is possible through the knowledge of the specific nature of an object, assisted by prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) awakened by the unseen principle of experience (*bhogādṛṣṭa*)."
For even those effects that are not perceived for the sake of enjoyment, and which have not been sought after by men,
may become productive of results due to the presence of an internal intelligence.

Therefore, in this context, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavidhi*) is as follows: one who desires the knowledge of Brahman in the form of devotion should cultivate that [knowledge] through sacrifices and other means accompanied by tranquility (*śānti*) and the like. Now, an objection may be raised: "Even in the injunction for the means to achieve devotion, would there not arise the same contingency of a logical circle (*cakraka*) and so forth as you have described? The answer is: No, it would not. For that injunction is established with a view toward the increase and the continuity of devotion. Likewise, there is no contradiction even in the injunction for the means to knowledge; for although [Brahman] is known in a general way, one proceeds [to practice] out of a desire to know it in its specific details.

Nor should it be argued that even if there is a distinction [between the two], the conceptualization of "known" and "unknown" is untenable; for even for you, one engages in debates and the like which consist of the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and questions. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with both the common person and the investigator. If it is then argued that for one who has thus developed the desire to know, there is an injunction regarding the means to that end out of a desire for its persistence, even in that case, since there is no difference in the result, one would simply ascend to that [same conclusion]; and as for the "knowledge" asserted by others, it has already been refuted.

He states that the ritual action must be performed throughout one's life (*yāvajjīvam*) in order to maintain the desire for the realization characterized by the many forms previously mentioned—this is expressed by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). However, if it were merely a means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) as stated by others, then in the view that this is an "ascension" (*anvāroha*), the response would have to be somehow interpreted through the persistence of that desire to know alone. The phrase "of that very [desire]" refers specifically to the object of the desire to know. The statement that it takes the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) is made with the intention that this realization is not, like a sacrifice or like a transcendental result (*apūrva*), a means that is produced once and then remains at intervals.

The expression "day after day" (*aharahar*) and so forth excludes both the notion that even a continuous practice can be accomplished in a single day—as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—and the notion that it must be accomplished with intervals between days; furthermore, the statement regarding its continuation "until death" (*āprayāṇāt*) [establishes its lifelong duration].

This is for the purpose of excluding the notion that [the practice] must be performed daily with a fixed limit such as one year. By the phrase "an excellence to be acquired through repeated practice," it is indicated that there is also a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*). "For the sake of its arising" means: for the sake of the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is intended to be accomplished by sacrifices and other means because it is desired as a continuous state. The word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) is to be distributed appropriately according to what is suitable. By the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), there is a rebuttal of what was previously stated, namely that [the practice continues] for hundreds of future births and so forth.

Even when the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has arisen, the abandonment of ritual action in the interim is not proper; for if the desire to know were interrupted, there would follow the consequence of the interruption of knowledge itself. Indeed, the persistence of knowledge cannot be established by a single instance of the desire to know, just as the persistence of eating cannot be established by a single instance of hunger. Even if its continuity is possible through an abundance of past merit, the intention is that one must nevertheless engage in practice to pacify potential obstacles. Previously, it was shown in the Sūtra that knowledge takes the form of meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and so forth.

Now, he states that there are sūtras regarding the necessity of following [the meditation] day after day until death, and likewise regarding the continuation of its constituent rites, saying: "And he will state... By these very sūtras, the scriptural passages concerning each respective topic are also indicated. By this, the contradiction with the sūtras and other authorities in the case of not accepting what has been stated by himself is reinforced. For by the sūtra itself, "Because it is seen even there until death," it is established that the rite must be performed for as long as one lives.

Indeed, because the phrase "practicing in this manner for as long as life lasts" is intended to be understood by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), and because the continuation of the duties previously mentioned—such as "in a pure family and in a pure place"—is restated here by the expression "practicing in this manner," the mention of the *agnihotra* and other rites in the Sūtra is intended to indicate that even those obligatory rites, such as the *agnihotra*, are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*).

Regarding the question of how ritual action—though described as a constituent part of the stages of life (*āśrama*) in the sūtra "And because it is enjoined, the work of the stages of life also [must be performed]"—can serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*), the sūtra "And as a cooperative factor" is cited to indicate the distinct application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*) of the same act. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is a collection of sūtras indicating simultaneous performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*) when rituals serve both as constituents of knowledge and of the stages of life, such as "In every way, those very [acts] possess both characteristics."

And the author of the *Vākya* states that the accomplishment of constant mindfulness (*dhruvānusmṛti*) arises precisely from discernment (*viveka*) and the other [factors]: "Its attainment results from discernment, detachment, practice, action, auspiciousness, non-dejection, and non-exultation, because of their occurrence and their etymological definitions. He also explains the nature of discernment and the others: "Discernment is the purification of the body through food that is not defective in terms of species, source, or cause. Here is the etymological definition: "When there is purity of food, there is purity of the *sattva*; when there is purity of the *sattva*, there is constant mindfulness. Detachment (*vimoka*) is the absence of attachment to desires.

"One should worship with tranquility" (*śānta upāsīta*) is the etymological definition (*nirvacana*). Furthermore, "cultivating the undertaking" (*ārambhaṇasaṃśīlana*) means repeated practice. And the etymological definition from the Smṛti has been cited by the Commentator: "Always permeated by that state" (*sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ*). "Performance according to one's ability" refers to the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth; its etymological definition is: "This one who performs action is the best among the knowers of Brahman," and "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting."

Truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, charity, non-violence, and freedom from covetousness constitute the auspicious way of life (*nīti*). The etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) is: "He is to be attained through truth," and "This dustless world of Brahman belongs only to them," and so forth. Dejection (*avasāda*) is the lack of luster in the mind born of depression due to unfavorable place and time, as well as the recollection of objects of sorrow and the like. Its opposite is non-dejection (*anavasāda*). The etymological explanation is: "This Self is not to be attained by one who lacks strength. Exultation (*uddharṣa*) is the satisfaction born from the opposite of that [dejection]. Its opposite is non-exultation (*anuddharṣa*).

The meaning is that excessive contentment is also an obstacle. The scriptural definition likewise states, "peaceful and self-controlled. Thus, it is stated that for one endowed with such restraints (*niyama*), the perfection of knowledge (*vidyā*) occurs precisely through the performance of duties prescribed for one's stage of life (*āśrama*).
This refers to the sevenfold means, beginning with discrimination (*viveka*), as taught by the author of the *Vākya*.

Now, he also refutes the reasons for the prima facie view—such as "because of contradiction" and "because of lack of authority"—by means of the words of those who know the intention of the author of the Sūtras, beginning with the verse: "In the sentence... (vākye). By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), it is made known that there is no contradiction between [the requirements of] tranquility (*śama*) and so forth on one hand and sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth on the other, and that this is in agreement with what has been stated by himself. Alternatively, the meaning is: neither by the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), nor by any one of the [preliminaries] such as discrimination (*viveka*), nor by ritual action (*karman*) alone, nor by tranquility and so forth alone. "For one who has desisted from prohibited, optional, and fruitless actions, the engagement in the limbs of knowledge appropriate to one's own stage of life (*āśrama*) is not contradicted by tranquility and the rest. (320)

He employs the phrase "the attainment of that" (*tallabdhi*) in order to demonstrate, without contradiction, that [meditation] functions as a means when combined with other practices. Here, the referent of the word "that" (*tat*) is indicated by the expression "of constant recollection" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ*); for it refers back to what was previously introduced there, namely, that "constant recollection would be meditation" (*upāsanaṃ syāt dhruvānusmṛtiḥ*).

The doubt raised by some—that it might be possible to establish a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of the seven stages beginning with *viveka* (discrimination) according to different *āśramas*, based on their mutual dependence in a single effect through *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction), such that they function and cease together—is also refuted. This is because [such an arrangement] is possible, as there is no contingency of contradiction due to their compatibility in a single instance; and because of the definitive statement (*nirvacana*), meaning from scripture (*āgama*) accompanied by reasoning (*yukti*), which serves as a determinative authority regarding supersensuous matters. In this context, [the passage] is intended to establish that knowledge (*vidyā*) is produced by ritual action (*karman*).

Regarding the question of what these [virtues] such as discernment (*viveka*) are, and how they are not in conflict with one another, the author of the *Vākya* himself has explained this; he states: "of discernment and the rest. This means both their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the specific characteristics that distinguish them from one another among those already mentioned. "Defiled by its species" (*jātiduṣṭa*) refers to garlic and the like. "Defiled by its source" (*āśrayaduṣṭa*) refers to the food of a Śūdra and the like. "Defiled by its cause" (*nimittaduṣṭa*) refers to that which is contaminated by hair and so forth.

Discrimination (*viveka*) is the separation, through purification, of the body together with its senses from impure food—food which has been distinguished from [impure sources] by being free from such defects—by means of the awakening of *sattva* that is devoid of the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*. He states the illustrative sentence: "Born... and so on. Here, the expression "etymological derivation" (*nirvacana*) refers to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "When there is purity of food, there is purity of *sattva*. In this etymological derivation, *sattva* refers either to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or the quality of *sattva*. Because it serves as an indicator for all things that require purification, the mention of the "body" (*kāya*) in the sentence is used [to represent them all].

That [state] also characterizes the group of instruments (karaṇa). Longevity, vitality, and so forth, as well as pure and impure food, have been described. Here, the word "liberation" (vimoka) refers to desire, anger, and likewise greed.

The intention is that the statement "non-attachment to desires" (*kāmanabhiṣvaṅga*) is an expression of a "blow to the root," because it aims at the non-contact with the aforementioned classes of things to be abandoned. Here, "desire" (*kāma*) is that which is produced by extremely intense attachment (*saṅga*), based on the scriptural statement: "From attachment, desire is born. By this, "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*) refers to persistent and firm grasping; in its absence, there occurs the cessation of the sequence described as "from desire, anger is born," and so forth. In the phrase "one who is tranquil should meditate" (*śānta upāsīta*), the word "tranquil" (*śānta*) refers to the absence of desire and the like by way of the cessation of the activity of the organs.

For one desiring to ascend the path of yoga, the *ārambhaṇa* (initial support) is the mental object (*cittālambana*) in the form of a beautiful basis (*śubhāśrayarūpa*). In the *Vivaraṇa*, however, it is stated that one should meditate upon the object of knowledge (*jñānālambana*). Its "cultivation" (*saṃśīlana*) means practicing it in a favorable manner. The phrase "again and again" is to be applied here because of the context concerning the limbs [of yoga] and because of the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "even by a mind engaged in activity" regarding the time of rising from sleep. For this very reason, there is no suspicion of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). And this [practice] is for the purpose of accumulating impressions (*vāsanā*) conducive to yoga and for the purpose of removing the impurities (*kaṣāya*).

The statement from the *Smṛti* is made with the intention of showing that the supplement to the Vedic definition—"Having become disillusioned with both childhood and scholarship, one then becomes a sage"—is presented because its meaning is not explicit. Here, the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is the teacher Dramiḍācārya, who is the commentator on the *Vākyakāra* (Brahmanandin). By him, Vedic scripture (*śruti*) was cited in other instances, whereas here it is the *Smṛti*. Alternatively, in other cases Vedic scripture was cited by the *Vākyakāra* himself, while here it is the *Smṛti* cited by the *Bhāṣyakāra* himself.

Although the phrase "whatever [being] he remembers" (*yaṃ yaṃ vāpi smarann*) introduces a general principle—as seen in the expression "always" (*sadā*) and so forth—nevertheless, in accordance with the subsequent statement, "Therefore, at all times remember Me," that [specific object] is understood because it constitutes the subject matter under discussion. The mention of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) is for the purpose of indicating the Smṛti rule that even a householder is liberated [by this practice]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the duties belonging to the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are also included. Although, in the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the inclusion of all constituent parts (*aṅga*) is required;

Nevertheless, the word "according to one's capacity" (*śaktitaḥ*) is used here with the intention that, in this context, performance according to one's ability is sufficient; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Performing that [duty] according to one's capacity, one attains the supreme goal. Furthermore, because there is no use of the desiderative suffix (*san*) in the passage, "This man of action is the best among the knowers of Brahman," the connection between ritual actions and knowledge is made explicit; thus, even the phrase "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣantaḥ*) is thereby restricted. And this statement is intended to show that ritual action, as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), is the cause for the full perfection of knowledge.

But it does not indicate the existence of one who knows the inactive Brahman, because it has been stated that the performance of ritual action continues as long as one lives; or rather, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) refers to abundance, or aims at the exclusion of those who know Brahman while being widowers and so forth. For they are inferior because they possess only the duties pertaining to their caste (*varṇadharma*). Therefore...

However, it is established by the sūtra, "But the other [is] superior, because of the indicative mark" (*liṅgāt*). In this context, the scriptural passage beginning with "In these mantras are the rituals... and ending with "...perform them constantly, O you whose desire is truth" (*tānyācarata niyataṃ satyakāmāḥ*) should also be considered. The word *kriyā* (action) is employed in the phrase "this very [Self]... (*tametam*) and so forth, in order to exclude mere concentration of the mind and similar practices. By the term *anāśakena*—meaning "by non-eating"—the word *tapas* (asceticism) is restricted here according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Alternatively, it may mean "by something other than that which causes destruction."

Even sacrifices and the like, if performed for the sake of enjoyment, are established by the Śruti and other authorities as leading only to destruction, which is of the nature of saṃsāra. Truth (*satya*) is speech that is beneficial to living beings and consistent with reality. Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the uniformity of the three instruments [of body, speech, and mind]. Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to remove the suffering of others, independent of one's own interest. Generosity (*dāna*) is the bestowing of wealth acquired through righteous means upon a worthy recipient according to the rules; by this, the cessation of greed is manifested. Alternatively, according to the root *daip* in the sense of "purifying," it may mean the purification of one's own side and so forth.

Regarding the root *ava* in the sense of "breaking," this refers here to the breaking of another's ego, in accordance with the Smṛti: "One should subdue those who revile the deities or the Guru to the best of one's ability. This is because the injunction "one should not engage in contentious debate" pertains to matters of personal whim. Here, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) consists in the avoidance of causing injury to living beings contrary to the scriptures, as established by the statement: "Not harming any living beings, except at sacred sites (*tīrtha*). Malice (*abhidhyā*) is the thought of doing harm to others.

For in the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like, the prefix *abhi-* signifies hostility, or constant remembrance of harm done by another, or a false obsession, or the notion that another's property should be seized; the cessation of these is non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*). In this way, the mention of a few [virtues] is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others as well, such as those recited together with straightforwardness (*ārjava*), compassion (*dayā*), and so forth. By the phrase "and so on" (*ityādi*), there is a summary of such qualities as freedom from pride (*amānitva*), freedom from ostentation (*adambhitva*), compassion toward all beings, patience, and lack of envy.

Considering that non-dejection (*anavasāda*) would follow as a matter of course, he provides a sentence with its reason concerning the nature of its opposite: "Place" (*deśa*). A "thing of grief" (*śokavastu*) is an object that causes sorrow; alternatively, the word *śoka* may be derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*), meaning "that by which one grieves. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to the cause of fear. Grief and fear are forms of suffering consisting of cognitions directed toward undesirable past or future objects. These two—due to "deficiency" and "recollection"—are connected with the phrase "the mind's lack of luminosity" (*manaso 'bhāsvaratvam*).

Non-luminosity (*abhāsvaratva*) is either the absence of luminosity or that which is opposed to it. That non-luminosity is produced by that [absence]. When there is a requirement for a further explanatory statement to manifest its nature, another sentence—"the dejection born from that"—is inserted in between. Dejection is the non-luminosity produced in that [state] or in that mind; the meaning is the incapacity to manifest as previously employed. Alternatively, one should construe it such that both the mind’s non-luminosity and the dejection born from it constitute "depression" (*avasāda*).

*Tajjam* means "born from that," namely, born from such a particular kind of compassion. Alternatively, this may be understood as follows: men possess a dejection of mind—such as being pained by the suffering of others—which is contrary to luminosity (*bhāsvaratva*); and from that [dejection] arises sorrow and so forth. Here, *bhāsvaratva* refers to the quality of illumination; its absence is [the opposite]. Regarding the statement that "dejection born from that is despondency" (*avasāda*), the commentary provides the elliptical completion (*vākyaśeṣa*) that its opposite is "non-despondency" (*anavasāda*). However, this is not explicitly stated in the verse itself for the sake of developing the students' power of inference.

"By one devoid of strength"—the meaning is "by one lacking the mental strength described as 'the steadfast one for whom pain and pleasure are equal. "Born from its opposite"—the meaning is "born from the notion that [pleasure] is caused by the qualities of place and so forth, or by future happiness, or by the happiness of kinsmen. Although "exultation" (*uddharṣa*) was mentioned previously, its opposite, "non-exultation" (*anuddharṣa*), should be inferred in the same manner; thus, although not explicitly stated in the verse, it is shown in the commentary. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts such passages as "content with whatever comes by chance," "the constant yogin," and "study, purity, contentment," he says:

Regarding "excessive contentment" (*atisantoṣa*): the meaning is that, like discontent (*asaṃtoṣa*), excessive contentment is also an obstacle because it causes one to engage with other sense objects. This is indicated by the prefix *ud-* in the word *uddharṣa*. Furthermore, its status as an obstacle is well-known from various accounts, such as those beginning with "intoxicated by the pride of power" (*aiśvaryamadamatta*). As for the word *api* in the phrase "the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) also," the particle *api* has the sense of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*) regarding possibility; it should be understood to apply to the previous etymological definitions as well.

He concludes by summarizing the established collection of principles intended by the words of the Sūtra—namely, that the utility of ritual actions (*karma*) has been set aside through their cessation-aspect, and that they are to be integrated without contradiction—using the word "thus" (*evam*). By the particle *eva*, it is indicated that this is not desired by others, or that statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) are being distinguished [as superior]. Thus, here the arguments regarding the non-utility and contradiction of ritual action, as well as the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for them, have been refuted.
And the phrase "and knowledge" (*vidyā ca*) refers to the meaning of the scriptural passage from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*.

And so says another Śruti: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he attains immortality by means of knowledge. Here, that which is denoted by the word "ignorance" is action prescribed for the [various] castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). "By means of ignorance"—that is, by means of action—"having crossed over death"—meaning, having dispelled prior karma that is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge—"by means of knowledge"—that is, by means of wisdom—"he attains immortality"—meaning, he reaches Brahman.
This is the meaning of the scriptural passage from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*: "Both knowledge and [ignorance]."

Now, he states that the scripture, which has been otherwise explained by the Mṛṣāvādin and the Samuccayavādins, actually reveals the very method we have described, by saying "tathā" (so it is). The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis; or the construction may be "and another scripture [also] says so."

The word *antara* (internal/intermediate) clarifies the distinction from the previously mentioned statement because it is clear in meaning by being devoid of the suffix *-san*, because it demonstrates the gateway for the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the production of the whole (*aṅgin*), and because it makes known that the culmination in the supreme human goal occurs through the performance of rituals—the details of which are explicitly taught—resulting in the realization of the fruit produced by the means of knowledge. As for the phrase "and knowledge" (*vidyāṃ ca*), the meaning is: he who, according to the scripture, knows both the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) and the "ignorance" consisting of ritual action (*karmarūpāvidyā*) as things to be practiced.

The two *ca*s have the sense of a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) of what has been stated. However, if they indicate what has not been stated, they include the specific details of the respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*), as well as the fruits of knowledge and the things to be removed, which are the means for attaining [the fruit] and the obstacles to it. In the phrase "both together" (*ubhayaṃ saha*), what is intended is the simultaneity in the mental apprehension of the two things to be performed—which will be established in the third chapter as being related as subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*)—and not their simultaneous status as objects to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*). For "togetherness" (*sahabhāva*) is spoken of in the context of being known (*vedyatva*); it does not mean that they are known simultaneously.

For indeed, the coexistence of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ritual action (*karman*) is impossible both at the stage of origination and at the stage of the removal of obstacles. In this context, the passages beginning with "They enter blind darkness" and "Into a darkness even greater than that" are intended to express a censure of each individually. One should not mistakenly assume that the particle *ca* and the word *saha* establish a simultaneous conjunction, because they can be accounted for otherwise. The phrase "those who delight in knowledge" means those who possess the enthusiasm for the arising of knowledge through disregard for ritual action.

For those devoted to action, the very nature of action—which is independent of knowledge—is indeed accomplished; yet liberation does not result from that alone. For those devoted to knowledge, since there is an absence of the cause [of action], knowledge itself is not possible, let alone liberation; such is the intended meaning of the word "furthermore" (bhūyaḥ). He establishes that the word "ignorance" (avidyā) here refers to the subject of action by means of the context with the words "here," but not everywhere.

In such passages as "dwelling within ignorance" (*avidyāyām antare vartamānāḥ*) and "the perishable is indeed ignorance, [it is] the notion of self in what is not-self," the term *avidyā* is employed in different senses. However, here, by the statements "he perceives only the Self" (*ātmany evānupaśyati*) and "performing actions here indeed" (*kurvann eveha karmāṇi*), knowledge (*vidyā*) and its constituent action (*karma*) are the subjects under discussion. That very same thing is here restated by the word *avidyā* for the purpose of making known its utility for knowledge (*vidyopayoga*). In order to dispel doubt and misconception—which have been explained in the commentary on the other [passage]—he clarifies the meaning of the words and the sentence with the phrase "by ignorance" (*avidyayā*).

The statement regarding the opposition to the arising of knowledge is made for the following reasons: (1) because sin is understood by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) either through the power of its constituent parts or figuratively, as it is the cause of misfortune; (2) to exclude the possibility that sacrifices and the like merely remove obstacles to the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); and (3) to distinguish [sin] from the attainment [of liberation], which is established by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts as being removable only by enjoined knowledge. By this, the interpretation of Yādavaprakāśa is also refuted. For if the "crossing over death" here were liberation itself, how could there be anything else to be accomplished by knowledge?
Furthermore, the use of the suffix *-ktvā* would be untenable, since it is impossible for something to be prior to itself.

If the cessation of the contraction of the intellect is [effected] by the karma known as ignorance, then the expansion of the intellect is that very same thing; thus, there is no possibility of another goal to be accomplished.
If the removal of obstacles is accomplished through ignorance [of reality], then the attainment of immortality would be established by itself, without requiring any other unseen factor. (322)
The Lord of living beings is naturally inclined toward instilling self-experience;
for those whose obstacles have been stilled, He is indeed the independent cause.

Although the word "death" (mṛtyu) may have a common application [to both ignorance and ritual action], it cannot possibly refer to something that is removed by knowledge or that stands in opposition to its attainment, based on the force of numerous clear Śrutis and Smṛtis such as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death. Furthermore, since there is a prohibition of other means in the passage, "There is no other path," it is impossible for ritual action to be combined with knowledge as a means to liberation. Since the status of ritual action as a means to knowledge has been established by the Śrutis and other authorities themselves, the term here refers specifically to that ritual action which is opposed to the means [of knowledge].

The inclusion of the word "ancient" (*prācīna*) is because, unlike knowledge, action lacks the capacity to oppose subsequent evil. The interpretation offered by others—that the phrase "having crossed over" (*tīrtvā*) means "having reached and remained"—is incorrect, as it is both strained and requires an unwarranted ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the attempt to explain that one "crosses over" action denoted by the term *mṛtyu* because sacrificial and other good deeds are opposed to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) is refuted by the fact that such an application contradicts the specific injunction regarding the purpose of the desire for knowledge.

In passages such as "This is the bridge," since there is no [physical] motion, the intention is that the root *tṛ* (to cross) signifies "attainment"; with this in mind, it is said "having discarded" (*apohya*). Since the word *vidyā* is used for scriptures and other things as well, he clarifies that its scope here is the knowledge of Brahman under discussion by saying "by means of knowledge" (*jñānena*). In accordance with scriptural passages such as "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman; the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," he says "the immortal Brahman."

Objection: Is it not the case that you have previously accepted the statement of others that liberation is simply the cessation of ignorance, and that this occurs solely through the knowledge of Brahman? Yet here, by the statement "The knower of Brahman attains [it]," it appears that another goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is admitted in this scripture. Response: Not so. Since by the term "cessation of ignorance" the cessation of the contraction of knowledge is intended, that very attainment of Brahman is identical to it according to the principle that the absence of one thing is the presence of another; thus, the meaning is the same.

Because of this, and in accordance with the natural sense of the word "liberation" (mokṣa), if one intends to speak of the cessation of the binding karma described as "ignorance" (avidyā), then only that much is to be accomplished through meditation. Upon the removal of the cause of the contraction of the intellect, the expansion of the intellect occurs spontaneously through the will of such a Lord, according to the principle of the flow of a river upon the breaking of a dam.

Therefore, by the statement "through knowledge one attains immortality," since the removal of obstacles is accomplished through knowledge, the experience of Brahman—which will arise spontaneously—is what is being described; thus, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following passages. Furthermore, although the attainment of Brahman is desired as the supreme human goal, the means for removing its obstacles is designated as a category distinct from things to be desired.
For all duties of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), which remove obstacles to that [attainment] and its means, are situated within the domain of occasional duties (*naimittika*). (Verse 324)

Here, by means of the instrumental case-ending in *karaṇa* and the two words *karman* and *jñāna*, it is indicated for the purpose of reinforcing the clear meaning that "the ripening of the *kaṣāya* [impurity] is through actions (*karman*), while knowledge (*jñāna*) is the supreme goal; when the *kaṣāya* has been ripened by actions, knowledge then proceeds. By this, it is established that the word *mṛtyu* here refers to that which is opposed to the means [of knowledge], that the connection of *vedānuvacana* and so forth is with the sense of the verbal root in *vividiṣanti* ("desiring to know"), and that the doctrine of their cumulative combination (*samuccaya*) is refuted.

The "cooking" (*pāka*) refers to the ripening of impurity (*kaṣāya*), which is evil, or of passion and the like produced by it; that by which something is cooked is the "instrument of cooking" (*pāka-nimitta*); and that by which one goes is the "path" (*gati*). From that [ripening] arises knowledge—not the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), nor liberation—but rather that which functions with excellence toward its appropriate object. This is the meaning. The fact that merit has the nature of evil, as well as the fact that both merit and demerit are to be dispelled by *dharma*, is established. Ignorance (*avidyā*), understood as the means for crossing over death, is simply that which is other than knowledge (*vidyā*), namely, prescribed ritual action (*karma*). As it has been said:
"He, too, relying on knowledge, performed many sacrifices, having taken his stand upon the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), in order to cross over death by means of [the practice of] avidyā.

Let the immediate context rest for now. With the intention that, in this very statement, there exists a reason—consisting in the inherent capacity of the facts, which is unimpeded and naturally attained—that establishes the subordinate status of ritual acts to knowledge (*vidyā*) and confirms the definition of the term *avidyā* and others as we have stated, he says: "in crossing over death. The word "perceived" contains a reason. The phrase "other than knowledge" (*vidyetarat*) is the etymological derivation of the word *avidyā* used here.

With the intention that, according to the logic of terms such as *abrāhmaṇa* (one who is not a Brāhmaṇa), it is appropriate for the function of "other than that" (*tadanya*) to refer to what is proximate within the context, he stated "the prescribed action" (*vihitaṃ karma*). This implies a restriction conveyed by the two words [of the compound], namely: neither un-prescribed action, nor knowledge of Brahman and so forth. By this, although the word *karman* in the passage "only while performing actions here" (*kurvann eveha karmāṇi*) is common to all types of action, its scope is restricted to the appropriate subject; for optional rites (*kāmya*) and the like are not to be performed throughout one's entire life. He states that the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence have been confirmed in his own exposition through the corroboration of the cited Śruti: [The verse: "One should perform the prescribed action here, Not even for a moment should one neglect it; For by performing action here, one obtains the world of the doer, But by doing it without attachment, one goes to the eternal state. [The commentary: The word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is used to exclude un-prescribed action. The phrase "here" (*iha*) is used to exclude the performance of action in other worlds. The word "even for a moment" (*api kṣaṇam api*) is used to exclude the idea that one might perform it at some other time. The word "neglect" (*tyajet*) is used to exclude the notion that one might perform it in a different manner. The word "world of the doer" (*kartuḥ lokam*) is used to exclude the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*). The word "without attachment" (*anāśritaḥ*) is used to exclude the performance of action with desire for results. The word "eternal" (*avyayam*) is used to exclude the attainment of the world of the doer. The word "state" (*padam*) is used to exclude the attainment of anything else. Thus, the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence have been established. The sense is that the performance of prescribed action is enjoined here for the sake of attaining the world of the doer, and the non-performance of it is enjoined for the sake of attaining the eternal state. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two injunctions. As for the objection that the word "action" (*karman*) is common to all types of action, we reply: it is true that the word is common, but its specific application is determined by the context. For instance, in the passage "One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice throughout one's life" (*yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*), the word "Agnihotra" is common to both the obligatory and the optional forms of the rite, yet it is understood to refer specifically to the obligatory form because of the context. Similarly, here, although the word "action" is common, it is restricted to the appropriate subject by the force of the context. Therefore, the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence are firmly established. Thus, the performance of prescribed action is enjoined here for the sake of attaining the world of the doer, and the non-performance of it is enjoined for the sake of attaining the eternal state. Consequently, there is no contradiction between the two injunctions. Hence, it is established that the word "action" in the passage "only while performing actions here" refers specifically to prescribed action. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the commentary on the first verse of the second chapter. [End of section] [The verse: "One should perform the prescribed action here, Not even for a moment should one neglect it; For by performing action here, one obtains the world of the doer, But by doing it without attachment, one goes to the eternal state. [The commentary: The word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is used to exclude un-prescribed action. The phrase "here" (*iha*) is used to exclude the performance of action in other worlds. The word "neglect" (*tyajet*) is used to exclude the notion that one might perform it in a different manner. The word "world of the doer" (*kartuḥ lokam*) is used to exclude the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*). The word "without attachment" (*anāśritaḥ*) is used to exclude the performance of action with desire for results. The word "eternal" (*avyayam*) is used to exclude the attainment of the world of the doer. The word "state" (*padam*) is used to exclude the attainment of anything else. Similarly, here, although the word "action" is common, it is restricted to the appropriate subject by the force of the context. "Yathoktam" (as stated) means: "relying on knowledge" (*jñānavyapāśrayaḥ*) means being established in the knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*); "having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyāmadhiṣṭhāya*) means intending to bring about the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*)—which arises from discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth—and which has assumed the form of devotion (*bhakti*). For it is precisely these two types of knowledge under discussion—namely, that arising from scripture and that arising from discrimination—that are clarified here. Therefore, the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) here refers to the obstacle to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Furthermore, [the interpretation of *yajña* as] "having performed" is improper; for that [action of performing sacrifice] was not mentioned as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Moreover, by the phrase "having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyām adhiṣṭhāya*), the fulfillment of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is already established by implication. Any suspicion that the word "having crossed" (*tīrtvā*) implies the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*)—based on the statement of the purpose, "to cross over death" (*tartuṃ mṛtyum*)—is also dispelled. Furthermore, what is expressed by the word *avidyā*, which indicates the Vedic terms to be supplemented, is precisely what is manifested by the word *yajña*. The meaning is: "he performed sacrifices" (*yajñān iyāja*)—that is, he carried them out.

Action, consisting of both merit and demerit, is an obstacle to knowledge. Because it obstructs the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and because its fruit is undesirable, both types of action are designated by the term "sin" (*pāpa*). Furthermore, this action's status as an obstacle to knowledge occurs through the intensification of *rajas* and *tamas*, which oppose the pure *sattva* that serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge. That sin is an obstacle to the dawn of knowledge is understood from the Śruti: "It is He who impels one to perform evil action, whom He wishes to lead downward."

The Lord himself has established that *rajas* and *tamas* are obstacles to the knowledge of reality, while *sattva* is the cause of the knowledge of reality—through such statements as, "From *sattva* arises knowledge. Therefore, for the production of knowledge, sinful action must be eliminated. And its elimination is achieved through *dharma* performed without regard for its fruits. Thus says the Śruti: "By *dharma* one drives away evil."

[Objection: Is it not heard in scripture that only evil (*pāpa*) is to be removed by *dharma*, while here, by saying "ancient karma" without qualification, the crossing over of even merit (*puṇya*) is described? To this, [the author] clarifies what was stated as being removable in the scriptural passage to be cited later, with the words "In knowledge" (*jñāne*). [Question: How can merit be removable by *dharma*, and how can it be denoted by the word "evil"? To this he says: "Brahman" (*brahma*). The expression "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*) is intended as an illustration, referring to the mixture of the censured and the uncensured. Here, "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*) means "being cognizable" (*bodhyatva*).

The statement in the *Vivaraṇa*, "one should observe," is made by way of its full significance (*vaibhava*). This is the intended meaning: it is recorded in the Smṛti that "that very same thing is dharma and that very same thing is adharma, depending upon each individual person. Therefore, even that which is established as a meritorious intention becomes sinful in the state of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

Due to the distinction between the states of desiring liberation and not desiring liberation, a single action for a ritual performer attains the status of both sin and merit, even though the goal to be accomplished remains the same. (325)
The dual nature of the enjoined hawk-sacrifice and others arises from two types of scriptural injunctions;
if this exists for a single act at one and the same time, how much more so when there is a difference in time? (326)

For even merit (*puṇya*), which is the sole means for attaining heaven in the form of preeminent pleasure, obstructs the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of unconditioned bliss—for the sake of achieving its own fruit, namely attachment to objects that are censured by the terms "obstacle" (*antarāya*) and "hell" (*niraya*). Therefore, it is logical that the *pravṛtti-dharma* (the path of action) must be dispelled by the *nivṛtti-dharma* (the path of renunciation). Furthermore, the definition of sin (*pāpa*) is its being known through scripture as a means to an undesirable result for the agent; [as it is said]: "Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds."

Furthermore, in the Śruti text, "All evils turn back from here," although the word *pāpman* (evil) used in the conclusion may be taken figuratively to refer to sorrow and the like, its primary sense alone must be accepted because it is possible for it to be the cause of both good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*). Even in the view that there is a single figurative application throughout according to the "umbrella-bearer" maxim (*chatrinyāya*), there remains a distinction of degree. Nor is it the case that [good] deeds...

One might suspect that, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *pāpman* here refers specifically to a particular kind of evil deed (*duṣkṛta*), just as the words *duṣkṛta* and *pāpman* are used interchangeably in other contexts. However, this is untenable because both terms are equally pervasive, making such a distinction impossible—just as one cannot distinguish between the words *haya* and *turaṅga*. Furthermore, it would render the qualifying term *sarva* (all) redundant. Moreover, the immediately following sentence, "For this world of Brahman is free from evil," naturally intends to proclaim the cessation of all things to be abandoned that have been under discussion.

Therefore, in this context, it is appropriate that the two words *pūrvapāpman* (prior sin) and *aparapāpman* (subsequent sin) have the same meaning without restriction. This being so, the word "sin" (*pāpa*) applies even to a specific kind of merit (*puṇya*), because the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical. Now, one might object: "It is accepted that *rajas* and *tamas* are opposed to knowledge; but does that [opposition] occur through conjunction with 'sin' (*pāpa*), through alternation, or by some other cause? Since there is no determining factor, the opposition of 'sin' to knowledge is difficult to ascertain; therefore, its nature is simply that of being a means to suffering. To this, he says: "Of this... (*asyeti*).

"Pure *sattva*" here refers to that *sattva* which has overcome *rajas* and *tamas*, and which produces illumination and so forth when employed. Even at the stage of the arising of knowledge, because the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) persist for persons, the word "increase" (*vivṛddhi*) is used to manifest its distinction from the other qualities present at that time. Through such statements as "the qualities are subject to karma," it is established that the qualities serve as the medium [for experience]; the point is that the fact that sin is a cause of suffering is not established by the exclusion of anything else.

Regarding the question of how one can conceive of a relationship between a means and that which employs it (*dvāra-dvāritva*) when there is no evidence for both being equally opposed to knowledge, the author states the evidence for the opposition of the latter [the means]: "Of sin," etc. In the Śruti passage beginning with "He indeed," the phrase "desires to lead downward" does not mean desiring to lead [the person] to hell; for in this context, the desire to lead upward does not have heaven and the like as its object. Rather, in the passage "He desires to lead him up from these worlds," the leading up from all the worlds, including heaven and so forth, is understood according to the natural sense of the words.

Therefore, in this context, "unrighteous action" (asādhukarma) must be that which leads downward and is opposed to the attainment of liberation (apavarga). Its opposite, which is the means to that [liberation], is prescribed here in such passages as "Worship Me. Furthermore, at the beginning of that [section], it is established that its quality of being the "most beneficial" (hitatama) consists in being the immediate means to liberation, based on the words "that which you consider most beneficial for a human being. That very same thing is what is understood here by the term "righteous action" (sādhukarma), even though it is used in a general sense, due to the force of proximity.

Furthermore, His status as the cause of that [action] has been specifically stated in such passages as, "I give him that yoga of discernment" (BhG 10.10). And the action that is opposed to that [discernment] by way of obstructing its arising is the action that brings about aversion toward the Lord; for when there is favor toward Him, there is no possibility of falling into a lower state. That unwholesome action is the primary cause of the downward descent has been made clear in the section beginning with, "Those cruel ones who hate Me... (BhG 16.18) and ending with, "...they go to the lowest state" (BhG 16.20).

Alternatively, the term "good action" (*sādhukarma*) here refers to the auxiliary factors required by the means under discussion. Furthermore, the status of action as a means to liberation—expressed by the word "leading up" (*unnayana*)—is not direct (*advāraka*); for its mediated nature (*sadvārakatva*) is established by scripture and other authorities. Therefore, "bad action" (*asādhukarma*), which stands in opposition to action that is an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga-karma*), is precisely what is contrary to the arising of knowledge. Moreover, the Lord's role as the instigator of good and bad actions here does not depend on the prior karma of the individual soul (*jīva*), as that would entail the faults of partiality and cruelty.

Nor is there a state of being an impeller, as in the case of wind, water, and so forth; for that would entail the futility of the scriptures and other such consequences, and it would contradict scriptural statements regarding the granting of intelligence and so on. Therefore, the phrase "whom he wishes to lead downward" (yamadho ninīṣati) is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) of a certain person's conduct, revealing their status as a doer of sin which serves as the cause for the desire to lead them downward. In this regard, when one begins a subsequent sin while still burdened by a prior sin, the loss of knowledge and the resulting contrary knowledge rooted therein serve as the means. This is corroborated by such passages as, "To whomsoever the gods grant [sin], they destroy his wisdom," and so forth. Although this was stated generally with respect to all gods and all sins, it applies to the present context as well.

It is unimpeded. Moreover, it is specifically sung [in the Gītā]: "I hurl [them] incessantly," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that sin is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge. Now, one might object: "Let knowledge be obstructed by the two kinds of sin mentioned in the Śruti, and let it arise through the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti-dharma); there is no need for the qualities of *prakṛti* to act as intermediaries in both cases. To this, he says: "Passion" (*rajas*).

The inclusion of the term "of the *sattva*" here is for the purpose of ascertaining that *sattva* is the cause of knowledge through its pervasive concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) with the exclusion of *rajas* and *tamas*, for the purpose of demonstrating the gateway of virtuous action (*sādhukarma*), and for the purpose of establishing what was stated—that it is the pure *sattva* which is the cause of the arising of knowledge. The sense is that since it is improper to abandon either of the two means established by *Śruti* and *Smṛti* when another alternative exists, nor is a mere option (*vikalpa*) appropriate, it is logical here that they stand in the relationship of the door and the doorkeeper (*dvāra-dvāritva*).

But surely, by the statement "greed is from rajas," its status as a cause for erroneous cognition is also established, since greed for an unattained object is a cause of delusion; this is made explicit by the passage beginning with "by which one regards dharma as adharma," and so forth.

To dispel the doubt that—on the basis of such Smṛti texts as "Action is not exhausted until it has been experienced"—knowledge might only be accomplished at the conclusion of the experience of the fruits of action, and that dharma would thus merely result in the attainment of pleasure in the form of the meaning of the word *dhṛti* (fortitude), [the author] determines the nature of the relationship between the object to be removed and its remover, established through both scriptural injunctions for expiation (*niṣkṛti*) and the distinct application [of dharma]. He concludes the two aforementioned points with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

It must be dispelled—the sense being that while infinite sins continue to accumulate, there will never be an occasion for their complete cessation through mere experience [of their fruits]; therefore, their removal must be effected solely by means of the expiations prescribed in the scriptures. Even so, one might argue that an expiation for such immeasurable sins is impossible; to this he replies with the words "that" (tat). The intention is that, according to the maxim beginning with "even a small portion of this dharma," it is possible to bring them to an end through the majesty of the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*) when performed without attachment to other fruits.
