In passages such as "and he who knows this thus," the mention of a fruit for the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture is intended as praise, or may be understood as indirect (paramparayā), or due to a difference in the qualified practitioners (adhikāribheda). Therefore, performance is primary; with the intention that for those who abandon it, there is an absence of the effect due to the absence of the cause, it is said: "by [the rite] being performed."

He cites a scriptural passage that clarifies how words such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and others, when occurring in the context of what has been acquired through study, possess their intended meanings, and demonstrates that even sin can be removed without the experience of its fruit: "In the same way... Therein, although the word *dharma* refers specifically to expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), it also includes the "duty of cessation" (*nivṛttidharma*) because there is no distinction made; this is due to the proximity of the knowledge of Brahman, as indicated by the passage beginning, "From knowledge comes bliss, the source of Brahman. Furthermore, even those other fruits perceived in the acts of giving and so forth—which are recited together with these rites and have results such as subjugating enemies—are indeed conducive to the accomplishment of the knowledge of Brahman. [This is] the fruit of the subsidiary parts (*aṅgiphala*).

And here it is clearly stated: "O wise one, do not undergo death again. Therefore, by means of the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), the fact that both worldly merit and demerit—both of which are designated by the term "demerit" (*pāpa*)—are to be ceased is established. Thus, the study of ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) must precede [the inquiry into Brahman]. Consequently, knowledge—which serves as the means for attaining Brahman—depends upon the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, the knowledge of the nature of those required duties, as well as the knowledge that mere rituals yield results that are limited and impermanent, is to be understood through the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*. Hence, that very [study] is to be declared as the prerequisite for the desire to know Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*).

To the question, "What follows from this? he says "That" (*tad iti*), intending that the knowledge consisting of meditation—which is the root of that [liberation]—is established as being dependent upon ritual action (*karma*). "That" means by the force of the aforementioned Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtra, reasoning, and tradition. "In this way" means by the manner in which desireless rituals serve to remove obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Granted that meditation, as an object of inquiry, has a dependence on its own constituent rituals, how does the inquiry into that [meditation] depend on the inquiry into all rituals? To this, he confirms the established point with a conclusion:

"—*ataḥ* (therefore). This means that it is impossible for the knowledge (*vidyā*) which is the means to liberation to be independent of the duties of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*). By the phrase "knowledge of the nature of the required action," [the author shows that] through the usage of elders, just as with rice and other grains, the specific details of ritual acts such as sacrifices—including their procedures (*itikartavyatā*)—must be known specifically via the *Mīmāṃsā* of rituals. Since an application (*viniyoga*) requires the knowledge of the nature of that which is enjoined by an injunction, according to the maxim of "not grasping the qualified without having grasped the qualifier" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*), there is a desire to know (*bubhutsitatva*) precisely that which is conjoined with its own nature as the means to the fruit, because it is accomplished by its own constituent parts.

Even though the worship is inconceivable, it is indicated that the action can nevertheless be conceived. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "kevala" (alone) is said with the intention that the encouragement toward knowledge (*vidyā*)—which occurs through the deprecation of ritual actions that are not auxiliary to knowledge—depends upon such knowledge of those actions. "Avaseya" means that which is to be accomplished; "mīmāṃsā" here refers to deliberation.

With the intention that—for those investigating the meaning of the scripture concerning worship, which includes both what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—the determination of the true nature of both is inevitable and must necessarily be accomplished through the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*; therefore, it is appropriate to state that [the inquiry into Brahman] is preceded by that [inquiry into ritual action], as it has not been previously established. By this, the claim that [the inquiry into Brahman] ultimately depends on an examination of ritual action, as well as the statement regarding the existence of the three-fold suffering (*tāpatraya*), is refuted. Alternatively, the word "only" (*eva*) suggests the exclusion of the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).
This is the refutation of the view that the fourfold prerequisites must precede [the inquiry into Brahman].

Furthermore, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, and so forth, cannot be accomplished without hearing the Mīmāṃsā; for without a determination of the specific fruit, instrument, procedure, and qualified agent, it is difficult to understand the nature of ritual action, its results, their stability or instability, the eternity of the Self, and other such matters. Moreover, the status of these as means is to be understood through application (*viniyoga*), and application is derived from direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so on; and that [application] belongs to the third book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras].

It is not merely that what we have stated is logical; rather, with the intention of showing that there is also a flaw in what you have stated, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*). Therein, he exposes the circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) by saying "In the case of the eternal" (*nitye*). The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "however" (*ca*), indicating the reversal of the status of what is about to be discussed from what has already been discussed. Here, the word "Mīmāṃsā" refers to both parts [of the system], because of the inclusion of the eternity of the self and so forth. And the word "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) extends up to "deliberation" (*vicāra*).

The point is this: what is intended here by the word *viveka*—is it certain knowledge (*niścaya*), or is it a superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*)? It cannot be the first, because that which is established by the entire *Mīmāṃsā* cannot logically be a prerequisite for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*); for the eternality of the self and other such matters will indeed be determined in the section concerning Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*). Nor can it be the second, because such a superficial cognition is common to both the sections on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) and Brahman, and thus it is inappropriate to mention it specifically here. Furthermore, as has already been stated, there is no reason to bypass the first alternative.

Nor is that [knowledge] the cause of detachment from other fruits and so forth, since the cognition of the attainment of immortality and the like is established in both cases. Nor is there any distinction [to be made] by means of the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others, because it is stated that the opportunity for them is blocked by the sequence beginning with Vedic study; furthermore, you yourself agree that in those systems there is a manifold perversion of discrimination regarding the supreme good and its means. For this very reason, they will be refuted. As for the corroborative passages such as "The world is not eternal," these must serve the purpose of discrimination precisely by following the Śruti.

But not independently; otherwise, what would be the need for the *Śārīraka*? If you argue that this is because doubt and other such states may arise elsewhere than there, then in that case, the establishment of discrimination (*viveka*) does not occur. As for what was stated here by Vācaspati—beginning with "The eternal and the non-eternal abide [together], thus they are 'eternal and non-eternal things'; the discrimination between their attributes, and between those two substrates, the eternal and the non-eternal, is the 'discrimination of eternal and non-eternal things'"—and continuing until: "Eternality is truthfulness; that which possesses it is eternal and true, and thus it is the object of one's reliance."

Impermanence is unreality; that which possesses this quality is impermanent and false. Thus, it is said to be an object of non-reliance. That which is real is established as permanent and blissful, and will therefore be an object of reliance; whereas that which is impermanent and unreal, being encompassed by the three types of suffering, will be abandoned. This is what is called the "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. This too is weak, because even though something is impermanent, its reality will be established on the grounds that it is not sublated.

Nor is it the case that the engagement of those performing ritual acts (*karmiṇaḥ*) in the investigation of karma and so forth proceeds from the thought that "eternal happiness is not to be pursued"; rather, it proceeds either from the delusion that it is achievable through karma, or from the perception of its extreme rarity. Furthermore, mere eternality and such qualities are not the cause for the absence of interest (*anāsthā*); interest arises precisely from [the object] being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) or a means thereto, while the absence of interest arises from the opposite. And these two—eternality and non-eternality—should be applied as appropriate to each case.

For even one who seeks liberation must renounce impermanent pleasure, according to the principle that "what is impossible, what has a miserable end, and what yields a result equal to its cost [is not to be pursued]," or else because of satisfaction derived from the attainment of superior pleasure. In the absence of such [superior pleasure], even the slightest pleasure is accepted. Furthermore, if even eternal [pleasure] were of the nature of suffering or neutral, how could it be worthy of reliance? This is because the subject under discussion is characterized by preeminent pleasure.

If it is argued that [the goal] is well-known, we reply: that knowledge is not established by means of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because such a relation is never observed. Nor is it established by scripture (*śruti*), because the superficial understanding based on such a source would be common to all [systems], leading to confusion; and as for definitive certainty, it is beset by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, it has been shown that the traditions and memories of other systems do not prove this point. Moreover, the desire to acquire the basis for the possibility of eternal bliss is common to all. And the impossibility of that [bliss] in other systems is quite evident.

The passage beginning with "Bliss is Brahman" and so forth is difficult to understand through those portions concerning ritual action (*karma*) and Brahman that have not been investigated, because such [a view] has been refuted in the *Pramāṇa-adhyāya* and the *Tarka-pāda*. Therefore, it is also impossible to maintain that the impossibility of an eternal fruit is established here in the first sūtra and elsewhere for the sake of relevance to the subject at hand, since you yourselves have not stated the meaning of the sūtra-sentences in this manner. Furthermore, there is here only a mere possibility of eternal bliss.

Furthermore, the impermanence of the happiness of heaven and so forth could not be established by another scripture or by inference, because it would be equally easy to state the opposite by those very same means—for instance, the argument "the happiness of heaven is impermanent because it is happiness" is sublated by scriptural texts such as those declaring its immortality (*amṛtatva*). Moreover, the determination of such figurative intent (*anyaparya*) depends upon the ascertainment of that [scriptural meaning]; otherwise, the undesirable consequence would follow that even the happiness of liberation is impermanent because it is happiness. And that non-occurrence of such a consequence results from the determination of the meaning of the Upanishads (*trayyanta*), which in turn depends upon that [ascertainment of the meaning of the scriptures]. Thus, there is a circular dependency (*mithassaṃśraya*).

Therefore, it is the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*) alone that is required here. As for the discernment of tranquility, self-control, and so forth as being means (*sādhana*), or their mere nature (*svarūpa*), it is said to have been already established; however, it is not the former, because that is to be accomplished in the section defining the means (*sādhanalakṣaṇa*) by the rule, "He should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth. Nor is it the latter, because in that context, those forms such as concentration and the like which are merely conducive to hearing (*śravaṇa*) are common to all scriptures and thus it is inappropriate to discuss them specifically here. However, regarding those conducive to *yoga*, such as the restraint of the external and internal organs, which relate to the hearing of the meaning of the Upaniṣads (*trayyantārthaśravaṇa*)—

Because [these qualities] have not been enjoined prior [to the inquiry], and because it is stated that one who possesses such knowledge must first be "tranquil and self-controlled" (*śānto dāntaḥ*), [they must be prerequisites]. Furthermore, do the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*) and so forth exist as cause and effect, or otherwise? In the first case, the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) should also be studied together [with the inquiry into Brahman], since, through the manner of "having examined the worlds," there is a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) with the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) via a traditional succession (*paraṃparayā*); otherwise, only the desire for liberation alone would need to be studied.

What is the purpose of mentioning the "tetrad"? Even in the second [case], there is a contradiction with one's own admission, because others have explained the sequence beginning with "dispassion from discernment" (*vivekādvairāgyam*). Here, he explains what was stated as "without hearing the Mīmāṃsā": "In the fruit," etc. In the *karmabhāga* (the ritual portion), the fruit is heaven and so forth; the means is sacrifice and so forth; the auxiliaries are the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; and the seeker is one desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). In the *brahmabhāga* (the knowledge portion), however, the fruit is liberation; the means is meditation (*upāsti*); the auxiliaries are tranquility (*śama*) and so forth; and the seeker is one desiring liberation (* mumukṣu*). Their "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is their specific form, which is excluded from that stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), as well as their mutual differences.

In this context, there is no lack of distinction between the means to be established (*sādhya*) in the statement that explains the nature of action and so forth through the determination of the fruit, the instrument, and other factors. This is because, in those various topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*), the understanding of the meaning of the great sentence—composed of mutually connected specific elements—is explained subsequent to the determination of the respective intermediate meanings of sentences. Furthermore, it is because the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*), which is the root of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the other [means], has as its primary purpose the instruction included within the determination of the fruit, the instrument, and so forth.

The mention of "action" (*karma*) here is intended to indicate meditation (*upāsti*) as well; or rather, by saying "it is performed," both are included. Furthermore, the word "action" is used even for meditation in the Sūtra: "And light [is the fruit] in action through practice," etc., where the Commentary states: "in action consisting of meditation. Elsewhere it is said: "Action consists of sacrifice and so forth, as well as that consisting of meditation. Moreover, the expression "mental action" is seen in the Smṛtis and other texts.

Some maintain that here, considering the word *karman* to refer exclusively to [rites] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an imitation of the method for determining their permanence or impermanence, but not of the method for determining [the nature of] certainty. Here, the meaning of what is being stated by way of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that reveals the incongruity is this: how can there be an understanding of ritual action—which consists of the cultivation of the three factors—without the ascertainment of the three required components of the fruit and so forth, namely "what," "by what means," and "how"?

And how can there be a certainty that the referent of words such as "heaven," which is connected to a qualification specified by "living" and so forth, is to be experienced in another body and in another place? And in the absence of that [certainty], how can there be the determination of a self that persists through prior and subsequent bodies—the very core of the refutation of the Lokāyata and Buddhist views on transmigration? Furthermore, since the experience of pleasure within the self can be established otherwise [as being merely a property of the body], how can the scriptural statement regarding the nature of pleasure be taken in its primary sense without [the certainty of] a self? For one who, in the absence of such a determination of the self, considers the body alone to be the self—

How can there be detachment from fruits pertaining to this world? Even for an eligible seeker who has realized the nature of eternal bliss, if they have not attained the certainty that the fruit of active dharma (*pravṛtti-dharma*) is entirely limited to the enjoyment of finite objects and is impermanent, whereas the fruit of abstinent dharma (*nivṛtti-dharma*) is supreme and eternal, how could there be a desire to renounce impermanent fruits such as heaven, and how could there be an attraction toward the knowledge of the eternal fruit found at the end of the Vedas? Therefore, in the doctrine concerning the practice of the fourfold means, one must accept an investigation into both parts [of the Veda] as the root of specific discrimination and the other qualities.

And thus, there is a dependence upon the investigation of karma; furthermore, there is the additional fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the nature of knowledge and bliss is intended. He states the specific defect regarding the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth with the words "of these" (*eṣām*). This means: of those [qualities] mentioned in the applicatory injunctions (*viniyojaka-vākya*) such as "one who is tranquil, self-controlled," and so on. "Application" (*viniyoga*) is the cognition of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgitva*); however, the *Nyāyasudarśana* uses the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*).

For when it is understood that tranquility (*śama*) and the other [qualities] are auxiliary members (*aṅga*), their status as means (*sādhana*) would be established by implication even if not explicitly stated. To the question "What follows from that?", he states that [the section on] application (*viniyoga*) depends upon the characteristics of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) established in the characteristics of the subordinate elements (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. To the objection that "the application of these means of knowledge should be considered within the Brahma-kāṇḍa itself," he replies with the word "sa" (that). That [application] belongs to the third [chapter]—namely, that which was stated in the third chapter of the Karma-kāṇḍa according to the sequence of connection previously mentioned. Here, however, in this third [chapter], we shall merely provide the refutation of objections by means of those very [means] already established earlier for the sake of brevity. The sense is that one should likewise observe here the reliance on the principles of other chapters.
This is the consistency regarding the meditations on the Udgītha and so forth.

The meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, although intended for the successful completion of ritual acts, consist in the vision of Brahman and thus depend upon the knowledge of Brahman; they must therefore be considered here [in this section] itself. Furthermore, since those very rituals—when performed without desire for their fruits—are means for generating the knowledge of Brahman, these meditations, which bring about their excellence, are all the more appropriately connected here. And it is universally accepted that these meditations depend upon the comprehension of the essential nature of the rituals.

Now, demonstrating another argument, he establishes the sequence of the inquiry into ritual action and Brahman here itself—due to its primary connection as being unfit for other locations—by means of the discussion on the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth, with the words "In the *udgītha*" (*udgīthe*). By the phrase "even those [meditations] for the sake of the success of ritual action" (*karmasamṛddhyarthānyapi*), the doubt is raised that while they were useful in the previous section, they are not so here; this is then resolved by the statement "the success of ritual action—that very [action] becomes more powerful" (*tadeva vīryavattaraṃ*).

The statement from the Śruti implies that there is no obstruction by powerful karmas to that which consists of the fruits of the qualities. The phrase "consisting of the vision of Brahman" contains a reason: they depend upon the knowledge of Brahman—for one who does not know the nature of the object to be superimposed elsewhere can never have a superimposition of it; furthermore, because the view of [the superimposition being] indeterminable (anirvacanīya) and so forth will be refuted later. And here, the intention is that the knowledge of Brahman is to be accomplished through the first two sections. He dispels the objection that these meditations on vision (*dṛṣṭy-upāsanā*) are of no use to the primary goal by showing their utility through an indirect means (*praṇāḍyā*), with the words "those [meditations]."

This means that the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth are to be set aside or rejected. Furthermore, the word "api" (even/also) here indicates a contradiction superimposed by another. Alternatively, having accepted the lack of utility in the preceding text, the connection [of this section] was established through the mere presence of similar applications, by stating that there is no other possible recourse for the expectancy [of the text]. Here, however, it is suggested that there *is* utility. "Those whose fruits are not intended" means they are devoid of the volition for results that lead to bondage. The knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is what is desired here. "Excellence" (*sādguṇya*) refers to the very prosperity previously mentioned.
But there is no cessation of deficiency; rather, [the causes] are those that bring about the perfection of karma and the production of its results.
From the excellence of karma arises the excellence of knowledge, and from the excellence of knowledge [arises the excellence of karma].
Therefore, there is no contradiction, as this is established through the distinction between individual instances. (327)

"Sutarām"—the sense is that this applies both with respect to itself and with respect to other forms of knowledge (*paravidyā*). By the phrase "right here" (*ihaiva*), not only non-connection (*ayoga*) but also connection with anything else (*anyayoga*) is excluded.
However, in the case of meditations such as viewing [the body] as Brahman (*abrahmadṛṣṭi*), there may be a single primary purpose;
yet, in this context, it is desired because of the logic regarding the causes for views and so forth that are conducive to knowledge (*vidyā*). (328)
In this way, there would be no over-extension [of the definition], because the recitation follows immediately upon the study;
and here, some kind of connection, which is desired by our opponents, is not precluded. (329)

To the objection that false perception (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is well-known even when the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not correctly understood, he replies with the words "of these" (*teṣām*). For this is not merely a false perception; rather, it is the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) of a contrary nature upon what has been correctly understood. Consequently, for one who does not know the constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), which serves as the substrate, as it truly is, it is impossible to conceive of an injunction regarding the perception of something else in its place.

"Agreed by all"—even those who deny everything find it impossible to refute when confronted by an investigator; the sense is that there is no disagreement regarding the cognition of pure existence (*sanmātra*) when considered directly. Now, one might object: even optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) require these [means of knowledge], which—though not constituent parts of the rites themselves—endow them with greater potency; thus, since the performance of those [rites] also requires both inquiry and ritual action, let the investigation into them occur within the Ritual Section (*karmakāṇḍa*) due to this mutual requirement. This is not so; for it has already been stated that such [inquiry] is impossible for one who does not know Brahman.

For this very reason, its study occurs only within the Upaniṣads themselves. As for the previous objection raised—that for one who has studied the Vedānta, reflection on that alone is possible—it is incorrect; for the injunction of study enjoins the study of the whole [Veda] in its proper sequence. Nor can the inquiry into the Vedānta now seek a prerequisite based on a study of the end of the Veda (trayyanta) undertaken by transgressing the injunction, or undertaken due to some calamity.

By this, the view that partial study and reflection might occur due to an excellence of detachment fixed by specific past merits (*prācīna-sukṛta-viśeṣa*) is also refuted, because even that would involve an improper transgression of the injunction for complete study. Furthermore, it has been stated that for one who has not mastered the ritual actions (*karman*), the acquisition of knowledge regarding the auxiliary sciences (*vidyā*) of those rituals is impossible to investigate. Moreover, attempting to fill in the deficiencies later through an indistinct preliminary investigation is a laborious and strained approach.

If it is argued that for one intent on the contemplation of Brahman, there should be comprehension of the constituent rituals of knowledge (vidyā) through the mere instruction of a teacher, then by that same logic, the inquiry into Brahman (brahmavicāra) itself should not exist. Therefore, the pure path is this: for one who has studied the entire text according to rule, a specific stage of conduct is prescribed for the remaining portion of the inquiry, just as it was previously. Thus, the path is purified.

The conduct of the Lord of Ascetics, which draws away the body of the crown of sacred learning and acts like thieves through its impure behavior, has—as it were—shattered the twenty-fold discipline; yet this very conduct has now restored that discipline. 330.
Thus ends the *Laghusiddhānta*.

Because action, known through the first part (*pūrvabhāga*) of the Mīmāṃsā, yields results that are meager and unstable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman, which is to be understood from the subsequent part (*uttarabhāga*), yields infinite and imperishable results, it is stated that after the knowledge of action—which has preceded—it is for that very reason that Brahman must be known. Thus says the author of the *Vṛtti*: "After the mastery of action as it has been practiced, there arises the desire to know Brahman (*brahmavividiṣā*)."

And he will state the unity of the two treatises on ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) and Brahman (*brahma-mīmāṃsā*): "This *Śārīraka* [Mīmāṃsā] is joined with the sixteen-chaptered [work] of Jaimini; thus is the unity of the treatise established."

In this work, *Tātparyadīpikā*, it appears as if the author intends to present the historical account stated by Yādavaprakāśa and his establishment of the irrelevance of investigating Sāṅkhya and other systems; setting that aside, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Mīmāṃsā. Whether one derives the form from the root *māṅ* (to measure) with the irregularity of the suffix *naṅ*, or from *māna* (to honor) with the addition of the suffix *nic* according to Pāṇini’s rule *mānbadha...* etc., this word is formed with the desiderative suffix *san*. The grammarians’ statement that it is derived from *māni* (to desire to know) is not far removed from this view.

For the determination of the primary meaning (*śakti*) of this term [mīmāṃsā] is derived from the usage of the elders in reference to that venerable inquiry which is prompted by a specific desire to know (*jijñāsā*), as well as to the excellent method (*nyāya*) associated with it. And they have said: "All reasoning designated as *mīmāṃsā* originates from the Veda," and so forth. However, when applied to the treatise (*śāstra*) itself—which consists of a compendium of such methods—the word *mīmāṃsā* is used figuratively (*bhākta*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction in describing it as "known" and "to be understood" through the division into earlier and later parts. Here, the construction of the sentence begins with "pūrvavṛttāt" (from what has preceded), while the remainder serves to support the logical reasons (*hetu*) found therein.

The sequential instruction on investigation is based on the Sūtra; however, in this [treatise], the unity of the treatise and its sequence are stated here as intended by the author of the Sūtra for the sake of clarifying that [instruction]. (208)

By the two terms *pūrvabhāga* (the former part) and *uparitanabhāga* (the latter part), the unity of the treatise—which consists of explanations arranged in a fixed sequence—is indicated. The cause of this [unity] is the sequential nature of the Veda, which is to be explained; this is shown in the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*) by the term *saśiraska* (together with the head). There is no tautology because the intended meanings (*tātparya*) of the words and the sentences differ. *Jñātasya* means of that which is known; *nirṇītasya* means of that which has been ascertained. *Avaseyasya* means of that which is to be determined, being present in an uncontradicted initial cognition. *Brahmajñānasya* means of the knowledge of Brahman, or the meditation upon Brahman.

Because, when the intention is merely to express the nature of Brahman, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is redundant here; because it is more appropriate to grasp a specific result by placing it in grammatical coordination with "of the known action" (*jñātasya karmaṇaḥ*); because it is improper to speak of knowledge—whether in the form of inquiry or in the form of ascertainment—as something to be attained (*avaseya*); and because [such knowledge] is not enjoined as a means toward the result being indicated.

Thus, here, according to the principle of coordination (*samanvaya*), although Brahman is to be known primarily as the infinite and inexhaustible fruit itself, it is also to be known as the object of its own worship by virtue of being the means for attaining that infinite and inexhaustible fruit; therefore, its mention as a subordinate element is perfectly consistent. However, by the statement "Brahman is to be known," its primary status is manifested. In this context, the reason for its being an object of inquiry is its presence in the mind through a preliminary cognition (*apātadhī*) characterized by purposefulness.

However, for that [inquiry] which occurs subsequent to the inquiry into karma, there is dependence upon it once obstacles have been stilled; and as for "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), it is the absence of any other such requisite. Therefore, with the intention of referring specifically to that inquiry which extends until the fulfillment of the detachment (*nirveda*) mentioned in the scripture, [the sūtra says] "from that very [karma]."

Thus it has been stated. Here, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended to exclude the insufficiency of the reason, for it is improper to negate a reason that is itself restrictive. Some, however, say that since the inquiry into Brahman might otherwise follow from other causes—such as its being non-essential or its being accessible to Śūdras—this teaching is intended to show disregard for any cause other than the knowledge of ritual action (*karma*). In this case, there would be much impropriety, as neither the primary thesis nor its reason, nor the reason for a further thesis, would have been stated.

By the very exclusion of the impossibility of the specific probandum (sādhyaviśeṣa) being preceded by the intended cause, the rejection of other causes and so forth follows by implication; this is indeed logical. "To be known" means "to be investigated. It will be stated that "investigation must be performed. Here, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of fitness (*arha*). In the phrase "from the knowledge of karma," "knowledge" likewise refers to investigation.

By stating "Brahman is to be known" (*brahma jñātavyam*), [the author] indicates through its natural sense (*svārasya*) and through reasoning that the meaning of the sentence is that Brahman alone is to be known; thus, those who argue otherwise are refuted. For this Sūtra is intended to remove the notion that [Brahman] is not an object of inquiry. Since the knowability of Brahman has not been established prior to this, the restrictive rule that "that alone is to be known" does not arise. Furthermore, how can one speak of the knowability of a specific established entity without first proving the possibility of words referring to established entities?

The proof for that [non-exclusion] follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*; moreover, a construction involving mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa-yojanā*) is not tenable. Here, as in the *Codanā-sūtra*, it is also untenable to claim that there is both the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with others through both word and meaning, and that there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because a mere thesis (*pratijñā-mātra*) that is irrelevant [to the context] cannot be established. Furthermore, the claim that "increasing faith in Brahman" and "the negation of others" are useful for the subject at hand is weak; even if those were accepted as theses, a reason (*hetu*) must still be inferred here.

However, if one were to deliberate upon that [Sāṅkhya], it would be redundant, as its means of proof have already been established by the sections beginning with *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* up to the end of the *Tarka-pāda*. Furthermore, how can those who assert that parts not mentioned in the *Śārīraka* are to be understood through Sāṅkhya and Yoga now deny them here? As for the point that portions contrary to the Veda are not to be respected, this was already established prior to the *Virodha-adhikaraṇa*. Now, while reinforcing his own stated positions regarding word-meanings (*padārtha*) and sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) even through the method of exposition (*vṛtti*), he demonstrates the correspondence between his work and their composition by following their system, saying: "Thus he says."

The author’s intention is also that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) serves as a cause [for the inquiry into Brahman], by virtue of its being established as preceding [the inquiry into Brahman] and not being otherwise accounted for. Here, "attainment" (*adhigama*)—derived from the sense "that by which something is attained"—refers to the inquiry (*vicāra*). The mention of "desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) is to be understood in the same way as the mention of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*).

To establish the meaning of the Sūtra he himself has stated, he confirms the unity of the scripture (*śāstraikya*) which was indicated [earlier] with the words "he will state. This is a future reference, as it concerns another section of the work yet to be explained. By the expression "being joined together" (*saṃhitatva*), he intends to show that the unity of the scripture here consists not merely in belonging to the same branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), but rather in being a single continuous composition (*aikaprabandhya*).

The meaning is that once the unity established by the investigation into the nature of the entire Veda’s meaning has been achieved, the two sections—the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *brahmakāṇḍa*—are joined together according to the maxim of the lost horse and the burnt chariot (*naṣṭāśvadagdharathanyāya*), because each is incomplete in itself and thus possesses a mutual expectancy. Furthermore, this commentary indicates the causes for the delusion regarding the division of the scripture and the means to dispel them: it makes known the difference in subject matter through the word *śārīraka*, which shows that its scope concerns all embodied beings; and it points out the difference in purpose, the difference in qualified aspirants, and the manifestation of the non-contradiction of their respective meanings with the very same finger. [This is indicated] by the phrase "by the follower of Jaimini."

This indicates the apprehension of a division [of the work]. The resolution, however, is given by the phrase "by that which has sixteen characteristics," meaning by the two sections consisting of twelve chapters. Regarding this, the author of the Sūtras manifested that [system] in three ways concerning the spheres of ritual action (*karman*), the deities (*devatā*), and Brahman, respectively from the sage Jaimini, Kāśakṛtsna, and Bādarāyaṇa. Thus ends the *Tattvaratnākara*.

Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Tantra* (PMS) and because of its function (*vṛtti*), any apparent contradiction in certain instances should be understood as being resolved through figurative usage (*upacāra*). By employing the counter-argument (*pratibandī*) "by means of the sixteen characteristics," it is shown that differences in intermediate subjects and so forth do not contradict the unity of the treatise (*prabandha*). By the very phrase "by Jaimini," it is indicated that the suspicion of a contradiction in meaning arises from a lack of understanding regarding the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the Sūtras; for [Bādarāyaṇa] will indeed demonstrate Jaimini’s agreement on many matters concerning the subject matter of the *Śārīraka*.

In passages such as "Jaimini [holds this] for the sake of pacifying delusion" (*vyāmohaśāntyai*), there is the mention of a disagreement in certain instances and its subsequent refutation. In cases such as "Jaimini [regards] the highest stage" (*parāśramaṃ jaiminiḥ*), the absence of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and other stages of life—though not explicitly formulated as a sūtra by Jaimini—was likely mentioned at some point and then rejected as a restatement, for the purpose of preventing those with desires from turning away from the duties of the householder. Otherwise, it would be inconsistent to state that Jaimini agrees with [Bādarāyaṇa] regarding the prohibition of falling away from the lifelong student and other stages, as seen in passages such as "But for one who has become that [stage], there is no returning to another state, even according to Jaimini. (*tadbhūtasya tu nātadbhāvo jaiminer api*).

Jaimini [asserts] non-qualification on account of the impossibility [of certain rites] in the Madhu-vidyā and others; Jaimini [also asserts] the existence [of qualification] because of the mention of alternatives (*vikalpa*) in passages such as "either... or..."—thus, even in these cases, there is no statement that contradicts the unity of the scripture. This is because a slight difference in expression does not contradict [the unity], just as there are differences in the explanations provided by oneself. By the mention of "being joined together" (*saṃhitatva*), it is demonstrated that the difference or non-difference of authors does not necessarily entail the difference or non-difference of the treatise, according to what is observed. For when there is a coherence of meaning, it is logical for a connection to exist through the intention of either one [author] or the intention of both. [This is so] due to the firmness of the dialogue with Brahmā and because there is no contradiction regarding the primary subject matter.
However, a contradiction with a non-primary element is set aside by virtue of the intended meaning (tātparya). || 209 ||

Or rather, just as one completes a remainder by removing the portions obstructed by a palace imagined by another, so too is the possibility of speaking of "junction" (saṃhitatva) here [in the case of phonemes]. 210.

Therefore, the distinction between the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā is due to the difference in the objects intended to be explained, just as there is a distinction between the *ṣaṭkas* (six-chapter sections) and between the chapters themselves. The Mīmāṃsā-śāstra begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and concludes with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), following a specific sequence determined by particular logical connections.

To the inquiry of one who is inattentive—asking, "Whence then is the manifestation of that difference, and even if difference exists, how can there be unity in the continuum?"—the author clarifies what is intended by the second commentary with the words "ataḥ" (from this). This means: from the authoritative tradition supported by reasoning. By the statement that [this] is what he intends to explain, it is indicated that although the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) and others in the *Karmakāṇḍa* aim to establish the excellence of ritual action, they lack any intention (*tātparya*) regarding the refutation of the deity's corporeal form and so forth, since those who lack certainty regarding the true nature of the deity are still capable of performing rituals.

For it has been stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "Just as the Venerable Jaimini’s presentation of the fruit of ritual action was intended to increase one's faith in that action. This has also been explained in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "In the section concerning the Deities (*Devatādhikaraṇa*), hyperbolic statements (*ativādāḥ*) were made so that those who have not heard the Vedānta might not lose faith in ritual action. The term "hyperbolic statements" refers to declarations made with another purpose in mind. The intention is that even by that much, the suspicion regarding the lack of authority of the Śruti—based on reasons such as its connection with impermanent things as asserted by outsiders—is dispelled; and from that very fact, one's own desired goal is accomplished.

Moreover, in this manner, within the first pāda of the ninth [chapter], among the two topics under consideration—namely, the fruit (*phala*) and the deity (*devatā*)—under the heading "And because of the fruit and the deity," and "Not from the injunction, for its quality is such," we shall explain those sūtras concerning the deity which begin with "Or the deity would cause [the sacrifice]," namely: "The substance to be given, intended for the deity, the deity does not cause [the sacrifice]. Why? Because, as in the case of agriculture and the like, it is logical that the action itself, being the means to the fruit, is what causes [the performance].

To this he replies: "Or rather, the deity should impel [the sacrificer], because the eating is for that purpose," as in the case of a guest. The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the doubt. The deity who is the intended recipient of the oblation (*havis*) should impel the seeker of results toward her own propitiation. Why? Because the eating is for that purpose; that is, because the eating of the oblation and its offering are for that purpose, being subordinate to it. For the deity, as the recipient (*sampradāna*), being the primary factor, impels the substance and its offering toward her own end.
Even though the deity is subordinate in sentences where the action is primary, [she remains the goal].
By the power of those respective mantras and so forth, it possesses the predominance of the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the deity is not an agent because of the absence of the fivefold attributes such as a physical body (*vigraha*); for its existence is established by the uncontradicted evidence of traditional texts (*smṛti*), figurative usage (*upacāra*), and the observation of other scriptural passages (*anyārthadarśana*). Therefore, just as a guest possessing a physical body and so forth is to be worshipped and employs the ritual service for his own sake according to his desire, so too does the deity. Furthermore, regarding the term *ārthapatya*: "artha" means prosperity (*vibhūti*) which is attained (*aryate*), or that which is sought after (*arthyate*). Consequently, one should not suspect that the deity is unworthy of worship due to the absence of such [prosperity], nor that it is ineffective because it does not grant what is desired.

The Supreme Deity indeed rules over everything, while another [deity] appointed by Her exercises various powers according to their respective jurisdictions. Nevertheless, the independent Deity would not be pleased by anything, nor does She please anyone; therefore, as to how She can be the instigator [of action], he says: "And thus, there is a connection with That."

Therefore, even though [the deity] is indifferent, the connection between the one who performs the service and the attainment of their desired fruit is established through such means as recollection (*smṛti*) and ritual application (*upacāra*), because the deity—though indifferent—is served by a royal policy characterized by compassion and generosity and thus becomes propitious; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is: "Or rather, because the word 'śara' (year) comes first, the sacrificial act would be primary. Here, the phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates a partial acceptance while setting aside the previous position.

Although the fivefold attributes of a deity, such as its corporeal form and so forth, are difficult to deny; although the recipient (saṃpradāna) is primary in relation to the substance and other factors; and although sacrifice, being synonymous with the propitiation of a deity, has that deity as its purpose; and although in established descriptive passages we learn the essential nature and other qualities of both the higher and lower deities for their own sake—nevertheless, in the injunctions regarding what is to be performed, ritual action in the form of sacrifice and the like is primary because it is enjoined as the means for attaining results such as heaven. Thus, by appearing as the goal to be accomplished, it impels the person toward action, while the deity and all else become subordinate to the action.

But surely we have heard that the deity who bestows the fruit possesses primacy by virtue of being the object of worship? To this, he says: "The scripture [declares] the deity to be subordinate. For we hear of the deity as having become subordinate with respect to the offering of the oblation (*havis*). That which consists of the propitiation of the deity—established through mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—is adopted as the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) that serves as the medium for the fruit arising at a later time from the enjoined action, which itself is momentary. Therefore, although the deity possesses actual primacy, it is subordinate to the ritual action, just like the verbal primacy that motivates one desiring the fruit.

"It is not the primary motivator. If that is so, how then does the guest function as the motivator? He explains it thus: "In the case of a guest, there would be a predominance of that [guest], and an absence [of purpose] regarding the ritual act. It follows that the guest is the predominant factor with respect to hospitality (*ātithya*); otherwise, since there would be no motivator for the ritual act intended for him, that act would simply not exist. If it is argued that the injunction for honoring him (*saparyā*) is itself the motivator, he replies to that: "Because it is a counter-measure (*pratividhāna*).
For the injunction for the ritual of hospitality is indeed issued precisely as a counter-measure to the arrival of the guest.

But the deity, being summoned by a person engaged in ritual action, becomes present for the sake of that person's desired object; it does not, however, follow from this that the deity is under the control of that person.
But when a guest arrives of his own accord, one should fulfill his own desired purpose; by complying with what he desires, one is prompted to perform service for him. (213)

Therefore, the statement regarding the preeminence of the guest is based on a discrimination between what is already attained and what is not yet attained. Just as there is never any harm in performing the ritual service for a guest even if that guest possesses a physical body and so forth—in fact, it results rather in the very attainment of his true nature—likewise, we see no success in refuting the deity’s possession of such attributes either. If it is asked, "What is the fruit even in establishing the subordinate status [of the guest]? the answer is: the strengthening of faith in ritual action even among those who have not yet determined the actual preeminence [of the deity].
Thus, in these sūtras, regarding the prior and subsequent positions:
This indicates that [the teachings] concerning possession by deities and so forth are not to be rejected. || 214 ||

Regarding the unity of the body and other such [attributes] asserted in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, their refutation does not appeal to those who recognize intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). (215)

Through the application of memory, through other scriptural observations, and because it was spoken by himself, that which he uttered cannot be denied by those other than the nihilists merely on the basis of words alone. (216)

When the meanings of what has been heard are denied through non-perception and fallacious reasoning, there arises the possibility of universal denial, resulting in the adoption of the views of the Cārvākas and others. (217)

The claim that the grammatical compounds and so forth heard in scripture are merely figurative is born of delusion; for you, however, there is the burden of postulating the non-existence of the powers of words and other such factors as taught in scripture. (218)

When considering what the door to the fruit might be for that which is momentary, it is better here to accept the alternative interpretation where the door is heard [in the scripture] rather than to construct one. (219)

The fact that deities have action as their purpose, and that ritual acts have them as their purpose, is established through different aspects; therefore, they do not deserve to contradict one another. (220)
By establishing the meditations on the sun and other deities within the sacrificial fire, Bādarāyaṇa has indicated that the preeminence of the deities is established by the very nature of the matter.
Furthermore, the perception of a deity’s form that has not been accomplished is not appropriate elsewhere;
nor should the procedure of perceiving [something as something else] be postulated everywhere without contradiction. (222)
Nor is the practice of austerity by the deities contradictory, because it is logically consistent with their engagement in such activity for the purpose of pleasing their own superior Lord. (223)
And for the Ruler, who desires to establish dharma by means of the Ghuṇī [science] and follows the dictates of his own karma, there shall be engagement in various respective duties.

The qualities and actions of animals, stationary beings, and insentient things, as well as their remedies, are regarded by the deities through their continuous attachment; this too has been heard in the scriptures.
The bestowal of different fruits occurs according to the specific types of oblations;
furthermore, provocation [of the deities] arises through prohibited acts, following the logic of the "king and so forth" (rājādinyāya).

If the nature [of the deity] in respect of the oblation and so forth is determined according to scripture, then it is appropriate that the respective nature of the one to be propitiated be accepted as such. (227)
Even though the meaning of a mantra is established through explanatory passages (arthavāda), where no contradiction is observed,
the Smṛti rooted therein is also not subject to sublation, just like its own source.

In various modes and in their distinct forms, the conceptualization of different deities occurs through the application of their respective names, in order to establish them as the objects of worship.
Those atheists who, failing to recognize their own dull-wittedness, have here spoken of dull-wittedness among the believers, are to be pitied by those of subtle vision. (230)
Even when the substance and the deity are common [to two mantras], the substance is more powerful;
this is because it is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whether it be perceptible or imperceptible. || 231 ||
The sacrificial nature of a substance established through perception is the domain of scripture;
likewise, the nature of the deity and its status as a dharma [are established] through their distinctness. (232)
Because it depends upon perception and other means of knowledge, cognition derived from scripture is delayed;
for this reason, there is a relative weakness even among the means such as direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The discrepancy between the material object and the deity does not arise from their being real or unreal;
for if the deity were false, how could it possess attributes such as differentiation? (234)
Whether its nature consists of words connected with meaning, or whether it consists of mere sound,
or even as it is grasped exactly as heard— verily, the deity is real.
Success through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth is accepted as being taught;
why then is that which is innate at birth not also accepted as being practiced among the gods? (236)

It is not appropriate to assume this here—as one might do when enjoining the vision of Deva regarding both an object and another location—because the injunction of the nature of *svarūpa* is more consistent [in the present case]. (237)

And according to the principle of the Rātrisatra and other such rites, by following the requirements of the injunctions, the deities are established as bestowers of fruits because they themselves constitute the fruit. (238)
Thus, by this ancient method, the doctrine that there is no divine being has been refuted;
the remainder will be addressed in the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "tadupari" (above that). 239.

The author of the Drāmiḍa-bhāṣya has also stated: "Starting from 'the form of the Creator of the universe is indeed manifest,' [he says] 'for no form is taught for a deity that is formless, since the scripture speaks of things as they truly are. Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not previously stated that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi*), whereas in the *Samanvaya* section it was stated otherwise? How, then, is there no contradiction? It is thus: because the two proceed by way of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*). And this is observed in other scriptures and in other sections (*kāṇḍa*) as well.

In this manner, contradictions imagined through false views (kudṛṣṭi) elsewhere must also be pacified. The phrase "like the division of the *Ṣaṭka*" serves as a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) regarding the *Karmakāṇḍa*, while "like the division of the chapters" applies to all three sections (*kāṇḍa*); the word "and" (*ca*) here includes other unstated divisions such as the *pādas*. Furthermore, the separate treatment of the *Śārīraka* from the *Devatākāṇḍa* is established by way of a counter-argument based on that very separation. Now, he clarifies—on the basis of what is established in the *Vṛtti*—the removal of the notions that [the *Brahmasūtra*] is a mere sequence of topics (*vinnakrama*) or a disjointed composition (*bhinnaprabandha*), by stating: "The Mīmāṃsā Śāstra."

The meaning is: "by a specific connection," that is, by a relationship such as that of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). And this [connection] is explained in the *Viṃśatilakṣaṇī* as the state of being accomplished by a single effort due to the accomplishment of a single purpose. This is for the sake of manifesting the unity of the work as a single treatise (*ekaprabandhya*). "With a specific order" means with a fixed order; the intention is that there is no sequence here based merely on the occasion (*avasara*) as in other treatises. In this regard, the distinction is as follows: "In this system, study is established as occurring prior to inquiry (*vicāra*) because of the injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, inquiry by one who has not studied the Veda is prohibited by the Śruti. (240)
The sequence of the twenty characteristics is not based on scriptural injunction (vaidha), but rather is logical (yauktika);
therefore, any consideration of a different order reveals its impropriety. || 241 ||

By the word "commencing" (*ārabhya*), the promise to investigate the meaning of the entire Veda is indicated in the *Dharmajijñāsā-sūtra*, because the term "dharma" (*dharma*) encompasses all established entities (*siddha*), things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), higher and lower levels, and the cause of the maintenance of the universe. Even the promise to investigate only the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) would be established therein either by the principle of "one [text] being the authority for another" (*tantratva*) or by repetition (*āvṛtti*). It is on this basis alone that the statement in the *Sāra* regarding the purpose of investigating ritual action is made. From the two specific promises concerning the two portions, the general promise is understood—just as in the *Nyāyasūtra*, from the mention of the "balancing of similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) and "balancing of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*), the "balancing of the counter-property" (*pratidharmasama*) is inferred. All of this has been stated in the *Saṅgatimālā*.

Nor should it be argued: "If the entire subject matter is established by the initial proposition alone, what is the purpose of the specific propositions? For this is appropriate both in the preceding chapters and here as well, due to purposes such as removing specific doubts. Furthermore, this opening—"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (Athāto dharmajijñāsā)—is not an irrelevant subject; for the intent is that just as elsewhere there is a fixed sequence of order through connection, so it is here. For in this context, since that which lacks a means of knowledge cannot be defined, the first chapter was devoted to the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Once the authority of the Veda has been established in its entirety, and since distinctions among its objects would be impossible—rendering all [notions] such as being a "subsidiary" (*aṅga*) untenable—the inquiry into the distinction between the subjects of the scriptures (*śāstrārtha-bheda*) proceeded immediately after the inquiry into the means of knowledge (*māna*). Some say it was an inquiry into the distinction between the scriptures themselves (*śāstra-bheda*). In that regard, once the distinction [between actions] is established through difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*), the definition of the "subsidiary" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) proceeds by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and title (*samākhyā*).

In the fourth [book], there is an inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), so that the remaining [subsidiaries] may be employed by their respective principals; some say this is an investigation into "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which consists in the requirement of the injunction. Once the subsidiaries have been enjoined, the order of sequence is set forth in the fifth [book] by means of direct statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), textual position (*pāṭha*), procedure (*pravṛtti*), principal action (*mukhya*), and section (*kāṇḍa*). When the meaning of the scripture has been established as possessing a specific order, the performer of those rites is declared in the sixth [book]. Thus, once the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*) has been taught, the general rule of extension (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) is established in the seventh [book]. In the eighth [book], too, the specific details connected with that [extension] are treated.

In the ninth [book], there is a manifold modification (*ūha*) of mantras and other elements that have been extended by analogy (*atideśa*). In the tenth, there is sublation (*bādha*), occurring where—among those things obtained through extension—there is an absence of purpose, or where it is obtained from another source, or due to an explicit prohibition. In the eleventh, there is the principle of common performance (*tantra*), which applies when both [the primary and secondary acts] possess the capacity for separate performance, yet share identity in place, time, and so forth. In the twelfth, there is the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), which occurs when one act falls within the middle of another performance and depends upon that performance.

They summarized this as follows: "By means of [the topics of] dharma, intellect, non-difference, auxiliaries, application, sequence, and agent; and by means of [the topics of] beginning, specific place, particularity, doubt, refutation, tantra, and repetition. Thus, when the ritual action had been reasoned out in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa* (the Section on Deities) consisting of four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*), the very deity to be worshipped through each respective rite was drawn forth (*nirakṛṣyata*) by way of distinctions in essential nature, qualities, and excellence.

And at its conclusion, because of the vision of Him in Hari, the elders of truth state that [the final section] was introduced as something to be investigated, saying: "They call Him Brahman; they call Him Brahman. Therefore, in the final book (kāṇḍa), the Supreme Deity—who is to be worshipped by all the dharmas taught in the twelve books (the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras) through both mediated and immediate means, and whose body is the aggregate of all deities as determined in the immediately preceding four books—is intended to be examined.

In that regard, the first chapter establishes the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all causal statements with Brahman by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "The concordance of sentences with Brahman—having set aside [the possibility of] being non-referential or having another referent—is demonstrated here by means of the first chapter. In the second chapter, the removal of suspected contradictions is treated.

By those two [the first and second chapters], Brahma is established through the process of origination (*utpatti-krama*); by the third and fourth, the excellence of the means and the fruit is shown. Thus, the specific sequence of the twenty chapters has been indicated merely in outline. Well then, in this case, how is the priority of the group of four [chapters] regarding the sixteen [categories] established? For even in the case of a reversal of order, it is not [invalidated].

As for the contradiction: although the authority of the Vedas and so forth are foundational, they can be addressed in their proper place within the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras); or, one might engage in reflection on Brahman after merely hearing that much. This is not so; for regarding the three aims of life (*trivarga*) practiced since time immemorial, the agent first becomes attached to them until he perceives their defects—this is the sequence of meaning.

Although there is no difference between the two cases regarding the immediate perception of limited or unlimited fruits, according to the maxim "if one can find honey in the mud itself," it is better to first undertake the contemplation of karma—which is free from conceptual construction and its like, and independent of knowledge—rather than the exertion of knowledge which is dependent upon karma. Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of sentences that constitute the limbs of those [meditations] depends upon the understanding of the meanings of terms such as "sacrifice" (*yajña*). Likewise, in various distinct meditations (*vidyā*), the investigation of injunctions for viewing sacrifices and their components depends upon the determination of the specific qualifiers of those views.

Furthermore, the cognitions regarding the examples such as the piling of bricks (*iṣṭakacita*) depend upon the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). Since the portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) abounding in ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman is studied according to the sequence of refinement established by the beginningless tradition of study, the sequence for investigating them is likewise logical. Moreover, this is the primary sequence (*mukhyakrama*) here, due to the order of the arising of the subsidiaries and the principal acts consisting of ritual action and meditation (*upāsanā*). Thus it has been stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "Because the relationship of cause and effect is accepted between the knowledge of ritual action and [the knowledge of] Brahman, the priority of ritual action is established, and the posteriority of the other."

And because those two [offerings] occur in a sequence, their respective deliberations should likewise follow that same order, just as in the case of the subsidiary rites of the Sarasvatī sacrifice. For instance, regarding the two sacrifices arising from a pair—based on the mantra "These two are indeed the divine couple"—when it is not determined which of the two has priority among the subsidiaries, the priority of the sacrifice to Sarasvatī is established by its *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; consequently, it is stated that the priority of its subsidiaries follows that sequence, according to the principle: "Or rather, the order of the subsidiaries follows the order of the principal, because they exist for its sake.
This is because the principles well-known in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) are here being summarized.
Remember also that which was stated in the preceding chapters: that the section on Brahman would be in vain.

The exposition of what was previously unknown, as well as its establishment by means of refutation, and in some cases an exception—by these, the meaningfulness of this [treatise] is established here. (243)

Now, if the Mīmāṃsā concludes with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement," then—since the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras] accept that only the dispassionate are qualified [for its study], and since an infallible, infinite fruit is determined therein—no one would succeed in performing the means for fruits such as heaven; consequently, the injunctions regarding optional rites (kāmya-vidhi) would suffer invalidity characterized by non-performance.

It is not so: for those who, out of delusion or due to obstacles, have rested after merely investigating ritual action; or those who, desiring only fame, gain, honor, and the propagation of their own doctrines, might contemplate the meaning of the Upanishads; or those whose dispassion has later subsided through the force of destiny—even though they have heard the *Śārīraka*, such persons would abandon the dharma of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*).
Even a wise man, when afflicted by illness, may engage in unwholesome things;
why then should that which is desired not likewise occur even in a wise person regarding forbidden acts? (244)
Even great beings are said to possess both types of cultivation due to desire;
for some, gradual liberation is likewise taught. (245)

For instance: first of all, by the injunction "one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," the grasping of the collection of syllables called the Veda—which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*—is prescribed by the act of study itself. The phrase beginning with "for instance" (*tathā hi*) is stated for the purpose of establishing the sequence and the logical consistency of the present subject matter: the inquiry into Brahman and the undertaking of the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*). (Verse 146)

Regarding this, keeping in mind the following dilemma—namely, whether one intends for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) to precede even the study [of the Veda], or whether it should precede the investigation of ritual action (*karmanirūpaṇa*) by one who has already studied the Veda—the author negates the first alternative with the word "first" (*prathamam*). The *Vivaraṇa* explains that the word "first" (*tāvat*) demonstrates that the immediate succession of the inquiry to the study of the Veda is accepted by all.

By this, it is indicated that—just as inquiry (*vicāra*) occurs immediately after study (*adhyayana*)—the subject matter to be explained possesses the nature of a single, continuous composition with a fixed sequence, which is the object of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of study established by a single injunction; that study, by the force of the injunction, has the entirety of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) as its object; and for that very reason, the same applies to the inquiry thereof. This is difficult for anyone who properly reflects upon both ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman to deny. Alternatively, the word *tāvat* may be used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

Furthermore, because the study of other scriptures is precluded by the disciplined study that follows immediately after the initiation ceremony at eight years of age—which is preceded by instruction in the rules of purity and conduct—the possibility of other prior conditions, such as the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) which might be presumed to be its root, is eliminated. By adopting the self-injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied," the necessity for its application is intended. Through the statement "by study, the mass of syllables is grasped," the attainment of refinement (*saṃskāra*) is indicated. Here, the particle *eva* (only) illuminates the fact that this restriction is the resulting consequence.

Although this injunction for study is obligatory (*nitya*) because of the sin incurred by non-performance and the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from its performance as a specific occasion (*nimitta*), nevertheless, since a visible fruit (*dṛṣṭaphala*) cannot be abandoned, when the mass of syllables is acquired through study undertaken for the sake of attaining that [visible fruit], there is no room here for another cause of acquisition. For even one who asserts that study is for the sake of the mandatory injunction (*niyoga*) must, by implication, prohibit reading from books and the like; it is for this very reason that there is also censure of those who read from written texts.

By the three [verses] beginning with "That which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*," it is indicated that neither merely a portion of one's own recited scripture (*svaśākhā*) nor the meaning of the Vedas is what is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*; rather, the sense is that study according to the traditional sequence is sanctioned by injunction. "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is enjoined and understood as the fruit; the meaning is that while other means might be possible, this fruit is restricted to a specific means. Since the restrictive particle *eva* is used, the restriction applies to something other than that [which is excluded].

Although there is no restriction regarding the essential nature of grasping the syllables, since that can be accomplished through other means as well, nevertheless, the restriction is justified on the grounds that the utility for recitation and so forth applies only to what has been acquired through formal study (*adhyayana*). Those who assert a restriction regarding the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) are likewise saved by this same reasoning.

In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of that study is and how it is to be performed, the following are prescribed through such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brahmin boy who is eight years old and teach him," and through specific instructions on vows and observances such as: "Having performed the *upākarma* rite according to rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being self-restrained, should study the Vedas for four and a half months. Thus, those matters required by the context are established.

Surely, by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), only the fact that one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied is understood. By that much alone, there is no obstruction to the opportunity for other scriptures which serve as causes for the attainment of the fourfold qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth; for it is possible to study [those others] even after that. Whether one studies them without the preliminary rites or having studied [the Veda] once, let one practice other scriptures—regarding this, he clarifies the nature, time, and qualification for study with the word "that" (*tat*); the meaning is that it refers to the initial study established by the universally accepted obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*).

"What is its form?"—does this mean an independent recitation like that of *japa* and so forth, or is it a non-recitation; or is it based on a different principle like the study of the *Gauḍa* [Veda], or like the *pārāyaṇa* (which is not repeated), or is it repeated like the threshing of grain? By the word "form" (*rūpa*), the inclusion of the fruit is intended; thus, even for the *Tūlikā*, the intent is that it consists of a repeated form until the goal is reached. "How? refers to the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*).

With the intention of showing that there must necessarily be a distinction and a harmony between those supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) which are accepted as being for the purpose of study—though they might be suspected of being for the purpose of teaching—and those [other texts] that require supplementation, he makes this specific mention by dividing them as "and by these instructions. The statement "having performed the *upākarma*, one should study" establishes the intended meaning of the Vedic injunction that "one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) should study," for it is precisely for the sake of the study of one who has been initiated that the *upākarma* and other rites are prescribed. "Diligent" (*yukta*) means attentive, or else, engaged in the observances (*vrata*) and so forth.

Those for whom the fifth is half are "half-fifth" (*ardhapañcama*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included the previously mentioned statements consistent with the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), such as: "But from this point onward, one should regularly recite the *Chandas* (Vedas) during the bright fortnights; and one should thoroughly recite all the *Vedāṅgas* during the dark fortnights. The "particular observances" (*vrata-viśeṣa*) are those accompanied by initiatory rites (*sopākṛti*), such as the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, and others.

The "particular rules" (*niyama-viśeṣa*) concern the distinctions in the time of Vedic recitation divided according to the bright and dark fortnights, the half-month, the fifth month, and so forth, as well as matters concerning place and other factors as stated in passages such as, "One should not study in the presence of a Śūdra."

Thus, it is understood that study (*adhyayana*) has as its fruit the acquisition of the mass of syllables (*akṣararāśi*), consisting of the repetition of what is uttered by the teacher—an instructor who knows the Vedas, is endowed with self-qualities such as steadfastness in good conduct born of a lineage of virtuous ancestors, and who initiates the student; and this [study] is characterized by specific vows and observances.

One might object: "Since the Vedic injunction *upanayīta tam adhyāpayet* (he should initiate him and teach him) prescribes the duties of the teacher, how can it be a rule required for the student's study? And how can it be established here that even by this implied scriptural authority (*upātta-śruti*), there is the prevention of opportunities for other scriptures? To this he says: *evam* (thus). This means: by the manner of enjoining the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), which is established by one's own injunction assisted by the aforementioned Śruti and Smṛti; [and] by the teacher [being defined] through such [qualifications] as "one who is distinguished by noble birth and learning" (*abhijana-vidyā-samudeta*).

One should not suspect that the passage is intent upon enjoining the act of teaching because of the mention of qualities (*guṇa*), following the logic of the statement regarding the qualities of a priest (*ṛtvij*); it is with this intention that the phrase "in a lineage of the virtuous" (*satsantāne*) and so forth is stated. Here, the words "composed" (*samāhita*) imply both proper conduct (*ācāra*) and personal qualities (*ātma-guṇa*). The term "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) clarifies the state of being fully endowed with knowledge. Furthermore, teaching from an unfit person is prohibited, and [the requirement] is restored when those qualities are lacking. Likewise, the loss incurred by the student is described in such passages as, "He indeed enters from darkness into darkness."

The fact that these qualities belong to the student is evident from such statements as "he should seek out a preparer" and "in him alone [the teacher should impart] the end of knowledge and action.
