Just as for those who maintain that the injunction to teach is the primary rule, the qualifications of the student—such as being eight years old—are for the sake of the teacher, so too the qualifications of the teacher are for the sake of the student. To indicate this parallelism, the phrase "endowed with specific vows and observances" and so forth has been cited; for by means of the two words ending in the genitive case, the qualified person (adhikārin) is also shown to be a specific observance, and because one who has been initiated at eight years of age is already encompassed by the injunction to study.

By the phrase "the teacher's utterance followed by the student's non-independent (anūñcāraṇa) utterance," independent utterance and the suspicion that reflection might enter into the meaning of the study-scripture are excluded. Just as, according to another view, the presence of a disciple suitable for teaching is considered an auxiliary factor due to its visible result [in the form of instruction], so too, in this view, there is a proximity conducive to the non-independent utterance. And such is the intended sense.

In this first chapter, disregarding specific details such as "once," "not once," "twice," or "thrice" according to the logic of threshing (*avaghātanyāya*), he says—"the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables"—intending that the purpose of repetition is established by the attainment of the result. By this, it is also indicated that the desire to grasp the syllables is a qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) [of the seeker]. Even though it is adopted as the fruit, its status as such is like being husked [of grain];
and the utility of even such grasping in sacrifices and other rites is difficult to deny. (247)

For one who desires the knowledge of the meaning here as the fruit [of study] according to injunction or permission, it is difficult to maintain that its status as a compulsory duty (nitya) would be lost due to its connection with a fruit. (248)

However, those who—regarding the injunction for the compulsory study (*nityādhyayana*) as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—postulate heaven as the fruit, being indistinguishable from all [desires] according to the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice, and who postulate the knowledge of meaning as the fruit in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), are also refuted by this [argument]: for it is logical that the apprehension of syllables, which is a perceptible result, should have the status of a fruit—even though it is distinct from pleasure—because, like the knowledge of meaning and so forth, it culminates in pleasure and the like.

Thus, both the non-deficiency of the syllables and the fruit of grasping the collection of syllables have been shown to constitute the nature of the meaning of the primary study (*adhyayana*), as to what its form might be. And so the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) states: "The function of a verbal root (*dhātu*) consists in a collection of momentary actions delimited by a single result, as in the case of 'he cooks rice' (*odanaṃ pacati*); otherwise, there would be the consequence of violating the indication of the present tense. For the meaning of the word 'present' is that which has begun but is not yet completed."

However, if action—which is momentary—were the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then because the moment of action already known prior to the utterance of the word has perished, and because the subsequent moment is yet to come, and because a simultaneous moment cannot be cognized and thus cannot be an object of the word, it follows that even if it were perceptible, its beginning, middle, and end could not be determined due to its destruction in each moment; consequently, neither its commencement nor its completion could be established. Therefore, he states that the term "studying" (*adhyayana*) applies to a collection of momentary actions delimited by the result of grasping [the text].

The statement that study consists of the non-original recitation performed by one initiated by a teacher clarifies that both injunctions—“one should initiate him” and “one should teach him”—prescribe that study must be preceded by initiation and other rites performed by the teacher.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the injunction "one should teach" (adhyāpayet) is intended as a restrictive rule regarding the means of livelihood? [Reply: Not so; for even one who has not been initiated (anupanetr) is seen to teach for that purpose, which would render the injunction for initiation (upanayana-vidhāna) useless. Nor is there a restriction of sequence such that "one should teach only one who has been initiated," because that would result in the injunctions such as "a Brāhmaṇa of eight years" being rendered unnecessary. Furthermore, teaching that [initiation] here for some other purpose is entirely inconsistent. Nor can a restriction regarding initiation be suspected here, since no other source is observed that establishes it. If it is argued that a Smṛti text is observed, we say no, because the mention of "eight years" and so forth would be redundant.

O King, there is no statement here of two means of livelihood (*vṛtti*); for initiation (*upanayana*) is not enumerated as such a means. Even if that were the case, the impossibility of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) has already been stated due to the absence of a motivator (*prāpaka*), and because [this objection] has already been answered. Therefore, this is simply an injunction (*vidhi*) required by the act of study. And in this context, the injunction would be one that prompts action (*prayojaka*), like the command "one should cause [someone else] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). For teaching (*adhyāpana*) also, being established as a means of livelihood just like officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), is not something to be enjoined.

Therefore, in this context, an eight-year-old Brahmin, desiring to acquire the Veda (*svādhyāya*), having been initiated by a teacher according to the aforementioned procedure, should approach him and study while observing the vows and rules as prescribed. This establishes the meaning of the scriptural injunction for study, including its supporting arguments. For this very reason, it is improper to assume that the performance [of study] is prompted by something else simply because no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is heard of in the injunction for study; for such an assumption would apply equally to both cases, since no such person is heard of in the injunction for teaching either. Nor is such an assumption made here.

The establishment of that [obligation] follows from the mere modification of the case endings in passages such as "A Brāhmaṇa... for those desiring offspring and so forth, and because it is supported by the Smṛti text, "A Brāhmaṇa should study. If it is argued that a child cannot be prompted by its own injunctions due to ignorance of its own entitlement (*adhikāra*), we say no; for, according to the principle of the "Niṣāda chief" (*niṣādasthapati-nyāya*), the performance is possible through others who are cognizant of it. Indeed, even for children and others who do not know their own entitlement, well-wishers—themselves knowing the utility of the rites—perform the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*) such as the birth rite (*jātakarman*).
However, in the case of Vedic study, it is appropriate for a child to engage in it through the instigation of authoritative persons and the like, since its success can be inferred therefrom.

For those who maintain that constant study is prompted by desire for results, how can there be in that case the characteristic of a mandate (niyoga) having the performance of the action as its objective? 249.
"For those who are awakened, [liberation occurs] through their own method, while for the unawakened it is from another;
yet, in postulating such a distinction in application, there would be the fallacy of the 'half-old woman' (ardhajaratīya)."

And as for the claim that, in the case of a student who has completed the hardship of study, the knowledge of meaning—which is perceived prior to reflection—is accepted as the purpose to be accomplished through the subject matter, in order to bring the injunction of study to its completion regarding entitlement (*adhikāra*); that too is weak. For if study were established from another source, it would be improper to postulate a further purpose for it based on an effect that is already established and is not itself the motive for that study. Rather, like other obligatory rites (*nitya*), this too is logically shown to have the mere performance of the mandate (*niyoga*) as its sole purpose.

If it is argued that something other than the visible result is also permitted [by the injunction], we say no; for then there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting even incidental gains such as profit and honor, since they too would be permitted by the injunction here. Nor can it be said that the injunction permits only the knowledge of meaning because it is useful for the performance of Dharma, and nothing else; for wealth and so forth are also useful for that purpose, and thus those too would be granted permission. While the knowledge of meaning may indeed be helpful to all injunctions, one does not disregard other visible results on the basis of this much distinction alone. (251)

If you argue that wealth and the like assist [the person] through their own inherent power, then knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda] would likewise be so; it would not be subject to the brow of a ritual injunction.
In its true sense, that [Vedic injunction] is authorized and manifested through the very power of the word;
let it be relied upon by those dependent on the injunctions for sacrifice, giving, and so forth. (253)
Moreover, it would follow that a single [action] possesses a dual nature because it consists of both an injunction and a permission;
furthermore, this would apply to the distinction between a primary action (*pradhānakarman*) and a subsidiary action (*guṇakarman*). (254)

Therefore, it is a well-known fact even in your own villages that at the very time of beginning the study of the Veda, teachers and others, intending what is beneficial for the boy—whether by their own intelligence or through the instruction of others—act as the instigators of that study. No one, however, is seen engaging in this with the thought, "I must assume the role of a teacher for another. Furthermore, those who wish him well, while instructing him, point out to the child the future results [of his learning].

And in the *Chāndogya*: Jābāla said to Gautama, "I shall dwell as a religious student (*brahmacarya*) under the Blessed One; I would approach the Blessed One"; and he was replied to by him: "Bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the teacher acts solely for the sake of the disciple, and that the student must obtain the sacrificial fee (*vara*) and other requirements from him. For this very reason, the claim made by some—that study is motivated by the teacher's desire arising from greed for the acquisition of wealth and the like—is refuted.

This is established in order to show that, even though its own injunction (*svavidhi*) may not be applicable, the application of the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*) is nonetheless untenable. For it is not possible to compel a boy (*māṇavaka*) to act without first making him understand his own purpose; otherwise, the teacher’s activity would amount to a mere forced exertion. Therefore, in the injunction for the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅgādhyayanavidhi*), the Brahmin and others—who are explicitly mentioned—are the qualified agents (*adhikārin*) acting with the intent of their own welfare; thus, there is no application [of the student] by any other [injunction].

By this, the argument raised by some—that if the impulsion (*prayukti*) of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) is not accepted, then since the impulsion of the ritual injunctions (*kratuvidhi*) must necessarily be resorted to, even Śūdras and others desiring those respective fruits would have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for study—is refuted; for study is impelled by its own injunction, which has a fixed agent just like the rite of consecrating the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Furthermore, the objection regarding the lack of a stated qualification (*adhikāra*) in the injunction for study is also answered by stating that the result is the apprehension of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), which is a visible effect (*dṛṣṭa*) similar to threshing (*vaituṣya*).

The Smṛti passage beginning with "upanīya" (having initiated) also does not enjoin teaching, nor does it take the status of being an *ācārya* as its result; for its purpose is merely to etymologize the word *ācārya* by way of restating a specific form of teaching already established through other means, just as it etymologizes words such as *upādhyāya*. Indeed, there is no reason here to assume an intention distinct from that. Nor is there a single, separate kind of *ācārya*-ship [distinct from the teacher of a portion], as there is no evidence for it. If it is argued that this is postulated because no other basis is observed, we say no.

This is because we observe that the ground for the application [of the term] is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) with the act of teaching, which is brought about by the restrictive condition of initiation (*upanayana*). For this very reason, even at a time subsequent to the initiation and so forth, the use of the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) is justified according to the principle of the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*) and others. However, previously, because it is difficult to anticipate the future, there is no usage due to doubt regarding the cognition of the ground for the application. Furthermore, if the Smṛti text here were intended merely to derive the meaning of the word, its source is seen to be nothing other than the linguistic usage of the elders.

If, however, it were intended as an injunction for the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), then one would have to assume that it is rooted in a scriptural text whose meaning is not known from worldly experience (*alaukikārtha*). And when there is a conflict between what is already established (*klpta*) and what must be assumed (*kalpya*), the established alone should be accepted. Furthermore, the scriptural mention of the suffix *-ktvā* and so forth—in passages such as "having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—is compatible even if [the acts] are not subsidiary parts (*anaṅga*), provided there is merely the commonality of having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) as stated in the Sūtra. [Objection: But surely, because of the natural force of the single-agent construction and the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), the relationship of principal and subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgitva*) would be established through a single performance (*ekaprayoga*). [Reply: That is not so; for the scriptural mention of *-ktvā* resides in Smṛti, and it may also function as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
In this case, the indicative mark (liṅga) residing in the direct statement (śruti) is indeed stronger, because it lacks any delay.

The *upanayana*, which is heard in the Veda as being for the sake of the single refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the boy—referred to by the term "Brāhmaṇa"—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the student's study (*adhyayana*) alone. This is because, despite its proximity to both fruitful activities—studying and teaching—it resides within the ritual action (*karmastha*) and thus possesses an internal indicative mark (*antaraṅga-liṅga*) that connects it to the study performed by the initiated boy. If it were intended for another purpose, there would be a need for an indirect application (*praṇāḍyā*). Thus, since the *upanayana* is enjoined for study by a direct Vedic indicative mark (*śrauta-liṅga*), to assume it is also an auxiliary to teaching would constitute a contradiction between what is already enjoined and what is being further enjoined (*viniyukta-viniyoga-virodha*).

For a non-hearing of the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) based on Smṛti is not capable of subverting a *liṅga* (indicative mark) based on Śruti; this is because it is obstructed by a double delay: Smṛti depends upon its own source (the Veda), and a restatement (*anūkti*) depends upon what was previously stated. [Objection: But surely, from the ātmanepada prescribed by rules such as Pāṇini 1.3.72 (*svarita-jita...*), initiation (*upanayana*) would be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the teaching (*adhyāpana*) residing in the initiator (*upanetṛ*). [Response: It would not be so, because it is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *sammānana* (Pāṇini 1.3.36).

The Grammarians (Śābdikas) maintain that this [present] undertaking has the sense of "not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāya*). They argue: "Intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*) means the connection of the fruit with the agent alone, whereas "not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāyatva*) is simply the absence of such a restriction. If this is argued, we say no; for even in the case of the *ātmanepada* ending prescribed by the rule beginning with *svarita* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), as in the example *ādadhīta*, the fruit is connected to both [the agent and another]. Nor is it the case that the fruit of the action cannot be connected to two conscious beings; for that is observed even in the instance: *jāyāpatī agnimādadhīyātām* ("Husband and wife should install the fire"). Furthermore, the claim that the fruit is not connected to a conscious being other than the agent is also refuted.

From the perspective of authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika*), in all scriptural matters, because there are scriptural declarations of results consisting of love toward one who is not the agent but the object of worship, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of losing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in cases such as *ādhāna*. Furthermore, in passages such as "one should sacrifice while practicing sorcery" (*abhicaranyajeta*), a result appropriate to that [action] is accepted even for the enemy (*bhrātṛvya*). And in the case of "he chooses the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*), the result is established even for those being chosen. Since the term "result of the action" (*kriyāphala*) is intended to denote the immediate result, its connection with the agent constitutes the state of being "intended by the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*).

As for the argument that the *Sammānanādi-sūtra* must serve to establish the connection of the agent with a remote result, this too has already been answered: because there is a deviation [in the rule] in cases such as "one should establish" (*ādadhīta*), where the result—namely, the status of being one who has established the fires (*āhitāgnitva*)—belongs to the agent even though it is mediated by the consecration of the fire. Now, one might object: "The very accomplishment of the consecrated fire, which serves as the basis for future obligatory and optional sacrifices, is the result for the agent; thus, there is no connection with a remote result. Do not say so.

In this case as well, since the very accomplishment of the student who has undergone the initiation (*upanayana*) rite is the fruit for the initiator (*upanetṛ*), it would follow that the sūtra concerning "honoring" (*sammānana*) and so forth would be rendered purposeless. If it is argued that the two sūtras are effective because the immediate fruit is either desired or not desired by the agent, we say no; for even an initiator who seeks the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) cannot fail to desire the rite of initiation for the one being initiated. Therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here is used solely to establish the connection with the agent. Likewise, by the expression "one should teach," the fruit does not accrue to the agent. Thus, in this manner, study is not prompted by another injunction.

And as for reflection (*vicāra*), is it enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*)? Not the first, because the [objection regarding] the lack of a subject matter and a fruit has already been refuted. Not the second, because it would not exceed the limit of what is prescribed.

For once the teacher has caused [the student] to grasp the *svādhyāya*, he too may desist. However, if [reflection] is prompted by compassion and the like, then it was already established that this is the case even prior [to the completion of study]. (256)
Therefore, thinking that according to the Guru’s view even the entire Mīmāṃsā system would not be established, those who wish to maintain the original position have refuted it. (257)
And study is a refinement of the Veda (svādhyāya); for from the injunction "the Veda is to be studied," it is understood that the Veda is the object of the action.

Although, in this way, the opportunity for other treatises is blocked until the letters have been grasped, there may still arise the doubt that such an opportunity might exist once the letters have been grasped. To prevent this even subsequently, the author clarifies—by rejecting the view that study is the object of an injunction—that it is, as previously indicated, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text), stating: "study" (*adhyayanam*). The particle *ca* serves to dispel that doubt; or rather, it is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*), serving to conjoin the nature of being a refinement with [the fact that it consists of] repeated recitation and so forth.

By those who maintain that "consecration (saṃskāra) is intended for the person alone through means such as recitation and sprinkling," it is accepted that even the consecration of study belongs to the agent alone. To dispel the doubt that [therefore] the intended meaning is not established, he says: "svādhyāya" (one's own Veda). And it has been stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "In the enumeration of consecrations, the consecration of the syllables is indeed appropriate; for 'svādhyāya' is clearly an action, and it is that which is directly consecrated.
Those who understand the imparting of excellence to the person through sprinkling and other such acts [are here addressed].
They too did not abandon their status as conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and karma in each respective case. || 258 ||
The impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by various specific actions resides in the person;
for it is determined that, when conjoined with those [actions], it brings about the respective effects. (259)

In this context, since study (*adhyayana*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), its status as an object (*karman*) serves as the reason; thus, there is no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This is the underlying point: here, no other meaning for the suffix *tavya* is possible. Consequently, whether the accusative case-ending or the suffix *tavya* itself denotes the object, there is no distinction between them. Furthermore, although grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) exist for the sake of an action, because the verbal sense (*bhāva-artha*) residing in the substance is for the sake of the substance, the principle of "beating" (*avahanti-nyāya*) and so forth is appropriate here.

Furthermore, it is established in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa* (1.4.23) that the acts of threshing and so forth constitute the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of their respective substances, and that these [actions] are twofold, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*). By the phrase "of one's own study" (*svādhyāyasya*), the impossibility of [the Veda] being something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth is indicated; for it is certainly not something to be produced, since its sequence is established from time immemorial (*anādi-siddha-krama*), and because there is no usage of constructing a sentence [from it] as there is in the case of previous utterances. Nor is it something to be modified (*vikārya*), since no change of state is observed, as is seen in the case of milk becoming curds and the like.

Nor does it consist merely in being something to be attained, for that would be incompatible with its having other functions [such as recitation]. Therefore, the understanding of its status as an object (*karman*), supported by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), is the reason for its being something to be refined (*saṃskārya*).

For "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) indeed means the production of fitness for another purpose. And it is appropriate that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) be something to be refined, because it provides knowledge of the four aims of human existence—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as well as their means; and because it serves as a means to those ends even in its own form through practices such as silent recitation (*japa*).

Now, one might ask: even if it is understood that the Veda is an object of action (*karman*), how can the Veda—which is not yet enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) and the like, and is not a physical substance (*adravya*)—be something to be refined (*saṃskārya*)? To this, he says: "For [the word] *saṃskāra* [is used] in the sense of a well-known convention (*hi* indicates renown); the particle *nāma* indicates excellence up to the point of gaining the approval of others. Here, the expression "making it fit for another purpose" is stated with the intention of referring to a refinement that, once produced in the Veda, will be useful for a future goal. Alternatively, the definition of refinement (*saṃskāra*) here is "the imparting of an excellence (*atiśaya*) to something already existing."

[This has been] explained. Therefore, even though [the *paridhi* sticks] are already in use, the term "fitness for another effect" (*kāryāntara-yogyatā*)—which implies fitness for a different function corresponding to that [new purpose]—must somehow be applied here with the intention of expressing a usage suited to that end. For it is heard in scripture that even when they have been employed as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), they remain fit for another effect in the form of assisting the ritual (*bhūtopakāra*) by means of that very same form. The underlying point is this: it is not the case that they cannot be consecrated simply because they have not been specifically enjoined for this purpose; for even in the absence of a specific injunction, their status as objects of consecration is possible precisely through the observation of their utility.

Furthermore, there is an application (viniyoga) both general and specific, such as "the Hotṛ priest acts with the Ṛgveda" and so forth. Nor is it the case that [the Veda] cannot be an object of ritual refinement (saṃskāra) because it is not a substance; for there is no contradiction provided it has been acquired through study as previously described. Moreover, the fact that [the Veda] is an object of apprehension is universally accepted even in the case of qualities and other categories.

Even though the excellence (*atiśaya*)—consisting of the Lord’s grace—which is to be accomplished by the action enjoined, does not reside in the Veda itself, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because that very excellence, being attained through study and apprehended by the cognition of the object of worship, restricts the subsequent action as appropriate according to the scripture. Whether or not an imperceptible excellence arises in rice and other materials through sprinkling and so forth, the stated principle applies universally.

[Objection: But surely, even though in cases such as "one offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*) or "gold is to be worn" (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*), one understands that the object (*karman*) lacks the status of being something to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth, the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) does not have the purpose of [merely] referring to the substance (*dravyārthatā*). Likewise, in injunctions for muttering (*japa*), such as "the Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) or "one should study the Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhīyīta*), the understanding of the object is no different. Therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that case; or else, in those instances too, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the object being something merely to be refined (*saṃskārya*). To this, he says: "The state of being something to be refined... (*saṃskāryatvam*).

The intended meaning is as follows: because it is impossible for groats and the like to have utility either in the past or the future; because recitation and the like necessarily have the syllables already grasped as their object; because it would be cumbersome to postulate numerous latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); because no other utility is observed to be accomplished by the latent impressions produced by recitation and so forth; and because a fruit is heard [promised] in those cases, one abandons the notion of a latent impression there. However, that would not be the case here, since the status of these as ritual actions (*karman*), once understood, remains uncontradicted.

On this very point, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states: "We maintain that the first study is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*), because it is measured as an action and because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is useful [for other purposes] even though no specific fruit is heard [in the injunction]. If it were claimed that even recitation (*japa*) and the like are purificatory acts, then the first study would not be a purification, since it is not useful for the entire Veda. Consequently, the status of being an action would contradict the nature of the Veda everywhere; therefore, the first study must be a purificatory act, while the others are primary acts (*arthakarman*)."

In this case, the fruit must be that which is mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice. Here, the wise maintain that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is an unintended object (*anīpsita-karma*), whereas in the former [type of injunction], it is considered an intended object (*īpsita-karma*), and the ritual action is regarded as being for its sake. If even recitation (*japa*) and the like were merely preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), then the only useful result of the Veda—which is the object of all such preparations—would be the comprehension of its meaning. However, since that [comprehension] would be useless regarding those portions of the ritual not authorized for performance, as well as regarding the *hum* and other such sounds, all studies of the Veda would consequently become purposeless acts.

In that case, the status of *svādhyāya* as the object of the action would be destroyed; therefore, the first study alone is the purificatory act (*saṃskāra*). [Objection: But even here, since no utility is observed, the argument remains untenable; for if one assumes utility solely on the basis of its being a thing to be purified (*saṃskārya*), there is a circular dependency. And they say: "A rule of purification does not enjoin the thing to be purified; rather, a rule of purification—which culminates in purification—applies to that whose utility is already established by another means of knowledge, and it does not postulate a purpose for the thing to be purified. To this, he replies: "For the sake of Dharma" (*dharmārtha*). For it is because no utility is observed that the scriptural injunction regarding the action is set aside in the case of groats (*saktu*) and the like.

The sense is that, because various visible and invisible purposes for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) are observed—just as in the case of *saktu* (barley-meal) and other substances—it is not logical to regard it as something that cannot be refined (*asaṃskāryatva*). Here, the statement that the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are to be known through the Veda is intended to demonstrate that the entire work is to be investigated (*mīmāṃsitavyatva*), by showing a common purpose that runs through all its parts; it is also intended to show that those [aims] taught in non-Vedic systems are not to be trusted. Even though some objects of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) and their means are established in the world, it is appropriate that wealth and pleasure in the form of sovereignty over the three worlds, etc., as well as their means, are to be known through the Veda.

The operation of the scripture is established even regarding worldly objects and desires through means such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice. However, while *dharma* may be perceptible in the form of substances and so forth, it is apprehended by the scripture specifically as a means to stability (*dhṛti*). As they say: "For their status as means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda; and since its nature as *dharma* consists in that [status], it is therefore not within the range of the senses."

Furthermore, liberation (mokṣa) is not perceptible to people like us. As for arguments such as "the self is at some time devoid of all specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), because it possesses non-eternal specific qualities, like a jar," they do not constitute valid inference because there is no subverting proof (bādhaka) against the contrary case (vipakṣa). If one were to state a subverting proof against the contrary case by relying on the scriptures that aim at liberation, then the inference would be futile. However, since liberation consists in the experience of Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss, there is no possibility of the application of a logical reason [to prove its absence]; if one were to attempt to prove the opposite of that, it would be contradicted by scripture (āgamabādha).

Moreover, it can also be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is never devoid of all its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because it possesses the nature of self (*ātmatva*), just like the Lord (*īśvara*). In this context, since dharma is a means for achieving the desired goal—just as wealth is—it is a particular excellence of the human aim; therefore, it too is designated by the term "means" (*sādhana*). Furthermore, it should be understood that both the *mantras* and the *arthavādas* appropriately convey the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) or assist in conveying them.

Even in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others such as the *vajra*, there is no injunction toward what is harmful (*anartha*), because they merely instruct on the instrumental part (*upāyāṃśa*) for achieving desired ends such as the destruction of enemies.
And in this case, protection may be obtained even from other terrible means;
for they declare that malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) can be overcome by a light expiation. || 261 ||
Furthermore, it is taught that "one who does not practice sorcery shall fall into the six [hells]";
by this, they understand that killing an *ātatāyin* (aggressor) is consistent with the Dharma.

But surely, the capacity to convey extraordinary human goals and so forth exists even in the Smṛtis and other texts; therefore, if the purpose is to be accomplished by other means, what is the use of the Veda’s refinement? Furthermore, there is no comprehension of meaning in the case of *hum* and similar sounds. Moreover, even if such comprehension were present in cases where the portion is not yet understood or not intended to be performed due to differences among persons, it would be of no use because it would lack the quality of extending to actual performance. Thus, in this context:

Because the utility of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is obtainable through other means, because it is impossible for the act of recitation (*adhyayana*) to be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the entire *svādhyāya*, and because a refinement of only a single part would not be supported by the Vedic word itself; and since, in the absence of its being an injunction for refinement, the position that it serves the purpose of a mandatory duty (*niyoga*) alone would otherwise result, he says: "by means of muttering (*japa*), etc. By the word "etc.," memorization (*dhāraṇa*) is included. "Even in its own form" means not only by way of the knowledge of the meaning. Alternatively, teaching (*adhyāpana*) may be understood as what is included by the word "etc."

Then, by its own nature—that is, by the mere nature of that which has been shaken off—according to the Smṛti text beginning with "the wise man, upholding the Ṛgveda. This is the intended meaning: knowledge is accomplished solely through the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) as acquired through formal study.

The injunctions (*vidhi*) are that which must be relied upon for subsistence; however, the explanatory supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) do not possess the capacity to be means for achieving *dharma* and so forth independently. Furthermore, there is a scriptural text (*śruti*): "By constant study of the Vedas, by truth, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. Such well-known purposes as the recitation of mantras (*japa*), which cannot be accomplished by any other means, are established. By that very fact, even in those portions intended for performance by those who are unqualified or whose actions would otherwise be purposeless, the status of being an object of refinement (*saṃskāryatva*) is logically justified.

Furthermore, the injunction for recitation (*japa*), even when its object is mere vocalization, does not subvert the fact that the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) has meaning as its primary purpose; for if it were to subvert all injunctions, it would result in self-contradiction. Nor is there a contradiction regarding the distinct application (*viniyoga*) when both purposes are intended, because there is no multiplicity of purposes through a single form. Thus, the *Nyāyasudarśana* states: "By its own nature it serves the purpose of recitation and so forth, while by its own power it brings about the comprehension of meaning; there is no contradiction due to the difference in forms, just as fire possesses both the powers of burning and illuminating."

The intended meaning is this: since the possibility of infinite purposes arises from the Veda once it has been refined by study, who would exert themselves in the pursuit of other treatises without first undertaking its investigation?
Thus, the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables, just like the recitation of mantras, accompanied by the prescribed rules.

One might object: "In this way, by one who has understood the utility [of study], the knowledge of the meaning must also be accepted as the fruit of the injunction; however, for one who has not understood the utility, even the grasping of the syllables cannot be recognized as a fruit. Therefore, since it is directly useful toward performance, let the knowledge of the meaning also be the visible fruit of the injunction to study, just like the grasping [of the syllables]. He refutes this objection under the guise of concluding the present topic with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning is: "in the manner of determining the nature of the enjoined act, its fruit, and so forth."

The possession of mantras and the possession of observances (niyamas) reside in the non-deficient pronunciation; their fruit is understood as being figuratively attributed [to the study]. "Mantras" refers to those that are constituent parts of the *kāṇḍavrata* and so forth, as well as those to be recited during the period of study, such as "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*) and others. "Observances" refers to those previously mentioned. Some maintain that the expression "as with mantras" (*mantravat*) is a statement of an illustration: just as the study enjoined regarding a mantra is accepted as culminating merely in the grasping of the syllables, so too is it here.

Others, however, maintain that it should be understood as being just like [the case] of those mantras to be recited at the time of the initiation (*upanayana*) for one who has merely been initiated, such as the mantras for placing fuel on the fire (*samid-ādhāna*), and so forth; others say it is like *hum* and other such syllables, or like specific mantras for neutralizing poison and the like. By the use of the words "merely" (*mātra*) and "conclusion" (*paryavasāna*), the cessation of the injunction both before and after the grasping of the syllables is negated.

The point is this: the word "study" (*adhyayana*) does not denote the knowledge of meaning, because there is no established linguistic usage for it in that sense; furthermore, in expressions such as "one becomes a Brāhmaṇa after having studied something," it is impossible for it to have meaning as its primary referent. Regarding study as the object of an injunction, its result is observed to be immediate, pervasive, and unavoidable.

If one were to postulate that something other than that [knowledge] is its fruit, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate that even a remote goal is the fruit, it would follow that the performance of the rite—which is itself produced by knowledge—would also have to be considered the fruit, just like the knowledge itself. Moreover, the fact that both the grasping of the text and the knowledge of its meaning are required without being separated from the subsequent injunction is equal for both. If the knowledge of the meaning were taught as having the ritual action as its object, then one might indeed have confidence in it even if it were partial or remote; however, this is not the case. Therefore, the knowledge of the meaning must be accepted solely on account of its utility.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, according to the logic of the *Samanvaya* section, it is proper to establish that the knowledge of meaning alone is the fruit by virtue of being an end in itself? [Reply: Not so; for that [logic] was stated only with respect to those portions that propound Brahman as unsurpassed bliss, whereas here, since we are considering the fruit of the study of the entire [Veda], it is inappropriate to posit such a heterogeneous result. [Objection: But in cases such as "Listen to the words of the elders," it is observed in common experience that the injunction to hear sentences culminates in the knowledge of their meaning. [Reply: No, because the purport in such instances is merely the instruction to listen to a particular sentence that serves as a landmark on the path—like a tree or other sign—and we observe that this is not always the case.

Furthermore, in some instances, the purposefulness of an instruction consisting of the hearing of a sentence is accepted out of necessity; however, this is not the case here, as it is observed in the world. [Objection: But surely, by such scriptural passages as "He who, indeed, with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity (*daivata*) are unknown... and by such Smṛti texts as "That which is studied without knowing the seer and the meter, being uncomprehended...", the knowledge of the meaning is established as something that must necessarily be accomplished, since faults are stated to arise from the opposite.

It is stated that in the absence of that [knowledge], study is fruitless, whereas in its presence, the attainment of all human goals occurs: "This man is a mere pillar, a bearer of burdens, who having studied the Veda does not understand its meaning; he who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness and, with his sins shaken off by knowledge, goes to the world of Brahman. Therefore, the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas is mandatory (*vaidha*). Not so.

Just as for one who is subject to passion (*rāga*), a fault is incurred by failing to perform acts such as approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), while the attainment of progeny and so forth is recorded in the Smṛtis as the fruit resulting from performing them according to the injunctions—so too would it be here. Therefore, the statement "one should know these [ṛṣis, etc. in each mantra" is intended to mean that at the time of performance, one must recollect the ṛṣi and other details for every individual mantra. For this very reason, the prohibition against using mantras whose ṛṣi and other attributes are unknown refers only to that much.

Therefore, since the praise of the knowledge of meaning through such passages as, "He who has studied [the Veda] is a mere pillar, and he who deliberates upon the sacrifice [without understanding it is likewise]," spontaneous engagement is encouraged. Furthermore, because the knowledge of meaning is necessarily required, one should not assume that the injunction for study extends so far as to include that knowledge—even within the context of a mandatory injunction—because [the injunction] is independent [of such a result], because an injunction remains indifferent toward what is already established by other means, and because even if it were to extend that far, it would not terminate in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by itself.

As for the objection raised by some: "Because the injunction to study extends up to the comprehension of the meaning—on account of such scriptural passages as 'Having studied the Veda from the teacher's family, according to the rule, and having returned home at the conclusion of the duties toward the guru, performing the rites of dharma in a pure place within the household, one should recite the svādhyāya,' and so forth; and on account of Smṛti texts such as 'Having studied, one should bathe'—the knowledge of the meaning, which consists of the Self, is also employed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent of ritual action, since it serves the purpose of that action; therefore, [the Self] is to be seen and heard..."

Since the Self—declared as the object of inquiry in such passages as "It is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon; that is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known"—is established as a subsidiary element of ritual action (karmaśeṣa) by not contradicting its inherent status as something to be refined (saṃskārya), just like rice-grains to be threshed; and since statements such as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman" declare that even one subject to karma possesses the nature of Brahman; and since universal authorship (viśvakartṛtva) is possible through the medium of karma; and since, when there is a conflict between what is already established and what must be assumed, it is logical to adopt the established; and since the individual soul (jīva), having attained the status of agent in rituals, is fit for refinement for their sake—therefore, this is so while the Vedānta texts have the individual soul as their primary referent.

Since there is no possibility of a scripture whose subject matter is an Īśvara distinct from that [Veda], for what could this single scripture and its sequential order be postulated? That argument, too, is refuted by the fact that [the Vedic texts] terminate merely in the acquisition of the syllables (akṣaragrahaṇa). Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras, by using expressions such as "having studied" (adhītya) and "having returned home" (abhisamāvṛtya), does not enjoin the knowledge of the meaning as a subordinate part of ritual action; for the use of the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*) rests solely upon the identity of the agent and so forth. Even if such a subordination were admitted, meditative worship (*upāsanā*) is something entirely different from the knowledge of the meaning required for the performance of rituals.

The knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts consists of this very nature [of Brahman]. Furthermore, the Self to be meditated upon is established by Scripture itself as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), and is not merely a conceptual construct. Moreover, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the individual soul and Brahman—just like that between the non-sentient (acid) and Brahman—is for a different purpose, as it would otherwise contradict their oneness. And let the injunction of such knowledge stand as it is; even so, there is no contradiction.

Because the one to be propitiated, like the agent, is to be investigated as being for the sake of the ritual action (*karman*), and because it is established by scripture that he is distinct from that which is subject to *karman*, the existence of a separate section (*kāṇḍa*) for the investigation of him is established. Even though here too the knowledge of the meaning is subordinate to the performance of the rite, it follows as a conclusion that it may also, according to its respective portion, be subordinate to the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the Supreme Brahman.

Nevertheless, since it is impossible to overlook the grave offense committed at the very outset when the objection is rooted in the necessity of understanding the meaning, one must disregard the *anvāruhyavāda* (the argument that proceeds by temporarily accepting the opponent's position) and instead cut off the root of the matter; with this intention, the word "only" (*mātra*) is used in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.

Since it is observed that the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) acquired through formal instruction possesses by its very nature the capacity to bring about the understanding of a purposeful meaning, a person who has completed his Vedic studies spontaneously engages in listening to Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the inquiry into Vedic sentences resulting in the determination of the specific nature and modes of those purposeful meanings understood from the studied Veda—upon seeing such meanings presented in a general way.

In this regard, once the nature of ritual action has been determined, one observes that the fruits of such actions are limited and unstable; yet, upon hearing certain Upaniṣadic passages within the portion of the Veda acquired through study, there arises an initial intuition that immortality constitutes an infinite and stable fruit. Consequently, one becomes qualified for the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, which consists of an inquiry into the Vedānta passages aimed at reaching a definitive conclusion regarding that [immortality].

Now, it might be argued that since the injunction to study culminates in the mere acquisition of syllables, the meaning of the Veda—which is understood only because it has been studied for another purpose—cannot be the intended object of the injunction's purport and thus should not be investigated. Consequently, the Veda would be meaningless; the injunction to study would not culminate in human welfare; and Mīmāṃsā itself could not even begin, as its subject matter would be absent and its opportunity blocked by the Smṛti rule, "Having studied [the Veda], one should bathe."

Dispelling the doubt as to how there could be such identity [between the Veda and the Mīmāṃsā], and demonstrating the unity of the scripture—which consists of the Veda as the subject matter and the Mīmāṃsā as its exposition—thereby indicating the meaning of the opening sūtra of Mīmāṃsā, he says: "In the study... Here, by the words *adhyayana* (study), *svādhyāya-nirṇaya-vicāra* (determination and inquiry into one's own recited text), and *adhīta-veda* (one who has studied the Veda), the unity of the subject matter, the fruit, the nature, and the qualified person (*adhikārin*) of the Mīmāṃsā is manifested. By the phrase "of that which has been grasped" (*gṛhītasya*), the cessation of the operation of the injunction is stated.

The statement that there is the perception of a purposeful meaning is for the sake of making known the culmination in human goals (*puruṣārtha*). "By its very nature" means without depending on the operation of an injunction; the phrase "by one who has mastered the meanings of words and their combinations" is to be supplied. This is the intended sense:

"Even though the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is undertaken for the purpose of memorization, it illuminates [its own meaning] by itself, like fire; in that regard, it is intrinsically authoritative as long as it is not sublated. (263)

The capacity of the word [to denote its object] is not obstructed by recitation, nor by meditation accompanied by the respective fruits prescribed in the Śruti; how much less so when it comes to the purpose of apprehension? (264)

One who, by means of a specific application (*viniyoga*), denies the capacity of the Veda to convey meaning, is himself refuted by self-contradiction, because he thereby subverts the cognition of the meaning derived from that very application. (265)
The injunction to study would either have the intended meaning as its purpose or it would not;
in the first case, there is the utterance [of the Veda], but in the latter case, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) cannot even arise. (266)
Moreover, validity here is difficult to establish on the grounds that it has the knowledge of the object as its fruit;
for if that [knowledge] is the fruit, then this [cognition] is the means of valid cognition, and if this is the means of valid cognition, then that [knowledge] is the fruit. (267)

If the injunction (*vidhi*), even when its meaning is *niyoga*, accepts the status of being directed toward an object, then it would likewise be for the sake of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), since it possesses the same eagerness for its own accomplishment. (268)

The Veda is a self-evident knower (*nirapekṣavedaka*); that is to say, unlike the speech of a human being, it does not depend upon another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) that has become its source. For this very reason, there is no possibility of suspecting a defect in its source, nor is there any obstruction to its investigation—this is the sense. The purpose here is the fourfold aim of human life (*caturvarga*). The objects possessing that [purpose] are the means thereto, consisting of ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*). Here, "the state of being made known" (*avabodhitva*) refers to the evident and undeniable capacity for producing a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*); and with the intention that "nothing is impossible in what is perceived," the word "because it is seen" (*darśanāt*) is used.

Even if [the Veda] were self-evident (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), one might argue that it need not be investigated because the object to be established (*sādhya*) is absent; to this he says: "Having perceived" (*gṛhītāt*). The connection is with the temporal qualification "having seen objects as they are presented" (*arthān āpātato 'vagamyamānān dṛṣṭvā*). Only the superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*) has been perceived; therefore, the intention is that the removal of doubt and so forth is what remains to be established. The first use of the word *artha* (object) implies something purposeful, thereby distinguishing it from the talk of a crow’s teeth and establishing the authority of the Śruti. The latter [use], however, indicates that superficial cognition acts as an impeller by generating an interest in investigating its own subject matter. Nothing whatsoever—whether already perceived or unperceived—should fail to be investigated.
Thus, even the objection has been refuted by the statement that [the object] is known at the very moment of its appearance. (269)

[Objection: "But surely, since it is the very nature of the word *yajati* (to sacrifice), there would be an initial comprehension even for those who have not learned its meaning; and in this case, there is no rule that such comprehension occurs only for those who have mastered the linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). [Response: This is not so, because even in the case of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the Veda, when the injunction for their study concludes with the mere grasping of the syllables—just as it does for the primary part (*aṅgin*)—such comprehension is impossible. Furthermore, if the injunction were uniform across all parts, there would be no reason to distinguish the study of the auxiliaries as extending up to the comprehension of the meaning. To this we reply: For one whose refined language (*saṃskṛta-bhāṣā*) has been practiced from childhood, that [comprehension] may indeed occur for him at first sight (*āpāta-mati*). However, in the case of the Veda, that would only be so for him personally. (Verse 270)

If this is so even when studying the Veda without its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), how much more so when studying it with them! Having gained an initial understanding of the meaning of the Veda, one should direct one's mind toward an initial understanding of the meaning of the auxiliaries. (271)
And some wise men, having attained an initial understanding born from the words of those who wish them well, indeed proceed to engage in investigation. (272)

Some, however, maintain that by grasping the syllables of the [mantra] limbs in a form suitable for assisting those limbs, one practices the state of possessing meaningful knowledge; they hold that this has a visible purpose and is thus expedient. (273)

Let it be granted that this is the initial understanding; however, even if that [knowledge] were distinct from it, one might argue that such knowledge should be accomplished by other branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*) alone. To this, the reply begins with "But as for its true nature" (*tatsvarūpe tu*). The sense is that the ascertainment of its specific form, distinguished from what was stated regarding the opposing view, is the result here that cannot be achieved by others. By the phrase "consisting of the investigation of Vedic sentences," the body of Mīmāṃsā is distinguished from other branches of learning. The statement that Mīmāṃsā consists of investigation is due to a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the two, or because the word "investigation" (*vicāra*) is derived in the instrumental sense (i.e., the means of investigation).

The statement that "the Veda has been studied" is intended to show that there remains nothing further to be done regarding the domain of ritual injunctions (*vidhi*), and it is also intended as a reason based on the fact that [the person] possesses a superficial understanding. The word "person" (*puruṣa*) contains a reason, namely, "because of the desire for a purpose. "By himself" means by his own will, independent of injunctions. For one who perceives a superficially useful object and desires its definitive determination, and who then engages in the means to that end, an injunction is indeed unnecessary. (274)
That investigation is established as the cause for determining one's own desired object through positive and negative concomitance; for even in that case, an injunction would be fruitless. (275)

Upon perceiving treasures, jewels, and the like, those who desire them proceed toward the identification of those objects according to their actual nature, entirely without being prompted by another. (276)
Therefore, neither the investigation nor its sequence is established here as a mandatory injunction;
for otherwise, the second [alternative] would be established simply by observing the defects [in the first]. (277)

Even though one might engage in [the study] on one's own initiative, this engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and taking refuge in them is intended to eliminate the possibility of independence from a teacher. Otherwise, there would be no fault in not doing so; but that is not the case, because the very absence of the certainty dependent upon him and the engagement in what is beneficial—which is contingent upon him—constitutes the fault. It is with this intention that it is said: "He who, having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, neglects inquiry, forgets his own exertion, and falls away from the goal."

[Objection: "If inquiry (*vicāra*) were thus not sanctioned by scripture, how could one engage in *mīmāṃsā* when the opportunity is blocked by injunctions such as 'having studied [the Vedas], one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)'? For the cessation from dwelling in the teacher's house—which consists of suffering—is already established by its own nature; therefore, it is only the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) that must be enjoined here. [Reply: Not so. For in this context, what is enjoined is precisely the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the ceremonial bath accompanied by specific observances (*saniyamaka-samāvṛtti-yukta*). Otherwise, since even the immediate succession following cessation would be established by its own nature, it too would be non-enjoinable.

Furthermore, even if reflection (*vicāra*) were mandatory, how could there be any occasion for it? If you argue that it is because the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*, we say no; for even in the *śruti*, it is stated: "having studied" (*adhītya*) and "having returned home" (*abhisamāvṛtya*). If you claim that in those cases the intention is merely to express a common agent and priority of time, and not immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then why should it not be the same in the case of the *smṛti*? Nor can it be restricted that the word "studying" (*adhyayana*) in the *śruti* extends up to the comprehension of the meaning, while in the *smṛti* it extends only up to the grasping of the syllables.

If it is argued that [the injunction for bathing] would be like [the rule] "that which has been studied," etc., we say no, because there is a distinction based on contradiction and non-contradiction. Suppose, then, that both Śruti and Smṛti enjoin study as a prerequisite for the knowledge of meaning; in that case, the injunction for bathing would not obstruct the opportunity for the scripturally mandated inquiry. If this is so, then the injunctions for bathing and the like—which are prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*)—would likewise not obstruct the opportunity for hearing (*śravaṇa*), just as the acquisition of wealth necessary for one's own use does not.
Those injunctions for bathing and so forth, which desire performance after having gained knowledge, naturally embrace the very Mīmāṃsā inquiry pertaining to their own respective subjects. (278)

Moreover, in this matter, those who do not know the specific measures, the constituent parts, the sequence, the agent, and so forth, are not even capable of correctly understanding a single rule for ritual bathing. (279)
Out of necessity, one engages in study and the like without prior reflection;
however, since there is an alternative course regarding the ritual bath (snāna), that "resort to necessity" should not be adopted.

And since it is authorized everywhere that one's own body-part does not constitute an intervention, therefore, in this case, the intervention by means of Mīmāṃsā does not create a contradiction. (281)

Alternatively, there is no contradiction even if the study [of the Veda] and the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) follow immediately one after the other. If it is argued that there is a contradiction because for those who have not investigated the nature of *dharma*, the performance of subsequent rites would be impossible, we say no; for even after the ceremonial bath, as long as the investigation continues, the performance of rites is possible—just as it was for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) while he was still under the care of his preceptor. Nor does performing rites based on the words of well-wishers contradict the principle regarding the exclusion of Śūdras (*apaśūdranaya*), because well-wishers direct one toward those duties appropriate to one's station, and because prohibitions such as "one should not teach him *dharma*" are observed.

If it is argued that the study of Mīmāṃsā would be useless since the performance [of rituals] could be accomplished otherwise, that is not so; for its study is justified by the desire to investigate the source when doubts regarding the opposite arise, as well as by faith in the authority of others, the reputation of the teacher, and so forth. In this very way, the continuity of the tradition from predecessors to successors is established. If it is argued that someone might, out of laziness, rely exclusively on written texts and the like as the sole authority, what of it? For others who are not lazy, the study of the scriptures remains possible.

If it is argued that for one who has completed his bath and is listening [to the Vedas], there might be an obstruction to his own duty (*svadharma*) due to activities for the sake of his teacher, we say: no; because those [activities] are prompted by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and cease once that is accomplished. As it is stated in the *Nyāyasudarśana*:

"For this injunction is intended to establish the rules regarding the means of grasping the syllables; the Smṛti declares that the status of religious duties (*dharma*) lasts until that [syllable] is grasped."

"After the Veda has been studied, the knowledge of its meaning arises spontaneously; however, that [spontaneous understanding] is neither the act of study itself, nor is it the motivator for religious duties (*dharma*). If this is so, for what purpose should the teacher expound the *Mīmāṃsā*? Is it for the sake of gain and the like, or for the sake of *dharma*? For one who is occupied with the duties of a householder, what opportunity is there to listen? And what opportunity does the teacher have to speak? For him, who seeks his livelihood, there is the time for acquiring wealth.

If this is argued, then hearing [the Veda] would also be like other activities for visible purposes that are permitted by injunction. Furthermore, even for a householder, there is some time for inquiry when [the Veda] serves as the subject matter of histories and so forth. At that time, Mīmāṃsā too would be employed as being conducive to its own goal, along with those [texts] that augment the Veda. And they divide the study of the Veda in this way: "First, the acquisition of the Veda; then inquiry, practice, recitation, and the giving of it to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold."

For some, such as those who have inherited wealth through family lineage or obtained wealth by chance, even the time for its acquisition must be considered as the proper time for hearing [the scriptures]. Furthermore, householders and others who follow the duties of their respective castes and stages of life without prior deliberation are seen in the Śruti and Smṛti as listeners of those very duties. Even for a householder, it is permitted by some that he should dwell with his teacher for two months every year for the sake of attaining superior knowledge.

As it is restated: "When he has settled down, he should live for two months every year in the house of a teacher, concentrated in mind, desiring further learning"—thus said Śvetaketu, "for by this method I learned more than before. [Objection: But is this not contradicted by those scriptures? For Āpastamba states his own view that once one has settled down, the obligatory duties (*naiyamikāni*) are heard [in the texts], such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, guests, and so forth. [Response: True.

By this [statement] as well, only an uninterrupted residence in the teacher’s house for two months is prohibited at that time; however, the opportunity for inquiry—which, like the speaker, leads to the hearer’s success—is not set aside.

Let it be that inquiry follows study, and let it have the entire [Veda] as its object due to natural inclination (*rāga*); nevertheless, if inquiry and its sequence are not based on scriptural injunction (*avaidhatva*), they may proceed according to one's own preference.
Because of the non-occurrence and the occurrence [of error], it is said that "it exists" in that regard. || 282 ||
Because investigation cannot be abandoned, because simultaneity is contradictory, and because faults are seen in a deviation from the order, this sequence indeed belongs to the Sūtra. (283)

In this context, "there" (tatra) means either in the Veda or in Mīmāṃsā; or it means when one proceeds according to one's own will. "Ritual injunction" (karmavidhi) here refers to the impulsion toward optional rites (kāmyakarman) or the performance of such rites; or, since no distinction is made, it includes obligatory rites (nityakarman) and others as well. By the term "essential nature" (svarūpa), it is indicated that the application [of the ritual] as a subsidiary to the higher knowledge (paravidyā)—for one who has renounced the fruit—is not being considered here. For that [application] is to be examined in the section on the "Means" (Sādhanalakṣaṇa); for upon its determination, one would understand that [the means] culminate in an infinite and stable fruit.

Alternatively, the sense is that although the fact that mere actions yield small and unstable fruits has not been examined in certain places; by the phrase "having been determined," the necessity of the determination of action having already occurred is intended. This has been explained in detail in the *Tātparya-tūlikā*: "In this regard, this obligatory action cannot be neglected, for it follows a person in all circumstances."
Whether one desires worldly enjoyment or seeks liberation, whatever person may be taken as an example,
for all of them there is indeed the undertaking of many karmas.
The obligatory daily rites, the occasional rites, and those that are prohibited must always be examined by everyone who desires to avoid the resulting transgression.
Those who do not fear sufferings should not engage in deliberation;
however, it is clear that for others, this much action must be deliberated upon.
Desirable action (kāmya-karma) is capable of providing enjoyment even without Brahman;
however, Brahman does not attain the capacity for liberation without action.
For it will be stated [in the Sūtras] that "there is a requirement for all [stages of life], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth";
thus, even reflection on a single portion of the Veda is declared to be prompted by the entire Veda.
"Therefore, since it must necessarily be considered, action itself is investigated first.

This means that having observed the limited and unstable fruits of actions, one determines—by the very words of the scriptures themselves—their nature with clarity. For in defining the essential nature of rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnihotra, there would be a classification of the heaviness or lightness of the resulting heavens according to the specific means employed. Furthermore, once it is established by the statement "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the Agniṣṭoma" that the Jyotiṣṭoma takes the form of the Agniṣṭoma, the determination of the spatial and temporal limitations of the heaven achieved thereby is made through such passages as "as much as one attains by the Agniṣṭoma."

In this regard, even the injunction for repetition is an indicator that the fruit is small for one who does not repeat [the rite]. Furthermore, with respect to the obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), a gradation of fruits according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life is recorded in Smṛti texts such as "for Brāhmaṇas, the fruit is that of Prajāpati," and so forth, depending on the specific qualified performer.

For when the nature of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices—such as the Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, and others—is understood, it is observed that the Vaiśvadeva and the rest yield measured results, as seen in the statements: "This indeed is the measure of the Vaiśvadeva," "This is indeed the lowest of these; from this, the subsequent ones become better. Therefore, regarding the passage, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible," the intended meaning is understood to be merely that its enjoyment lasts for a long time.

Although this quality of having inexhaustible fruit could potentially be led to as a remote consequence by virtue of being an ancillary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*), nevertheless, because there is no intention to convey that meaning here, it is not so interpreted. Thus, only when the nature of the ritual action—characterized by the *soma* oblation and having limited results—is established, does the restriction [to those results] in passages such as "We have drunk the *soma*" arise from such Smṛti texts as "Immortality is a state lasting until the dissolution of all beings."

Furthermore, once the distinction in the nature of the rituals that accomplish various fruits such as heaven (*svarga*) and self-sovereignty (*svarājya*) is established, the limited nature of that which is designated by the word "heaven" therein is proven. Moreover, the determination of the gradations among fruits—as seen in passages such as "whatever sacrifice one studies"—is possible only through the ascertainment of the heavy and light natures of the rituals themselves. And because the nature of the ritual that pleases the worshipful deity is determined to be subject to origination and destruction, there is the perception of instability in its results, such as union (*sāyujya*) with that deity.

Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating that the *Śārīraka*—whose subject matter is the inquiry into Brahman from which all obstacles have been removed—is a specific branch of *Mīmāṃsā* distinguished by its unique nature and fruit from other branches of knowledge, and for the sake of establishing the particular object to be determined, the phrase beginning with "furthermore, [the study] of... was stated. Here, the word "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) denotes the fruit known primarily through the end of the three Vedas (*trayyantapradhānavedyaphala*); by this, there is an exclusion of the secondary fruits such as the attainment of food and so forth belonging to those of recent times, as well as the fruits of injunctions regarding meditations (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*) constructed through other types of connection. It has been established that the immortality mentioned in the ritual section (*karmabhāga*) is merely relative.

However, with the intention that this [work]—unlike the former [Mīmāṃsā]—is largely established as being based on the perception of no contradiction and supported by a portion of the Vedānta which is determined to be consistent, it is stated: "because of the initial cognition of an infinite and stable fruit. For here, it is not possible to postulate qualities such as smallness or instability through inferences regarding the nature of a "fruit," as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Because it is unconditioned (*anavaccheda*), the embodied one (*śārīra*) here is the one whose body is the universe; the scripture (*śāstra*) that proceeds with reference to him is called *Śārīraka*.

For it will be stated in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*: "That very [Self] is the unconditioned embodied Self (*śārīra-ātman*); for this reason, the scripture which proceeds by taking that Supreme Brahman as its subject is designated by the learned as *Śārīraka*. Thus, it is the *Mīmāṃsā* of the *Śārīraka*, i.e., the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*; [the word *tasyām* means] "in that [work]. The meaning is that one "enters into" (*adhikaroti*) it—that is, becomes intent upon it—with the thought that it is for one's own sake, and not because one enters into it on account of some other preceding matter.

The intention is that once the immediate succession to the inquiry into Brahman is established through reasoning, the immediate succession to the scripture whose subject matter is that [Brahman] is also established.

The fact that [the Veda] is apprehended, that it is a fruit, that it possesses meaning, and that its entire investigation proceeds from passion—all this has been stated here as something unprecedented. (284)

And likewise, the Vedānta texts demonstrate that the fruit of mere ritual action is perishable, whereas the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is imperishable: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes; for that which belongs to him becomes merely finite. Indeed, the eternal is not attained by means of the non-eternal. For these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts. Having examined the worlds acquired by action, let the Brāhmaṇa arrive at detachment: 'There is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created.'"

To gain knowledge of That, one should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. To him, who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint, that wise teacher imparts in truth that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the Imperishable, the True Person.

The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; he does not face death again. He sees That as One; seeing thus, he does not see death. He becomes the Lord of His own Self (*svarāt*). Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal in this very world; no other path for going exists. [He sees] the Self as distinct...

"And considering him the impeller, being favored by Him, he thereafter attains immortality," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "Is there not seen merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the smallness of the fruit of ritual action and the like? For the sake of strengthening a conviction contrary to what is heard [in scripture], the attainment [of the fruit] must also be stated; furthermore, the determination of the nature of ritual action here is for the purpose of removing obstacles to spontaneous engagement. As for the reason, it is simply the immediate perception of infinite and stable fruits—whence does this arise? To this he says: "In that manner" (*tathā*). The meaning is: "so that the purpose of this Sūtra may also be in accordance with the aforementioned method. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Here, the mention of "woundedness" (*kṣati*) and "perishability" (*akṣayi*) is indicative of smallness and so forth. The citation of the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as) serves to increase one's faith regarding another matter that is not explicitly stated, by means of a confirmed analogy. "The world" (*loka*) means that which is to be perceived or enjoyed. If it were taken in the sense of a physical place, there would be no syntactical connection with the terms "here" (*iha*) and "thereafter" (*amutra*). "Accumulated by action" (*karmacitaḥ*) means obtained through worldly actions.

By the general statement "the accumulation of merit," [the author] says "it is finite" (antavat) in order to dispel the delusion that even that which is accomplished through the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti-dharma) is subject to decay. Because this is consistent with the meaning of the cited scriptural passages, and because the finitude of the nature of the action itself is not what is intended to be stated here, the statement regarding its finitude is made by way of its result.

This is because of the preceding statement, "O Gārgī, he who, without knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years [is miserable]," and also because of the subsequent statement, "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable.
