Once it is established that the term "finite" (*antavat*) refers to ritual action devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, it follows easily that the same reference applies to the phrase "those who have accumulated merit" (*puṇyacitaḥ*) and those that follow.

Just as there is a distinction of fruits such as heaven or self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) in rites devoid of knowledge, so too there might be a possibility of a distinction of fruits even in the case of certain obligatory (*nitya*) rites; furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for the sake of all desires," the passage cited here would have to refer only to the majority of cases. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). The meaning is: "by those that are unstable," i.e., by those enjoined as means to unstable fruits. Through the connection with the phrase of the text, "That is stable" (*dhruvaṃ tat*), the absence of the status of having a stable fruit is established.

He reinforces the absence of the attainment of a permanent fruit for those who possess the rule of returning, because it is impossible for them to uproot all karma—[stating] "rafts" and so forth. They are unstable; they are incapable of leading one to the further shore of darkness. Those fools who rejoice in this inferior karma which has been described as eighteenfold, they return once again to old age and death. For there is indeed a defect in the wording here.

Now, the author states a verse—beginning with "parīkṣya"—which, in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtras, combines the determination that actions lack the capacity to produce eternal results as a cause for world-weariness (nirveda), along with the fact that the knowledge of Brahman yields infinite fruit.

This scripture has been explained in the *Sāra*: "A Brāhmaṇa—one devoted to the study of the Vedas—having examined with the help of *Karma-mīmāṃsā* the worlds acquired through ritual action (*karmacitān*) as being perishable by nature because they must be attained through worship, and having reached a state of world-weariness (*nirveda*), thinking that 'the Uncreated'—the eternal Supreme Person—is not attained through 'the Created'—ritual action—he should, for the sake of knowing That, approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a knower of the Vedānta, and firmly established in Brahman."

[He was one] who had realized the nature of the Supreme Person. And that teacher spoke—that is, he declared—to him who had approached him properly that Brahma-vidyā, by means of which specific knowledge one may know that Imperishable, True Supreme Person. [This is so] because there is no syntactical connection between "he should approach the teacher" and "that wise man spoke to him," and because [the latter] has not been previously established as a duty. Furthermore, the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is prescribed even for injunctions in the Vedic language, according to the rule: "In the Chandas, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [may be used]."

In this context, regarding the portion that restates what is already established by logic (*nyāya*), the word *brāhmaṇa*—though denoting a caste—is stated as "one devoted to the study of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsarataḥ*) so that, through *ajahallakṣaṇā* (a type of metaphorical indication where the primary meaning is not abandoned), it may refer to the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) who are useful for the investigation of the subject matter at hand, namely those who have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). They also etymologize the word *brāhmaṇa* as "one who breathes (*aṇati*) Brahman. The phrase "by virtue of being the object of worship" (*ārādhyakṣayitvena*) is an elliptical expression indicating the destruction of merit (*sukṛta*). The mention of "Karma-mīmāṃsā" is a statement implied by the sense of the passage.

In accordance with the masculine gender of the word *akṛta* and by the force of the supplementary context (*vākyaśeṣa*), the Supreme Person is shown as the substantive. Here, because the word "is not" (*na asti*) cannot negate the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is uncreated, and because it would not connect with the phrase "by action," and because a negation of origination is not required here, the meaning is for the sake of a clear understanding of that [Supreme Person]. In this context, "having fuel in hand" refers to Brahman.

Some say it is for the purpose of hearing the Vidyā, for the sake of the intermediate rite of initiation (*upaneyana*), and for the sake of the external signs [of a student]. For it is said in the *Chāndogya* to Jābāla by Gautama: "A non-Brāhmaṇa is not fit to explain this; bring fuel, my dear, and I will initiate you. Others, however, say: the initiation was appropriate for Jābāla because he was uninitiated; but elsewhere, the mention of "having fuel in hand" is intended as an indication that his hands were not empty.

For it is indeed seen in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā: "They, with fuel in their hands, returned in the forenoon; having brought them near without yet initiating them, he spoke this. And in the speech of Prajāpati, regarding the single Indra who returns with fuel in his hand for many questions, the phrase "he came again" is repeated. For in that case, initiation is neither seen nor intended to be performed multiple times. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras will state only this much: "Because of the reference to the purificatory rites (saṃskāra)."

Since one who has merely studied a single branch of the Veda—though described as a *śrotriya*—does not contribute to the present context by the mere fact of having studied his own portion of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*), the word *śrotriya* here is shown to refer specifically to a *śrotriya* who is "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*). He states that the term *brahmaniṣṭha* is intended to signify both the capacity for clear exposition and the highest degree of benefit through unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), by describing him as "one who has directly realized the nature of the Supreme Person."

Because it is stated, "to one whose mind is tranquil" (*praśāntacittāya*), "tranquility" (*śama*) here refers to the cessation of the activities of the external organs. In this context, tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) serve the purpose of providing the attention necessary for hearing (*śravaṇa*). However, in passages such as "one who knows thus, being tranquil and self-restrained," they serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*) for one who has already understood the meaning through hearing. Regarding the phrase "by which" (*yena*), since a change in gender would be forced, it indicates that the opening statement is general—namely, that it qualifies knowledge (*vidyā*) in its entirety.

And thus they employ [the following] sublation there: "Is it the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) or the destruction of external objects (bāhyārthabhaṅga), and so forth? With the intention of excluding Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña by means of the two terms "imperishable" (akṣara) and "real" (satya), which negate modification in terms of essential nature (svarūpa) and intrinsic being (svabhāva), he says: "the Supreme Person" (paramapuruṣam). The qualification "in reality" (tattvataḥ) is used to cast aside speech that is subject to doubt or error, as well as incomplete speech.

The traditional authorities (smaranti) declare: "Even a teacher becomes a non-teacher if he neglects what has been heard [from the scriptures]. To dispel the misconception that this refers merely to the failure to explain the meaning of the conduct (*vṛtta*), he says: "he should proclaim" (*prabrūyāt*). It would be strained to follow a reversal of the word order by overriding the injunction perceived at the outset through the phrase "he should approach" (*abhigacchet*); therefore, with the intention that the phrase "he spoke" (*provāca*) cannot be construed as referring to the past, he says: "He [should go] to the guru alone. The restrictive nature (*niyamavidhitva*) of the rule is indicated by the emphatic particle (*eva*). As for the phrase "he spoke": [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the preceding portion.]

He states another reason for its being a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, "because it is not otherwise established" (*aprāptatvāt*). Although some may engage [in this practice] out of passion (*rāga*) with a view toward gain and the like, nevertheless, this is enjoined as a duty (*dharma*) for a teacher who is free from such motives, in relation to a worthy disciple; thus there is no contradiction. He also states that the *liṭ* (perfect tense) specifically teaches the sense of the *liṅ* (optative/injunctive)—namely, "even in the case of an injunction" (*vidhāv api*).

Intending to show that the knowledge of Brahman leads to the attainment of the eternal, unsurpassed bliss that is the subject of the context—by virtue of its being the means for attaining the Brahman designated by the word "supreme" (para)—he says: "the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). To dispel the suspicion that even one who has attained Brahman might undergo rebirth and so forth—on the analogy of [attaining] heaven and other such states, and based on passages such as "these worlds"—he says: "not again. Here, "death" (*mṛtyu*) refers to dying; or it may refer to what was stated in such passages as "death is considered by the wise to be delusion" (*moha*).* *Moha* (delusion) is defined as death by the wise. (Katha Upanishad 2.6.8) *Note: The provided text contains a partial citation from the Katha Upanishad.*

The sense is that when evils are destroyed without remainder, nothing undesirable—characterized by death—shall exist, and following the ways of the world would be a matter of one's own choice. In this context, "seeing That alone" (tadekadarśana) is either the means or the fruit. This is because the statement, "There is no consciousness after departing," occurs within the section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).

By means of the words of the Elder (Vasiṣṭha), he dispels the apprehension that knowledge might be lost for one who is liberated, and he clarifies the cessation of death and its effects with the words "He does not see. Even though the liberated one perceives the suffering of others at that time and his own past suffering, those two do not constitute anything adverse to him, because they lack the qualities of being dependent upon him and being present. For this is indeed observed even during the state of bondage. However, in that state, the experience of suffering due to the suffering of others and the grieving for what has passed are caused solely by the limiting adjunct of karma (*karmopādhika*).

By the passage beginning with "The seer sees neither disease nor suffering," and so forth, it is established that even when all things are being seen, there is no perception of anything adverse to oneself. Here, the term "the seer" (*paśya*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) who perceives Brahman, as is evident from the context of the same section where it says "he sees that One. Furthermore, the term "sees" (*paśyati*) can also apply to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as seen in such usages as "the Seer sees the one who sees. Since everything is seen as having Brahman as its essence, there is no contradiction between "seeing that One" and "seeing all."

It is not merely a state of effortless omniscience; rather, other kings possess perishable worlds rooted in prescribed karma and remain subject to dependence on the Lord (Īśvara). With the intention that there should be freedom of action through the cessation of this dependence on the Lord, he says: "He is self-ruling" (*sa svarāṭ*). For this very reason, even while remaining under the sovereignty of the Lord, the statement of the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭuka*) that "self-ruling" means "independent" is not contradicted.

The scriptural denial of other means to immortality confirms that the statement regarding immortality being achieved through ritual action (*karman*) has another purpose; this is shown by the phrase "him alone" (*tameva*). Furthermore, because the reference here is to the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) as qualified by His attributes and manifestations, the position of the opponents—that liberation occurs for the individual soul (*jīva*) alone through the cognition of its own undifferentiated nature or through the cognition of it as distinct from the Supreme Person—is refuted. He states that the idea that the cognitions of identity or difference are causes of immortality is rejected by the scripture itself with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*).

The meaning is: "from that," namely from the contemplation of distinctness in the form of worship (*upāsana*). "Favored by him" (*tena juṣṭaḥ*) means made an object of affection by the Impeller (*preraka*). By this, it is stated that the stable grace of the Supreme is itself the gateway to the fruit. For it is also heard in scripture: "By the grace of the Creator. Now, one might object: here, the contemplation of both "the Self" and "the Impeller" together has been taught; therefore, it appears that knowledge of something other [than the Self] is also a cause of liberation. True; however, that does not detract from the primacy of the Impeller.

In passages such as, "A certain wise man beheld the inner Self, with eyes turned inward, desiring immortality," the reference is also to the vision of the individual soul (jīva) as an auxiliary to the higher knowledge (paravidyā). The word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to reinforce what has been stated by other scriptural passages as well, according to the maxim that "the majority [of evidence] shall be more powerful."

But surely, from the mere study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), it is already known that ritual actions have heaven and the like as their fruit, that heaven and the like are perishable, and that the meditation on Brahman has immortality as its fruit. Consequently, one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) should proceed directly to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). What need is there for the inquiry into Dharma? If this were so, then one would not even proceed to the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (the inquiry into the embodied self), since everything would be known from the study of the Vedas together with their auxiliaries. True; yet—

If it is argued that while an initial comprehension certainly exists, nevertheless, because a sentence aided by logic (*nyāya*) is what determines the meaning, even an initially comprehended meaning does not transcend doubt and error; therefore, for the sake of its ascertainment, an inquiry into the Vedānta texts must be undertaken—then please consider that for that very same reason, an inquiry into *dharma* must also be undertaken.
